# 01 — Program preparation (unlace-analysis)

```yaml
Anchors:
  - crates/unlace-analysis/src
  - crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition
```

Everything in this chapter runs **before any function is decompiled**. The
`unlace-analysis` crate is unlace's port of the layer Ghidra keeps *outside* its C++
decompiler — the Java loader, the analyzer tier, and the Listing — rebuilt against
unlace's own symbol/type tables. Untagged prose in this chapter therefore describes a
port of a **Ghidra Java analyzer or loader** (named per pass), not of the C++
decompiler; `(angr)`, `(ida)`, and `(unlace)` mark the other lineages, matching each
pass's row in `crates/unlace-decomp/phases.toml`. An analyzer named
below is a settable option under its own name (`--option <id> on|off`) where it
is a judgment call; a pass whose default behaviour is simply the correct reading
of the image (marked "always on" in its section) has no flag, and a refinement of
a flagged pass rides its parent's flag (`funcdisc_recursive` rides
`funcstart_patterns`; the DWARF layout, variant-part and discriminant-naming arms
ride `dwarf`). Defaults, symptoms, and flip guidance live in the generated
catalog, [`docs/options.md`](../options.md), and are not repeated here.

## 1.1 The tier contract

A program-prep analysis is an implementation of
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/pass.rs (AnalysisPass)`: it declares the phase
it feeds (P0/P1, a few feeding back to P2), a stable `id()` that doubles as its
option name, and one method `run(&AnalysisCtx) -> AnalysisOutput`. The contract has
three load-bearing properties:

- **Pure and read-only.** A pass sees only the parsed object (`object::File`), the
  raw image bytes, the opened load image, the resolved `Architecture`, the image's
  own on-disk path, and (for Listing consumers, §1.6) the built Listing. It mutates
  nothing. The path is the one input that is not the image's *content*: it is what
  lets a pass reach a companion file the image only names — a `.pdb` sidecar today,
  a `.dSYM` bundle or a `.gnu_debuglink` target tomorrow. It is derived once, at the
  context build, from the load image's own filename
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/passes.rs (image_on_disk_path)`) and is
  absent unless that filename resolves to an existing file, so a synthesized or
  in-memory image cannot make a pass probe the working directory.
- **Additive and total.** A pass only ever contributes *more* knowledge — names,
  types, entries, flags — and never fails: a malformed section, an unknown magic, or
  an out-of-range offset yields an *empty* output, never an error or panic.
- **Facts, not effects.** The output is a flat struct of typed fact lists
  (`pass.rs (AnalysisOutput)`): function/data symbols, sized data globals, discovered
  entries plus an optional name overlay, no-return functions, no-fall-through call
  sites, read-only ranges, string literals, library prototypes, processor-context
  paints, tracked register values, call-fixup tags, DWARF stack locals, source-line
  comments, and FID renames. Merging two outputs is concatenation; deduplication is
  the committer's job.

The passes never touch the pipeline live, and the pipeline never calls an analyzer:
the two meet exactly once, at a commit seam. `crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs
(bootstrap_from_object)` runs every registered pass at `load file`
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/passes.rs (run_default_analyses_per_pass)`) and
**stashes** each load-time pass's output keyed by its id. The commit happens later,
at `read symbols` (`engine.rs (commit_pending_analysis)`) — after the CLI's
`option` lines have been applied — so a disabled load-time pass's already-computed
facts are simply dropped at the gate (`engine.rs (analysis_pass_enabled)`; an id
with no registered gate fails *open*, so a new pass runs by default). Deferred
work is dispatched after those options are known: a disabled Listing consumer, AIF
gap walk, or operand-reference scan is not invoked at all, and its commit gate
remains as a defensive check. This is semantically load-bearing
for AIF: speculative SLEIGH decoding can paint processor context, so `aif off`
means no speculative decode, not merely discarding its discovered-entry facts.
The stash is drained on commit, so a second `read symbols` cannot double-commit.

Stash-at-load is the default, but it only pays when computing the facts is cheap
relative to the chance of using them. A pass whose sweep is expensive and whose gate
is normally off is *deferred* instead — kept out of `passes_for` and run from the
commit point by `passes.rs (run_deferred_entry_passes)`, where the gate is already
in effect. `funcstart_patterns` (§1.5) is the one entry pass in that category: its
whole-image pattern sweep is a fixed load-time cost on every subcommand and is
discarded on every default run. Deferring an entry pass is output-neutral because
the commit's entry arm is idempotent by address and resolves each name from the
fully merged `entry_names`, so merge position never changes what installs; the
deferred run rebuilds the object view exactly as the load-time run does,
`relocrebase` (§1.2) included, so a relocatable object still yields entries in the
loaded image's address space. It is dispatched *before* the deferred Listing build,
whose walk takes the committed entry set as extra roots.

`engine.rs (commit_analysis_output)` then installs the merged facts into the engine
once, each arm idempotent against the loader's own funcsym stream: a function fact
no-ops where `find_function` already resolves (a real `.symtab` name always beats a
discovered one), and it is listed beside any same-named function at another address,
as the funcsym stream lists one, because every overload and template instance of a
qualified name is a function of its own (`engine.rs (register_overload)`); sized data globals and string symbols skip occupied addresses (the plain label arm does not), no-return facts resolve by
**address** first (`find_function_across_scopes` — stable across demangling, which
renames the funcsym before install) with a name fallback for imports, and rename
facts (FID, ObjC, PDB) pass a **label gate** (`engine.rs (is_generic_placeholder_name)`)
that only ever overwrites an engine `sub_*`/`func_*`/`FUN_*`/`LAB_*` placeholder. Two fact
kinds are not installed globally: DWARF stack locals are parked per function and
re-seeded into each freshly-rebuilt `Funcdata`'s `ScopeLocal` at decompile time (the
`map addr`/`seed_mapped_symbols` path), and the `error(nonzero,…)` call-site list is
stashed on the `Architecture` for the per-function flow override (§1.7).

The console dispatcher in `crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs
(bootstrap_from_file)` releases its format-probe buffer before entering the
object loader, ending that allocation before loader initialization and analysis.

The entry arm is where a single-function run pays for the whole inventory: a
`createFunctionIfMissing` per discovered entry costs about a kilobyte, so an image
whose `.eh_frame` enumerates every function (377,429 on a 51 MB Android `.so`)
spends some 315 MB of a run that reads one of them. `lazyfuncs` (default **off**)
splits the commit: anonymous `sub_<addr>` entries retain compact addresses and
registration order instead of allocating names and name-index slots
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine/lazy_inventory.rs (inventory_symbols)`).
Names are generated when enumerated; address and anonymous-name selection use
the compact entries without constructing the whole canonical inventory. Real
names and entries carrying other commit facts keep their symbol records.
The entry starts are parked on the `Architecture`
(`crates/unlace-middle/src/infra/architecture.rs (set_lazy_entry_starts)`)
and no `Function` is created. An entry some other fact of the same commit attaches
to is not parked — a committed name (`_INIT_<i>`, the entry oracle's `main`), a
no-return verdict, a FID rename, an address-keyed prototype (library, `elfmain`,
DWARF, demangled), locals, comments, tracked registers or a format site
(`crates/unlace-console/src/lazyfuncs.rs (fact_entries)`) — because
each of those lands on the `Function` itself and would otherwise be dropped; the
string and data arms also treat a parked start as occupied, as they would its
`Function`. Flow still reads such an entry as a function rather
than code to follow into — `crates/unlace-middle/src/substrate
(ArchFlowEnv)` consults the parked set once the symbol table declines — so a
`BRANCH` into a lazy entry stays a tail call. The raw walk `bejoin evidence` makes
of a function and its callees stops at a parked entry for the same reason
(`crates/unlace-bandb-core/src/p4_calls/bejoin/evidence.rs (destination)`):
its verdict is cached once per image, before any `Function` is materialized, so a
walk that ran on into a tail-called entry would swap a big-endian pair's halves in
every later read. Materialization then happens on read,
at two depths: the console gives the *selection* its `Function`
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (ensure_function_symbol)`), and after
a drive `crates/unlace-console/src/lazyfuncs.rs (materialize_callees)`
gives every parked entry the p-code read one — transfer targets plus code addresses
taken as *values*, a Thumb pointer's odd value naming its even start — while
`crates/unlace-console/src/decompile_step.rs (decompile_one_prefollowed)`
drives again while that makes progress. The value case is load-bearing:
`crates/unlace-emit/src/p9_emit/coreaction_render.rs (ActionConstantPtr)`
types a constant as a code pointer, and the printer names it, only through a global
Symbol, so a merely-stored function address would lose both. Only parked entries
are materialized — never a constant that merely looks like an address, nor a
p-code-relative `BRANCH` offset — so the lazy symbol table is always a subset of the
eager one. The saving is a property of one function's run: a whole-binary surface
materializes what it walks.

String literals still commit eagerly with the option on. A literal's symbol
shapes the lift that reads its address: with it, a Rust or Go `(ptr, len)` call
argument renders through the `char[N]` symbol; without it, the `fatstr` rule
rewrites the pointer into a bounded literal and the finished lift no longer holds
the address. Planting only the literals a finished lift references therefore
renders different bodies.

CLI loads gate `objc` and `strings` before their pass runs. This is earlier than
the normal commit-time option filter: a disabled pass produces no discarded fact
tree, while an enabled pass reaches the identical commit. The `functions`
inventory suppresses `strings` because string data cannot change a function row.
Object-backed loads share segment slices with the normalized input image and copy
a segment only when relocation or an asserted-byte overlay writes it; deferred
discovery parses the shared input instead of constructing a second load image, and
reads the MIPS lazy-binding transfers the loader proved from that object view.
Thin Mach-O inputs use a private read-only file mapping shared by the loader and
analysis views (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/image_bytes.rs`). The console
recognizes that mapped input before reading a complete format-probe buffer.
The input must remain unchanged for the duration of analysis; private mapping
does not provide a snapshot of external writes. In-process writes use owned
segment overlays. `UNLACE_LOAD_MMAP=off` selects the owned path for every loader
and CLI probe. Non-regular files, failed mappings, other formats and fat-slice
normalization retain the owned input path.
CLI architecture, language and runtime-hint probes inspect the mapped view too,
avoiding file-sized temporary buffers before the engine starts.

Two timing consequences shape the tier. First, anything that must influence the
**loader itself** runs before any `option` line exists, so load-time gates are
bridged across the process by environment variables the CLI exports:
`UNLACE_DEBUGLINK` (`debuglink`),
`UNLACE_MACHO_ARM64E` (`macho-arm64e`),
`UNLACE_MACHO_SLICE` (`--slice`), `UNLACE_ARM_ISA` (`--isa`),
`UNLACE_DYLD_IMAGE` (`dyldimage`, `--image`), `UNLACE_DYLDCROSSREFS` (`dyldcrossrefs`). For those,
the option rows exist for discoverability while the live gate is the env var. The
external-artifact paths `unlace_fid_db` and `unlace_pdb_path` are different: they only
*locate* the artifact, and only as one tier among others (`pdb` also searches
beside the image, §1.4) — the `fid`/`pdb` passes stay flag-gated at the deferred
commit (`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (analysis_pass_enabled)`). Second,
anything that must **decode instructions** cannot run at load at all — the engine's
loadimage is attached to the SLEIGH translator only *after* the load-time pass list
runs — so the Listing build, its consumers, and `operand_refs` are deferred to the
commit point too (§1.6).

The XML `<binaryimage>` datatest path never constructs an `ObjectLoadImage` and never
stashes an output, so the entire tier is structurally inert on the 675-assertion
parity oracle; only real binaries feel it.

(unlace) The load image is two halves, and only one of them is single-threaded.
The bytes — the vma-sorted segment list and the containing-segment-else-
closest-greater walk over it — are `SegmentBytes`, held behind an `Arc` and
published through `LoadImage::shared_bytes`
(`crates/unlace-sleigh/src/loadimage.rs (ImageBytes)`); the reader is
the 512-byte window and the `Rc<AddrSpace>` an incoming address is checked
against, which is per-reader because space identity is pointer identity. A
second reader over the same bytes is `SharedBytesImage`, and both it and
`ObjectLoadImage` serve reads through the one `windowed_load_fill`, so there is
no second copy of the read semantics to drift. Every site that writes the bytes
— the dynamic-relocation patch at construction, an `--assert bytes` overlay,
`adjustVma` — runs at load time and requires sole ownership of the `Arc`; an
overlay requested after publication fails closed.

## 1.2 Load image

`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (ObjectLoadImage)` is the
real-binary `LoadImage` backend — the substitution for upstream's GPL-licensed
BFD loader (`LoadImageBfd`), rebuilt on the permissive `object` crate with the C++
interface semantics preserved exactly: the same 512-byte read buffer, the same
containing-segment-else-closest-greater walk with gap zero-fill, and the same
"initial address unmapped → `DataUnavailError`" contract in `loadFill`. Two
deliberate corrections inside that contract. The first: the buffer's
`bufoffset` is claimed at the top of a fill, *before* a byte is read, and a failed fill **releases it
again** (upstream throws with it still claimed). Left claimed, the buffer's own
fast path answers every later request within 512 bytes of the failed address out
of a buffer that was never filled — stale bytes, reported as a successful read.
Nothing upstream reads twice near a failure, which is why it never surfaced
there; a caller that probes addresses in order (the extern-slot
classification of §0.2) walks straight into it.

(unlace, GH-510) The second: **a read longer than the buffer is served straight
into the caller's slice**, bypassing the buffer entirely
(`crates/unlace-sleigh/src/sharedbytes.rs (windowed_load_fill)`,
over `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (fill_span)`).
Upstream stages every read through the 512-byte window and copies the answer
back out of it with `memcpy(ptr,buffer,size)`, which for a longer request reads
past the end of the buffer — a silent heap over-read kept out of reach only by
upstream's own callers, none of which ask for more than sixteen bytes. unlace's do
ask for more: the `.asm` data tail of a project export reads each named global
at its declared datatype size, and the same copy spelled as a Rust slice panics
instead of over-reading, so any image carrying a string or typed global of 512
bytes or more — `/bin/ls` among them — aborted the whole `decompile-project` run
before its output directory was created. A span that
long could never be answered out of a 512-byte window anyway, so serving it
directly caches nothing that would have been cached, and the window a
neighbouring short read is being answered from is left as it was. Nothing else
about the read changes — the same segment walk, the same zero-fill past the last
segment it crosses, the same unmapped-start `DataUnavailError` — and a request
of 512 bytes or fewer still follows exactly the path it always did.

The mapping unit is the ELF **`PT_LOAD` segment** (what the OS actually maps), not the BFD
section list. Where upstream returns a BFD target string for the Java side to
re-map, unlace resolves the SLEIGH language id directly off the object header
(machine + endianness + class → e.g. `x86:LE:64:default:gcc`). An `EM_BPF` (247)
object takes `eBPF:LE:64:default` or `eBPF:BE:64:default` by its byte order, the
same two ids the vendored `eBPF.opinion` declares, so a `clang --target=bpf -c`
program loads without `--target`. An `EM_S390` (22) object of the 64-bit class
takes `s390x:BE:64:default`; the 31-bit class has no language and still needs
`--target`.

(unlace) ELF target selection also reads declared instruction and ABI requirements
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipstarget.rs`). MIPS ELF32 can
carry 64-bit instructions with 32-bit pointers: the ISA flags select the register
width and release, while ABI2, O32, O64 and EABI32 select the compiler model.
The wide-register O32 model retains four-byte integer argument and return
slots, even-register alignment for pairs, and stack arguments after the
16-byte register save area. A scalar result uses the low word of `v0`; a
declared 64-bit result joins the low words of `v0` and `v1` in ABI order.
Each returned word also defines the sign-extended value of its full register.
Callers can test that full register without losing the call result or widening
the logical return slots.
Incoming integer words are sign-extended into the full general registers;
full-register reads retain the same four-byte argument slots. Struct and union
results, including four-byte aggregates, use a hidden result pointer in `a0`,
with subsequent arguments assigned after it using the usual pair alignment.
ELF32 wide-register languages retain full-width decoder addresses and use the
existing truncated-space pointer flow to recover their four-byte stack base.
The physical stack register remains eight bytes wide.

MIPS FPR width is selected independently from `.MIPS.abiflags` CPR1 size, its
FP ABI, GNU FP attributes and the legacy FP64 header flag. The shared ABI reader
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsabi.rs`) accepts records
from sections or `PT_MIPS_ABIFLAGS` segments and rejects conflicting records. O32 defaults to
paired 32-bit FPRs, except on Release 6; declared FP64 uses whole 64-bit FPRs.
FPXX code runs with either width, so its CPR1 size is only a minimum: a
Release 6 FPXX image uses the R6 decoder, whose FPRs are 64 bits wide.
Pre-R6 MIPS32 code that declares 64-bit FPRs keeps the MIPS32 decoder and
prints a `[unlace target]` note, because no bundled MIPS32 language has 64-bit FPRs.
FP ABI `ANY` (zero) supplies no evidence: it can accompany a concrete ABI in
either metadata source, including repeated GNU tags or sections. The shared
reader applies this rule before merging declarations, for both target selection
and hard/soft-float argument evidence. Explicit CPR1 width remains independent,
and two different concrete declarations still conflict.
Release 6 retains its R6 decoder when the ELF also declares microMIPS; the
per-function ISA markers choose ordinary or microMIPS decoding. MIPS16 plus
microMIPS, and MIPS16 plus Release 6, still require an explicit target.
The FP32 wide-register languages preserve 64-bit integer instructions and
use paired storage for double-precision operations. Conflicting declarations,
malformed metadata and combinations without a bundled model require an explicit
target rather than silently changing FPR width.
ELF64 without ABI bits uses the 64-bit-address default model. Contradictory or
unsupported declarations require an explicit target. An ELF32 wide-register
image with no ABI declaration uses the existing O64 default with a diagnostic;
Processor-specific machine or ABI-extension declarations are left to their
processor-specific selector. This generic path does not infer those targets.
Explicit `--target` always wins. An automatically selected MIPS language never
retries with a different ISA or ABI when its specification is unavailable.

O32 aggregate arguments preserve memory order within their four-byte slots.
Big-endian models left-justify structs and unions; little-endian models keep
their native justification. Separate compiler declarations carry this distinction
for both FPR widths without changing scalar extension or register-pair rules.
Octeon selection reconciles the MIPS machine flags, ELF class and N32 flag,
ISA-extension and register-width declarations, and GNU floating-point
attributes (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsocteon.rs`).
BE N32/N64 soft-float profiles select Octeon, Plus, II or III; the qualified
III hard-float profiles select the `hard` compiler model. Plus requires its
distinct ISA-extension declaration: indistinguishable legacy flags retain the
base Octeon target. Conflicting, incomplete or unsupported profiles require an
explicit target, which always takes precedence. Legacy vendor FP header bits
do not override standard attributes. The shared reader in
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsabi.rs` accepts matching
section and `PT_MIPS_ABIFLAGS` records, rejects malformed or conflicting records,
and treats FP ANY as unspecified. Call recovery uses the same evidence, including
in images without section headers. Non-Octeon target selection is unchanged.
Octeon III accepts the VZ capability declaration emitted by its compiler;
this does not assert that every privileged VZ instruction is modeled.
Octeon N32/N64 selection does not intercept ELF32 O32 images, including
little-endian images carrying Octeon machine flags: they retain generic MIPS
selection, and an explicit target still takes precedence.

(unlace) A RISC-V ELF whose `Tag_RISCV_arch` attribute lists `zcmp` or `zcmt`
selects the `RISCV:LE:32:Zcmp` or `RISCV:LE:64:Zcmp` language
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/riscvzc.rs`), whose processor
spec sets the `Zcmp` context bit so the `c.fsdsp` encoding space decodes as the
Zc stack and jump-table instructions (§2). The attribute is read from the
`.riscv.attributes` section, or from the `PT_RISCV_ATTRIBUTES` segment when the
image has no sections; extension names are compared with their versions
stripped (`zcmp1p0` is `zcmp`). An image that also declares `zcd`, or `c`
together with `d`, has no bundled language and requires an explicit target.
Every other RISC-V image keeps the default selection, including one whose
attribute blobs are malformed, truncated or conflicting, and `--target` always
wins.

(unlace) An ELF32 whose `e_machine` is 249 (`EM_NANOMIPS`) selects
`nanoMIPS:LE:32:default` or `nanoMIPS:BE:32:default` by its byte order
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/nanomips.rs`). The neutral
object parser has no architecture for that machine, so the id is read from the
ELF header itself, before the per-architecture table that would otherwise
report an unsupported machine. nanoMIPS is its own encoding, not a mode of
MIPS32: instructions are one, two or three 16-bit units, each stored in the
image's byte order, with the major opcode in the top six bits of the first
unit. The language (`specs/Ghidra/Processors/nanoMIPS`) covers the nanoMIPS32
integer instruction set in all three lengths, the system and EVA instructions,
and the p32 calling convention: eight integer argument registers `a0`..`a7`,
further arguments on the stack from offset 0, the result in `a0` (and `a1` for
a 64-bit value), and `s0`..`s7`, `fp`, `gp` and `sp` preserved. `SAVE` and
`RESTORE` lift to one store or load per listed register at `sp - 4`, `sp - 8`,
... relative to the frame's outer edge, plus the `sp` adjustment, so a prologue
and epilogue read as ordinary callee-saved traffic and `RESTORE.JRC` is a
return. The temporaries `t0`..`t5`, `t8` and `t9` are deliberately not declared
killed by a call: a compiler that knows a callee's register use keeps values in
them across the call, and declaring them killed would cut those values off.
The floating-point, DSP and 64-bit instruction groups are not decoded yet; an
image that uses them stops at the first such instruction. No option controls
any of this, and an image for any other machine is unaffected.
(unlace, GH-1632) A Synopsys ARC ELF has no architecture in the object reader, so
its machine is read from the ELF header
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/arctarget.rs`).
`EM_ARC_COMPACT2` (195, ARC EM and HS) selects `ARC:LE:32:ARCv2` or
`ARC:BE:32:ARCv2` by the image's byte order (§2). `EM_ARC_COMPACT` (93,
ARC600/ARC700) is not mapped: its 16-bit encodings differ and it has no
language yet, so it still needs an explicit `--target`. A relocatable ARCv2
object's `bl`/`b` (`S25W_PCREL`/`S25H_PCREL` and their `_PLT` spellings, the
displacement from `P & !3`), middle-endian long immediates (`32_ME`) and data
words (`32`, `PC32`) are applied (`reloc_apply.rs (classify_arc)`); the
small-data forms against `_SDA_BASE_` and the GOT forms are not.

(unlace, unlace#680) A WebAssembly relocatable object (`.o`) has no `name`
section; its function and global names come from the `WASM_SYMBOL_TABLE`
subsection of its `linking` custom section (version 2), for every index the
`name` section does not name (`loader/format/wasm.rs`). An undefined symbol
is named only when it carries `WASM_SYM_EXPLICIT_NAME`.

(unlace, unlace#678) A relocatable object for a 16-bit machine is laid out
inside its address space instead of at 0x400000, which is past its end: an AVR
object from `SMALL_RELOC_BASE` (0x100), an MSP430 object from
`MSP430_RELOC_BASE` (0x200, the first RAM address, above the special-function
and peripheral registers the processor spec names, so a laid-out global does
not print as `TBCCR5`); every other machine keeps 0x400000
(`reloc_object::reloc_base`, also used by the FID relocation map).

(unlace, unlace#676) Six more ELF machines are read from the header
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elfmachinetarget.rs`), because the
object reader either has no language stem for them or no architecture at all:
`EM_AVR` (83) selects `avr8:LE:16:default` (`gcc` model), `EF_AVR_ARCH_AVR6`
the ATmega256 language and `EF_AVR_ARCH_XMEGA1`..`7` `avr8:LE:24:xmega`;
`EM_MSP430` (105) `TI_MSP430:LE:16:default`; `EM_HEXAGON` (164)
`Hexagon:LE:32:default`; `EM_LANAI` (244) `lanai:BE:32:default`; `EM_LOONGARCH`
(258) the ilp32 or lp64 language of the ELF class, single-float when the
`e_flags` ABI is single-float and double otherwise (soft-float has no language
of its own); `EM_AMDGPU` (224) the GFX9, GFX10 or GFX11 language of
`EF_AMDGPU_MACH` (gfx900-gfx90c and gfx90a; gfx101x/103x; gfx11xx; and the
matching generic targets). RDNA images take the wave32 language, because the
wave size is in the kernel descriptor, not the ELF header; wave64 code and
GFX9.4, GCN 1-4 and GFX12 images still need an explicit `--target`.

(unlace) The AVR-Dx parts (AVRxt core) have their own languages,
`avr8:LE:16:avrda`, `avrdb`, `avrdd` and `avrdu`, chosen with `--target`; the ELF
header cannot tell an AVR-Dx part from an Xmega. They share `avr8xt.sla`: I/O at data address 0,
so `in`/`out` and `lds`/`sts` reach the same bytes; R0-R31 outside the data space; and a
16-bit PC. Each series has its own pspec, `avr8dx_<series>.pspec`, which
`tools/gen_avr_dx_pspec.py` writes from Microchip's Apache-2.0 AVR-Dx device pack. The pspec
labels every data-space register `<instance>_<register>` (`PORTA_DIR`, `TCA0_CNT`), so a
peripheral access prints by name, not as `dat_400`.

(unlace) The MSP430 families have their own languages, chosen with `--target` (an MSP430 ELF does
not name its device): `TI_MSP430:LE:16:f1xx`, `f2xx`, `g2xx`, `f4xx` and `i2xx` on `TI_MSP430.sla`, and
`TI_MSP430X:LE:32:f5xx`, `f6xx`, `fr2xx` (with FR4xx), `fr5xx` and `fr6xx` on `TI_MSP430X.sla`. Each
has a pspec, `TI_MSP430_<family>.pspec`, which `tools/gen_msp430_pspec.py` writes from TI's BSD-3
MSP430 GCC support files (the `<device>_symbols.ld` of every device). An address is labelled with
the name every device of the family gives it, the spelling most of them use, and left unlabelled
where the devices disagree (LCD_B against LCD_C, Timer_A against Timer_B); the legacy first-timer
names (`TACTL`) count as the current ones (`TA0CTL`). A word port's halves take the byte port
names code uses (`PAOUT` is labelled `P1OUT`, its high byte `P2OUT`). The peripheral space (to
0x1ff, or 0xfff on the 5xx/6xx/FR cores) is volatile. The `default` languages keep Ghidra's F1xx
pspec.

(unlace) The TMS320C28x device families have their own languages, `tms320c28:LE:32:<family>` (f2802x,
f2802x0, f2803x, f2805x, f2806x, f2807x, f2823x, f2833x, f2837xd, f2837xs, f2838x, f28002x, f28003x,
f28004x, f280013x, f280015x, f28e12x, f28p55x, f28p551x, f28p65x), chosen with `--target`, on
`tms320c28.sla`. Each has a pspec, `tms320c28_<family>.pspec`, which `tools/gen_c28_pspec.py` writes
from TI C2000Ware's BSD-3 device support headers: each peripheral instance is a variable of a register
structure (`volatile struct ADC_REGS AdcaRegs;`) that the family's linker command file places
(CPU1's on a dual-core part), so every register is labelled `<instance>_<register>`
(`AdcaRegs_ADCCTL1`, `EPwm1Regs_TBPRD`) at its word address, with 32-bit registers on even words, and
each instance's frame is volatile. Lines under `#if` are kept as a CPU1 build compiles them.

(unlace) The PIC18F Q-series families have their own languages, `PIC-18:LE:24:Q10`, `Q20`, `Q24`,
`Q35`, `Q40`, `Q41`, `Q43`, `Q83` and `Q84`, chosen with `--target`. Each family has a pspec,
`pic18q_<family>.pspec`, which `tools/gen_pic18q_pspec.py` writes from Microchip's Apache-2.0
PIC18F-Q device pack. It labels every SFR except the core registers, which SLEIGH already names.
Q10 has the classic core and runs on `pic18.sla`. The other families have the K42/Q core and run on
`pic18q.sla`, which `pic18.sinc` builds with `SFR_PAGE` 0x4 and `ACCESS_LOW` 0x500. On that core:
- the core registers sit at 0x4d8-0x4ff;
- access-bank 0x60-0xff is data 0x460-0x4ff;
- access-bank 0x00-0x5f is data 0x500-0x55f, so a variable reached by access and by bank is one
  address;
- a 12-bit `MOVFF` operand finds the core registers on page 0x4.

`pic18q.cspec` keeps 0x480-0x4ff out of the global ranges, as `pic18.cspec` does with
0xf80-0xfff. Q71 has no language: its PPS registers differ between pin counts. The three-word
`MOVFFL` is not decoded.

Five further machines are routed the same way:
- `EM_68K` (4) selects `68000:BE:32:Coldfire` when `e_flags` names a ColdFire ISA
  (`EF_M68K_CF_MASK`), `68000:BE:32:default` for `EF_M68K_M68000`, and `68000:BE:32:MC68020`
  otherwise (gcc's default `-m68020` has no flag).
- `EM_OPENRISC` (92) and `EM_XTENSA` (94) take the language of the header's byte order.
- `EM_CSKY` (252) selects ABIv1 when `e_flags` bits 28-31 are 1, and ABIv2 otherwise, in the
  header's byte order.
- `EM_TI_C2000` (141) selects `tms320c28:LE:32:default` (cl2000 EABI objects).
- `EM_CUDA` (190) selects the SASS language of the `sm_NN` in `e_flags`. The SM number is in
  bits 8-15 from ELF ABI version 8 (CUDA 12.8 ptxas), and in bits 0-7 before that. An
  architecture with no SASS language (sm_30, sm_32) still needs `--target`.

(unlace) TI compilers (cl2000 and its siblings) emit every branch target inside a function as a
`$C$L<n>` symbol typed `STT_FUNC`, local, size 0. The ELF symbol-table inventory skips these
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/tilocallabels.rs`), so they are not decompiled as functions
of their own.

(unlace) PowerPC32 ELF APU requirements are read by
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppcaputarget.rs` when the
default-off `ppcapu` load-time option is on. SPE and embedded floating-point APUs
then select the e500 decoder. The option stays off until the e500 model recovers
scalar call arguments held in its 64-bit registers. Shared requirements such as
ISEL do not identify a processor and retain the generic decoder, including its
AltiVec support. `EF_PPC_EMB` alone likewise does not select a processor. Unknown
APU versions and malformed or unsupported requirements keep the generic decoder
and print a `[unlace target]` note. Explicit `--target` takes precedence. A
selected language never falls back to a different ISA if its specification is
missing. The explicit e500mc target uses the standard PowerPC32 FPR argument and
return convention, while its 64-bit integer results keep the explicit `r3:r4`
pair (`r4:r3` little-endian) with the high word first.
The SPE compiler models join 64-bit integer arguments from aligned pairs of
32-bit GPR slots, preserving byte order and spilling the whole argument when
no aligned pair remains. Following arguments use the remaining register or
stack slots, and struct/union arguments are passed indirectly.

(unlace) A PowerPC64 ELF image's compiler spec follows the ABI version in its
`e_flags` (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppc64elfv2target.rs`).
The ABIs differ in the frame header below the parameter save area: ELFv1's is
48 bytes (back chain, CR, LR, two reserved doublewords, TOC), ELFv2's is 32
(back chain, CR, LR, TOC). The first stack argument, the ninth doubleword of
the save area, is therefore at SP+112 under ELFv1 and at SP+96 under ELFv2. A
big-endian image that declares ABI version 2 (musl, `-mabi=elfv2`) selects
`PowerPC:BE:64:default:elfv2` (`ppc_64_be_elfv2.cspec`); version 1 and an
unspecified version keep the ELFv1 default model. A little-endian image that
does not declare ABI version 1 is ELFv2, whose ABI requires a POWER8
processor, so it selects the Power ISA language `PowerPC:LE:64:A2ALT:default`
(`ppc_64_isa_altivec_le.sla`, the same ELFv2 `ppc_64_le.cspec`): the generic
language does not decode `popcntd`, `isel`, `ldbrx` or VSX, and 55 of the 114
functions of a static musl ppc64le image halted on them (10 with A2ALT, all on
`0x00000000` trap words). A little-endian image that declares ELFv1 keeps
`PowerPC:LE:64:default` and is read with ELFv2 offsets. Explicit `--target` takes precedence, and the explicit
`PowerPC:BE:64:A2ALT` language offers only the ELFv1 model.


(unlace) **A Go image composes the `:golang` compiler field instead**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (language_id_for)`,
option `goabi auto|off`, default auto, carried as the `UNLACE_GOABI` loadtime
environment gate — the `sourcelang` pattern, because the id is composed inside
`load file`). Go's register ABI is not the platform C ABI: under the `gcc`
model a Go function's RAX/RBX/… arguments are scratch, so its parameters are
invisible, a second return value is dead-coded away and the statements feeding
it are deleted (`func pair(a,b int) (int,int)` rendered
`long pair(void){ return v1 + v2; }`). The vendored golang cspecs
(`abi-internal` default, `abi0`, the write-barrier/duff helper models) exist
for x86-64, x86-32 and AArch64, so the override fires only on those three
little-endian architectures when the effective source language is Go (the
`UNLACE_SOURCELANG` force included); everywhere else the composed id is
byte-identical to before, and `elf_language_ids` enumerates the golang ids so
the resolves-in-the-DB gate proves them vendored. Measured on a stripped
go1.22 hello-world (1,544 functions): functions with recovered parameters
544 → 992, functions reading a never-assigned register local 853 → 501, zero
failures either way.

(unlace) **A 32-bit Delphi PE composes the `:borlanddelphi` compiler field**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (language_id_for)`, option
`delphiabi on|off`, default on, carried as the `UNLACE_DELPHIABI` loadtime
environment gate, the `goabi` pattern). The vendored `x86delphi.cspec` makes
Delphi's `register` convention the default model: the first three arguments
in EAX, EDX and ECX, the rest on the stack, the callee popping them, EAX the
return. Under the PE's `windows` model those three registers are scratch, so a
method loses `Self` and its first arguments and a call through a VMT slot
prints with none. The override fires only on an I386 PE that holds the
`TObject` class name and at least two VMTs under one layout
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/delphi/mod.rs (is_delphi_image)`, the
`delphi` pass's own detection); every other image composes the same id as
before, and `elf_language_ids` enumerates the Delphi id so the
resolves-in-the-DB gate proves it vendored. A Windows API entry point is
`__stdcall` whatever its caller's compiler, so under the same gate the pass
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/delphi/delphiabiimports.rs`
binds every resolved import, at its IAT slot and its jump thunk, to the
`__stdcall` model (a model-only fact; a parked Win32 signature keeps its
pieces and takes the model). A Borland-mangled `@` name is a Delphi package
export and keeps the register default; a C runtime import keeps `__cdecl`.
A delay-load thunk (`__imp_load_<name>`, which saves ECX and EDX and jumps to
`__tailMerge`) is image code, not an import, and is left out; the delay IAT
slot it fills is bound like any other import.
Without this a call such as `SetFilePointer(h, lo, &hi, 0)` read its first
three arguments from EAX, EDX and ECX and its fourth from the first pushed
word (`SetFilePointer(hFile,a1,a2,(unsigned int)hFile)`). The image's own
routines all take the register model, so a `stdcall` callback or `cdecl`
helper is read with register arguments.
Measured with `--option delphi on` on two Inno Setup stubs (344 and 919
decompiled functions): functions with parameters 207 → 272 and 619 → 801,
functions reading a never-assigned register 166 → 147 and 575 → 441, calls
printed with an empty argument list 621 → 110 and 2,245 → 914, zero failures
either way.

On AMD64 ELF with `goabi auto`, the Go function-table pass
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pclntab/goabi0.rs`)
compares the original defined text symbols with the pclntab entries. A
symbol `name.abi0` must match a pclntab entry at the same address named
`name`, which keeps the binding independent of the name chosen for display.
The pass checks the linker's function-data base against the matching
`runtime.firstmoduledata` and bounds `FUNCDATA_ArgInfo`'s offset entry by its
own function record. The complete incoming list must describe consecutive
eight-byte scalar inputs from offset zero, covering the whole area declared
by `_func.args`. Since the list excludes results, there is no room for a
nonzero stack result. A missing list, gaps, narrower inputs, aggregate or
truncation markers, generic dictionary arguments and an area with extra
bytes keep inference.

The function must have the ordinary FuncID and no flags other than the
optional assembly flag. Its nonempty ELF text symbol must end within the
pclntab function extent and cover at most 256 mapped bytes. After loader
attachment, the commit checks those bytes with a context-isolated SLEIGH walk
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pclntab/goabi0_leaf.rs`).
The walk must reach a decoded near return at the symbol boundary without a branch,
call, processor user operation or stack-pointer write before the return.
This keeps private runtime tail transfers and thread-exit paths under the
existing model. The model-fact commit binds a qualifying function and direct
calls to a bounded copy of the stack-input model. Stripped images lack the
alias proof. Call-bearing functions, independently proven result storage,
other input shapes and source types require separate evidence.

The AArch64 Go `abi-internal` model contributes zero net stack-pointer
movement when a call returns
(`specs/Ghidra/Processors/AARCH64/data/languages/AARCH64_golang.cspec`).
`BL` places the link in a register, and the callee restores its own frame;
there is no additional eight-byte pop. The model therefore states
`extrapop="0"`. A nonzero value makes `ActionExtraPopSetup` insert an
artificial stack-pointer addition after each call, disconnecting a saved
argument and an earlier recursive result from their later loads. This
correction changes only that model's return stack effect: its stackshift,
stack-argument offsets, register banks and other Go models remain as stated.
The AArch64 C model already has a zero extra pop.

(unlace) **The default model follows the image's Go release**
(`crates/unlace-middle/src/infra/architecture.rs
(unlace_go_stack_default)`, run right after the cspec's models are registered).
The register ABI reached amd64 in go1.17 and arm64 in go1.18
(`crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/goreg.rs
(register_abi)`); 386 never got it, and its golang cspec already defaults to
`abi0`. An older image passes every argument on the stack, so under
`abi-internal` its calls lost all their arguments (`main.add3();` in a go1.16
build). Such an image takes `abi0` as its default model. The AArch64 `abi0`
model states `extrapop="0"` for the reason given above for `abi-internal`:
`BL` pushes nothing, so with the eight-byte pop every call moved the caller's
stack pointer and its later outgoing arguments read as stores to its own
parameters. The release is the
one on the load options, read by
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/gobuildinfo.rs
(go_toolchain_version)` from the build-info blob in either form: the inline
strings of go1.18+, or the pair of pointers to Go string headers that go1.13
to go1.17 wrote, resolved through the image. An image with no blob (before
go1.13) is placed by the pclntab format of its named table section
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pclntab/mod.rs
(format_last_release)`): the go1.2 layout ends at go1.15 and the go1.16 layout
at go1.17, so the first is a stack image on both CPUs and the second on arm64
only. An image with no release keeps the cspec default. The cspec's `abi0`
states no output, because a Go stack result sits after the arguments at an
offset the model cannot give, so a callee's stack result is still not shown as
a return value. On a stripped go1.16.15 build `main.main` went from
`main.add3(); os.Exit();` to `main.add3(dat_4e7738,2,7); os.Exit(v1);`. The
same test removes the goroutine register below: before the register ABI `g`
lived in thread-local storage and R14/x28 were ordinary registers, so
`goroutine_register` names none and a function that used the register as
scratch no longer prints `g`.

(unlace) **The default model follows the image's Go version**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/gobuildinfo.rs
(go_uses_stack_abi)`, applied in the object bootstrap right after the
architecture is built). The register ABI reached amd64 in go1.17 and arm64 in
go1.18; 386 never got it, and its golang cspec already defaults to `abi0`. An
older image passes every argument on the stack, so under `abi-internal` its
calls lost all their arguments (`main.add3();` in a go1.16 build). IDA 9.5's
golang plugin makes the same choice from the version (golang.so 0x7570). The
version comes from the build-info blob, in either form: the inline strings of
go1.18+, or the older pair of pointers to Go string headers, which is read
through the image's sections. Without a blob the pclntab magic gives a range:
`0xfffffffb` (go1.2-1.15) is stack, `0xfffffff0`/`0xfffffff1` (go1.18+) is
register, and `0xfffffffa` (go1.16-1.17) is stack on arm64 and undecided on
amd64, which keeps the cspec default. A stack-ABI image then takes `abi0` as
its default model (`set_default_model("abi0")`). The cspec's `abi0` has no
output, because a Go stack result sits after the arguments at an offset the
model cannot state, so the callee's result is still not shown. Measured on a
stripped go1.16.15 build: `main.main` went from `main.add3(); os.Exit();` to
`main.add3(dat_4e7748,2,7); os.Exit(v1);`. The same version decides `goreg`:
before the register ABI `g` lived in thread-local storage and R14/x28 were
ordinary registers, so `unlace_goreg::goroutine_register` returns `None` for an
image the bootstrap's `UNLACE_GOVERSION` places before go1.17 (amd64) or go1.18
(arm64); that variable is now set from either build-info form
(`go_version_any`). In the same go1.16 build, a function at 0x404140 used R14
as scratch and printed `g = a4;`; it now prints a plain local.

(unlace) **Function ends come from the `pcsp` table**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pclntab/mod.rs
(pcvalue_span)`). Each `_func` points at its `pcsp` pcvalue table; the sum of
the table's pc deltas (in `minLC` quanta) is the length of the function's own
code. The `fde_bodies` extent the pass reports is that end, bounded by the
next functab entry, so the `int3` padding between functions is outside it
(IDA golang.so 0x23950 takes the end the same way). On a go1.26 build the
first function, `internal/cpu.Initialize`, ends at `+0x5e` rather than at the
next entry's `+0x60`.

(unlace) **A bounded literal ends the NUL-scan row it starts inside**
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (commit_analysis_output)`,
under the `fatstr` gate). rustc packs literals back to back without
terminators, so the NUL scan glues a literal to the next one. When a bounded
fact (a `&str` record or a `Location` file name) starts strictly inside a
NUL-scan row, the row is cut at that start before the strings are planted.
IDA's rust plugin splits at every referenced byte (rust.so 0x6e60); unlace
splits at the starts it has evidence for.

(unlace) **With the golang cspec active, the goroutine register becomes the
named, typed global `g`** (always on;
`crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/goreg.rs`, installed by
the architecture build right after the cspec `<global>` decode —
`crates/unlace-middle/src/infra/architecture.rs (unlace_install_goreg)`).
The register ABI pins the current goroutine in a register — `R14` on amd64,
`x28` on arm64, the values the vendored golang `register.info` files state —
which the cspec lists as `unaffected` and no `<pentry>` names, so every access
rendered as a phantom local (`v3; // r14`) fed by unexplained arithmetic. The
install mirrors a cspec `<global><register/>` (the register's storage joins
the global scope; the vendored spec itself stays pristine) and maps a type-
and name-locked `g` symbol typed `runtime.g *` over it. `runtime.g`,
`runtime.gobuf`, `runtime.m` and `runtime.gsignalStack` are synthesized shells
carrying exactly the fields whose offsets the runtime source states for the
register-ABI era, and the layouts are **versioned off the image's own
toolchain**: the build-info blob's version string
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/gobuildinfo.rs
(go_toolchain_version)`) travels on the load options
(`crates/unlace-middle/src/p0_knowledge/loadoptions.rs
(go_version)`) — set by the object bootstrap from the image's bytes before the
loader parses them and the sleigh build runs, because the shells are interned
inside the cspec decode, upstream of every per-image fact write. The image's
own version wins over a release the caller stated; a load without explicit
options publishes it as `UNLACE_GOVERSION`, and clears that variable for an image
with no version, so a stale value from an earlier load cannot leak in. It selects the release's layout
(`crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/goreg.rs (GoLayout)`):
go1.23 inserted `g.syscallbp`, go1.25 dropped `gobuf.ret`, and with both
perturbations the liblink-stable anchors (`stackguard0` 0x10, `_panic` 0x20,
`m` 0x30, `stktopsp`..`goid` 0x80..0x98) land identically while
`syscallsp`/`syscallpc` and everything inside `runtime.m` after `morebuf`
shift with the gobuf width. The `runtime.m` shell is verified field-for-field
against go1.22.10 and go1.25.3 through `profilehz` (linux/amd64 `sigset`; a
PE Go binary's empty `sigset` would shift the tail from `tls` on — the shell
is a reading aid); `g.m` carries the completed
`runtime.m *`, so `g->m->curg` chains render named end to end, while `m`'s
own goroutine pointers stay `void *` (a pointer taken to a still-incomplete
composite would survive the factory's clone-and-re-key completion pointing at
the stale type). An access past a modeled prefix renders as an offset off the
shell — still anchored. An image with no parsable build-info version takes
the release its explicit load options state, else the go1.22 baseline. A golang target with no pinned register (x86-32 reaches
`g` through TLS) is untouched. Measured on the stripped
go1.22 hello-world: functions declaring a phantom `// r14` local 267 → 23,
functions reading named `g->` fields 7 → 297, the preemption-request store
rendering `g->stackguard0 = 0xfffffffffffffade` exactly as the runtime source
spells it; with the `runtime.m` shell, functions indexing raw bytes off
`g->m` fall 166 → 42 and ~77 render named `curg`/`locks` reads — and on a
go1.25 build the versioned layouts keep those same names at that release's
shifted offsets (53 `curg` readers, `syscallbp` rendering where it exists).

The loader's symbol
stream — defined FUNC symbols plus the resolved import stubs of §1.3 — is
`@VERSION`-stripped, demangled (§1.4) and **character-sanitized** before each
name is installed as a `FunctionSymbol`, and the loader's read-only section ranges are applied to the
symbol-table property map eagerly at bootstrap (loader markup, not a gated pass):
they are what lets the printer prove a constant points into read-only memory and
render a string literal.

(unlace) **The loader's tables, the notes and `.interp` are not read-only program data**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/elf.rs (is_loader_table)`).
BFD sets the read-only bit on any allocated, non-writable section, which is as
true of `.interp`, the `SHT_NOTE` sections, `.dynsym`, `.dynstr`, `.gnu.hash`,
`.rela.*` and the version tables as it is of `.rodata`. Nothing in the program
reads those, but the read-only range is the *only* thing
`PrintC::pushPtrCharConstant` asks before it replaces a constant with the
characters at that address, so a number whose value happens to land in one came
out as a string. A PIE that calls `puts((char *)0x4a3)`, `puts((char *)0x320)`
and `puts((char *)0x3a0)` printed `puts("uts")`, the tail of the dynamic string
table's own `"puts"` entry, `puts("d-linux-x86-64.so.2")`, the middle of the
loader path in `.interp` at `0x318`, and `puts("\x03")`, a byte of the
`.note.ABI-tag` kernel version
(`crates/unlace-analysis/tests/fixtures/loadertablestring_x86_64`). In
real builds `bash`'s `rl_do_lowercase_version` returned `"_ungets"` for
`0x1869f` and coreutils `ls` compared a pointer against `"loc"` for `0x12c7`.
Those sections therefore do not carry the read-only bit: `SectionKind::Metadata`
(the `SHT_SYMTAB`/`SHT_DYNSYM`/`SHT_STRTAB`/`SHT_RELA`/`SHT_REL`/`SHT_RELR`/
`SHT_HASH`/`SHT_DYNAMIC` family), `SectionKind::Note`, the GNU dynamic-info types
`SHT_GNU_HASH` and `SHT_GNU_verdef`/`verneed`/`versym`, which `object` reports
as `SectionKind::Elf(sh_type)`, and the section named `.interp`, which is plain
`SHT_PROGBITS` and differs from `.rodata` only in its name. The same
classification gates `operand_refs`: a scalar operand that lands in one of these
sections is not a data reference, for the reason its `.got`/`.plt` exclusion
already exists.

(unlace) **An unusable section table is dropped, not fatal**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elf_shdr.rs
(tolerate_unusable_section_table)`). An ELF's section table is link-time metadata;
what the loader obeys — the entry point and the `PT_LOAD` map — lives in the ELF
header and the program headers, which is why `readelf -l` still prints a full
segment map for an image whose `e_shoff` is garbage. `object` nevertheless
validates the section table eagerly inside `File::parse`, so a single out-of-range
`e_shoff`, a wrong `e_shentsize`, or an `e_shstrndx` naming no section rejected the
whole image and every unlace surface exited 1 with "not in recognized object file
format". Packers, `sstrip` and CTF authors all produce that shape deliberately. The
image bytes are therefore normalized once, at the same canonical read point as the
Mach-O fat-slice peel, by clearing `e_shoff`/`e_shnum`/`e_shstrndx` — the encoding
of "this ELF has no section table" — so the loader and every analysis pass below
see the same recovered view. The test is pure header arithmetic and runs before any
parse, so an image whose table is usable is passed on byte for byte; the rewrite is
kept only if the rewritten copy actually parses, so corruption elsewhere still
reports `object`'s own error rather than a misleading one about the section table.
What was dropped, and what survived it, is reported on stderr. The CLI surfaces
that parse the image themselves rather than through the loader (`strings`, `crypto`, `blobs`,
`xrefs`, `decompile-graph`, the call graph) read it through the same normalization
(`elf_shdr (read_image)`), so a recovered image is recovered everywhere.

(unlace) **A PE DOS header whose `e_magic` is not `MZ` is repaired, not fatal**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/pe_dosmagic.rs
(tolerate_corrupt_dos_magic)`). The DOS header's only load-bearing fields are
`e_magic` and `e_lfanew`, the file offset of the NT headers; every header the loader
reads — the `PE\0\0` signature, the COFF and optional headers, the section table —
lives behind that pointer. `object` identifies the format from the leading bytes
alone, so an image whose first byte was overwritten (a CTF image ships `0x15 'Z'`,
`e_magic` `0x5a15`) was "Unknown file magic" on every surface although `e_lfanew`
still led to an intact PE. When the file is no format `object` recognizes and
`e_lfanew` points at `PE\0\0` clear of the magic itself, `MZ` is written over
`e_magic` in the loaded copy, at the same canonical read point and before the
data-directory clamp below, which reads the headers behind it; the file on disk is
never modified. Any other file, including every image that already parses, is passed
on byte for byte with no parse performed, and the format sniff that routes `load
file` to the object loader admits the same images. Like the clamp, the repair is kept
even when the copy still does not parse: the signature settles which format the
file is, so the caller reports what is actually unreadable in it. The repair is
reported once on stderr and, with the other two header repairs, recorded on the
loaded program (`ConsoleProgram::load_notes`), which `functions --summary --json`
publishes as its `warnings` array.

(unlace) **A PE data-directory count larger than its own header is clamped, not
fatal** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/pe_datadirs.rs
(tolerate_oversized_data_directories)`). A PE's optional header ends with an array
of `IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY` entries whose length is declared separately, by
`NumberOfRvaAndSizes`, and the two can disagree: `SizeOfOptionalHeader` bounds how
many entries are physically there. Windows trusts the bound and reads
`min(declared, what fits)`; `object` slices exactly the declared count inside
`ImageNtHeaders::parse`, so one oversized `u32` rejected the whole image with
"Invalid PE number of RVA and sizes" before a byte of code was mapped — the shape
a packer produces by overwriting the field (a reported Invius-packed image
declared 1531532893 in a 224-byte optional header holding the 16 real
directories). The count is therefore clamped to what the header holds at the same
canonical read point as the section-table repair, so the imports are read from the
real table rather than fabricated, and a count that already fits is passed on byte
for byte with no parse performed. Unlike the section-table repair, the clamp is
kept even when the rewritten copy still does not parse: a count larger than its own
header is wrong however the rest of the file reads, so keeping it lets the caller
report whatever is actually unreadable instead of a header count that was never
the whole story.

(unlace) **A PE's header page is mapped, read-only**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/pe_headers.rs (header_region)`).
Windows maps a PE in two parts: `SizeOfHeaders` file bytes are copied to
`ImageBase` as `PAGE_READONLY`, and only then is each section copied to
`ImageBase + VirtualAddress`. `object`'s neutral view enumerates the sections
alone, so everything below the first section's RVA — the MZ stub, the PE
signature, the COFF and optional headers, the section table — was mapped nowhere,
and an address there answered "is not mapped in this input" on every surface,
including `decompile --define-function`. A compiler puts no code in the header, but
a hand-built or packed image may: a reported keygenme declares
`AddressOfEntryPoint` `0x154`, the byte immediately after its own two-entry section
table, so its declared entry was unreachable. The region is therefore published to
the segment and section walks as one more mapping unit, `DATA | READONLY`. It is
read-only, not executable, both because that is what Windows does and because it
keeps the executable-region scans of §1.6 out of the MZ/PE bytes of every PE — so
function *discovery* invents nothing in a header. Its extent is `SizeOfHeaders`
clamped twice, to the file length and to the first section's RVA, so a malformed
value — the same field a packer overwrites two paragraphs above — can never shadow
real content; a clamp to zero publishes nothing. No other format defines one
(`ObjectFormat::header_region` defaults to `None`), because an ELF's `PT_LOAD`
headers already describe whatever of the header is in the mapping.

(unlace) **The one thing that makes a header page code is the image saying so**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/pe_headers.rs
(declared_entry_in_header)`). Mapping the page was not enough to *decompile* the
keygenme above: the header page is no section, so the executable-section filter of
§1.6 rejected the entry as implausible code, and both of that image's sections
carry characteristics `0xc00000e0` — `CNT_CODE|INITIALIZED|UNINITIALIZED|READ|
WRITE` with `MEM_EXECUTE` clear — so there was no executable section for any other
candidate to land in either. Its whole inventory was the two Import Address Table
slots, and once those were correctly withheld from the batch set (§1.9)
`decompile-all` answered `count: 0` on an image `decompile --addr 0x400154`
renders in full. Where `AddressOfEntryPoint` points into the header page the
region is therefore published `CODE | READONLY` instead of `DATA | READONLY`, and
that one address is exempt from the executable-section filter. Nothing is guessed:
the image names the address the OS jumps to, and no section flag ever spoke for
bytes that are in no section. Three things keep it that narrow. An
`AddressOfEntryPoint` of `0` is the "no entry point" encoding, which `object`
reports as `ImageBase` — inside the page — so it is rejected rather than declaring
the `MZ` signature to be a function. Only the entry is exempt, never a `.pdata`,
TLS or export candidate. And an entry inside a section the image flags
non-executable is **not** exempt: there the flag is a statement about those bytes,
and unlace answers it by naming the cause and the `--define-function` that overrides
it (§1.9), rather than overriding it silently.

(unlace) **A segment's zero-filled tail is mapped, not a hole**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (Segment::mapped_size)`).
Every format states a segment's RAM footprint separately from the bytes the file
supplies for it — ELF `p_memsz` over `p_filesz`, PE `VirtualSize` over
`SizeOfRawData`, Mach-O `vmsize` over `filesize` — and the excess is the
zero-initialized data the loader is expected to materialize: `.bss`, and the tail
of any `.data` whose trailing zeros the linker declined to write out. unlace copied
only the file extent into each segment, so an address in that tail matched no
segment, `loadFill` hit the "initial address unmapped" contract, and the surfaces
above it reported an address the image plainly maps as covered by no loaded
segment — a reported keygenme keeps its globals at RVA `0x8740`, inside a `.data`
of `VirtualSize` `0x7a8` over `SizeOfRawData` `0x200`, and reading them was
refused with the advice to unpack an image that was never packed. Each segment
therefore records its RAM footprint alongside its bytes, and the
containing-segment walk answers over the footprint; the part of the read past the
file extent falls into the zero-fill `copy_segment` was already doing for the
straddling case. A data segment with no file bytes at all — a `SizeOfRawData` `0`
section, an ELF `.bss` of its own — is kept for the same reason instead of being
dropped as empty. The footprint is trimmed at the next segment's vma so a declared
size can never shadow real content, and the trim only ever shortens the *tail*:
segments an image stacks at one address (a COFF `.obj` read through the linked
path described later in this section) map exactly what they mapped before.

The tail is recorded only for a segment the image marks as **data**. An
executable uninitialized region is a packer's staging area — `UPX0` is
`VirtualSize` `0x9000` over `SizeOfRawData` `0`, executable — and its file-time
contents are not its run-time contents, so materializing zeroes there does not
recover the code, it feeds 36 KB of `add [eax],al` to the flow walk of §1.6 in
place of the honest `DataUnavail` that stops it. Measured on the in-repo UPX PE:
without the carve-out, the packed entry stops reporting `Unable to load 512
bytes` and decompiles to 16,883 lines in 19.6 s, where the answer that helps is
`unlace unpack`. The consequence is that an image whose only load segment is `RWX`
does not get its `.bss` read either; that is the conservative direction, and the
address still resolves through the section walk, which has always described the
whole footprint.

(unlace, GH-1426) **Where declared segments overlap, the first in address order
serves.** An image can declare an address more than once: two `PT_LOAD`s over
one page from different file offsets, a Mach-O segment or PE section whose
extent runs into another's. The load image neither merges them nor rejects the
image. Its segment list is sorted by start address with a stable sort, so
segments that start together keep the order the image's table lists them in;
the tail trim above ends each zero-filled tail where the next segment starts;
and the containing-segment walk takes the first segment whose mapped extent
holds the address
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (SegmentBytes::find_section)`,
upstream `LoadImageBfd::findSection`'s first match). So a lower-starting
segment's file bytes shadow a higher-starting one's, the first-listed of two
segments at one address shadows the second, and any segment's file bytes shadow
another's zero fill. That is a static rule, not a runtime one: Linux maps
`PT_LOAD`s in program-header order with `MAP_FIXED`, so the *last* one wins page
by page, and Ghidra imports the later one into default memory and the earlier
as an overlay. unlace's bytes, and so its decompilation, follow this rule; `unlace
read --json` lists every other segment that declares a listed address in its
`provenance` ranges' `overlaps`
(`crates/unlace-cli/src/disassemble/provenance.rs`), so the choice is
visible rather than silent.

**Character sanitizing** (`symbolnamechars`, `off|safe|ident`, default `safe`;
`crates/unlace-middle/src/p0_knowledge/symbolnamechars.rs`) is the
last step of that name reduction, and it is the only one that treats the name as
*bytes*. A symbol name is unvalidated binary data, and it is printed verbatim
into the `// Function:` header comment, the `.h` prototype, the definition, every
call site and the `.asm` label. Three shapes therefore restructure the C document
rather than merely look odd — a `*/` closes the header comment early and turns
the rest of the line into code, a raw `0x0a` splits each of those five renderings
across two lines, and a `//` comments out the remainder of the line it lands on —
and a fourth breaks identity rather than syntax: the name is decoded with
`String::from_utf8_lossy`, so two symbols differing only in an invalid byte
become the same `String` and the export carries two definitions and two
prototypes with one name.

`safe` (the default) rewrites exactly that structural set and nothing else: an
ASCII control byte (`0x00`–`0x1F`, `0x7F`), a `"`/`'`/`\`, a `*` or `/` that
forms `*/`, `/*` or `//` with its neighbor (both characters of the pair), and
every byte of an invalid UTF-8 sequence. Each becomes its `_x<hh>` hex escape
rather than a single `_`, because a single `_` is not injective — `a"b`, `a'b`
and `a\nb` would all collapse to `a_b`, reproducing the redefinition defect with
a different trigger — and the escape costs nothing legible, since `safe` fires on
no name a real toolchain emits. A lone `*` or `/` is left alone (it is not a
comment delimiter), as are `.`, `$`, `@`, `-`, `+`, `<`, `>`, `(`, `)`, `;`, `{`,
`}` and all valid multi-byte UTF-8; `::` survives intact, because §0.4's scope
splitter reads it. `ident` additionally reduces each `::` component to
`[A-Za-z0-9_]` through the same routine the Itanium RTTI recovery uses for a
class name (`unlace_symbolnamechars (sanitize_ident_chain)`, called unconditionally
by `unlace_itaniumrtti (sanitize_class_name)`), which is what a reader who intends
to *compile* the export wants; it is not the default because the most common
name in the wild that is not valid C is gcc's clone suffix
(`err_fatal.constprop.0`, `main.part.1`, `add_fdes.cold`), which appears on most
`-O2` binaries and which `safe` is a measured no-op on. `off` restores the
verbatim bytes for someone auditing what a binary literally claims.

The sanitizer runs at the **mint** — after the demangler, so it sees the reduced
name rather than the `_ZN…` envelope, and before the scope splitter, so it never
contends with `symbolnamerepair` over the same empty component — and it covers
the second channel a name arrives through as well: an analysis pass's recovered
name (a DWARF `DW_AT_name`, a Go `pclntab` entry, a PDB public symbol) is
sanitized in `unlace-analysis`'s pass driver
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/pass.rs (AnalysisOutput::sanitize_names)`)
before the commit boundary of §1.4 sees it. That driver renames the facts that
carry a name of their own — symbols, prototypes and their parameters, locals —
but a struct or union tag, a member, an enumerator and a typedef live inside the
datatype a fact merely points at, so the DWARF pass escapes the `safe` set where
it first reads a `DW_AT_name`
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/dwarf/mod.rs (die_name)`), for
every DIE below the unit; the unit's own name is a path and stays verbatim. Under
`ident` those type-side names keep the `safe` spelling, because folding them
further could merge two distinct types onto one interned name; under `off` they
are verbatim like every other name. Like the other gates consumed inside
`load file` it is carried by a process environment variable. Print-time
sanitizing would be the wrong seam: §0.4 explains that the string in the symbol
table is the key `unlace decompile <name>` and `load function` are passed, so a
name only the printer fixed would be one the tool could no longer be asked for.

The **data** half of those same two symbol tables is read alongside the function
half (`loadimage_object.rs (data_symbols)`): every defined, named `STT_OBJECT`
entry with a non-zero `st_size`, deduplicated by address, `.symtab` before
`.dynsym`. Zero-size entries are dropped because the linker's section-boundary
markers (`__bss_start`, `_edata`, `_end`) are exactly the sizeless ones, and a
sizeless symbol would plant a name on the first byte of whatever object follows
it. Each surviving entry becomes a named `undefined<size>` global — the same
shape §1.4's DWARF data globals use, and for the same reason: a size-1 entry does
not contain a 4- or 8-byte access, so the printer's covering-symbol query would
miss and fall back to `dat_<addr>`. The behavior matches IDA Pro and Ghidra,
which both name data objects from the symbol table independently of any debug
info, and it is what makes `fprintf(stderr, ...)` read as an error path instead
of `fprintf(dat_61a0, ...)` on a stripped binary (GH-184). The stream is
collected at `load file` but committed at `read symbols` (DIV-26/DIV-76).

A PE image has no sized data symbols, but its export directory names data too:
`msvcrt.dll` exports `_iob`, `_environ` and `__argc`, and a COM DLL exports its
`IID_*` constants. Each named export whose address lies outside every code
section is kept as a **lookup name only** (`pe_iat.rs (data_exports)`), so
`xrefs --to _iob` and `disassemble` resolve it.
It never becomes a global: an export carries no extent, and a one-byte symbol
would not cover a wider access, so mapping it would trade `dat_<addr>` for
extra casts and raw addresses. A declaration (`--assert data ...`, DWARF) that
supplies the real extent names the storage in emitted C.

A Mach-O image takes the same rule (`macho_stubs.rs (data_exports)`). Its
"exports" are the external defined `nlist` entries, and every one of them used to
enter the function stream: a `__DATA,__data` global, an Objective-C class object
in `__objc_data`, Swift type metadata in `__TEXT,__const`, an `N_ABS` value. Each
then listed in `unlace functions` and decompiled by name to an
`UndefinedInstructionException` body. Now only an export inside a section the
loader classifies as code enters it; the rest are lookup names, under both their
symbol-table spelling (`_audit_global`) and the C spelling (`audit_global`), and
a decompile by either name answers that it names data, where, and that `unlace
read` shows its bytes. One more symbol is excluded the same way: an `N_SECT`
symbol's kind comes from its section's name, and the Mach header symbol
(`__mh_execute_header`) is numbered into `__text` while addressed at the image
base, outside it. A Mach-O symbol is a function entry only when its address lies
inside a code section.

Mach-O data symbols then join the `datasyms` stream themselves
(`macho_stubs.rs (data_symbols)`): every named `N_SECT` symbol inside a non-code
section, local ones included, plus the header symbol, demangled as the function
stream's names are. An `nlist` records no size, so each extends to the next
symbol of its section or the section's end, the way `lldb` sizes Mach-O symbols,
**capped at 8 bytes** (`MAX_DATA_EXTENT`, one 64-bit scalar or pointer). The
extent is what lets the covering-symbol query find the name at the access width,
so `counter += 1` and `return audit_global` read by name, and every pointer to
the object renders `&name` (`MetaClass(&gMetaClass)`,
`&original_NSManagedObject_init`). The cap exists because the gap is a guess: a
release image is stripped of its local symbols (`-x`), so the gap after an
exported object often holds unnamed data (Swift's lazy metadata caches follow
`__dyld_private`), and Go's region markers (`runtime.rodata`, `go:string.*`)
label hundreds of kilobytes; uncapped, every access there would render as an
offset into the wrong name. Inside the cap the guess can still cover alignment
padding, so an access narrower than the extent renders as a partial access of
the named object (`(short)half`, `*(char *)&flag = 1`).

The `nlist` is not where a Mach-O image keeps its exports, only where `object`'s
`exports()` looks for them (the `LC_DYSYMTAB` external-defined range). `dyld` binds
against the **export trie** (`LC_DYLD_EXPORTS_TRIE`, or the `export_off` range of
`LC_DYLD_INFO`), and the two disagree on a stripped image: `strip -N` removes every
`nlist` entry and keeps the trie, and a Swift framework can ship 17 external `nlist`
entries beside a trie of 219 names. `macho_trie.rs (exports)` walks the trie and
`macho_stubs.rs (named_exports)` appends, in address order, each trie name the `nlist`
does not already hold at that address. The trie's names take the `nlist` exports'
rule: one in a code section is a function entry, spelled as the symbol table spells
its names (`_audit_exported_function`), so a stripped image lists what its
unstripped original lists and the C spelling resolves the same way (at an entry
another name already holds, it is a lookup alias of that entry); any other is a
lookup name and, inside a non-code section, a `datasyms` entry sized like an `nlist`
symbol. A re-export names another image's symbol and is skipped, a
stub-and-resolver export names its stub, a thread-local export its descriptor, and
an absolute export is a value, never an entry or a global. On 32-bit ARM the trie
marks a Thumb function with the low address bit, which the `nlist` does not
carry, so an odd address whose even neighbour lies in a code section names that
even entry; an odd address in data keeps its bit, since an exported byte may sit
there. A trie name in code is
also a discovery seed: an `LC_UNIXTHREAD` executable with no `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS`
exports its crt `start`, which is how its entry is found at all. An exported
`_main` is a real symbol at the `LC_MAIN` entry, so `machomain` (§1.5) stands down
for it as it does on an unstripped image.

The trie is untrusted input, so its walk is bounded by its own size, never by what
it claims. Each node is entered at most once (a cycle or a shared child ends there);
a ULEB128 wider than 64 bits or an offset past the end drops the node; an empty edge
label drops the edge and a name over 64 KiB the node's remaining edges; the bytes
read are capped at four per trie byte and the names kept at sixteen per trie byte
(real tries hold about three). `resolve_imports` runs about twenty times per load,
so the export list is kept for the last two images, keyed by the bytes it is read
from: the load commands, the `nlist` array, the string table and the trie.

A **declared extent is never trusted to be representable.** `st_size` is a 64-bit
field of the image that no header check validates, while the type factory sizes
types in a 32-bit `int4`, so the commit clamps the declared size into `1 ..=
int4::MAX` **before** narrowing it — the same shape §1.4's DWARF globals use, even
though those arrive already bounded. Clamping after the narrowing inspects the
wrong number and lets two whole classes of size through: one whose low 32 bits are
zero becomes a size-0 type, which the symbol table rejects, and one whose low 32
bits have the sign bit set becomes a negative size. Neither cost only the symbol.
`engine.rs (commit_analysis_output)` applies its arms in place and propagates the
first error, so a rejected symbol abandoned every later arm — prototypes, context
paints, tracked registers, call-fixups, DWARF locals and line comments — and the
pending stash is taken by then, so a second `read symbols` cannot retry; a
negative size was worse still, indexing the type factory's fixed-size caches out
of bounds. `crates/unlace-middle/src/substrate/dtype.rs` therefore also
refuses a negative size at both cache lookups, as an ordinary error rather than an
invariant, because sizes reach them from image bytes. The clamp is saturating, not
narrowing: a hostile extent stays hostile — a symbol claiming ~2 GiB still covers,
and so shadows, every unnamed address above it, exactly as a legal `st_size` of
`0x7fffffff` already does — but it is now a symbol with a wrong extent rather than
a load that fails or a process that stops.

Precedence is what makes this safe to add underneath the existing sources. The
loader's data symbols commit **last** (`engine.rs (commit_analysis_output)`),
after the DWARF globals and after the detected string literals, and each is
skipped where a function or a covering data symbol already sits. So a
DWARF-described global keeps its DWARF-recovered extent and a detected string
keeps its `char[N]` typelock; the loader arm only fills addresses neither source
reaches. That residue is the interesting one: a copy-relocated libc extern
(`optind`, `stdin`, `stdout`, `optarg`) has a real `.bss` address and a `.dynsym`
entry but no DIE in the program's own `.debug_info`, so nothing else could name
it. Relocatable files use the same stream after rebasing each defined data
symbol through its allocated section's load VMA. COMMON symbols use their
allocated storage binding, not the alignment encoded in their original value.
Undefined symbols, absolute values and symbols in unallocated sections do not
become data globals. The extent and name filters, precedence and `datasyms`
gate are unchanged. A relocation that folds an index bias into its addend
(`table-0x35` in an x86 displacement, an i386 `@GOTOFF` operand) leaves a single
constant, which names whichever object contains the folded address, exactly as
on a linked image; only a base kept apart from its bias reaches
`globalarrayanchor`.

With `symbolnamechars ident`, imported data basenames become collision-safe C
identifiers before being mapped into the engine symbol table
(`crates/unlace-console/src/dataidentifiers.rs`). Readable stems
survive (`tempfile.3` becomes `tempfile_3`); a numeric suffix is added only for
an actual collision, and an address-based name is used only when no stem
remains. C keywords and leading digits receive identifier-safe adjustments.
Valid accented names remain intact. The default `safe` mode keeps ordinary
binary spellings unchanged. Data-name folding is deferred until installed and
pending names can be reserved together, so `counter.3.1` cannot capture an
existing `counter_3_1`. Original data spellings remain lookup aliases for
`unlace xrefs --to` and `unlace read`, without adding duplicate mapped objects.

Format dispatch is by magic (`engine.rs (is_object_binary)`): ELF, thin or fat
Mach-O, PE (`MZ`, validated downstream by the typed PE parser), and bare COFF
objects recognized by a whitelisted leading `IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_*` u16 — anything
else routes to the XML front-end (§1.8). Per-format knowledge is funneled through
one trait, `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/mod.rs (ObjectFormat)`:
the compiler-model id (ELF → `gcc`/`default`, PE → `windows`, with a resolve-time
fallback retry to the arch default when the preferred model has no vendored spec),
the section-flag translation, import resolution (§1.3), and extra constant ranges
(the MIPS GOT). Two format specifics live above the trait:

- **Relocatable objects** (angr, always on) — a pre-link object
  does not say where its bytes live, and each format fails that differently. An
  ELF `.o` has no program headers, so the faithful loader maps zero bytes and
  every lift fails. A COFF `.obj` does present segments, but stacks every section
  at VMA 0: the faithful loader maps whichever sorts first and every symbol
  collapses onto address 0, so with MSVC function-level linking (`/Gy`, one COMDAT
  `.text` per function — the default for real builds) all but one function
  disappear. A Mach-O `MH_OBJECT` places its sections one after another from 0, so
  it maps, but none of its relocations is applied: an arm64 `.o` decompiled to an
  empty body, its flow ending at an unrelocated `bl`, and an x86-64 one read its
  globals at junk addresses. `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/reloc_object.rs (RelocLayout)`
  reproduces angr CLE's relocatable backend for all three: lay each memory-resident,
  non-empty section out above `0x400000` (`RELOC_BASE`, matching CLE so addresses
  line up with angr's), apply the relocations, rebase defined symbols, and bind
  each undefined extern to a synthetic call target in an extern area above the
  sections so calls render by name (an extern reached by a plain data relocation
  on the operand of an x86 `call`/`jmp`/`jcc`, an MSP430 `call #imm` or an m68k
  `jsr`/`jmp` (xxx).L or `bsr.l` counts as code too, so i386, MSP430 and m68k
