  libcalls are named) (the next 4 KiB page plus one; on a 16-bit
  machine the next 16 bytes, so AVR's 4 KiB `rcall` still reaches every libcall). A section header's size is a claim the file
  need not back, so the layout allocates zero-fill only for data — `SHT_NOBITS`
  storage and a data extent past the end of the file — and at most 256 MiB of it
  per object (`reloc_object.rs (ZERO_FILL_LIMIT)`); code is laid out at the bytes
  the file holds, because absent bytes are not instructions. A section cut short
  this way is laid out at its reduced size, one left with no bytes is dropped,
  and each is named on the loader's diagnostic line. A Mach-O object takes every section but
  the `S_ATTR_DEBUG` ones (`__DWARF`, `__LD,__compact_unwind`). Its symbols hold
  addresses in the object's own layout, so their section offsets are taken
  against the section's `addr`, and the assembler's `ltmp`/`l_`/`L` labels name
  no function. `reloc_apply.rs (classify_macho)` reads the relocation by its
  `r_type`: ARM64 `BRANCH26` (a call when the word is `bl`), `PAGE21`, `PAGEOFF12`
  (`add`, or a load/store scaled by its access size, which the one type does not
  say), `GOT_LOAD_PAGE21`/`PAGEOFF12` and `TLVP_LOAD_*` through a synthetic slot,
  `POINTER_TO_GOT`, `UNSIGNED`, and an arm64e `AUTHENTICATED_POINTER` written as its
  plain target; x86-64 `GOT_LOAD`, `GOT` and `TLV` through a slot and
  `SIGNED_{1,2,4}`, the rest by their generic kinds. An `ARM64_RELOC_ADDEND` is the
  addend of the relocation it precedes. `reloc_object.rs (macho_target)` adjusts the
  target value. A section target (`r_extern = 0`) keeps the referent's pre-link
  address in the field, so the value is the section's move, plus for a
  PC-relative field the place's pre-link address. A `SUBTRACTOR` pair is the minuend
  less the subtrahend. An x86-64 `SIGNED_k` field already holds the addend less
  `k`, which `object` subtracts again, so `k` is added back. The rebased view
  writes the laid-out `addr` into each `section_64` and moves each `N_SECT`
  symbol's `n_value` with its section (`relocrebase.rs (patch_macho)`). The analyzer tier's
  rebased view (`relocrebase.rs (rebased_view)`) writes the same reduced
  sizes into its section headers, so no pass scans the declared extent. COMMON symbols instead reserve their
  full size (ELF `st_size`, COFF symbol value), using the ELF alignment carried
  by `st_value` or a 16-byte synthetic alignment for COFF, in a separate synthetic
  area after the maximum undefined-symbol slot extent. Their addresses are
  reused for repeated references, remain disjoint from extern slots, and do not
  move ordinary undefined targets. The analyzer’s rebased view retains the COMMON
  extent as a separate loaded-address range. The project loader includes this
  extent in its program-object ranges, so generated headers declare referenced
  COMMON globals; unresolved external slots remain excluded. Invalid alignment, address overflow or an
  allocation beyond the object's address width leaves the relocation unresolved,
  rather than assigning overlapping storage. This loader correctness repair in
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/commonalloc.rs (CommonAllocator)`
  needs no inference option; it retains the existing treatment of unbacked
  synthetic storage. An adjacent SPARC `sethi`/`jmpl` pair
  carrying `HI22`/`LO10` relocations to the same symbol with zero addends also
  identifies that symbol as code, even when the ELF marks it `STT_NOTYPE`.
  The jump must use the register written by `sethi` and discard the link or
  write `%o7`; an ordinary address materialization or data load does not qualify.
  This lets existing tail-call recovery resolve a named external destination
  and preserve its delay-slot arguments. The relocation encoder handles generic
  absolute, relative, PLT-relative, and image-offset fields at 8/16/32/64 bits in
  the object's byte order (an s390x `*DBL` field, `PC32DBL`/`PLT32DBL` and their
  16-bit forms, holds `(S + A - P) >> 1` and rejects an odd value), plus the instruction fields and ABI formulas for ARM
  `CALL`/`JUMP24`/Thumb branches/`REL32`/`PREL31`, Xtensa `SLOT0_OP` on
  little-endian cores (the operand of the relocated instruction by its opcode:
  `L32R`'s negative literal word offset from `(P + 3) & !3`, `CALLn`'s word
  offset from `(P & !3) + 4`, and the `J`, `BRI12`, `BRI8`/`RRI8`, `LOOP` and
  narrow `beqz.n`/`bnez.n` byte offsets from `P + 4`; `ASM_EXPAND`,
  `ASM_SIMPLIFY` and the `DIFF*` relaxation records are no-ops; `R_XTENSA_32` is
  partial-inplace, so the word it patches keeps the part of the addend GNU `as`
  left there, such as a jump-table row's case offset, and receives `S + A` plus
  that word), OpenRISC (`EM_OPENRISC`,
  told apart by `e_machine`) `INSN_REL_26`/`PLT26` jumps and calls, the
  `HI_16_IN_INSN`/`AHI16`/`LO_16_IN_INSN` halves, the split `SLO16` store
  immediate and the `32`/`32_PCREL` words, C-SKY `bsr32`
  (`PCREL_IMM26BY2`: `(S + A - P) >> 1` in the low 26 bits, the instruction's
  two halfwords high first), the A32 and Thumb-2
  `MOVW`/`MOVT` pairs (`MOVW_ABS_NC`/`MOVT_ABS` and the `PREL` forms, 43..50:
  the low half of `(S + A) | T` or the high half of `S + A`, less `P` for
  `PREL`, with `A` the REL addend already in the imm16; sweep re-run), AArch64 branch/page/low-12
  forms, PowerPC `REL24`/`PLTREL24`/`LOCAL24PC`/`ADDR24` calls (32- and 64-bit;
  a `-fPIC` object's `PLTREL24` addend locates the caller's `.got2` for the
  linker's call stub and is not added to the target), the 14-bit conditional
  branches, the absolute (`ADDR16*`, including the 64-bit `DS`, `HIGHER` and
  `HIGHEST` forms), PC-relative (`REL16*`) and TOC-relative halves, and the
  `REL32`/`REL64`/`UADDR*` data words, and 32-bit SPARC `WDISP30`/`WPLT30`/
  `HI22`/`LO10`/`PC22`/`PC10`/`DISP32` forms. A PowerPC64 ELFv1 object names each
  function by its `.opd` descriptor: the function symbol is registered at the
  code the descriptor's `R_PPC64_ADDR64` points at, a branch relocated against a
  descriptor's symbol, or against `.opd` plus a descriptor's offset (a call to a
  `static` function), reaches that code, and the descriptors (with their TOC)
  are the loader's ELFv1 descriptors, as a linked image's are. The TOC base is
  `.toc + 0x8000`; an object with no `.toc` (medium-model code that reaches its
  data through `@toc@ha`/`@toc@l` halves) still has the one the linker's `.got`
  would give it, 256-aligned after the other sections, plus `0x8000`. An
  undefined `.TOC.` resolves to that base. AArch64 also covers `ADR_PREL_LO21`,
  `LD_PREL_LO19`, `CONDBR19`, `TSTBR14` and `MOVW_UABS_G0..G3` (the checked
  groups range-checked). RISC-V covers `HI20`/`LO12_I`/`LO12_S`,
  `PCREL_HI20`/`PCREL_LO12_I`/`PCREL_LO12_S`, the 8-byte `CALL`/`CALL_PLT`
  `auipc`+`jalr` pair, `BRANCH`, `JAL`, the two compressed branches, the
  `ADD`/`SUB`/`SET` data families and `32_PCREL`; `RELAX` and `ALIGN` are no-ops,
  since the layout keeps the assembler's bytes. A `PCREL_LO12` names the label of
  its `auipc` rather than the target, so each section's `PCREL_HI20` values are
  kept by place and the low half takes the low twelve bits of that value.
  MIPS relocations go through
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsreloc.rs (Gp)`. An o32
  or N32 REL object keeps each addend in the field it patches, so a `HI16`, or a
  `GOT16` against a local symbol, takes the low half of its addend from the next
  `LO16` against the same target, as the GNU linker pairs them; an N32/N64 RELA
  object states its addends. Either way, consecutive records at one offset form
  one expression, as the GNU linker chains them regardless of ABI or record
  form: each operation's result is the next one's addend, a REL record's field
  is read once for the first operation, and only the last operation writes.
  `%hi(%neg(%gp_rel(f)))` is `GPREL16`, `SUB`, `HI16`, which an N32 object spells
  as one record per operation at the same offset; an N64 record packs up to
  three operations, its second using the `r_ssym` special symbol (zero, `$gp`,
  the input `$gp` or the place), and its chain continues into the next record
  at that offset until an `R_MIPS_NONE`. A REL record that is not followed by
  another at its offset therefore rereads whatever earlier expressions wrote
  there. Each operation computes what the GNU linker does, including a 32-bit
  result truncated before a later 64-bit one. PC32 always keeps the low 32 bits
  of `symbol + addend - place`, including when an earlier R32 result was
  zero-extended; signed overflow does not reject that displacement. Range checks
  on other operations apply only to the final value. An expression with an
  operation that cannot be applied writes nothing and reports each of its
  records; a packed record whose operations resume after a `NONE` is rejected
  on its own, ending the expression before it without disturbing it. A
  GP-relative value against a local symbol, and every `GPREL32`,
  adds back the input `$gp` that a partial link recorded in `.reginfo` or an
  `ODK_REGINFO` entry of `.MIPS.options`: absent, it is 0; malformed or
  conflicting, the expressions that need it fail as unresolved. Neither `$gp` nor a GOT exists before link, so the layout makes
  what the linker would: a GOT after the object's other sections, with one entry
  per symbol and addend a `CALL16`/`GOT16`/`GOT_DISP`/`CALL_HI16`-style
  relocation names and one per 64 KiB page a local `GOT16` or a `GOT_PAGE`
  reaches (sized from the relocations before any is applied), then the
  small-data sections (`.sdata`, `.sbss`, `.lit4`, `.lit8`, `.srdata`), and `_gp`
  `0x7ff0` past the GOT's start. A global definition of `_gp` in the object is
  overridden, as the default linker script's assignment overrides any input
  definition: relocations against `_gp` resolve to the layout's. A local `_gp`
  is not the linker's symbol and keeps the object's own value. `_gp_disp`
  resolves to `_gp` less the place (the PIC prologue adds `$t9`, the function's
  entry) and a global `_gp` or an undefined `__gnu_local_gp` to `_gp`. The GOT's entries hold what the relocations put in
  them and nothing writes them, so the loader reports its range foldable
  (`dynreloc_const`, beside the MSVC FP constants). The exception is the entry
  of an undefined weak symbol, which the run-time loader fills with the
  symbol's address, or 0 when nothing defines it: each such symbol gets its own
  entry holding 0, reported as an import slot outside the foldable range and,
  when a call reaches it, named after the symbol as an Import Address Table
  slot is, so `if (f) f(x);` keeps its test. A `GOT_PAGE` against the symbol
  reaches that same entry and its `GOT_OFST` is the addend alone, the decay GNU
  ld applies to a symbol that does not bind locally. A direct call or address
  relocation against the symbol still resolves to its synthetic extern, the
  address the function is entered at. Otherwise
  `lw $t9, %call16(f)($gp); jalr $t9` decompiles to a call of `f` wherever `$t9`
  is seeded with the entry. `R_MIPS_JALR`, a hint naming the function a `jalr`
  calls, is not applied; microMIPS, MIPS16, R6 PC-relative and TLS relocations
  are reported unsupported. `CALL16` marks its symbol as a code extern, so the
  call renders by name. A relocation that addresses its symbol's GOT slot
  (x86-64 `GOTPCREL`/`GOTPCRELX`/`REX_GOTPCRELX`, AArch64 `ADR_GOT_PAGE`/
  `LD64_GOT_LO12_NC`, RISC-V `GOT_HI20`, ARM `GOT_PREL`) gets one: a pre-link
  object has no GOT, so the layout reserves a synthetic one after the sections,
  one pointer-sized slot per target holding the target's address, and encodes
  the field against that slot. The slots are read-only and reported with the
  `dynrelocs` constant ranges, so a load through one folds to the target and
  `mov rax, [rip+sym@GOTPCREL]` reads as `&sym`. This is the linker's own
  GOTPCRELX relaxation reached by folding rather than by rewriting `mov` into
  `lea` in the image, as IDA does. An entry that cannot be encoded is left
  untouched and classified by reason (unsupported, unresolved target, missing
  TOC, section bounds, required veneer, alignment, range, or invalid encoding).
  The loader reports exact failure totals in at most eight groups with three
  samples per group, once per public load, so machine-readable output remains
  valid and stderr stays bounded. The
  result feeds back into `ObjectLoadImage` as the same segments/sections/funcsyms
  triple the linked path produces. The loader also retains the original section
  index, section name, section-relative offset, symbol binding, and
  defined/undefined provenance beside each synthetic VMA. Front-ends expose that
  coordinate as `.section+0xOFFSET` or `SECTION_INDEX:0xOFFSET`; a bare numeric
  selector first means a mapped synthetic VMA, then falls back to a raw function
  offset only when exactly one definition matches. Name and raw-offset collisions
  report every candidate instead of taking symbol-table order, and only a symbol
  marked undefined is classified as external. Linked ELF inputs retain the
  symbol-table definition addresses separately from resolved import-stub
  addresses, using ELFv1 code entries rather than descriptor addresses and
  folding the ARM Thumb state bit. These addresses follow loader VMA shifts.
  A name matching one executable definition and only import stubs selects the
  definition in both selector resolution and canonical name lookup; both entries
  remain in the inventory. Multiple executable definitions or unclassified
  executable competitors remain ambiguous, and explicit address selection
  remains literal. A load of any format, linked or relocatable, still reports
  one name per address (the first in symbol-table, import-stub, `.dynsym`
  order, the one the symbol table installs for call sites: on Mach-O the first
  `nlist` entry, locals ahead of externals as the linker writes them, on a PE
  the first COFF function symbol, and an ELF `.localalias` (gcc's local name for a recursive weak function) only when no other name holds its address; a PowerPC64 ELFv1 image keeps every name, as
  before), but no longer discards the other distinct names there: they
  become lookup-only aliases
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (ObjectLoadImage::func_symbol_aliases)`,
  raw addresses with any Thumb bit), which the console appends to the
  canonical entry at the normalized address. So a local veneer name, a
  `.localalias` or a strong symbol ahead of its weak alias no longer hides the
  name after it, and an exported name that also labels a PLT stub selects the
  definition by the rule above instead of the stub. An alias never becomes the
  reported name, so `unlace functions` and whole-binary output keep the name
  its callers print. Nor does it outbid a function's own name: when that rule
  does not settle a name, the candidates it reaches only through a loader alias
  are dropped before the remaining tie-breaks, so a static `shared` still wins
  over another function's same-address alias `shared` and a name that selected
  one function keeps selecting it. An alias whose address no entry holds yet
  (discovery has not named it) is still a candidate there, so a lookup sees the
  same candidates with or without discovery. Mach-O and PE kept only the first
  name until GH #1357, so a second `nlist` label at one entry (`_audit_export_b`
  beside `_audit_export_a`, two local labels, a function `ld64` folded into an
  identical one) or a MinGW pair (`_fpreset`/`fpreset`) did not select its own
  function. A Mach-O export is also reported in its C spelling (`audit_export_a`)
  by the export stream; at an entry the symbol table named, that is the same name
  again, and lookup already retries a Mach-O name with its `_`, so it is not kept
  as an alias (two exports at an entry only the export stream names, as in a
  kext's `__TEXT_EXEC`, are two names and both are kept). That retry narrows
  its candidates by the decorated spelling, so `audit_shared` selects the
  function named `_audit_shared` over another one's `_audit_shared` alias, as
  `_audit_shared` itself does. Loaders that publish no section
  records, including the XML corpus loader, prove a numeric VMA by probing one
  byte from the load image instead. Which sections are memory-resident
  is the one question that stays per-format — ELF's `SHF_ALLOC` bit and COFF's
  `Characteristics` content bits minus the link-time-only sections (`.drectve`,
  `LNK_REMOVE`, the discardable `.debug$S`/`.debug$T`) — and it is asked through
  `ObjectFormat::is_alloc_section`, alongside `ObjectFormat::relocatable_layout`,
  which decides whether a given file needs this path at all.
  A REL-style relocation table (COFF, 32-bit ELF) stores its addend in the field
  being patched rather than in the entry, so the in-place value is read back and
  added; a RELA entry carries the whole addend and reads back zero.
  ARM function symbols additionally retain the ABI state bit while branch
  relocations are applied. `R_ARM_CALL` and `R_ARM_THM_CALL` convert `BL` to
  `BLX` (or back) when a typed target crosses the ARM/Thumb boundary. A
  cross-state jump cannot make that transition in place, so it is left
  untouched and reported as requiring a linker veneer instead of being encoded
  as a branch in the wrong instruction set. Untyped and undefined targets do
  not infer state from their synthetic slot address. AArch64 branch, page, and
  low-12 relocations preserve the instruction's opcode/register fields, and
  read and write the instruction little-endian in a big-endian object too
  (A64 code is little-endian in every image; only data follows `EI_DATA`), while
  PowerPC64 `REL24` and TOC-family relocations preserve big-endian instruction
  layout and DS-form low bits. SPARC `WDISP30` and `WPLT30` rewrite the 30-bit
  word displacement of a `call`, computing `S + A - P` modulo 2³² so a call
  can cross the signed-address boundary or wrap around address zero;
  `HI22` writes bits 31..10 of `S + A` into a
  `sethi` and `LO10` the low ten bits into a format-3 immediate, leaving the
  upper `simm13` bits as the GNU linker does; `PC22`/`PC10` are the same two
  fields over `S + A - P`, and `DISP32` is the 32-bit PC-relative data word.
  The split forms truncate rather than range-check, and reject a REL-style
  implicit addend, which cannot be reassembled from one half. SPARC64 (V9,
  unlace#677) takes the same forms plus the medium-low 44-bit triple (`H44`
  into a `sethi`, `M44` bits 21..12 and `L44` bits 11..0 into simm13), the
  medium-any `HH22`/`HM10`/`LM22` halves, `DISP64`, and the branch
  displacements `WDISP22` (`Bicc`/`FBfcc`), `WDISP19` (`BPcc`/`FBPfcc`) and
  `WDISP16` (`BPr`, split d16hi/d16lo), range-checked; a `WDISP30` call whose
  ends do not fit 32 bits is range-checked as a signed 32-bit displacement.
  GOT/TLS forms that need linker-built tables remain unsupported. LoongArch
  (unlace#677) covers the `PCALA_HI20`/`PCALA_LO12` pair (`pcalau12i` takes the
  page delta of `S + A + 0x800`, so the signed low twelve bits land on the
  target), the 8-byte `CALL36` `pcaddu18i`+`jirl` pair, and the `B26`, `B21`
  and `B16` branch displacements, each encoding-checked; `RELAX` and `ALIGN`
  are no-ops, since the layout keeps the assembler's bytes. The `object`
  crate's generic `LoongArchBranch` reading of `B16`/`B21`/`B26` (a plain
  integer field) is never used. Lanai (`EM_LANAI`, unlace#677), for which the
  object reader has no architecture, is told apart by `e_machine`
  (`reloc_apply::classify_elf`): `R_LANAI_25` writes the absolute word address
  of a `bcc` into bits 24..2, `R_LANAI_21` the absolute 21-bit address of an
  SLS/SLI access into bits 22..18 and 15..0, `HI16`/`LO16` the halves of
  `S + A` into an RI immediate, and `R_LANAI_32` a big-endian data word; the
  absolute fields are range-checked. CUDA cubins (`EM_CUDA`) are told apart
  the same way:
  - `R_CUDA_ABS32_LO_32`/`HI_32` write the low or high word of `S + A` into
    bits 32..63 of the 128-bit SASS word (the 32-bit immediate);
  - `R_CUDA_ABS47_34` writes `(S + A) >> 2` into bits 34..80 (the `CALL.ABS` target);
  - `R_CUDA_64` is a data doubleword;
  - the yield and unused-clear relocations are no-ops;
  - the constant-bank `CONST_FIELD*` offsets stay unsupported. Hexagon (unlace#677, little-endian
  RELA) covers the PC-relative branches `B22`/`B15`/`B13`/`B9`/`B7_PCREL`
  (`(S + A - P) >> 2` dealt into each form's ABI bit mask, range-checked),
  their extended `_X` forms (the low six bits of `S + A - P`), the `immext`
  payloads `B32_PCREL_X` and `32_6_X` (bits 31..6 into mask `0x0fff3fff`), and
  the low six bits of `16_X`, `11_X`, `10_X` and `6_X` for the instruction
  classes measured against `ld.lld` (by top byte, or bits 25..20 of a duplex
  for `6_X`), ORed in as the linker does. Other classes and `8_X`, `12_X`,
  `9_X`, `7_X` are reported unsupported and leave the field untouched.
  AVR (unlace#757, little-endian 16-bit words) covers `13_PCREL` (`rjmp`/
  `rcall`) and `7_PCREL` (`brbs`/`brbc`), the word displacement from the next
  instruction (an `rjmp`/`rcall` whose ends both lie in the first 8 KiB wraps at
  4 KiW, as a device with at most 8 KiB of flash does and the 16-bit-PC avr8
  language's `rel12addr` models, so an -O0 object's libcalls past 4 KiB are
  reached; unlace#976); the nine `LDI` forms (`LO8`/`HI8`/`HH8` of `S + A`, of its
  negation, or of the word address `(S + A) >> 1`) into `ldi`'s split K; `CALL`
  (the 22-bit word address of `call`/`jmp`); and `16_PM`. AMDGPU (`EM_AMDGPU`,
  no object architecture, told apart by `e_machine`) covers the 32-bit literal
  halves `REL32_LO`/`REL32_HI` (`S + A - P`, the `s_getpc_b64` pair of every
  call and global) and `ABS32_LO`/`ABS32_HI`, and the `ABS32`, `REL32`, `ABS64`
  and `REL64` data words; the GOT forms stay unsupported. A TI C2000 object (`EM_TI_C2000`) counts symbol values, symbol sizes and `r_offset` in 16-bit words, while its section sizes and bytes are in bytes. The layout keeps byte VMAs and scales those three by the address unit (`loader/wordaddr.rs`), so a function's entry, extent and relocation sites land on its bytes. Its relocations (`reloc_apply::classify_c28x`, TI SPRAC71C table 11-5) write word addresses, the target's byte address halved: `R_C28X_ABS22` (5) and the type 20 cl2000 puts on `LCR` calls fill the 6 + 16 bits of an `LCR`/`MOVL #22bit` word pair, and `R_C28X_ABS16`/`ABS32` fill data words, each with its REL addend read from the field. eBPF objects are REL-only and every program ships as one,
  so its three instruction forms are encoded rather than written as plain words:
  `R_BPF_64_64` names the 16-byte `lddw` (a map or global reference) and lands
  `S + A` in the two 32-bit `imm` fields at +4 and +12, the addend read back from
  those same halves, with the opcode, registers and offset untouched;
  `R_BPF_64_32` is the `call` to a BPF subprogram (source register 1, the high
  nibble of the register byte little-endian and the low nibble big-endian) and
  writes `(S + A - P) / 8 - 1`, the displacement in instructions from the next
  instruction, into the `imm` at +4; its addend is the field's own `imm` in
  instructions past the symbol, `(imm + 1) * 8`, which is `0` for LLVM's `-1`
  against a function symbol and the callee's offset when a static callee is
  named by its section symbol; `R_BPF_64_ABS64`, `R_BPF_64_ABS32` and
  `R_BPF_64_NODYLD32` are the data words of `.maps`, `.BTF` and `.BTF.ext`.
  A `call` whose `imm` is a helper id (source register 0) carries no
  relocation; it reaches the `syscall` space, where the pspec
  `<default_symbols>` label at that id names the callee
  (`bpf_map_lookup_elem`), as a Ghidra function created at a labelled address
  does. Only a label outside the default code space names a call this way: a
  code-space label such as ARM's or AArch64's `Reset` at address 0 does not, so
  a call to an unresolved weak function at 0 keeps its `sub_0` name.

  An undefined symbol reached through any branch or call instruction field —
  not only a call-spelled one — is bound to a named extern slot. A tail call is
  spelled as a plain jump relocation (`R_ARM_JUMP24`, `R_AARCH64_JUMP26`, a
  PowerPC64 `REL24` with its link bit clear), and the branch is patched to point
  at the synthetic slot either way; leaving that slot unnamed makes the *calling*
  function undecompilable, because the flow walk follows the branch into memory
  the layout never backed. The call/jump distinction itself is kept where it is
  load-bearing — the ARM `BL`/`BLX` interworking rewrite — and is not what
  decides whether an extern is named.

  Laying the object out synthetically splits the address space in two, and every
  pass in this chapter reads the *other* half: each one re-parses the file through
  its own `object::File`, which reports the **pre-link, section-relative**
  addresses the linker has not yet assigned. Mixing the two in one inventory is
  what produced a phantom `sub_<section-offset>` beside every real function, a
  single DWARF function at address 0, and string literals that never attached to
  the loaded image at all. `relocrebase` (unlace, always on) closes that by
  rebasing the analyzer tier's **input** rather than each output fact — necessarily
  so, because a fact is a bare address by the time it reaches `AnalysisOutput`, and
  in a relocatable object every section sits at address 0, which makes `.text`+0x20
  and `.rodata`+0x20 the same number. Worse, the fields that matter are not offsets
  at all until their relocation is applied: an unrelocated `.eh_frame`
  `initial_location` reads back as its own section offset, and an unrelocated
  `DW_AT_low_pc` reads 0 for every subprogram (as does every `DW_FORM_strp`, so the
  whole object's DWARF collapses onto one function named after whatever string sits
  at `.debug_str`+0).
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/relocrebase.rs (rebased_view)`
  therefore re-presents the object to the tier: each laid-out section carries the
  loader's own relocated bytes and its load VMA (ELF `sh_addr`, COFF
  `VirtualAddress`); each section the layout skipped — every `.debug_*` table — has
  its relocations applied here, resolving a target in a laid-out section to that
  section's load VMA and a debug-to-debug target to its own section-relative offset,
  which is what a single-object link leaves in place; and each ELF symbol defined in
  a laid-out section has its `st_value` shifted by **its own section's** delta,
  since the layout is non-contiguous and there is no single global offset (a COFF
  symbol needs no shift — it is reported as `VirtualAddress + value`, so the section
  write already moved it). A debug section stored compressed (ELF
  `SHF_COMPRESSED`, zlib or zstd: `-gz`, and the default of some toolchains) is
  inflated before its relocations are applied, because their offsets address the
  uncompressed bytes; the relocated bytes are appended to the image and the section
  header points at them, uncompressed. Patched in place, the relocations corrupted
  the compressed stream and such a `.o` lost all of its DWARF (`int apply(int k,int
  a,int b)` printed as `unsigned long apply(unsigned int a0,…)`). Each patched field is written in the object's own byte
  order (ELF `EI_DATA`), the implicit addends of a REL table read in it, so a
  big-endian object (PowerPC, MIPS, SPARC, ARM big-endian) is rebased as a
  little-endian one is; it used to keep the pre-link view, so `unlace functions`
  listed each of its functions twice (`0x0 scale` beside `0x400000 scale`) and a
  MIPS PIC function's `$t9` was seeded at its section offset rather than its
  entry, so its `addu gp,gp,t9` never resolved and every call and global through
  the GOT stayed a load from an unknown `t9`. Over 959 relocatable objects the 441
  whose output changes are all big-endian: the `t9` variables left in MIPS PIC
  functions drop from 3,352 to 25, string literals printed rise from 6,766 to
  18,169, and no function is added or lost. Every pass then produces an
  already-rebased fact with no source change of its own.
  A field with no relocation still yields an address in no laid-out section, so
  `unlace_relocrebase (retain_in_image)` **drops** exactly those rather than letting a
  pre-link address through — that is the phantom class. The single exception is a
  no-return fact, which the commit resolves by name when its address does not
  resolve (an undefined `exit` in a `.o` has never had one); it is kept with its
  address zeroed. The Listing/xref tier takes the other answer and declines outright
  for a synthetically laid-out object (§1.6): it exists to find functions an image
  has no symbol for, and a pre-link object always carries the symbol table the
  linker is about to consume.

  Binding an undefined symbol to a synthetic slot resolves the *reference* and
  loses the *value*, and for one class of symbol the value was never elsewhere to
  begin with: MSVC never encodes a floating-point literal into the instruction
  stream — x87 and SSE both load one from memory — so the compiler emits each
  literal as a COMDAT whose **name spells it**. `__real@8@3ffec90fdaa22168c000`
  is π/4. COMDAT folding then keeps the definition in exactly one translation
  unit, so in every other object that symbol is undefined: no section, no bytes,
  a slot with nothing behind it, and an expression written entirely in opaque
  addresses (`(… * dat_402020 + dat_402040) * dat_400ae0`). `msvcfpconst` (unlace,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/msvcfpconst.rs (plan)`, always on) reads
  the value back out of the name. Three spellings are accepted:
  `__real@<size>@<20 hex>`, an x87 80-bit extended datum (a 16-bit
  sign/exponent field then a 64-bit mantissa carrying its **explicit** integer
  bit) plus the storage width the program loads it at — `4` for `float`, `8` for
  `double`; and the two bare-bits forms `__real@<16 hex>` (IEEE double) and
  `__real@<8 hex>` (IEEE float, which is what MSVC has emitted for a `float`
  literal since VS2005 — the 20-hex form is the VC6-era one). The decode is
  exact rather than approximate: the source constant was a `float` or a `double`
  before the assembler widened it, so at most 53 of the mantissa's 64 bits are
  set and the `f64` image is lossless. Every x87 encoding class with no faithful
  `f64` image is **refused** rather than approximated — an Inf/NaN exponent, a
  denormal or pseudo-denormal (whose true scale is one binade away from the
  normalized formula), an unnormal, and any value outside `f64` or, at `@4@`,
  outside `float` — as is every other mangling, `__xmm@`/`__ymm@` included: a
  wrong 16-byte datum is worse than an honest `dat_<addr>`.

  As with `dynrelocs` below, decoding is only half of it. The undefined half
  gets the decoded bytes materialised as a segment at its extern slot, which is
  what makes the address readable at all; but the *defined* half needs nothing
  materialised and still renders `dat_<addr>`, because folding a read-only global
  is gated program-wide by `option readonly` (default off). Both halves are
  therefore reported as `ObjectLoadImage::dynreloc_const_ranges` — the same
  narrow "constant by construction, not by policy" exception list `dynrelocs`
  fills on the linked path, carried to `Architecture::dynreloc_const` and folded
  by `ActionVarnodeProps` with global propagation still off (§3.4). Listing only
  one half would be worse than listing neither: one operand of an expression
  would come out a literal and the operand beside it stay opaque. A defined
  COMDAT's mapped bytes are cross-checked against its own name before its range
  is admitted, which is also what keeps the relocatable-object fidelity hazard
  away from this path — a read-only section in a `.o` holds *pre*-relocation
  bytes, but a `__real@` COMDAT carries no relocation, and a disagreement between
  the bytes and the name drops the range with a warning rather than folding it.
- **Mach-O read-only sections** — a Mach-O section carries no write bit of its
  own, so `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho.rs (section_bits)`
  derives READONLY from the neutral section kind `object` assigns, which knows
  `__TEXT,__cstring` by name and nothing else. Every other literal section
  (`__TEXT,__oslogstring`, the kernel's `__TEXT,__os_log`, `__objc_methname`)
  read as unknown, so it was not read-only and a reference to one of its strings
  printed as the string's symbol (`_os_log_impl(...,s_10006c0cf,...)`) even
  though `unlace strings` found the text. Two facts the image states settle it. A
  section of type `S_CSTRING_LITERALS` is a pool of coalesced literals and is
  `DATA | READONLY` like `__cstring`. And a loaded section lying wholly inside a
  segment whose initial protection is readable but not writable (`__TEXT`, never
  `__DATA_CONST`, which dyld writes before protecting it) is READONLY
  (`macho.rs (readonly_segments)`, `macho.rs (in_readonly_segment)`, applied by the
  object load image to every non-NOLOAD section); this covers the kernel's
  `__os_log`, an `S_REGULAR` section. Strings in either now print as literals.
- **Mach-O fat/arm64e** — a universal binary is peeled to one slice's bytes
  before anything else parses it, because `object::File::parse` has no fat arm
  and rejects the whole file with "Unsupported file format"
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/macho_fat.rs (select_fat_slice)`;
  preference `--slice`/`--target`, else x86-64 → arm64 → first), so the loader,
  every pass, and the deferred-Listing stash all see the same thin slice. The
  peel is one policy with two readers: the engine dispatch, and the canonical
  image read every surface that parses the file for itself goes through
  (`macho_fat (peel_fat_image)` from `elf_shdr (read_image)`, the same point the
  ELF and PE header repairs above are applied). Reading the file directly instead
  is what made `strings`, `xrefs` and the `functions --summary`/`--reachable-from`
  call graph exit 1 on a universal image whose `functions` inventory loaded fine,
  and what made `--slice` inert on those surfaces — it steers both readers, so a
  slice named on the command line selects the same image the inventory reports.
  An
  arm64e slice selects the Apple-Silicon pointer-auth SLEIGH spec instead of
  generic v8A unless the `macho-arm64e` env gate is off
  (`crates/unlace-middle/src/p0_knowledge/macho_arm64e.rs (MACHO_ARM64E_ENV)`).
  Modern Mach-O pointer slots are chained-fixup entries, not pointers;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho/chained.rs (ChainedFixups)`
  parses `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS` into a VMA→resolved-pointer overlay. It
  decodes the generic 64-bit formats and the arm64e family (`ARM64E`,
  `ARM64E_USERLAND`, `ARM64E_USERLAND24`). An arm64e authenticated rebase stores
  a 32-bit offset from the image base plus its signing context (key, address
  diversity, 16-bit diversifier). The slot reads as `imagebase + offset`, and the
  context is kept beside it (`ChainedFixups::auth`, which also records an
  authenticated bind's context). A bind entry names an import whose address is
  unknown statically, so it is absent from the pointer overlay — a consumer
  misses and falls back rather than reading a wrong address — but its ordinal is
  resolved through the blob's imports table to the symbol it names
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho/chained.rs (bind)`),
  which is what lets a `__objc_classrefs` slot bound to `_OBJC_CLASS_$_UIView`
  be named without an address. The bind also keeps its addend: the import
  record's (`DYLD_CHAINED_IMPORT_ADDEND*`) plus the entry's own (eight bits in
  `PTR_64`, a signed 19 bits in a plain arm64e bind; an authenticated bind spends
  those bits on its signing context and has none). A C++ RTTI record points at
  `vtable for __si_class_type_info + 16` this way, so a slot whose addend is not
  zero holds an address inside the import, not the import itself.
  A bind whose ordinal is out of range or whose name cannot be read is still
  kept, unnamed. The loader writes the resolved rebase values into the image it
  maps, and a zero into each bind slot (`dynrelocs`, §1.3). The header is the
  image's own bytes, so the walk is bounded by the file rather than by its
  counts: a `seg_count` stops at the end of the blob, every address computation
  wraps instead of overflowing, all of an image's chains share one hop budget of
  the file's length, and the walk reads at most one page start per 2-byte entry
  of the blob (`chained.rs (walk_segment)`). An honest image decodes each slot
  once and reads each page start once, so neither bound changes what it yields;
  thousands of segments sharing one 65535-entry start table would otherwise read
  it once per segment.
  An image that predates chained fixups keeps its
  binds as the `LC_DYLD_INFO` opcode program instead, and the slot itself holds
  zero in the file;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho/dyldinfo.rs (resolve_dyld_info_binds)`
  replays that program (segment+offset, symbol, bind, advance; weak binds
  included, lazy and arm64e threaded binds not) to the same `slot → import name`
  answer. The resolver also records which segments the
  linker flagged `SG_READ_ONLY`, the Mach-O statement that dyld maps the segment
  read-only once its fixups are in (`__DATA_CONST`); `dynrelocs` (§1.3) reads
  it as the `PT_GNU_RELRO` of a Mach-O.
- **Apple kernelcaches** (unlace, `kernelcache`, default `auto`, env-bridged) —
  an iOS kernelcache ships as an IMG4 or bare IM4P DER container around an
  LZFSE or `complzss` payload, and decodes to an `MH_FILESET` kernel
  collection: one Mach-O header per `LC_FILESET_ENTRY` (the kernel and every
  kext), all sharing one file, one `__LINKEDIT` and one
  `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS` table. Before the fat peel, both readers above run
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache.rs (peel)`. It
  walks the DER only as deep as the IM4P (type, description, payload, an
  optional KBAG, an optional compression record with the decoded size), refuses
  a payload that carries a KBAG because it is encrypted, and decodes the
  payload by its magic: LZFSE (`bvx2` FSE blocks, `bvxn` LZVN blocks, `bvx-`
  stored blocks; v1 `bvx1` headers are refused) or `complzss` (Okumura LZSS,
  checked against the header's size and Adler-32). A decoded size different
  from the IM4P's record is an error, not a truncation. The record also bounds
  the decode: output stops, with an error, as soon as it would pass the
  declared size. Whatever the record says, output also stops at 64 times the
  payload (at least 16 MiB) and never past 1 GiB, so a small payload cannot
  claim a gigabyte. An FSE bit stream may preload bytes from
  before its payload, as the reference encoder's does, but consuming them is
  a truncation error rather than a read of zeros. Symbols a block claims beyond
  its raw size (a valid block exceeds it only by padding literals and literal-only
  triples, at most 50 per block in two real kernelcache streams) are charged
  to the input's length, so all-header blocks that decode to nothing stop
  quickly. Then, for an
  `MH_FILESET`, every rebase of the collection's fixup table is written into
  its slot — the kernel formats `DYLD_CHAINED_PTR_64_KERNEL_CACHE`,
  `ARM64E_KERNEL`, `ARM64E_FIRMWARE` and `X86_64_KERNEL_CACHE` are decoded in the same
  `chained.rs` as the userland ones, targets are offsets from the collection
  base, and pointer-authentication bits are dropped. The kernel-cache formats
  name the collection a target lies in by its `cacheLevel`, xnu's index of the
  boot (0), System/pageable (1) and Auxiliary (3) collections
  (`pexpert/gen/kcformat.c`). Only targets at the collection's own level can be
  rebased from this file's base. Neither the header nor the chains state that
  level (xnu learns it from whoever loads the collection), so it is read from
  the collections the `__PRELINK_INFO` plist links: no `_BootKCID` is the boot
  collection (0), `_PageableKCID` an Auxiliary one (3), and `_BootKCID` alone is
  a System collection or an Auxiliary one built without a System collection,
  told apart by whichever of levels 1 and 3 its chains name (neither can point
  into the other's level). With no plist, or chains naming both, the level is
  unknown and no kernel-collection target is written; a target at another
  level is kept aside with its level and offset, and counted as damage of the
  walk, because only the file of that collection holds its base
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho/chained.rs (resolve_kernel_cache_levels)`).
  Those targets are what a macOS System or Auxiliary collection
  (`SystemKernelExtensions.kc`, `AuxiliaryKernelExtensions.kc`) uses for every
  pointer into the kernel: a kext's call slots, the vtables and metaclass
  pointers its classes inherit. `kernelcache-boot` (unlace, default `auto`,
  env-bridged through `UNLACE_KERNELCACHE_BOOT`) resolves them from the other
  file. The plist names each linked collection by UUID, `_BootKCID` for level 0
  and `_PageableKCID` for level 1, as a 16-byte base64 `<data>` value. `auto`
  takes the first 4096 entries the directory of the input lists, in name
  order, keeps the regular files other than the input whose first 16 bytes are an
  `MH_FILESET` header (at most 16), and reads each whole until every wanted
  UUID is found; a path value names one regular file, which may be an IMG4 or
  IM4P container, or a directory searched the same way; `off` reads no other
  file. A candidate is the linked collection only if
  its `LC_UUID` or its own plist's `_PrelinkKCID` equals the wanted UUID, so a
  boot collection from another build is never used: its offsets would land on
  other functions. For a match, each slot gets the linked file's base (its
  lowest file-backed segment address, the rule the own level uses) plus the
  offset, pointer-authentication bits dropped. Then each such address that a
  section symbol of the linked file defines inside an instruction-bearing
  section is named: the kernel entry's symbol tables are read before the
  kexts', each distinct entry header once, under the same work budget as the
  bind below
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/linked.rs (resolve)`).
  The names reach the loaded entry as symbols of its own: its symbol table is
  copied to the end of the file with one `N_ABS | N_EXT` symbol per named
  address after it, the names follow, and the entry's `LC_SYMTAB` is pointed at
  the copy, its string table keeping its offset and growing to reach the new
  names
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset.rs (append_bound_symbols)`).
  That is the form the collection bind below leaves an import in. The builder
  of a collection turns each bind of a kext's symbol-pointer sections (`__got`,
  `__auth_got`) and of `__auth_ptr` into a rebase, so after the peel the value
  of such a slot is the only record of what it is bound to: the import walk
  makes each 8-byte slot of those sections that holds a bound import's address,
  and that the indirect-symbol table did not name, an import slot of that
  function
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/macho_stubs.rs (push_kext_bound_slots)`),
  and a call through it prints the kernel function's name. A data target (a
  vtable, a metaclass object) is rebased and not named. The load note states,
  per level, how many pointers were rebased from which file and how many
  functions were named, or how many stay unresolved and why (the option is off,
  the plist carries no UUID for the level, no file with that UUID was found).
  An unresolved slot keeps its packed word. A collection with no target at
  another level reads no other file, so every other input is unaffected.
  Then one entry is cut out as a thin Mach-O by copying
  its header and load commands to file offset 0. Nothing else moves: every
  entry's file offsets are already absolute in the collection, so its
  segments, symbol table and indirect-symbol table read correctly in place. The
  copy is refused if any of the entry's file-backed segments starts inside the
  header it would overwrite. `auto` takes the `MH_EXECUTE` entry (the kernel);
  any other value names an entry by its bundle id, exactly or by a unique
  case-insensitive dotted suffix (`IOSurface`), a miss lists the
  candidates, and `list` stops the load with every entry id, each followed by
  what the collection's `__PRELINK_INFO,__info` plist says of it (version, load
  address, the `IOClass` of each of its `IOKitPersonalities`;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset/prelink.rs (kexts)`,
  a small XML plist reader that resolves `ID`/`IDREF`). A pre-fileset
  (prelinked) kernelcache is one `MH_EXECUTE` kernel that carries its kexts
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset/prelinked.rs (rebase)`).
  Its pointers are not in a fixup table but threaded through the words
  themselves: `__TEXT,__thread_starts` (iOS 12-14) opens with a word whose bit
  0 picks a 4- or 8-byte hop unit, then lists each chain's offset from the
  image base up to `0xffffffff`. A chain word with bit 62 clear is a rebase:
  authenticated (bit 63) it holds a 32-bit offset from the base, otherwise a
  43-bit sign-extended address with its top byte in bits 43..50, exactly as
  xnu's `rebase_threaded_starts` reads it; bits 51..61 hop to the next word.
  `__TEXT,__chain_starts`, which `ld -static -fixup_chains` writes for SPTM,
  TXM and other static images, holds a pointer format, a count and each
  chain's offset from the base, and its chains are walked by the
  `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS` decoder in `chained.rs (chain_starts_rebases)`.
  Every rebase is written into its slot before anything reads the image, so
  `auto`, which loads the kernel, already sees real pointers (iOS 14.8 A12:
  338,665 pointers, and 37,000 IOKit class and method names where there were
  none). The kexts come in two layouts
  (`fileset/prelinked.rs (entries)`). Up to iOS 11 each is a whole Mach-O in
  `__PRELINK_TEXT` at the plist's `_PrelinkExecutableLoadAddr`, its segments
  spread over the `__PLK_*` and `__PRELINK_DATA` ranges, its file offsets
  relative to its own header and not always consistent; from iOS 12 they are
  merged into the kernel's own segments, `__PRELINK_INFO,__kmod_start` points
  at each one's header, which describes only its `__TEXT_EXEC`, and the plist
  names it by `ModuleIndex` (failing that, `__kmod_info`'s `kmod_info_t` name
  does). Each kext header's segment and section offsets are rewritten to the
  absolute offsets of their addresses, and a merged kext's code sections get
  the instruction flags its stripped header no longer carries. `list` prints
  these entries, and a kext is chosen by the same names as in a fileset
  (`fileset/prelinked.rs (cut)`). On a merged cache the kernel already holds
  every kext, and a kext alone keeps the kernel's non-code segments beside
  its own code, because they hold its data. On an older cache a stripped kext
  has no symbols and untyped `__got` / `__stubs` sections, so each one chosen
  gets a symbol table of the kernel symbols its `__got` slots, stubs and `bl`s
  reach, each absolute at the kernel address in the undefined range, where a
  fileset kext's bound imports sit, plus an indirect-symbol table for those
  sections, which are retyped to non-lazy pointers and 12- (16-, for
  `__auth_stubs`) byte stubs; the import walk then names its stubs and slots
  after the kernel functions they reach. Several entries, or `all`, go through
  the same `merge` as a fileset's, the kernel's `__PRELINK` segments dropped
  so nothing is mapped twice. iOS 11.4.1 A10: `all` loads 197 entries (34,425
  functions, 8.9 s); IOSurface alone loads in 0.5 s with its calls named
  `OSUnserializeXML`, `lck_mtx_lock`, and so on.
  A comma-separated list or `all` loads several entries as one image
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset/merge.rs (merge)`):
  their segment commands are concatenated at their collection addresses (one
  shared `__LINKEDIT` kept), and a symbol table, indirect-symbol table and
  `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` are rebuilt behind the collection. The entries' symbols
  are renumbered into one local / external-defined / undefined order; a
  symbol's section ordinal moves to the merged section list, or, past the 255
  ordinals an `nlist` can name, to the first merged section of the same kind
  (code or data), since only the kind is read from it; and each stub or
  pointer section's `reserved1` moves to its entry's part of the merged
  indirect table. The rebuilt header goes in front of the collection, so every
  file offset moves by the header's page-rounded size; the kernel's
  `LC_UNIXTHREAD`, `LC_UUID` and version commands are kept. The collection's
  `__BRANCH_STUBS` / `__BRANCH_GOTS` segments, where a release cache's
  cross-entry branches land, are added to whatever is loaded, which sends even
  a single entry through this path when they exist. `unlace functions` on the
  whole iOS 16.4.1 collection takes 45 s and 1.5 GB and lists 166,184 entries. A kext calls into the kernel and into the kexts it depends on
  with a direct `bl` that the collection's builder resolved, so the only record
  of the callee's name is the kext's undefined `nlist`; when the chosen entry is
  not the kernel, each undefined symbol that another entry exports from an
  instruction-bearing section is rewritten to `N_ABS | N_EXT` at that address,
  the kernel's definition winning over a kext's and an ambiguity between kexts
  left unbound. Each distinct entry header is read once, however many entries
  name its offset; a segment's sections are read only as far as its own
  `cmdsize` holds them; and because every count and offset comes from the file,
  the walk stops at a work budget proportional to the collection's size (4
  units per byte of commands, sections and name bytes visited, at least one
  million), and the undefined names copied never exceed the file
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset.rs (bind_to_collection)`),
  and the Mach-O import walk names each such symbol of an `MH_KEXT_BUNDLE` as
  an external function
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/macho_stubs.rs (push_kext_bound_imports)`).
  `off` passes the bytes through untouched: an IMG4 is then an unrecognized
  format, and a bare `MH_FILESET` loads as one image with no symbol table. The
  load prints one `[unlace]` note naming the container, codec, chosen entry and
  how many pointers and symbols were bound. Measured on an iOS 16.4.1 A13
  kernelcache (21 MB IMG4, 72 MB decoded, 233 entries, 445,860 fixups), the
  peel costs about 0.15 s per read and `unlace functions` on the kernel takes
  3.7 s and 429 MB.
  The choice is read live from `UNLACE_KERNELCACHE`, and the `unlace` CLI exports
  it from `--option kernelcache` for the whole invocation, with `dyldimage`,
  the other option that chooses which image of a file is read
  (`crates/unlace-cli/src/loadtime.rs (export_image_selection)`).
  Exporting it only around the engine's load left every surface that reads
  the image itself on the default entry: the `xrefs` reference walk then
  decoded the kernel's bytes from a kext's function list and answered
  `count: 0` for a kext function with five callers, while `strings`, `crypto`,
  the `disassemble --as data` provenance and the call graph behind
  `decompile-all` and `decompile-graph` described the kernel. The peel also
  returns the collection's entry map, every entry's segment ranges by bundle
  id, with each distinct header read once, the loaded entry first, within the
  same work budget
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset.rs (fileset_map)`).
  The walk decodes only the loaded entry, so `xrefs` uses the map to say when
  the address it was asked about is in another entry, naming it, or in none:
  for `--to` the rows are only the loaded entry's references to it, and for
  `--from` nothing was decoded there.

(unlace) **Mach-O load tolerance**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/machotolerance.rs`). A segment,
section, symbol table or string table whose file range runs past the end of a
truncated or hand-edited Mach-O used to fail the whole load: `object` checks the
symbol table eagerly in `File::parse`, and the loader reads each segment's file
range when it maps it. `clamp_out_of_file_ranges` clamps each such range to the
bytes the file holds (segment `filesize`, section `size`, `nsyms`, `strsize`) in
a copy of the image, applied at the same two points as the ELF and PE header
repairs, and says so once on stderr. Virtual sizes are untouched, so the rest of
each data segment still reads as zero-filled memory and nothing is invented. A
Mach-O with `LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO[_64]` `cryptid != 0` still loads, but its
encrypted range is App Store ciphertext that decompiles to noise, so the engine
load names it once (`encryption_note`): `Mach-O is encrypted (LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO
cryptid 1): file bytes 0x4000..0x... are ciphertext and decompile to noise;
decrypt the app first`.

(unlace) **dyld shared cache.** A cache file is not an object file: it is a main
file starting `dyld_v1`, sub-caches beside it (`.01`, `.27.dylddata`,
`.44.dyldlinkedit`, ...) and a `.symbols` file, each a header plus a mapping
table that places its bytes at virtual addresses, with thousands of images
spread across them. The loader works on one image and turns it into a thin
Mach-O before anything else parses it, at the same two points the fat peel
uses: `bootstrap_from_object_with_isa` and `elf_shdr (read_image)`, both of
which call
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/dyldcache.rs (read_selected_image)`
when the file opens with the cache magic (`bootstrap_from_file` routes a cache
to the object path before reading it whole). The image is chosen by
`dyldimage` (the `UNLACE_DYLD_IMAGE` bridge, which the CLI's global `--image`
sets, and which the console accepts before any image is loaded, since choosing
the first one is its job). It matches a full install name, then a unique
basename, then a unique basename minus its last extension (`libobjc.A`), and a
one-image cache needs no choice. Several images can share one program: `dyldimage A+B+...` rebuilds `A`
with the segments of the companions `B...` appended (all but their
`__LINKEDIT`), their named symbols (exports and `.symbols` locals) added as
locals with renumbered section ordinals, and the names of their own calls
(their islands and their own stubs, which `own_stubs` makes `xrefs.rs
(collect)` resolve through each companion's indirect table) merged into the
note. A companion's stub and pointer sections are retyped to `S_REGULAR`,
because the merged indirect-symbol table is `A`'s alone. The merged header and
load commands no longer fit before `A`'s first section, so they get pages of
their own and every segment follows them. A Mach-O reader that keeps the last
`__TEXT` it sees would then take a companion's, so the function-starts and
`__unwind_info` readers keep the first. On iOS 16.4.1,
`CoreFoundation+libobjc.A.dylib` loads in 2.6 s and 430 MB, and libobjc's
`class_copyMethodList` decompiles in that program with every call named, as it
does on its own. The cache is read through
file handles, never mapped whole, so the cost follows the image, not the 3 GB
of the cache. Every header field is read only when it lies below the header's
own `mappingOffset`, which is how `dyld_cache_format.h` adds fields. That one
rule picks between the old and new image tables, the plain and the
slide-carrying mapping tables, the unnamed (`.N`) and named sub-cache entries,
and the 32-bit (file-offset keyed) and 64-bit (cache-offset keyed) local-symbol
entries. Each sub-cache and the `.symbols` file must carry the UUID its main
header records.

The rebuild (`dyldcache/extract.rs (DyldCache::extract)`) keeps every
segment at its cache address and lays the segments out page-aligned, `__TEXT`
first at file offset 0, so the rewritten header and load commands sit where the
original ones did. It refuses an image whose commands no longer fit before its
first section. Data pages are copied with their mapping's slide info applied at
slide zero (`dyldcache/slide.rs (SlideInfo::apply)`). v2 chains carry a
`delta_mask` link plus `value_add`, and a page may list several chains in an
extras array. v3 chains carry an 11-bit link at bit 51: plain pointers keep a
51-bit target with a top byte, and authenticated ones keep a 32-bit offset
from `auth_value_add`. v4 chains (32-bit caches) keep the link in the top two
bits of a 32-bit word: a value with no bits above 15 is a small positive
integer, one whose bits 15 to 29 are all set a small negative one
(sign-extended), and anything else is a pointer plus `value_add`. v5 chains
carry a 34-bit runtime offset from `value_add` and the link at bit 52. Each
slot therefore holds its unslid
target; the PAC key and diversity of an auth pointer are dropped, because the
decompiler does not model them. v1 needs no rewrite at slide zero. A 32-bit
cache (`arm64_32` on watchOS) holds 32-bit Mach-O images: a 28-byte header,
`LC_SEGMENT` commands with 32-bit fields and 68-byte sections, 12-byte nlists
and 4-byte pointer slots. The rebuild reads and writes either layout through
one table of field offsets (`extract.rs (Width)`), the local-symbols file's
nlists follow the cache's width, and a stub's `ldr w` is followed like its
`ldr x`. An `arm64_32` Mach-O, thin or rebuilt from a cache, loads as
`AARCH64:LE:32:ilp32` (`loadimage_object.rs (compose_language_id)`). On the
watchOS 10.0.1 cache of a Watch5,1, `libobjc.A.dylib` rebuilds, lists 1,073
functions and decompiles with its cross-image calls named. The cache's images share one `__LINKEDIT`,
so the image gets a private one. It holds the image's nlists, a compact string
table read in spans around the names actually used (the shared pool is tens of
megabytes and an image's names are scattered through it), the indirect-symbol
table, and copies of the export trie, function starts and data-in-code. The
local symbols the cache moved to `.symbols` replace the `<redacted>`
placeholders left in the image's own table, and every indirect-symbol index
and `LC_DYSYMTAB` boundary is renumbered by the difference in count. Without
the `.symbols` file the placeholders stay, nameless, rather than giving
thousands of functions one shared name. On iOS 16.4.1, the local symbols take
CoreFoundation from 7,137 unnamed functions of 11,922 to 764. Linkedit
data the rebuild does not carry (code signature, split-segment info, the rebase
and bind opcodes the cache builder already applied) is zeroed in its command.
On the iOS 16.4.1 arm64e cache (44 sub-caches) and the iOS 14.8 arm64 cache
(one file, slide v2), all 2,715 and 2,121 images rebuild and parse; the
rebuilt `__text` of an image matches an independent extraction of the same
build byte for byte, and its data differs only where that extraction left
chained pointers undecoded.

A `dyldimage` value may join several names with `+`
(`Foundation+CoreFoundation`), and the loader then works on all of them as one
program, so a call from one image into another can be followed without a
second run. `dyldcache.rs (DyldCache::select_all)` resolves each name the
way a single one is resolved; since `+` also occurs inside install names
(`libc++.1.dylib`, `libc++abi.dylib`), `dyldcache.rs (select_images)`
takes from each piece the longest run of `+`-joined pieces that names an
image, a run ending only at the end of the value or before a non-empty piece,
so `libc++.1.dylib` stays one image and `libc++` is not read as `libc`. Then
`dyldcache/merge.rs (DyldCache::extract_merged)` rebuilds each image on
its own, as above, and joins the results into one thin Mach-O (an entry named
twice, or two entries sharing a header, count once, and one image is rebuilt
exactly as before). The joined file opens with a header page of its own,
because the segment commands of several images need not fit in the padding
before the first section of one (the rebuilt Foundation of iOS 16.4.1 has
2,808 bytes spare and CoreFoundation's segment commands take 4,904). Every non-`__LINKEDIT` segment follows at its
cache address, images in address order, and one `__LINKEDIT` closes the file.
It holds one symbol table, ordered as `LC_DYSYMTAB` requires (locals, external
definitions, undefined symbols), in which each symbol's section ordinal is
moved past the sections of the images before it. A Mach-O symbol names its
section in one byte, so the images may hold at most 255 sections together and
a larger selection is refused with that count. The indirect-symbol tables are
concatenated, their entries renumbered to the merged symbol table, and the
`reserved1` of every stub, symbol-pointer and thread-local-pointer section is
moved to its image's part. The function starts of all images are decoded,
sorted and written as one table counted from the lowest `__TEXT`, and
`macho_entry.rs (walk)` counts from the first `__TEXT` command for that reason.
The `unlace.dyld.xrefs` notes are joined, without the call targets that now lie
inside a loaded image (the image's own symbol names them). The identity
commands (`LC_ID_DYLIB`, `LC_UUID`, the dylib list) are those of the image
named first. Export tries and data-in-code are not carried: every export of a
cache image is also an external definition in its symbol table. A joined
Mach-O holds one `__objc_classlist`, `__cfstring`, `__swift5_types` (and so
on) per image, so the ObjC, CFString and Swift passes read every section of a
name (`objc/sections.rs (sections_named)`), not the first. On the iOS 16.4.1
cache, `Foundation+CoreFoundation` lists exactly the 50,742 and 11,166
functions the two images list alone. In a sample of 24 functions (12 from
each image) the decompiled text matched the single-image text except in two
ways: a reference into the other image now resolves to its symbol, and a
local may be renamed where its name collides with a symbol of the other image
(`ptr` became `ptr_2`). A call through a stub island still renders as a named
import of the calling image.

The CLI widens the selection on demand
(`crates/unlace-cli/src/followimages.rs (apply)`). Before `decompile`,
`disassemble` or `xrefs` loads a cache, each `0x` address of the request that
the selected images do not hold is looked up in the segment ranges of every
image (`dyldcache.rs (follow_images)`), and the image that holds it is
appended to the selection, up to `--follow-images N` images (default 2; 0
turns the lookup off). A stub-island address belongs to no image; for
`decompile` and `disassemble` the stub is followed (up to four hops, the same
walk that names cross-image calls) and the request is rewritten to the
function it jumps to. `xrefs` leaves such an address alone, since the island is
what the call sites reference. Each step prints a `[unlace]` note on stderr,
and past the limit the note names the image to add.

An explicit target changes only language selection: the parsed container still
owns section mapping, image base, symbols, and imports. Container header class is
independent of decoder instruction width, so ELF32 can be decoded with a 16-bit
x86 language. An endian disagreement is reported on stderr rather than refused:
`--target` is the flag that overrides what the container declares, and a
byte-swapped decode of a mislabeled image is a legitimate use of it. Empty targets
and the `default` sentinel select the detected architecture and retain the
compiler-model fallback; the loader and console normalize these requests
identically.
This separation lets a recognized container remain loadable when `object` reports
its architecture as unknown. In particular, PE/COFF machines `0x01c0`
(`IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_ARM`) and `0x01c2` (`IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_THUMB`) are both
treated as little-endian ARM32 for language selection; what each says about the
decode mode is the shared ARM mode table's answer (§ the TE paragraph below), a
whole-image Thumb paint for `THUMB` on a PE and the entry-bit walk for `ARM`.
Their sections and PE image base still come from the container parser.

Bare THUMB COFF objects use the typed COFF reader before architecture selection:
the generic `object` magic dispatcher omits machine `0x01c2`. The shared
`loadimage_object::parse_object` entry point preserves the original machine,
sections, and symbols, and is also used when analysis or a CLI inspection
command reopens the image. It retains the typed reader's header and section
validation; it does not rewrite the machine bytes to another architecture.

(unlace) **A DEX file is mapped whole at address 0** (`option dexmodel` governs
what the engine does with it). `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_dex.rs
(DexLoadImage)` maps the file as one read-only code segment, as Ghidra's
`DexLoader` maps its `.dex` block; Ghidra also copies each method's
instructions to a second block, which unlace does not need, so an instruction's
address is its file offset. The format probe is the `dex\n` magic followed by a
three-digit version and a NUL. The same dispatcher that routes TE images
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (bootstrap_from_image_with_isa)`,
and `bootstrap_from_file` for the console) routes a DEX file to
`engine.rs (bootstrap_from_dex_bytes)`, which decodes with
`Dalvik:LE:32:DEX_Android12` unless `--target` names another Dalvik language,
installs one function symbol per method with code, named as the DEX model does
(chapter 00), hands the model to the `Architecture`, and turns on
`readonlypropagate` for the image. At the analysis commit each method's DEX
prototype is locked onto its symbol, after the `option` lines, so `dexmodel off`
also leaves the signatures to recovery. No analysis pass runs over a DEX image:
the method table is the complete function inventory.

An APK is a zip; `loadimage_dex.rs (is_apk)` claims one whose central directory
lists a root `classes.dex`. `loadimage_dex.rs (load_dex_models)` inflates
`classes.dex`, `classes2.dex`, ... in that order (stored or deflated entries;
zip64 and other methods are refused) and maps each at the next 64 KiB boundary
after the previous one, one DEX model per file. Index spaces are per file, so
each function's snapshot carries the model whose mapping holds its entry
(`architecture.rs (Architecture::build_arch_handle_for_entry)`): a constant-pool
index resolves in the method's own file. A call into a class defined in another
file of the APK prints by name through that pool. Its target is linked across
the files by `crates/unlace-middle/src/p0_knowledge/dex/links.rs
(MethodIndex)`: a method reference is the declaring class's descriptor, the
name and the prototype descriptor, which name the same method in every file, so
an index of every defined method by that key, plus each class's superclass for
a method a subclass inherits, resolves an `invoke` in any file to the code
address of the method it runs. `links.rs (calls)` lists every `invoke` of the
loaded files that way, and `unlace xrefs` answers from it for DEX and APK input
(`--to` a method: its call sites in every file; `--from` a method: what it
calls, a framework method that no loaded file defines appearing by name with
no address).

The on-device forms of a DEX file load the same way, through
`loadimage_dex.rs (load_dex_models)`. A **compact DEX** file (`cdex` and a
three-digit version, ART's `compact_dex_file.h`) is parsed by the same reader
(`dex/format.rs (DexFile)`): its header is 0x88 bytes, the offsets of its
string data, type lists, class data and code items count from the header's
`data_off`, and a code item packs registers, ins, outs and tries into four 4-bit
fields and the instruction count into 11 bits, with a preheader of 16-bit
additions before the item for larger values (`DexFile::read_code_item`). An
**ODEX** (`dey\n`) wraps one DEX file at its `DexOptHeader`'s `dexOffset`; it
decodes with `Dalvik:LE:32:ODEX_KitKat`, whose tables hold the quickened
instructions an optimized file may contain (`loadimage_dex.rs (dex_language)`).
A version-027 **VDEX** (Android 12 and later) lists its sections in its header;
the DEX section holds one DEX file per checksum, each 4-byte aligned after the
previous one's `file_size`, and runs to the section's end so a compact DEX file's
shared data stays reachable. Each entry must carry a DEX or compact DEX magic,
and a VDEX of any version other than 027 is refused as `Unsupported VDEX version`. An **OAT** file is an ELF whose `oatdata` dynamic
symbol starts with `oat\n` and a version; up to Android 7 it embeds the DEX
files, which are found by their own headers (a DEX magic on a 4-byte boundary
whose header size, endian tag and file size hold up), since the `OatDexFile`
records that locate them change with every OAT version. An OAT whose `oatdata`
holds no DEX file is refused (`Could not locate DEX file inside the OAT file`),
not read as an empty image. Every form is
synthesized from `tests/stages/fixtures/dex/hello.dex` and `tries.dex` by
`tests/stages/fixtures/dex/containers.py`.

(unlace) **A stripped ELF's separate debug information** (`debuglink`,
default on, a load-time gate read through `UNLACE_DEBUGLINK`). Distributions
strip their binaries and ship the symbol table and DWARF in a separate file.
When the image has no `.symtab`,
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elf_debuglink.rs (companion_symbols)`
looks for that file the way gdb does: the GNU build-id note names
`<dir>/.build-id/<xx>/<rest>.debug`, accepted only if its own build-id matches,
and `.gnu_debuglink` names a file next to the image, in its `.debug/`
directory, or under `<dir>/<image's directory>/`, accepted only if its CRC32
matches. `<dir>` is each entry of `UNLACE_DEBUG_DIRS`, then `/usr/lib/debug`.
Failing a companion, the XZ-compressed ELF in `.gnu_debugdata` (Fedora's
MiniDebugInfo, decompressed with `lzma-rs`) supplies a function-only symbol
table. The companion's defined function symbols join the loader's function
symbols; an address that already has a name keeps it. A companion that carries
DWARF also feeds the DWARF analyzer
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/dwarf/mod.rs (DwarfPass)` runs
over the companion when the image has no `.debug_info`), since the addresses
are the image's own; MiniDebugInfo has no DWARF. A debug file that `dwz -m`
compressed (Fedora/RHEL `-debuginfo`, Debian/Ubuntu `-dbgsym`) keeps the
strings and partial units several packages share in a supplementary file its
`.gnu_debugaltlink` names with that file's build-id;
`elf_debuglink.rs (find_altlink)` looks for it at the named path (absolute,
with `/usr/lib/debug` also tried under each `UNLACE_DEBUG_DIRS` root, or
relative to the debug file), then by build-id under the debug directories,
and accepts it only if its build-id matches. The DWARF analyzer then sets it as
gimli's supplementary `Dwarf` (`Dwarf::set_sup`), so names in
`DW_FORM_GNU_strp_alt` / `DW_FORM_strp_sup` resolve. A DIE reference into
another unit, `DW_FORM_ref_addr` into a partial unit of the same file (what
`dwz` makes of a single file, and how an LTO unit reaches its early-debug
units) or `DW_FORM_GNU_ref_alt` / `DW_FORM_ref_sup` into the supplementary
file, is keyed in the unit's DIE snapshot by `.debug_info` offset with a high
bit for each kind (`analyzers/dwarf/mod.rs (die_ref)`), and
`mod.rs (graft_foreign)` takes each referenced DIE, its subtree and its
ancestors from a snapshot of the unit that holds it (`ForeignUnits`, one
snapshot per unit, its own unit DIE left out) into the referring unit's
snapshot, again for what those reference, up to 32 rounds and 65,536 DIEs. The
type mapper and the declaration walks then resolve them as they resolve a
unit-local reference. A reference still unresolved leaves its prototype
untyped rather than `void`. The loader also reports a `PT_LOAD`
that maps an address another `PT_LOAD` already mapped from different file bytes
(`elf_debuglink.rs (overlapping_loads)`), a shape only a hand-made or hostile
image has; which bytes win is unchanged.

(unlace) **A Mach-O image's `.dSYM` bundle** (`debuglink`, the same gate). A
binary shipped without DWARF takes it from the bundle `dsymutil` wrote beside
it: `<name>.dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/<name>`, and for a framework or app
the bundle named after the wrapper (`Foo.framework.dSYM` next to
`Foo.framework`), each enclosing directory up to three levels tried.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/macho_dsym.rs (find_dsym)` accepts a
candidate only when its `LC_UUID` equals the image's, so a dSYM of another
build is never applied. A universal dSYM is read slice by slice, and the thin
slice carrying the image's UUID is the one that feeds the DWARF analyzer
(`analyzers/dwarf/mod.rs (DwarfPass)`), which runs over it as it does over an
ELF companion. An image with no `LC_UUID` takes no dSYM. Beside a `*.kext`
bundle the `*.dSYM` bundles of its directory are also read, in name order (at
most 64), since a kernel extension's dSYM is often named for its bundle
identifier; the UUID check still decides each one.

(unlace) **MS-DOS `MZ` executables load as relocated real-mode images.**
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_mz.rs (MzImage)` claims a file
with an `MZ` (or `ZM`) header that is not the stub of a newer format: a `PE\0\0`
signature at `e_lfanew`, an `NE`/`LE`/`LX` one there past the old header, or an
image the `object` crate opens as PE keeps the object path. Bytes 0x3c..0x40 are
read as `e_lfanew` for the `NE`/`LE`/`LX` test only when the header reaches past
them and the relocation table does not cover them (deark's rule); otherwise they
are code or a relocation entry, and a stray `LE` they happen to point at does not
turn a DOS program away. The load module is
the file from the header's paragraph count to the size its page fields declare
(an overlay past that is not mapped), and it is placed at segment 0x1000, linear
0x10000, as DOS would place it at some free paragraph: each relocation-table
entry adds 0x1000 to the word it names, and one that names a word outside the
module is skipped and reported. The entry is `(0x1000 + CS) * 16 + IP`, with the
segment add wrapping as the CPU's does, so PKLITE's `FFF0:0100` lands on the
first module byte; an entry outside the module is refused. The dispatcher
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (bootstrap_from_mz_bytes)`) hands
the relocated bytes to the raw-image path as one in-memory `CODE` mapping, with
the `x86:LE:16:Real Mode:default` language unless the caller names another and
the entry as its seed, so `rawdiscover` widens the inventory from it and the
entry is reported as the image's, together with the relocated words the call
sweep reads (`mzsweep`, below). It then states the code segments the image
names to the 16-bit x86 decoder
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/realmodecs.rs (paint)`): the
entry's CS from its `CS:IP`, and, for every relocation whose word is the segment
of a far `CALL`/`JMP ptr16:16` (`9a`/`ea`, offset, segment) with a target in the
module, that segment at the target (`MzImage::code_segments`). The target must
also lie below the next segment the image names (every relocated word, and the
entry's CS): a far branch lands in its own segment, while a `9a`/`ea` byte that
is the tail of another instruction (`b8 9a 10 ba ..` is `mov ax, 0x109a; mov
dx, seg x`) implies a target past that segment, in code another CS runs, and
stating that CS there would wrap its near branches in the wrong segment. A
segment holds from its point up to the next one, so a near branch in the
entry's segment wraps IP inside that segment instead of taking the linear sum,
and the raw-image call sweep, which runs before the descent, already decodes a
far-called segment with its own CS. The header's
minimum allocation is not mapped: a flow into uninitialized memory is a flow
into nothing, not into zeros that decode as `ADD [BX+SI],AL`. A PKLITE or LZEXE
stub is named on load, since its code is a decompressor in front of a packed
body (issue #1288); the note sends a PKLITE file to `unlace unpack`. Surfaces that
need an `object::File` refuse an `MZ` input with a capability error, as they do
a TE.

(unlace) **PS-X EXE, N64 ROM, a.out, Amiga hunk, PEF and NE executables,
OMF objects and libraries, and Android boot images load from their own headers.** These containers hold code for processors unlace
decodes, but the `object` crate reads none of them, so each was refused as an
unknown format and had to be mapped by hand as a headerless image, which for
the three relocatable ones is also wrong: a flat mapping leaves every
relocated word holding a link-time value. Each has a bounded parser under
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/retroimage.rs (parse)` that
turns the file into one description: a contiguous module of bytes as the
platform's loader would leave them in memory, its base address, the SLEIGH
language, the entry point, the mapped ranges with their kind, the names the
container gives addresses, and any register the container fixes for the whole
image. The dispatcher
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine/retroimage.rs (bootstrap_retro_bytes)`)
hands that module to the raw-image path, so discovery, naming and every option
behave as they do for a headerless image; what the command line supplies there
(`--target`, `--base`, `--entry`) the header supplies here. `--target` still
overrides the language. The ranges are published as the load image's sections
in place of the single whole-file code range, so the call sweep of
`rawdiscover` reads only the ranges that hold code, and a read-only range is
marked so. Every named code address is a discovery seed and takes the
container's name; a named data address becomes a global of that name. There is
no option: before this the same file was an error.

The format is claimed from the first 32 bytes
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/retroimage.rs (is_retro_image)`),
after the TE probe and before the MZ and object-file ones; an NE file, whose
header follows its MZ stub, is claimed when `e_lfanew` names `NE`, and only
then is the whole file read. Every size and
offset is untrusted: arithmetic is checked, a module may not exceed 256 MiB,
and what a parser cannot honor (a relocation outside its segment, a malformed
relocation program) is skipped and reported on stderr rather than guessed.

- **PS-X EXE** (`psx.rs`): the magic `PS-X EXE`, then little-endian `pc0`,
  `gp0`, `t_addr`, `t_size` and the bss range in a 0x800-byte header. The text
  that follows the header is mapped at `t_addr` (clamped to the bytes the file
  holds), the bss range after it as zero fill, `pc0` is the entry and must lie
  in the stored text, and a nonzero `gp0` is `gp`'s tracked value over the
  image, so a `gp`-relative access folds to its address. The language is
  `MIPS:LE:32:default`.
- **N64 ROM** (`n64.rs`): the first word is the PI configuration word
  `0x80371240`, whose stored byte order tells a big-endian (`.z64`),
  byte-swapped (`.v64`) or little-endian (`.n64`) dump; the latter two are
  converted. The boot code at ROM offset 0x40 copies up to one megabyte from
  ROM offset 0x1000 to the entry address in header word 2 and jumps there, so
  that segment is the one mapped range and its first byte the entry. Two
  revisions of the boot code subtract 0x100000 or 0x200000 from the header
  word first; they are told apart by the CRC-32 of the boot code. Code the
  boot segment later copies from elsewhere in the ROM is not mapped. The
  language is `MIPS:BE:64:64-32addr`.
- **a.out** (`aout.rs`): a 32-byte header whose first word is the magic
  (OMAGIC 0407, NMAGIC 0410, ZMAGIC 0413, QMAGIC 0314) and a machine id, in
  one of three dialects: NetBSD's network-order `flags, mid, magic`; SunOS's
  big-endian word with its machine type (1 to 3) below a toolchain version;
