  and the host-order word of Linux and the i386 BSDs. A file is claimed only
  when the machine id is one of the table's (m68k, i386, SPARC, ARM), which
  also picks the byte order of the rest of the header, the page size and the
  language. Where the text starts in the file and in memory follows the
  dialect and the magic; when the entry point is not inside the text at that
  address, the text is placed at the page the entry is in. Data follows the
  text (on the next page boundary unless OMAGIC), then bss as zero fill. The
  `nlist` symbols of the text, data and bss name their addresses, less the
  leading underscore and without debugger records, object-file names and
  assembler-local labels. A file with no entry address and with relocation
  records is a relocatable object: it is loaded at 0, each undefined or
  common symbol is given a slot in a range appended after the bss, and each
  external relocation record of m68k and i386 adds its symbol's slot address
  to the field it names, so a call to an undefined function is a call to a
  named address. Section-relative records need nothing at base 0. SPARC and
  ARM relocation records are not applied, and the load says so.
- **Amiga hunk** (`hunk.rs`): `HUNK_HEADER` (0x3f3) with no resident library
  names and the memory size of each hunk, then each hunk's blocks to its
  `HUNK_END`. AmigaDOS allocates the hunks separately; here they are placed
  one after another from 0x10000. `HUNK_CODE` and `HUNK_DATA` contents are
  copied, `HUNK_BSS` and the part of a hunk past its stored contents are zero
  fill, and each `HUNK_RELOC32`, `HUNK_RELOC32SHORT` and `HUNK_DREL32` entry
  adds its target hunk's address to the word it names. `HUNK_SYMBOL` names
  are kept, `HUNK_NAME` and `HUNK_DEBUG` skipped. The entry is the first byte
  of the first hunk, which must be code. An overlay tree ends the load with a
  note; a library or object unit (`HUNK_UNIT`) is not claimed. The language is
  `68000:BE:32:default`.
- **Android boot image** (`androidboot.rs`): the `ANDROID!` magic, AOSP header
  versions 0 to 2. The kernel is the module, based at `kernel_addr` and entered
  at its first byte; its size is bounded by the module limit and it must fit the
  32-bit address space. The language comes from the kernel's own header: an
  arm64 `Image` (`ARM\x64` at 0x38) is `AARCH64:LE:64:v8A`, an ARM `zImage`
  (0x016f2818 at 0x24) is `ARM:LE:32:v7`, and any other kernel is refused. The
  ramdisk and second-stage loader are not mapped; each is named in a note. The
  command line is not surfaced. A page size that is not a power of two, or a
  kernel or ramdisk that runs past the file, is refused.
- **PEF** (`pef.rs`): the tag `Joy!peff` with architecture `pwpc`; a CFM-68K
  fragment is refused. Each instantiated section (code, data,
  pattern-initialized data, constant) is placed in header order from
  0x10000000 at its alignment, pattern-initialized data is expanded by
  running its five-opcode pattern program, and one eight-byte slot per
  imported symbol follows the sections. Each section's relocation program
  from the loader section is then run: the instructions add a section's
  address, or an import's slot address, to successive words, with the
  position, the import index and the two section variables as state, and the
  two repeat instructions replaying the blocks before them. A program is
  bounded by a step budget and by its section, and one that leaves either is
  cut short with a note. The main symbol of a PowerPC fragment is a
  transition vector in the data section: its first word is the entry and its
  second the TOC, which is `r2`'s tracked value over the image, so a
  TOC-relative load reads its slot. Code is named from the export table (a
  transition-vector export names the code its first word points at), from the
  traceback table after each function (a zero word, flags with the
  offset-present and name-present bits, the distance back to the function
  start and the name), and from the import table: an import names its slot,
  and each cross-fragment glue stub (`lwz r12,d(r2)` followed by the fixed
  five-instruction tail that saves the TOC and jumps through the vector) takes
  the name of the import whose slot its TOC entry holds. `r2` is known at each
  function's entry only: after a cross-fragment call the caller reloads it
  from the linkage area the glue stored it in, and that store is not modeled.
- **NE** (`ne.rs`, Win16 and OS/2 1.x): an MZ stub whose `e_lfanew` (with a
  header of at least four paragraphs) names an `NE` header. Under
  `x86:LE:16:Protected Mode:default`, where a far address is selector *
  0x10000 + offset, segment n of the segment table is placed at n * 0x10000
  with selector n (its stored bytes, zero to its minimum allocation), so a
  near branch stays in its segment and a far pointer reads as its target.
  Each segment's relocation records are applied as the Windows loader does:
  an internal reference (a segment and offset, or a movable entry's ordinal
  resolved through the entry table), an import by ordinal or by name, written
  as the target's offset, selector, far address, 32-bit offset or 48-bit
  pointer, added to the stored value for an additive record and otherwise
  along the chain the stored words link (0xFFFF ends it). Each distinct import
  gets a two-byte slot (a RETF) in a segment after the module's own, named
  `MODULE_ordinal` or after the imported name, so every far call to it reaches
  a named function. The entry table's exports are named from the resident and
  non-resident name tables (`entry_N` when unnamed); the entry is `CS:IP`, or
  for a library without one its first code export. The automatic data
  segment's selector is the tracked value of DS and SS over the image.
  Operating-system fixups (the floating-point emulator's) are counted in a
  note and not applied; resources are not mapped.
- **OMF** (`omf.rs`): a THEADR or LHEADR record whose name fills it opens an
  object, a library header record (page size a power of two from 16 to 32768,
  flags 0 or 1, zero padding, THEADR at the next page) a library, whose modules
  are read in order from page boundaries (the dictionary is not used). The
  records (LNAMES/LLNAMES, SEGDEF, GRPDEF, EXTDEF/LEXTDEF/CEXTDEF,
  COMDEF/LCOMDEF, PUBDEF/LPUBDEF, LEDATA, LIDATA expanded, FIXUPP with its frame
  and target threads, MODEND) of every module are laid out as one program: the
  segments one after another at their alignment (at least a paragraph), from
  0x10000 under `x86:LE:16:Real Mode:default`, or from 0x400000 under
  `x86:LE:32:default:windows` when USE32 code dominates; the communal
  variables after them; then one slot per external that no module defines
  (16 bytes in 16-bit code, so a far pointer to it is `:0000`; a RETF where a
  far pointer or segment fixup names it, else a RET). An external a module of
  the same library defines resolves to that public. Each fixup adds to its
  site the target's offset from its frame (the frame's paragraph in 16-bit
  code: a segment, a group's lowest member, the segment that defines an
  external, else the external's own paragraph; zero in flat 32-bit code), a
  self-relative displacement, or the frame's paragraph for a segment base.
  The entry is the first MODEND start address, else the first public in a
  code segment. A 16-bit image with a DGROUP group fixes DS at its paragraph.
  COMDAT records, fixups of iterated (LIDATA) data, import definitions and
  segment selectors in 32-bit code are counted in notes and not mapped.

Surfaces that need an `object::File` refuse these inputs with the capability
error a TE or MZ input gets.

(unlace) **An MS-DOS executable's functions start with DS holding its data
segment** (`mzdgroup`, default on, `MZ` loads in real mode only). A near data
pointer is an offset into the segment DS holds, and a function's DS is an input
the decompiler cannot see, so without a value every global read printed as a
pointer constant resolved against DS 0 (`*(int *)0x308e`) and no two functions
shared a global. DOS starts a program with DS holding its PSP; a compiled
program's startup code loads the linker's DGROUP into DS before it calls into
the program, and the program's functions keep it there. The loader
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mzdgroup.rs (startup_ds)`)
reads that segment off the entry code: it decodes forward from the entry
`CS:IP` and tracks the 16-bit registers that hold a segment of the module — one
loaded from an immediate whose word the relocation table names (`mov dx,
DGROUP`), CS at the entry, or a relocated word read through `CS:` — carried by
register moves, segment-register moves and a `push` the next instruction pops.
Every other write forgets a register (by the instruction's p-code outputs); an
`INT 21h` forgets the registers the DOS function in AH returns in (AX, BX and
CX for the version call Turbo C's startup makes between `mov dx, DGROUP` and
`mov ds, dx`; a write to AL keeps the function number in AH), an `INT 21h`
whose function is not listed forgets every general register and ES, and a
non-DOS interrupt, an `INT 21h` whose function is not known or one that returns
a pointer in DS (`1Bh`, `1Ch`, `1Fh`, `32h`, `4Bh`, `5Dh`, `63h`) forgets DS as
well. The walk ignores backward branches, forgetting each register assigned
between such a branch's target and the branch, and after an instruction that
does not fall through it resumes at the next forward branch target; at a
branch target a register keeps its segment only when every path into the
target brings the same one, so a DS load on a path that exits (a DOS 1 version
check that loads `CS` into DS to print a message) does not reach the code after
it. DGROUP is the segment DS holds at the first call, or at a DOS exit no branch
target follows, and it must start inside the load module; a return, an
indirect or far jump, an undecodable byte, a branch into the middle of an
instruction or 512 instructions end the walk with none, as EXEPACK's stub does
(its `push cs; pop ds` ends in a `retf`). The segment at the first call is only
DGROUP when the program keeps it, so the walk reads on past that call through
the rest of the startup, taking each call to return with every segment register
but ES kept, and decodes each direct callee the startup enters with a known DS
up to its returns (128 instructions at most, `keeps_ds`). A callee that returns
with another known segment in DS (an `init` routine that loads the data segment
after a banner printed with DS = CS), or a path of the startup that ends with
another known segment still in DS (a first call made with a scratch segment,
then `main` with the real one), states nothing. A routine the startup calls
with another known segment in DS while DGROUP comes back afterwards is
recorded as entered with another DS: Borland C++'s StartExit walks the `_INIT_`
and `_EXIT_` tables through DS. The segment is stated as DS's tracked value
over the load module
(`crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/mzdgroup.rs (apply)`),
keeping every other tracked register (the spec's `DF = 0`), and is left out at
the entry address, where DS holds the PSP, and at each routine recorded as
entered with another DS. `ActionConstbase` then starts each
function with `DS = COPY DGROUP`, so `segment(DS, 0x308e)` folds to the linear
address and the read is the global `dat_3dfbe`, and the segment resolver reads a
constant near pointer against DGROUP. A function that loads another segment
into DS is read with that one from the load on. The assumption is the
compiler's, not the program's: hand-written code that runs functions with
another segment in DS (an interrupt handler entered with the interrupted
program's DS that does not load its own) is read against DGROUP, which is why
`mzdgroup off` exists; it leaves DS an unknown input. On the unpacked
DAZZLE.EXE of issue #1288 (Turbo C, DGROUP `3af3`) 1,388 near-pointer
dereferences in 136 of 295 functions become 44 (the entry point's PSP reads
and code that loads DS from memory), and 1,537 named global references replace
29.

(unlace) **A managed .NET assembly loads from its CIL method bodies** (`cil`,
default on, a PE with a CLI header only). The native code of a managed PE is
one jump to `_CorExeMain`; the program is ECMA-335 metadata and CIL, so read
as x86 the image has one function. The dispatcher
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (bootstrap_cil)`) takes a file
whose PE data directory 14 names a CLI header, whose metadata reads and which
has at least one method body, unless the caller names a target language or
sets `cil off`
(`crates/unlace-middle/src/p0_knowledge/cil.rs (cil_enabled)`);
every other input keeps the object path. The image
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_cil.rs (CilImage)`) is the PE
mapped by RVA at 0x400000, through the raw-image path as the language
`CIL:LE:64:default`. Only the extent the file backs is mapped, and a section
table that spreads that extent past 64 times the file size (the alignment
ratio of a managed image is 16) or past 1 GiB is refused, so a small file
cannot ask for a large allocation.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_cil/metadata.rs (Metadata)`
reads the metadata root, the `#Strings`, `#US` and `#Blob` heaps and every
table of the `#~` stream: the row size of a table depends on the row counts of
the tables its columns index, so all 45 schemas are stated even though the
loader consumes eleven. Each method with a body is one function. It starts at
the first instruction, after the tiny or fat header, is named
`Namespace.Type::Method` (a nested type under its enclosing type, joined with
`.`), and takes its prototype from its signature
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_cil/sig.rs (method_sig)`): a
reference is a pointer, an array reference a pointer to its element, a string
a pointer to UTF-16 text, an enum its underlying type. Overloads share a
name and are told apart by address.

CIL leaves two things out of the instruction bytes that a decoder needs, and
the loader supplies both before anything is decoded. The first is operand
types: `add` adds whatever the evaluation stack holds.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_cil/body.rs (type_body)` walks
each body's control flow from its first instruction carrying the stack as a
list of kinds (int32, int64 or native or reference, float32, float64), as the
verifier does, and records for each reached instruction the depth before it,
the class of its operands and a call's argument count. Those are painted over
the instruction as the decode context `cilctx`; an instruction the walk did
not reach keeps the default and decodes as unimplemented. The second is what
a metadata token names. Each token operand is rewritten in the mapped image:
a `call`, `callvirt`, `newobj` or `ldftn` to the address of the method, a
static field access to the field's address, an instance field access to the
field's offset, `ldstr` to a NUL-terminated UTF-16 copy of the `#US` string
laid out after the image, and `ldtoken` of a field with initial data to that
data. A method of another assembly, or one with no body, gets an address in an
unmapped range from 0x10000; it is named and prototyped but is not a function
of the inventory. A generic parameter in the signature of such a member is
replaced by the argument its `TypeSpec` parent or `MethodSpec` instantiates it
with, so `List<int>::get_Item` returns an int32. `throw` calls a no-return
helper at 0x1000.

The runtime, not the image, lays out a class, so the loader gives each class
of the assembly a layout of its own (`CilImage::layout`): the instance fields
in declaration order, each at the next naturally aligned offset after an
8-byte object header or after a base class of the same assembly, and from
offset 0 in a value type. The same layout becomes a struct type the method's
`this` and every reference of that class point at, so a field access prints
`this->field` and the offset never shows. A class with an explicit layout, an
interface and an enum get none, and an access to a field of one refuses the
body.

A body the walk cannot follow is refused whole and left unpainted, so it is
listed and decodes as unimplemented instead of as a guess: one with an
exception-handling clause (a `finally` runs on every exit, which a branch
does not say), a value type on the stack whose size the assembly does not
give, `ldarga`, `calli`, `jmp`, a checked conversion or arithmetic (`.ovf`),
`localloc`, the object-copy instructions, a vararg call site, more than 16
arguments or 64 stack slots, and a stack that differs between two paths into
one instruction. Two methods may share one body, but a body whose bytes only
partly coincide with another's is refused as well: every body is typed from
the bytes as the file holds them, before any token is rewritten, and two
overlapping bodies would otherwise paint and rewrite each other.

A method's extent is its body. The bytes between two bodies are the next
method's header and alignment, and metadata follows the last one, so the
bootstrap states each method's end and the inventory, the listing and the
size filters report the body's own length instead of the distance to the
next entry. A stated end is not a flow that stopped short, so the notes a
real-mode image prints about one (`ConsoleProgram::extent_cut_by_flow`) stay
silent. The load image
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_cil/image.rs (CilLoadImage)`)
answers every read as the raw image does and replaces its section table: the
raw image is one buffer, which its loader reports as one code section, while
here the method bodies of each PE section are one code run and the PE
headers, the CLI header, the metadata and what the loader lays out after the
image are data. A sweep of the code sections, as the project export's
assembly listing makes, therefore lists the methods and the few header bytes
between them rather than the whole file. The string inventory still scans
the PE's sections, so it lists the names in the metadata heaps.

(unlace) **UEFI TE images take a bounded container path of their own.**
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_te.rs (TeLoadImage)` parses a
file the format probe claims. That probe reads more than the `VZ` signature —
two ASCII letters an unrelated file can open with — and also requires an EFI
subsystem and a `StrippedSize` leaving room for the header it counts, so a
non-container keeps the headerless-image guidance instead of being routed into
the TE parser or refused as a TE; the machine word is deliberately not part of
the claim, so a TE for a machine unlace has no binding for is told so by name. One
dispatcher (`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (bootstrap_from_image_with_isa)`)
routes every front-end's file load to the TE or the object loader, and the
section table is classified by the same `SectionKind` rule and flag rule the PE
loader applies to the same characteristics. The TE header remains authoritative for
the machine, image base, entry point, data directories, and section table; an
explicit target can select only a width- and data-endianness-compatible SLEIGH
language. Each section's file offset subtracts the stripped-header bias while
its loaded address retains the original image-base-relative VMA. File offset zero
is retained at `ImageBase + StrippedSize - 40`, and the read-only mapping
continues up to the adjusted `BaseOfCode`, so it covers the TE header, the
section table, and the alignment slack behind them. That region has two extents
and they coincide only when the image was linked with SectionAlignment equal to
FileAlignment: the file BACKS it up to the first section's adjusted raw offset,
while it is MAPPED up to the adjusted `BaseOfCode`, with the difference reading
as zero. Deriving the file length from the RVA delta instead refuses an
ordinary 0x200-file-aligned image outright. The file-backed part must lie
inside the file, and a section's adjusted raw range must begin at or after the
section table describing it — the TE analog of a PE section starting at or
after `SizeOfHeaders`; truncated or overlapping input is rejected rather than
completed with synthetic bytes.
`VirtualSize` bounds each section's mapped extent when nonzero, file-alignment
padding beyond that extent is not exposed, and a virtual tail beyond the
initialized bytes reads as zero — a firmware module is loaded into a zeroed
buffer, so unlike the object loader's packer-staging refusal that tail is
faithful. It is still not *evidence*: the literal-pool constant ranges are built
from the file-backed extents only, so a read landing in a tail the image carries
no copy of is never folded to a constant. The parser rejects arithmetic overflow,
overlapping or out-of-file ranges, directories outside mapped sections, and
entries outside file-backed code before allocating section contents. Byte
assertions atomically replace a complete span within one mapped header or
section and may materialize a zero-filled virtual tail; unmapped,
cross-boundary, and wrong-address-space writes are rejected. The entry is named
at the analysis commit, after options such as `namestyle` are applied.

Language selection reuses the object loader's `compose_language_id` over the PE
machine word, so a TE and a PE carrying the same machine select the same SLEIGH
variant; only the compiler model follows the UEFI bindings (C/cdecl for IA-32,
the UEFI x64 convention with the arch-default fallback for x64, AAPCS for
AArch32, AAPCS64/LP64 for AArch64), and an explicit compatible target remains
authoritative. The ARM decode-mode policy is one table in
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (pe_arm_mode_policy)`,
read by both PE-family loaders: `ARMNT` declares a wholly Thumb image on every
container and is painted as such; `ARM` may interwork on every container; and
machine `0x1c2` is read as its container family names it — `THUMB` on a PE,
painted wholly Thumb, and `ARMTHUMB_MIXED` on a TE, interworking — a decision
made once there rather than in each loader. Where the policy leaves the mode to
the entry bit, on a TE or a PE alike, an odd entry arms the entry-reachable Thumb walk
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/entrythumbflow.rs (entry_thumb_flow)`,
always on), run at the deferred analysis commit after image-scoped overlays so
it follows the effective instruction stream: it seeds `TMode=1` over each
executable range as one region write, decodes the flow reachable from the
normalized entry through fall-through, direct branches, and direct
mode-preserving `BL` calls (an interworking `BLX` target keeps the mode its
encoding selects), restores every run of values the range already held rather
than the one at its start, and publishes exactly the decoded instruction ranges
as bounded `TMode=1` paints under its own gated pass id — written to the
context database at once as well as stashed, because the deferred Listing
consumers decode the same bytes before the stash is committed. Decoding inside
the walk masks only the `TMode` bits out of the language's context writes
(`set_context_write_mask`): a Thumb `blx` runs `globalset(TMode=0)` at its target,
which would flatten every Thumb address above that target for the rest of the
walk, and the seed already answers the mode question for the whole range.
Other context writes still propagate, including the IT condition at the next
instruction, so guarded branches and returns retain their fall-through. The
previous write mask is restored when the walk finishes, even at its budget. The
walk covers file-backed executable bytes plus successfully applied byte
overlays clipped to executable mappings. Adjacent and overlapping spans merge
before decoding, so an instruction can cross their boundary, while unwritten
gaps and tails remain excluded: zero-filled bytes can decode as Thumb no-ops.
Only enabled analysis passes supply no-return seeds to the entry walk and the
later Listing consumers. An unconditional direct call to one of those callees
has no fall-through; an IT-guarded call, including `BLX`, retains the successor
reached when its condition is false.
The walk is bounded at 4096 instructions; reaching the bound publishes the ranges
walked so far, reports the truncation once on stderr, and leaves the unreached
code at the language default, so the load never fails on the size of the image.
The pending entry is consumed before the walk runs, so a failure cannot re-arm
it, and a walk that publishes nothing leaves the context partition as it found
it. A wholly Thumb image can opt into the explicit `--isa thumb` range paint
instead.

PE entry discovery and Listing seeds normalize the low bit according to the
selected decoder before deduplication and naming. A 32-bit ARM decoder clears
the Thumb bit; a non-ARM override preserves an odd address even when the header
machine is ARM, THUMB, or ARMNT. The header-page entry exemption and the loader's
reported image entry use the same selected-decoder convention. Container-only
discovery, which has no selected language, retains the automatic machine policy.

The parsed entry and named sections are retained as format-neutral program
metadata (`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (ProgramImageMetadata)`),
populated by the object loader as well, so the project README no longer
re-parses the input and reports the entry through the inventory on every path.
A TE image has no `object::File` of its own. The loader maps it directly (above),
and the analyzer tier reads it through a rebuilt PE view (`objectview`,
default-on; `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/objectview.rs (te_as_pe)`).
The TE header replaced `StrippedSize` bytes of DOS, PE and optional headers, and
every section's `PointerToRawData` still counts from the original file, so the
view is a freshly written header of exactly `StrippedSize` bytes — machine,
subsystem, entry, `BaseOfCode`, `ImageBase` and the two data directories a TE
keeps — in front of the TE file from its section table on. Every raw pointer
then stays valid as it is. If `StrippedSize` is too short for a PE header, the
header is padded and every raw pointer is moved by the padding. At the commit
(`engine.rs (run_object_view_passes)`) the view goes through the same per-pass
list and gates an object image's bytes go through, and it becomes the deferred
Listing tier's image. A TE therefore gets strings, the `pemain` UEFI entry
prototype, prologue starts and the Listing consumers. On top of that comes the
headerless-image discovery a `--raw-image` load uses (`rawdiscover`, §below),
seeded with the container entry over the TE's `CODE` sections. It runs after the
entry Thumb walk, so a mixed-mode ARM image's Thumb code is decoded in the mode
that walk painted. With `--option rawdiscover off` that walk is skipped and the
load says so once on stderr. With `--option objectview off` the view is dropped
and the passes do not run. The object-view consumers (`strings`, `crypto`,
`xrefs`, `decompile-graph`, and the graph-backed `functions`/`decompile-all`
filters) read the same PE view through the shared image read.

(unlace) **Static unpacking.** A packed image is the one input on which the whole
tier is honestly useless: it maps a loader stub and a compressed blob, so every
address the original program used is absent until something recovers it.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/upx` reimplements the recovery in-process --
the UCL NRV2B/NRV2D/NRV2E decoders (`nrv.rs`), the LZMA1 decoder (`lzma.rs`), UPX's
branch-target filters (`filter.rs`), and one reconstruction walk per target family. `unlace unpack` is the
only caller; nothing on the load path unpacks implicitly, because the recovered
file is an artifact an analyst reads and names, not a hidden rewrite of their input.

The two families share nothing but the codecs, because the packed layouts do not
resemble each other. An ELF (`upx/elf.rs`) carries its `PackHeader` in the tail and
its payload as one block stream per original `PT_LOAD` plus the gaps between them.
A PE (`upx/pe.rs`) carries the `PackHeader` in the header padding immediately before
the compressed data -- outside the tail window entirely -- and holds the whole image
in a single block, followed by a trailer that the packer's own loader consumes at
run time and the unpacker replays instead: the original PE header and section table,
then one record per rebuild -- where the stripped import list starts, where the
relocation stream starts, and the icon count the resource rebuild restores -- then a
pointer back to that header. `win32/pe` (PE32) and `win64/pe` (PE32+, amd64) are the
same walk; they differ only in word size: eight-byte import thunks whose ordinal
flag is bit 63 instead of four-byte ones with bit 31, and `DIR64` relocations
instead of `HIGHLOW`. The optional-header magic sets the word size, and both the
packed header and the recovered one must have the size the PackHeader's target
format names; a PE32+ whose PackHeader claims `win32/pe`, or the reverse, is refused
as unsupported before anything is rebuilt. A PE header that does not parse is
reported as what it is; the tail scan that serves every other target can still find
such a file's PackHeader, but a PE PackHeader has no overlay field, so it is never decoded
as though it had one -- that misreading is what used to answer a valid `win64/pe`
file with "PackHeader declares an overlay outside the file".

UPX filters only the code, and every rewritten branch target carries the code's
distance from the image's first section as a bias, so the unfilter takes that bias
rather than refusing a code base that does not start the image. `win64/pe` uses the
`ctok` filter (`0x49`) alone; `win32/pe` adds the plain calltricks `0x11`-`0x16` a
`--brute` pack can choose.

The import descriptors, thunk arrays and hint/name entries UPX strips out of the
image come back from the trailer's compact list. The DLL *names* are not in the
trailer at all; they stay in the packed loader's own import table, which the trailer
addresses by offset. That table is found by agreement with the trailer rather than
through the packed image's import data directory, because retargeting the directory
at a decoy is the first thing a repacker does to a UPX image, and the witness in
`tests/fixtures/upx_packed_pe_i386.exe` is exactly that. Where the original's import
names were one contiguous run, the trailer says where it started and they are
written back there in order; where they were scattered -- every MinGW image -- UPX
leaves each descriptor's name address and each thunk's hint/name address in place
and only the strings go back where those already point. A `KERNEL32` import by
ordinal is recorded as the offset of the packer's own loader thunk for it, and the
ordinal is read out of that thunk rather than out of the offset.

The agreement is over the *set* of DLL names, not a position-by-position walk. The
loader table holds one descriptor per distinct DLL, while the original image may
import a single DLL across several descriptors -- a 32-bit MSVC witness names seven
DLLs from thirteen, `KERNEL32.DLL` four times -- so the two lists differ in length
whenever a binary does that, and a positional comparison can never agree on one. It
did not merely lose the table: it reported the image as corrupt. The table also
carries the stub's own `KERNEL32.DLL` descriptor even when the original imports
nothing from that DLL, so one such descriptor is allowed beyond the set.

Base relocations are rebuilt the way `upx -d` rebuilds them. UPX strips an EXE's
relocations when it may, marking the packed header `RELOCS_STRIPPED`, and its own
unpacker then zeroes the recovered header's relocation directory; `unlace unpack` does
the same. The relocations UPX keeps -- every DLL's, and every ASLR image's, which on
win64 is nearly all of them -- were rebased to zero, byte-swapped in place and
recorded as a delta-coded position stream; the rebuild decodes the stream, restores
each pointer, and lays the positions out as a fresh `.reloc` table (one block per
page, padded to four bytes), with the 16-bit `LOW`/`HIGH` lists a PE32 may append.
Entries of a kind UPX does not keep -- anything but `DIR64` in a PE32+ -- were
dropped when it packed, so they are not in the result either. An export directory
UPX moved out of the image -- a DLL's always, an EXE's with `--compress-exports=0`
-- is rebuilt at its original address in the compact layout UPX's `Export::build`
writes, forwarder strings included. A TLS directory needs no step: UPX's own
`rebuildTls` is empty. The resource directory comes back with every leaf UPX moved
repointed, unless UPX could not clear the original's (its pieces were not
contiguous), in which case the original's is still in the image and stays. What
comes back is the packed copy whole, names included: UPX's packer lays the directory
out afresh with every name string behind the directories and data entries, and
clears only the original's directories and data entries, so the original's names are
still in the image at offsets the packed copy's entries do not point at.

Which trailer records exist is read from the trailer's length rather than predicted
from the data directories. The packer writes a record only when it had something to
put in it, while UPX's own unpacker predicts each one from the original's
directories, and the two disagree on an image whose import directory names no DLL or
whose relocations are all of a kind UPX drops -- `upx -d` then reads the next record
as this one and fails. The three records are 8, 5 and 2 bytes and no two sets of them
sum alike, so the length names exactly one set, and a length no set reaches is
refused as a PE feature this tier does not rebuild. The resource record is the one
the length cannot leave out: the packer writes it exactly when it gives the packed
header a resource directory, which it does only for an original with one, so a
trailer without it for an image whose two headers both have a resource directory is
refused as damaged rather than unpacked with its resources left unrebuilt.

The rebuilt header matches what `upx -d` writes in two ways and keeps the original's
in two. The bound-import directory is zeroed -- its table lived in header slack the
packed file's own headers took over -- and so is the checksum, which covers bytes
the rebuilds re-laid out. The import-address-table directory and `SizeOfHeaders`
keep the original's values, which `upx -d` zeroes and recomputes, and each rebuilt
import descriptor's `OriginalFirstThunk` names its `FirstThunk` array rather than
the zero `upx -d` leaves; with those set aside the file is byte-identical to
`upx -d`'s. Data past the packed file's last section is the original's overlay -- a
signature, a MinGW image's COFF symbol table -- and is appended again at the
original's offset. With nothing dropped from the image, the original's length says
how long that overlay was, and the packed file's tail can carry more than it on
either side. UPX 3.9x writes its stub's relocation block twice; the second copy
spills past the last section's declared end, and the spill and its zero padding to
the file alignment sit in front of the overlay, where `upx -d` copies them too. Bytes
appended to the packed file afterwards -- a signature, a payload -- sit behind it. So
the overlay is read from past a front of exactly the spill's shape, and only for its
own length; neither shifts it. The reconstructed file must
be exactly the original's length, or short of it only by what UPX itself drops: the
trailing `.reloc` section of an image packed without relocations (its directory is
gone too), or debug data that started the overlay (the debug directory stays).

Every size and offset these rebuilds follow comes from the file, so each walk is
bounded by the bytes the file holds. The loader-table scan reads only section
bytes present in the file -- a section past the end of the file maps nothing, and
one at the top of the address space does not wrap -- and reads at most two
descriptors per four bytes of the file, about twice what an honest image needs; a
trailer naming more than 256 distinct DLLs is refused as unsupported, since UPX can
pack more. A resource tree that reaches one directory or data entry twice is refused: UPX's packer writes
the directory out afresh with every node once, even for an original whose linker
shared a subtree, so only an edited file has one, and following it lets a small tree
fan out into an exponential walk. The leaves it moves may not add up to more than
the packed file. An export rebuild is sized as its strings are read, and refused once
it outgrows the image -- every name pointer may name the same long string. The output
file is laid out, and refused if it would be longer than the declared original,
before anything is allocated for it.

What is not rebuilt is named. The `win64/arm64` and `wince/arm` targets exit with
their names; so does PackHeader version 14, UPX's exact-layout PE mode, whose trailer
stores the original headers and the gaps between sections verbatim instead, and so
do versions before 12, older than any layout UPX's own unpacker still reads.

(unlace) **NEOLite.** A second packer, recognized before UPX is asked and on evidence
of its own, so nothing about the UPX arm -- including what it answers for a file that
is not packed at all -- depends on this. `crates/unlace-analysis/src/neolite.rs`
takes an image with a `.NEOpack` section that **owns the entry point**; the section
name alone is a string anyone can write into a header, and it is the entry landing
inside the stub that says the stub runs first.

The layout is the opposite of UPX's, and it is why this is recoverable statically at
all. NEOLite compresses each original section in place and appends only its two
loader sections, leaving the original section table untouched -- so every virtual
address and virtual size in the packed file still describes the original image, and
"where does this decompress to" is a question the file already answers. What the
stub computes at run time is then only what the file also still holds: the original
entry point is the operand of its `push OEP; ret` hand-over, and the original import
directory is inside the `.rdata` that was just decompressed.

The codec is an LZX derivative rather than anything UPX carries. A block transmits
757 Huffman code lengths -- 721 main, 28 length, 8 aligned -- through a 19-symbol
code-length tree, DEFLATE-style with the run codes 16/17/18, each length delta-coded
modulo 16 against the previous block's so consecutive blocks pay only for what moved.
The main alphabet merges match length and position slot the way LZX does
(`256 + slot * 8 + len_slot`) over LZX's 58 position slots and its three repeated
offsets, and only the eighth length slot escapes to the length tree, which indexes
DEFLATE's length base/extra tables. Distances come out raw or, when the block's
aligned tree is not the uniform three-bit one that means "verbatim", as high bits
plus a three-bit aligned symbol. Symbol 720 ends a block and introduces the next
one's trees.

Completeness of a code table is the whole validity test a section's bytes get, and it
carries real weight: a packer routinely leaves resources uncompressed, and the only
thing separating those bytes from a stream is that their first block header does not
build a complete canonical code. A section that fails it is carried through exactly
as it stands rather than decoded into nonsense. The rebuild then restores three
things beyond the bytes -- the entry point, the import data directory, and
`CNT_CODE | MEM_EXECUTE | MEM_READ` on the section the recovered entry lands in,
because the packer rewrites every section to plain read-write data and a `.text` that
does not claim to be code is a section the executable-section filter skips. No other
section's flags are touched: the narrow claim is the one the entry point itself
warrants. Only PE32 x86 is rebuilt; any other optional-header magic is declined by
name, which is why the parse reads the entry point and section table before it looks
at the magic at all.

Refusing beats guessing, in both arms. The output is a file a reader will
disassemble and believe, and a subtly wrong one is more expensive than none: an
unreversed filter leaves every call target wrong while every size still adds up. So
each arm proves its own reconstruction rather than assuming it -- both of the
packer's Adler-32s, a total that equals the original file size the header declares
to the byte, and every rebuilt directory confined to the section the recovered
header says owns it. The PE arm adds one guard the ELF arm does not need: which
trailer steps run depends on which data directories the original image had, so an
unimplemented one would silently desynchronize every later read. The walk therefore
tallies the trailer bytes it consumed against the trailer's real length and refuses
a mismatch, on top of naming base relocations, TLS, bound and delay-loaded imports
up front. Everything unimplemented -- the CL1B, DEFLATE, ZSTD and BZIP2 methods, the
64-bit and ARM PE targets, the `ctojr`/PowerPC/RISC-V filters -- is a named refusal
and writes no file.

Two codecs sit behind that walk, chosen per block by the `b_info` method id. The UCL
decoders cover methods 2-10; method 14 is LZMA, which is what `upx --lzma` and
`upx --best` write and therefore what most recently packed binaries carry. UPX does
not wrap LZMA in a container: a block is a raw LZMA1 stream with no properties/size
preamble and no end-of-stream marker, prefixed by two UPX bytes that spell the coder
parameters -- `pb` in the low three bits of the first, `lc` and `lp` in the low and
high nibbles of the second. The uncompressed length comes from the block header, so
the decoder runs to a known size rather than to a marker, and a stream that stops
short is an error and not a partial block. The one place it relaxes the NRV arm's
contract is input consumption: an LZMA range coder holds lookahead bytes it never
uses, so trailing slack is a property of a valid stream, and the packer's Adler-32
over the decoded bytes is what proves the block instead.

(unlace) **Decoding without the metadata.** Discovery can fail on an image whose payload
is intact: a repacker that strips the `PackHeader`, a private packer that borrows only
the codec, a blob a reader located by hand. `no UPX PackHeader found` is then a correct
answer and a dead end, and the missing input -- where the stream is -- is something the
reader already has. `unlace unpack --raw-lzma START:END` supplies it: discovery is skipped
entirely and that range is decoded as one raw LZMA1 stream. Endpoints are virtual
addresses, resolved through the object's own section table (the table the address was
read out of) and clamped to the bytes the file stores for that section, since a
section's virtual size routinely runs past its raw data and the excess is zero fill, not
stream; `--raw-offsets` reads them as file offsets, which is also the only reading
available for an image no object parser recognises.

The consequence that shapes the decoder is that **no `b_info` exists to declare the
uncompressed length**. `lzma::decompress_exhaustive` therefore runs the same decoder to
the end of the *input* instead of to a length: the recovered size is a result, capped by
the caller rather than predicted, and running out of input is this mode's ordinary
ending rather than the `Truncated` refusal a declared length earns. A corrupt stream
still fails, because a bad distance or an unreachable model index is a different fact
from a short one. By default the range's first two bytes are the UPX parameter prefix;
`--lzma-props` names `pb`/`lp`/`lc` for a stream that carries none, and the prefix is
synthesized so one decoder path serves both.

What this arm produces is a payload, not a program: no imports, no relocations, no
rebuilt header, and none of the reconstruction proofs the walk applies -- there is no
declared size, no `UPX!` marker and no Adler-32 to check it against. That is why it is
an explicit override and not a fallback the `PackHeader` search reaches on its own. The
refusal path is unchanged and deliberately so: an image that genuinely is not packed
still exits `1` naming that, because an `unpack` that exited `0` on everything would
trade a right answer for a reachable one.

(unlace) **PKLITE.** The DOS packer, recognized after NEOLite and before UPX by its
decompressor stub at the DOS entry point, so a file without one reaches the UPX arm
exactly as before. A Windows or OS/2 program (`e_lfanew` naming a `PE`, `NE`, `LE`
or `LX` header) is never PKLITE's, even when its DOS stub is a PKLITE file: the
program is the new-style executable, which PKLITE does not pack.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/pklite` is a port of deark's
`pklite` module (MIT; the notice is in the module header and `NOTICE`): `stub.rs`
reads the parameters out of the stub, `decode.rs` is the decoder, and `mod.rs`
rebuilds the file. A packed EXE enters at `FFF0:0100` -- the start of its code --
and its load module is the stub, the compressed program, a compressed relocation
table and an 8-byte footer holding the original `SS`, `SP`, `CS`, `IP`; the 1990
betas put the data before the decoder instead. Without extra compression (`-e`) the
stub's header also keeps a copy of the original MZ header.

Nothing trustworthy *declares* the parameters. The version word at `0x1C` is
routinely wrong, so the compression mode and the data's position are read from the
stub's machine code, walked component by component against known byte patterns:
the intro (whose `MOV DX` immediate keys the descrambler some versions run over the
rest of the stub, an XOR or ADD chain undone in place before anything else is
read), the copier (whose `MOV SI` immediate locates the decompressor), and the
decompressor (whose immediate is the compressed data's paragraph, and whose
literal-copy loop, length table and register setup say whether extra compression,
large compression or the v1.20 code tables are in use, plus any XOR key on match
offsets). Every component that matches no pattern is a named refusal.

The codec is LZ77 over an 8 KiB window with fixed Huffman codes for the match
length and the distance's high five bits. Control bits come from 16-bit words read
least-significant first, and the next word is fetched the moment the last bit of
the current one is consumed, ahead of the data byte that follows; extra compression
XORs each literal with the number of control bits left at that moment. One length
code escapes to a byte that is a longer length, the stop code, a no-op, or an
uncompressed area, whose eight-byte `PKLITE` signature and length byte are restored
in the output while the history gets zeros (two registered PKZIP 2.04 builds put
stale memory there instead, matched by content). The relocation table is the short
form (count byte, segment, offsets) normally and the long form (count word per
`0x0FFF`-paragraph segment) under extra compression, byte-swapped when the stub's
descrambler is the ADD kind.

The rebuild uses the kept header copy only when its registers agree with the footer
and its relocation count with the table; otherwise it writes a 28-byte header with
the code 16-byte aligned, the footer's registers, `MAXALLOC` from the packed file
and `MINALLOC` estimated from the stub's own free-memory check, as deark does.
The kept copy runs up to the original relocation table, and PKLITE does not record
the bytes between that table and the code, so those are zero. An overlay is carried over when
the decompressed module ends exactly where the recovered header says. The format
has no checksum, so the proofs are structural: the stream must end on its stop
code, the relocation table must end where an 8-byte footer still fits before the end
of the load module, and a match may not reach before the output or behind an
uncompressed area. A file whose stub stores a `PK` signature into the PSP is
unpacked with a warning that the program checks for it at run time. A PKLITE COM
file is decompressed whole. As with UPX, nothing on the load path unpacks
implicitly; the runtime hint names the stub (`PKLITE packed: run 'unlace unpack'`).

(unlace) **The PC memory outside a DOS program is volatile** (always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/pcmemory.rs (paint_volatile)`).
Three regions of the first megabyte change or are read behind the program's
back: the interrupt vector table (linear 0x0-0x3FF), which the CPU reads on
every interrupt and other resident programs rewrite; the BIOS data area
(0x400-0x4FF, segment 0x40), whose timer tick at 0040:006C and keyboard buffer
and shift flags the BIOS interrupt handlers update; and video memory
(0xA0000-0xBFFFF, segments A000, B000 and B800), which the display adapter maps
and whose VGA planes a read or write reaches through the adapter's latches.
Read as ordinary memory, Turbo C's `delay()` calibration in the DAZZLE.EXE of
issue #1288 (`mov al,es:[bx]; l: mov dl,es:[bx]; cmp al,dl; jz l` with ES 0x40,
BX 0x6C) folds to `while (true) {}`, and the first of two writes to one VGA
address is dropped as a dead store. The `MZ` dispatcher therefore paints the
three ranges `volatile` when it loads the image, before any symbol is mapped
(the property is copied into a symbol as it is mapped, see `--assert
volatile`), skipping a range the load module overlaps (a module larger than
576 KiB would reach 0xA0000) and doing nothing under a language other than x86
real mode. Only accesses whose address the decompiler resolves into a range
are affected: an access through ES or DS holding the constant 0, 0x40 or a
video segment. A near access through a DS whose value is not known prints as
`*(short *)0x96` and is not resolved to linear 0x96, so it does not become
volatile. A `--raw-image` load is not painted: its addresses are its own (a
`.COM` program mapped at 0x100 is PSP-relative), so unlace cannot tell its low
addresses from the machine's, and `--assert volatile` remains the way to state
it. On DAZZLE four of 295 functions change: the tick poll and `delay()` keep
their reads, a video-mode probe keeps its read of the EGA switches at 0x487,
and the hard-disk parameter vectors at 0x104 and 0x118 are read where the code
reads them.

(unlace) **A WebAssembly module loads as a flat image of register-form code.**
(#1634; always on, no option: before it the module did not load at all.) A
module (`\0asm`, version 1) has no addresses: code is a list of bodies for a
stack machine, linear memory is its own index space, and globals and tables are
index spaces too. The decompiler works on addressed code that reads and writes
storage locations. Two steps at load close the gap, and after them a module is
an ordinary image.

*The module.* `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/wasm.rs (Module)`
reads the type, import, function, table, memory, global, export, start, element,
code and data sections and the `name` custom section's function and global
names. Every count is checked against the bytes left in its section before
anything is allocated, and a malformed section is an error with a reason; a
damaged `name` section only loses names.

*The layout.* `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_wasm.rs (WasmImage)`
gives each index space a fixed place in one 32-bit space:

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| `0x00000000` | linear memory 0 at its minimum size, zero except where an active data segment with a constant offset places bytes (a later segment wins an overlap) |
| `0x80000000` | code: every defined body, lowered, in function-index order |
| `0xd0000000` | globals, 16 bytes apart, each holding its constant initial value |
| `0xe0100000` | tables, as 4-byte code addresses, filled from the active element segments |
| `0xf0000000` | imported functions, 16 bytes apart, with no bytes behind them |

A linear-memory address in the program is therefore the address the decompiler
prints. A memory whose minimum exceeds 2 GiB, or a 64-bit memory, is refused. A
function's name is the `name` section's, else its export name, else (an import)
its field name, demangled as an object file's symbol is; a defined function with none is named at `read symbols` like
any other unnamed entry. An import is a named call target (`UndefinedExternal`,
as an object file's undefined symbol is), listed by `functions` and never
decompiled. Its declared signature is parked on it
(`loadimage_wasm.rs (WasmImage::prototypes)`), since it has no body to recover
one from; a defined function's signature is left to the decompiler, because a
locked `i32` parameter could no longer be typed as the pointer its body uses it
as. Each named global is a data symbol of its width, and each table is typed an
array of code pointers named by its export (else `table<N>`), so an indirect
call prints as `(*table0[i])(...)`. Read-only: the code; an immutable global
whose initializer is a constant; and a table nothing can write, which is one
that is neither imported nor exported in a module whose every body was lowered
(a lowered body holds no table write, an unlowered one may).

*The lowering.* A body is validated code, so the height of the operand stack at
each instruction is a static fact, and so is the type of each slot.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/wasmlower.rs (Lowering::lower)`
walks a
body with the validation algorithm's control stack and type stack and writes one
16-byte record per operation that still does something once the stack is gone:
the opcode, a type code where the opcode alone is untyped (`local.get`,
`select`), the stack height it runs at, and its immediates, with every branch
and call target already an address. Operand `k` from the top of the stack is
register slot `height - k`; a local is a register; a parameter arrives in an
argument register, and the first records of a body copy each parameter the body
reads to its local and zero every other local it reads. So `local.get 1; local.get 0; i32.mul` is `s0 = l1; s1 =
l0; s0 = s0 * s1`, which the decompiler's ordinary dataflow turns back into one
expression. The rest of the mapping:

- `block`, `loop`, `end`, `nop`, `drop` and the reinterpret casts leave no
  record. `if` is a branch past its true arm when the condition is zero, and
  `else` a branch past the false arm.
- A branch (`br`, `br_if`, `return`) that carries values to a label expecting
  them at a lower height is preceded by `move` records; a conditional one whose
  moves must not run on the fall-through path is a `br_unless` around them.
- `br_table` is a bounds test that branches to the default label, then an
  indirect jump through a table of addresses stored after the record; the
  decompiler's own jump-table recovery reads it as a `switch`. A target that
  needs moves gets a trampoline after the table.
- A call is one `arg` record per parameter, the call, and a `result` record.
  `call_indirect` loads its target from the table's region; `return_call` is
  the call followed by the return.
- A global is the memory at its slot. The exception is the mutable `i32` global
  the `name` section or an export calls `__stack_pointer`: the toolchain
  convention for the linear-memory stack, lowered to the stack-pointer register,
  so a frame carved from it is recovered as stack locals instead of printed as
  arithmetic on a global.
- Code the validation rules make unreachable is dropped.

A body is refused, and becomes a single `unsupported` record (it decompiles to
`unsupported();`), when it does not validate or uses something outside this
slice: SIMD, reference types and table instructions, exceptions, atomics,
passive-segment instructions, a function type with more than one result, a
memory other than memory 0, more than 8192 locals, 1024 parameters or an
operand stack deeper than 1024 (the registers the language names), or branches
whose carried values would lower to more than four records per byte of the
body (compiled code stays under one; the bound keeps a hostile body from
lowering to gigabytes). The load
prints one `[unlace wasm]` note with the count and the first reason. Segments
whose offset is not a constant inside their memory or table are counted and
reported the same way.

*The language.* `specs/Ghidra/Processors/Wasm/data/languages/Wasm.slaspec` gives
each record its p-code; the language id is `Wasm:LE:32:default` and a module
decodes as nothing else. The compiler spec passes arguments in the `a<N>`
register range, returns in one register per value type (`ri0`, `rl0`, `rf0`,
`rd0`, so an `i32` result is never read as the stale half of an earlier `f64`
one), keeps locals and stack slots across a call, and uses linear memory as the
stack space. Operations p-code has no operator for are user ops (`rotl`,
`rotr`, `ctz`, `fmin`, `fmax`, `fcopysign`, `memory_copy`, `memory_fill`,
`memory_size`, `memory_grow`, `trap` for `unreachable`); `f*.trunc` and
`f*.nearest` are the `FLOAT_TRUNC` and `FLOAT_ROUNDEVEN` user ops that chapter
05 types as float to float.

The dispatcher is `crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs
(bootstrap_wasm_bytes)`. Surfaces that need an `object::File` (`strings`,
`xrefs`, `decompile-graph`) refuse a module with a capability error, as they do
a TE. Measured on a 2.6 MB Go `wasip1` module: 1792 functions load in 0.08 s
and every body lowers. Checked by compiling the printed C of functions from
`tests/fixtures/wasm/calls.wasm` beside their source and comparing results on
random inputs (`crates/unlace-cli/tests/wasm_cli.rs`), and by
`tests/stages/wasm-module.toml`.
(unlace) **The Device memory of an M-profile image is volatile** (always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/cortexmdevice.rs (paint_volatile)`).
The ARMv7-M and ARMv8-M memory maps make two regions Device memory on every
part: the Peripheral region (0x40000000-0x5FFFFFFF), where a vendor maps its
on-chip peripherals, and the System region (0xE0000000-0xFFFFFFFF), the Private
Peripheral Bus with the NVIC, SysTick and System Control Block and the vendor
system space above it. A load there may return a new value each time and every
store has an effect, so read as ordinary memory the first of two writes to a
peripheral register is deleted as a dead store, two reads of a data register
merge, and a status-register poll is hoisted out of its loop. An image is
M-profile when its language is `ARM:*:32:Cortex` or `ARM:*:32:v8-m`, or when it
is an ARM ELF whose build attributes state `Tag_CPU_arch_profile` `'M'`. The ELF
loader paints both regions `volatile` after it maps the sections and before any
symbol is mapped (a symbol takes the property as it is mapped, see `--assert
volatile`); a raw-image load under a Cortex-M language does the same. A range
the image maps itself (a section linked into the Peripheral region, or a raw
image based there) is left out, since its contents are the image's own. Only
accesses whose address the decompiler resolves are affected: a register
reached through a pointer held in a structure or passed as an argument is not.

A Mach-O image also carries its dependency list and run paths, read from the thin image's own load commands by `loader/macho_dylibs.rs`. Every `LC_LOAD_DYLIB`, `LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB`, `LC_REEXPORT_DYLIB`, `LC_LAZY_LOAD_DYLIB` and `LC_LOAD_UPWARD_DYLIB` becomes a `Dylib` that keeps the command that named it, its install name and its current and compatibility versions; each `LC_RPATH` becomes a run path, kept as written. Both lists are in load-command order and are exposed by `ObjectLoadImage::macho_dependencies`. They are facts the file states, so no option gates them. The walk is bounded by the header's `sizeofcmds` and each command's `cmdsize`; a command that runs past the input ends it and an unterminated string is dropped. A fat file is peeled before the loader sees it, and any input that is not a thin Mach-O yields an empty list. A relocatable object names no dylib and carries none.

(unlace) **A Lua `luac` chunk parses into its prototype tree.** (#1263, first step: the container only. No option: nothing loads it yet, so no output changes.) `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/lua.rs (LuaChunk::parse)` reads a chunk of Lua 5.1 to 5.4 into plain tables: the header and its byte order, every prototype in dump order with its source name (NULL means the enclosing function's), line-defined range, parameters, vararg flag and stack size, the raw instruction words, the constant pool (nil, boolean, integer, float and raw-byte string), upvalue descriptors (5.2 and later), nested prototypes, and the debug lines, 5.4 absolute line anchors, locals and upvalue names. Each release's field order and tag values follow its own dumper; 5.3 writes float as tag 3 and integer as 0x13, the reverse of 5.4. Every count is checked against the bytes left before anything is stored, nesting stops at 200 levels, and a truncated or malformed chunk is an error. A 5.2 header carries no byte-order mark, so a big-endian 5.2 chunk is read as little-endian; 5.3 and 5.4 chunks take their byte order from `LUAC_INT`. Decoding the instructions and naming the functions from the parsed tree are the next steps.

**PE resource tree.** `crates/unlace-analysis/src/pe_resources.rs (resource_entries)`
walks `IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_RESOURCE` through `object`'s `ResourceDirectory` API
and returns one flat record per leaf: type, name and language ids, then the data's
RVA and size. Named (string) entries read as id 0. The walk is depth-capped at 8
and bounded at 65536 records, so a hostile directory cannot recurse or allocate
without limit. It is a reader only: nothing in the decompile path consumes it
yet, so no default output changes and it needs no option. The version-info strings
still come from the UTF-16 key scan in `unlace-cli`'s `sbom/pever.rs`.

## 1.3 Loader markup

Import naming exists because a CALL into a linkage stub carries no symbol: without
it `FlowInfo`'s call query finds nothing and every library call prints
`sub_<addr>(...)`. Each format reconstructs the stub→name map from its own linkage
structures, and all of them emit the same `ImportSym` currency into the loader's
funcsym stream:

- **ELF** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elf_plt.rs
  (resolve_plt_imports)`, the `ElfDefaultGotPltMarkup` analog): build
  `got_slot → name` from the dynamic relocations, then decode each `.plt*` stub's
  indirect jump per architecture (x86-64/x32, i386, AArch64, ARM, RISC-V, SPARC,
  s390x)
  and match the *decoded* GOT target against the map — self-correcting, since PLT0
  and IRELATIVE/IFUNC stubs jump to non-symbol-bearing slots and fall out
  automatically. `.plt.sec`/`.plt.got` outrank `.plt` so the CET call target wins.
  On SPARC the stub and the key coincide (`R_SPARC_JMP_SLOT`'s offset is the PLT
  entry itself), so a `sethi %g1`-headed word that is a relocation key is named
  when a complete entry fits behind it: 12 bytes for ELF32 (SPARC, SPARC32Plus),
  32 for ELF64, whatever the word's offset from the start of the scanned window.
  An s390x stub (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/s390xplt.rs
  (decode)`) is `larl %r1,slot; lg %r1,0(%r1); br %r1` from both GNU `ld` and
  `lld`; the PLT header starts with the same `larl` but continues with `mvc`,
  so it names nothing.
  `option ifuncfpret` (on by default, x86-64) adds a second pass that DOES name those
  IRELATIVE IFUNC stubs — `ifunc_<resolver>`, keyed off the `R_X86_64_IRELATIVE`
  resolver-address map — so a tail `jmp` to a glibc math/mem/str dispatcher's stub
  is recovered as a `tailcalljump` to a discovered function instead of flowing into
  the stub and rendering `(*dat_...)(...)`; the FP-return-type recovery it unblocks
  is a Ghidra-divergent follow-up (`docs/features/ifuncfpret/proposal.md`).
  Two ABIs need special handling: PowerPC (ELFv2 `.plt` is a NOBITS data table, not
  decodable code; PPC32 uses its own secure-PLT stub shape), and **MIPS**, which
  has no PLT and no jump-slot relocations at all — its resolver walks the
  `.MIPS.stubs`/GOT layout from the dynamic table (`DT_MIPS_LOCAL_GOTNO`/
  `DT_MIPS_GOTSYM`) and marks the external GOT slots constant, so with
  read-only propagation the `lw $t9, off($gp); jalr $t9` sequence folds to the
  named import (the bootstrap turns `readonlypropagate` on for MIPS only).
  Only a slot that holds its import's stub address is marked. An import with no
  lazy stub (its address is taken, or the reference is weak) has a slot holding
  0, which the dynamic linker overwrites with the import's address at load
  time; folding that 0 printed `(*NULL)(a0)` for the call and folded a weak
  `if (hook) hook();` guard away, so such a slot stays variable and reads like
  an x86-64 `-fno-plt` GOT call, `(*dat_<slot>)(a0)`. The slots of what the
  image itself defines are covered under `dynrelocs` below.
  PPC32 linked images use
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppc32_imports.rs (resolve)`:
  a zero-addend `R_PPC_JMP_SLOT` names its call target directly inside an
  allocated, writable, executable NOBITS `.plt`, after the reserved 72-byte
  header. Secure-PLT entries are pointer slots instead: complete `r11` load,
  `mtctr r11`, `bctr` stubs in executable sections are named only when their
  decoded address matches such a relocation in the non-executable `.plt`.
  Absolute stubs encode the address directly. For PIC stubs, the loader instead
  exposes validated relocation-slot metadata through
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppc32_imports.rs (pic_slots)`.
  Duplicate relocations, nonzero addends, data-symbol relocations and slots
  outside the allocated writable non-executable `.plt` are rejected. This
  metadata neither names executable stubs nor adds global no-return contracts.
  The `ppc32picimports on` mode consumes it during P2 flow, in the
  selected caller's register context. Metadata is available after loading even
  when the option is off, so `on`/`off` changes require no reload for an image
  loaded without `abi`. Entering or leaving `abi` requires reloading the image
  because its loader identities persist for that image. The default is `off`.
  `DT_PPC_GOT`, GOT headers and `.got2` locate tables, not the value of r30.
  Both ELF byte orders are supported. BSS-PLT and absolute-stub naming remains
  independent of this option. This does not add a sectionless PPC32 resolver.
  The `ppc32picimports abi` mode additionally resolves short and long PIC stubs through
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppc32picimports.rs (resolve)`.
  A PIC stub loads its target from `r30` plus a displacement, so its import is
  whatever `r30` its callers hold. The stub is named only when every transfer
  into it is reached by the proof and all of them select the same `JMP_SLOT`.
  The proof walks the image once from every entry: exported and local symbols,
  call targets, relocated code pointers, the ELF entry, `DT_INIT`/`DT_FINI` and
  `.eh_frame` function starts. A local symbol or FDE start that only other
  functions branch to (a `.cold` part) is not an entry; their walks continue
  into it. Each walk starts from symbolic registers: the caller's values of
  the nonvolatile registers, the entry stack pointer and return address. It
  tracks constants, stack offsets, the stack words that hold a saved
  nonvolatile register, the return address or a back chain, and loads from
  words whose runtime value the image fixes (code, read-only data and
  relocated GOT entries). `bcl 20,31` reads the program counter; it is not a
  call. Counted conditional branches decrement CTR on both successors, and
  indirect LR/CTR targets discard their low two bits. Joins keep equal values
  only. A stack word below `r1` holds nothing
  the walk knows: a signal frame or a callee's frame can overwrite it at any
  time, and a callee also writes its return address to `4(r1)`. `stwcx.` may
  store nothing and `stwbrx` stores reversed bytes, so neither saves a
  register. Scalar stores invalidate every saved word overlapping their actual
  effective-address range, including unaligned reversed and indexed floating-point
  stores. Only vector stores apply their instruction-defined alignment mask.
  The return address stays in registers and the frame's save
  words: a walk that stores it anywhere else, moves it to a special register
  other than LR and CTR, or calls through it forgets everything (below).
  A call to an import, or through a register, continues at the next
  instruction with `r1`, `r2` and `r13`-`r31` kept, as the SysV calling
  convention guarantees. A call to local code uses that function's summary:
  the nonvolatile registers every return restores, and whether it returns at
  all. Summaries come from the callee's own walk. They start from the
  strongest claim and weaken until no caller's view changes. This greatest
  fixed point is sound for recursion by induction on the depth of a call that
  returns. A callee whose walk forgets everything may return anywhere in the
  code that called it, so each caller's walk forgets everything as well. A
  straight-line helper ending in `blr`, such as libgcc's
  `_savegpr_N`/`_restgpr_N`, runs in the caller's state instead, unless it
  reads LR. The helper recognizer, normal walk and unresolved-edge walk share
  opcode-19 classification: only CR operations and `isync` are known fallthrough
  forms. TAR transfers and other unmodeled forms refuse a straight-line helper
  and flood the affected walk instead of applying skipped register writes or
  restores. A linked TAR branch is also a potential exception call site.
  A tail branch into another function returns through LR: to the
  walk's caller for the entry return address, and to a known address of the
  same code for a constant LR. Any other LR, such as the return address a
  call left behind, makes the branch an unresolved jump. A branch or table
  jump to an entry strictly inside its own function (a label whose address a
  computed goto takes) continues the walk there instead. The walk does not continue past a call to an import that its own
  proven slot names on the base ELF no-return list (`abort`, `exit`, `err`,
  `__stack_chk_fail`, `__cxa_throw`, `_Unwind_Resume`, `std::__throw_*` and the
  like) — the list `on` mode and the `noreturn_known` marking of the named stub
  also use, so the three agree on every import. It also stops after a call that is the last instruction of its FDE
  range or sized symbol (a stub that call would run into if it returned is
  never named), after `sc` with `r0` = 1 or 234 (`exit`,
  `exit_group`), and after an unconditional trap.
  Each landing pad in an LSDA call-site table is entered from the calls in
  its range, with their nonvolatile registers. A jump table is followed when
  the target is the table base plus a table word (PIC) or a table word itself.
  The index is shifted by two. An unsigned `cmplwi` the branch has passed, or
  the shift's mask, bounds it, and every bounded entry inside the jump's
  function is a target. An unbounded table is read until its first target
  outside the function. An entry outside the function is no case label, but
  a stub it runs into is never named. A target inside the dispatch sequence itself is never
  a case label. Any other indirect jump might reach any instruction of its
  function, including the GOT-pointer setup, so that walk forgets everything.
  It then floods what it reaches: a stub entered from there gets no evidence,
  and its summary keeps nothing. The failure stays scoped to what that
  function's walk reaches.
  A load resolves imports about twenty times; it holds its image buffer in an
  `ImportProofScope` (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppc32picimports.rs`)
  so those resolutions share one proof. The scope borrows the immutable buffer,
  so its address identifies the image while the load runs; nothing is copied or
  retained once the load ends. The console carries the proof with the stashed
  bytes to the deferred analyses at `read symbols`. An image resolved outside a
  scope is proved on each request, so another image can never reuse its
  identities, whatever its length or hash.
  The soundness argument rests on the toolchain and ABI, stated as
  assumptions. (1) Stub provenance: the linker writes a PIC stub's address
  only into branch fields (`R_PPC_REL24`, `R_PPC_PLTREL24`, `R_PPC_LOCAL24PC`).
  No relocation yields it for data or address arithmetic, and the stub has no
  symbol an input object could name. So no code pointer (a return address,
  function pointer, jump-table or landing-pad target) holds a stub address.
  The one exception, a call immediately before a stub, is a fallthrough site.
  An uncertified transfer elsewhere therefore cannot enter a stub; that is
  why one failing caller withdraws only the stubs its own walk reaches. The
  proof checks the observable part. A stub is never named when a data word,
  relocation, symbol (other than a local label at its start), the image entry,
  `DT_INIT`/`DT_FINI`, a landing pad or a branch points into it or into its
  padding. The same holds when a computed constant equal to its address is
  stored or passed, or when an unresolved jump's function contains it.
  Dynamic relocations in code reject the image. (2) Calling convention:
  imports and functions called through registers restore `r1`, `r2` and
  `r13`-`r31`. Local code is not trusted; its summary is proven. (3) A
  function's switch tables and computed gotos target its own code: its FDE
  range or sized symbol, else the code between neighbouring entries and stubs.
  (4) Exceptions are raised by calls, as in C and C++ without
  `-fnon-call-exceptions`. The unwinder enters a landing pad with the throwing
  call's nonvolatile registers. (5) Only a frame's own function writes its
  register save words, at fixed offsets from `r1` or its frame pointer. A
  pointer from elsewhere, or one the walk cannot compute, addresses a program
  object, so a callee given a local's address cannot overwrite the saved `r30`
  or LR. Only the dynamic linker writes GOT words, with their relocated
  values. No code rewrites a saved context (a `jmp_buf` or a signal's
  `ucontext`), and no function keeps a return address it received in a
  register other than LR for other code to jump to.
  (6) Compiled code does not run past the end of its FDE range or sized
  symbol, and the listed no-return functions do not return. (7) A function's
  address is taken through a relocated data word or a symbol, so the seeded
  entries are the only ones. Under these assumptions every runtime path to a
  stub starts at a seeded entry and follows modeled edges. The walk's state
  over-approximates every runtime state, so a constant `r30` at every
  transfer into a stub is the runtime `r30`. A stub's name is the slot its
  callers really load: code that moves `r30` between the linker's base and a
  call (as hand-written assembly can) is named after the slot it reaches, not
  after the linker's label. `DT_PPC_GOT`, a valid GOT header and a retained
  `_GLOBAL_OFFSET_TABLE_` symbol locate the GOT but never establish `r30`;
  GNU ld can discard an empty `.got2` while callers still use its per-object
  base. Duplicate relocation slots, nonzero addends, data symbols and
  incomplete stubs provide no import identity. A `.gcc_except_table` without a
  readable `.eh_frame` rejects the image, and an FDE whose LSDA cannot be read
  makes its function's walk forget everything. The walk is bounded by 64 visits
  and table reads per code word; an image that exhausts it gets no PIC names. Both byte orders
  are supported. Off keeps PIC stubs unresolved; BSS-PLT and absolute stubs
  are unaffected. In the console, set the option before `load file`; CLI
  options are bridged before either loader runs. The `abi` mode is opt-in because
  the proof walks every function:
  about 0.3-0.4 s for libstdc++ or libc, which makes listing a PPC32 PIC
  image's functions 1.1-1.8x slower and a single-function decompile up to 3x.
  The default path and other formats pay nothing, and the proof runs once per
  image content. Resolved PPC32 import names take
  precedence over local stub labels, which remain aliases. Existing library
  prototypes, no-return facts and name-based xrefs therefore see the same
  imported identity, including when a terminal call has no mapped fall-through
  bytes. This does not add a sectionless PPC32 resolver.
  Every input named so far is keyed on the section table — `object` builds its
  dynamic-relocation iterator by scanning it for `SHT_REL`/`SHT_RELA`, reads
  `.dynsym` as a section, and the stub scan finds `.plt*` by name — so an ELF
  whose section table is absent or unusable gets its bytes and none of its import
  markup, and every library call prints `(*dat_<slot>)(...)`. None of that
  information is actually section-bound.
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elf_dynseg.rs (dynamic_imports)`
  reads it out of `PT_DYNAMIC` instead — `DT_SYMTAB`/`DT_STRTAB`/`DT_SYMENT` for
  the names, `DT_JMPREL` (with `DT_PLTREL`/`DT_PLTRELSZ`) and `DT_RELA`/`DT_REL`
  for the slots they attach to, `DT_PLTGOT` as the i386 GOT anchor
  `_GLOBAL_OFFSET_TABLE_` otherwise supplies — translating each virtual address
  through the `PT_LOAD` map, which is how the run-time loader finds the same
  tables. It runs only when the section-driven resolution produced **nothing at
  all**, so it adds names to an image that had none and can never move a name on
  an image whose sections are intact. The PLT is deliberately not reconstructed
  as a range: with no section name left there is no honest bound for it, and a
  guessed sub-range of an executable segment names stubs off by an entry.
  Each executable `PT_LOAD` window is handed whole to the same per-architecture
  decoders, and the decoded-GOT-target match above decides which instructions in
  it were stubs — the relocation slots are the bound. PowerPC and MIPS are
  excluded: neither resolves through a `.plt` code section at all, and both need a
  section-derived anchor this path cannot supply.
- **Linked-image dynamic relocations** (unlace, `dynrelocs`, always on): the
  loader maps the `PT_LOAD` bytes the *linker* wrote, which is
  not the image a process runs. Every slot filled by a dynamic relocation —
  `R_*_RELATIVE`, `R_*_GLOB_DAT`, `R_*_JUMP_SLOT` — is left at zero for the
  run-time loader to complete, and in a PIE (which is the default link mode of
  every current toolchain) that is the whole `.got` plus every relocated function
  pointer in `.data.rel.ro`. A call through such a slot therefore reads a null
  target and can never resolve, which is the `(*dat_<addr>)(...)` rendering of a
  callee that is a *named function in the very same image*. Zero is not an
  ambiguity to be judged; it is a byte the run-time image never holds.
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/dynrelocs.rs (resolve)` reads
  the tables the way the run-time loader finds them, through `PT_DYNAMIC`
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/dynrelocs/dtable.rs
  (dynamic_relocations)`): `DT_RELA`, `DT_REL` and `DT_JMPREL` entries, the
  `DT_RELR` bitmap (an even word is a `RELATIVE` slot, an odd word marks the
  next 63 or 31 slots), Android's `DT_ANDROID_RELR`, and Android's `APS2`
  packed `DT_ANDROID_REL[A]` stream (SLEB128 groups sharing offset delta, info or
  addend), with symbols read from `DT_SYMTAB`. Section headers are not consulted,
  so an image whose section table is stripped or forged is still relocated; an
  image with no `PT_DYNAMIC` falls back to the section walk. For each entry it
  computes the value the dynamic loader would store: for `RELATIVE` the image's load bias plus the addend (unlace maps a
  linked image at the vaddrs it declares, so the bias is zero and the value is the
  addend); for `GLOB_DAT`/`JUMP_SLOT` the symbol's address, **and only when that
  symbol is defined in this same image**. An undefined one is an import — its
  value lives in another object, there is nothing to write, and the PLT/import
  naming above already covers the call — so it is skipped and that path is
