  untouched, lazy-binding stub contents included. A `REL` table (32-bit ELF)
  carries no addend field, so the in-place word is read back as the addend, the
  same in-place convention `relocobjects` uses; a `RELR` slot always holds its
  addend in place. The word-sized absolute relocation (`R_X86_64_64`,
  `R_AARCH64_ABS64`, ...) against a defined symbol writes `S + A`. An
  `IRELATIVE` slot is left alone, since only running the resolver gives its
  value, but the resolver is a function no symbol may name: it joins the
  function symbols as `ifunc_<addr>` unless one is already there (`ifunc_<addr>`
  is IDA's spelling). Architectures are named by their relocation types: x86-64,
  AArch64, i386, ARM, PowerPC64, RISC-V and s390x; a machine with no entry
  produces nothing rather than guessing at a number that means something else
  there.

  Applying the relocation is only half of it. `.got` is `SHF_WRITE`, so nothing
  downstream would trust a value read out of it, and the constant fold of
  read-only storage is gated program-wide by `option readonly`
  (`readonlypropagate`, default off — turning it on would fold every `.rodata`
  read in the program, a far larger change than this one). The narrow warrant is
  `PT_GNU_RELRO`: the linker's own statement that the segment is `mprotect`ed
  read-only once startup relocation finishes. So the written slots that RELRO
  covers are reported twice — through `getReadonly` (which paints
  `Varnode::readonly` as for any read-only section) and separately as
  `ObjectLoadImage::dynreloc_const_ranges`, carried to
  `Architecture::dynreloc_const` and into every per-function handle, where
  `ActionVarnodeProps` folds a read-only varnode inside one of those ranges even
  with global propagation off (§3.4). The halves are useless apart: relocating
  without the constancy leaves the load unfolded, and declaring constancy without
  relocating would fold the call target to zero. Slots outside RELRO — a
  `RELATIVE` pointer in ordinary `.data` — are still filled in, because that IS
  the value at process start, but are never declared constant, because the
  program may legitimately overwrite them.

  A MIPS dynamic image relocates its primary GOT with no relocation records at
  all (glibc's `elf_machine_got_rel`), so the walk above never reaches it. Its
  first `DT_MIPS_LOCAL_GOTNO` entries are local: page or full link-time
  addresses, to which the run-time loader adds the load bias. Entry 0 (the lazy
  resolver) and entry 1 when its top bit is set (the GNU module pointer) are
  written at run time. The global entries that follow map one to one onto
  `.dynsym` from `DT_MIPS_GOTSYM` to `DT_MIPS_SYMTABNO`, and for a symbol the
  image defines the run-time loader stores the address its lookup binds the
  name to, which the linker already wrote as the symbol's value. At unlace's zero
  bias each of those slots holds its run-time value, and only the run-time
  loader ever writes one, so
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsgot.rs (const_ranges)`
  reports every local entry after the reserved ones, and every defined symbol's
  global entry whose contents are that symbol's value, as constant beside the
  import-stub slots above (`ElfFormat::const_ranges`; MIPS folds read-only
  loads). `lw $25,%call16(add64)($gp); jalr $25` to a function of the same image
  becomes a call to `add64`, a `%got` page load plus `%lo` names the static or
  global it addresses, and a PIC jump table's base folds, so its switch is
  recovered. A `jr $25` tail call through such a slot is a one-destination
  table, which `tailcalljump` (§2.2) takes as a call or copies in. A
  default-visibility definition in a shared object can be interposed by another
  object's definition of the same name; the fold names the symbol the access
  binds by and gives it the body this image carries, the choice this pass makes
  for a `GLOB_DAT` slot of a defined symbol. Undefined, common, absolute, TLS
  and `STT_GNU_IFUNC` symbols are skipped, as is a multi-GOT image's secondary
  GOT, which `R_MIPS_REL32` records relocate. Every slot is read from the
  allocated section that holds `DT_PLTGOT`, so a count that claims more entries
  than that section holds stops at its end.

  This is a different path from `relocobjects`/`relocrebase` above, which own the
  *pre-link* `ET_REL` object; a relocatable object's relocations are applied by
  the layout pass and this walk does not run for it.

  A Mach-O has the same two halves in Apple's format, and takes them under the
  same gate through
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/machorelocs.rs (resolve)`. A
  chained-fixup image stores no pointer in a fixed-up slot at all: the word is a
  packed `dyld_chained_ptr_*` entry whose high bits carry the chain's next hop,
  so `__objc_selrefs[0]` reads `0x001000010000090c` in the file where the running
  program holds `0x10000090c`, and anything that folds such a load without
  unpacking it folds to garbage. dyld unpacks every chain at load; the loader
  does the same on its own segment copies, writing each rebase the §1.2 resolver
  decoded (bind slots, being imports, are left as the linker wrote them, exactly
  as an undefined ELF symbol is). The constancy warrant is the segment flag
  `SG_READ_ONLY`, which the linker sets on `__DATA_CONST` to tell dyld to remap
  the segment read-only once the fixups are applied — the same promise
  `PT_GNU_RELRO` makes — so the rebased slots of such a segment join
  `dynreloc_const` and fold, while a rebase in writable `__DATA` is written but
  not declared constant. The Objective-C reference slots live in `__DATA`,
  outside this warrant; their constancy comes from the metadata instead (§1.4,
  `objc`). A classic
  image (`LC_DYLD_INFO` rebase and bind opcodes) needs no write: its rebased words
  are already the unslid pointers, and its bound slots are already zero or a
  stub-helper address.
- **Data-held pointers** (unlace,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/dataptrs.rs (data_pointers)`):
  the read-only twin of the two writers above, for `unlace xrefs`. A word in data
  that holds `&audit_target` is a reference no instruction makes, so the
  instruction walk never reports it, and calling it a call edge would be wrong.
  But a rebased image lists every such word, because its loader must fix each
  one up: a chained-fixup Mach-O threads them on its chains (the rebase carries
  its target), a classic Mach-O lists them in its `LC_DYLD_INFO` rebase opcodes
  (interpreted here; the slot already holds the unslid target), a
  position-independent ELF carries a dynamic relocation for each, and a PE lists
  them in `.reloc`. The ELF list is read here, not through `dynrelocs` (whose
  writes are an option of the loaded image): a `RELATIVE` word holds `B + A`, and
  so does every packed `SHT_RELR` slot (Android's `SHT_ANDROID_RELR` is the same
  encoding under other constants), whose addend is the word it holds; an
  absolute word, `GLOB_DAT` or `JUMP_SLOT` against a symbol the image defines
  holds `S + A`. The absolute kind is how a shared object stores its own exported
  functions, which are preemptible (`R_X86_64_64 audit_target` for the first entry
  of a callback table). The relocation numbers are per machine
  (`dataptrs.rs (pointer_relocs)`), each checked against `llvm-readelf -r`
  on a shared object linked for it: x86-64, i386, AArch64 and ARM share
  `dynrelocs`' triple; RISC-V has no `GLOB_DAT` and fills its GOT with the
  absolute `R_RISCV_64` / `R_RISCV_32`; PowerPC64's `JMP_SLOT` is a word only
  under ELFv2 (`e_flags` ABI 2), an ELFv1 PLT slot being a copied function
  descriptor; and a 32-bit PowerPC `JMP_SLOT` is a word only under the secure PLT
  (`DT_PPC_GOT`), the BSS PLT patching code instead. PowerPC also has an
  unaligned absolute word, `UADDR32` / `UADDR64`, which GNU ld emits for a
  pointer at an unaligned offset (a packed struct); a 32-bit one against a local
  symbol stores `B + A`, binutils having folded the symbol's value into the
  addend, which is what glibc's loader adds. A machine with no entry is
  not guessed at: MIPS relocates its local GOT entries without a relocation, so
  its relocations would be a partial list presented as a whole one, and SPARC's
  could not be verified. The list keeps each word whose target is in an
  allocated section, and says how much of the metadata it covers
  (`Coverage`), because an empty list is only an answer when that metadata was
  read in full. `Complete` names the source. `Partial` names it too, plus
  what was not read: an allocated `SHT_REL`/`SHT_RELA` section whose `sh_link` is
  not the dynamic symbol table (the generic relocation walk skips it, and so does
  `resolve`), a table section whose bytes lie outside the file or are not a
  whole number of entries (skipped the same way), a table the dynamic section
  declares (`DT_RELA`, `DT_REL`, `DT_JMPREL`, `DT_RELR`, `DT_ANDROID_RELR`) that
  no readable section covers (an image without section headers), an
  Android-packed table (`DT_ANDROID_RELA`), `SHT_RELR` entries that name more
  slots than the file has words (a valid table names distinct aligned words the
  file holds, so decoding stops there and a crafted table cannot multiply
  memory), a PE base-relocation directory outside every
  section or a block that does not fit in it (the blocks are walked here, a
  zero-size one ending the walk as it ends the loader's), a Mach-O
  `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS` blob outside the file, a chain walk that stopped
  short (`ChainedFixups::damage`: a truncated header or start table, a pointer
  format the walk does not decode, a chain that leaves the segments' file data,
  kernel-collection rebases whose own collection level is unknown), a
  rebase-opcode stream that
  ends in an operand or names a segment the image lacks, and slots with no file
  data to read (`dynrelocs.rs (unread_tables)`). `Unsupported` is metadata
  unlace does not read: a machine above without an entry, a relocatable object's
  relocations, a Mach-O image's `LC_DYSYMTAB` local relocations, the static
  relocation sections an `--emit-relocs` executable keeps, and the rebases of an
  image built into a dyld shared cache or kernel collection (`MH_DYLIB_IN_CACHE`:
  the cache's slide info or the collection's chained fixups hold them, and the
  image's own `LC_DYLD_INFO` is empty or absent, which would otherwise read as
  complete). `None` is an image
  with no pointer-relocation metadata at all (a non-PIE ELF executable, whose own
  pointers carry no relocation, a PE without a base-relocation directory or with
  one of size 0, which the loader treats as none, a
  non-PIE Mach-O executable without rebase opcodes): its pointers are plain
  words no metadata tells from integers, and guessing would make an empty answer
  mean two things. Metadata that exists and lists nothing is complete with no
  rows: an ELF PIE without a pointer relocation, a chained-fixup image that only
  binds, a slid Mach-O (`MH_PIE`, a dylib or bundle) whose `LC_DYLD_INFO`
  rebases nothing, a PE directory of only padding. Each non-complete coverage
  carries its reason. A bound slot is not
  listed, since it holds an address of another image. `unlace xrefs` reports these
  as separate `pointer` rows with that coverage, never merged into the
  instruction rows or the call graph (`docs/cli.md`). On x86 an instruction can
  embed an absolute address, so a 32-bit PE's `.reloc` also lists every
  `push offset f` and `jmp [slot]` operand in `.text`; a word that lies inside a
  decoded instruction referencing the same address (the instruction's bytes, as
  its own decode measures them, cover the word) is that instruction's row and is
  left out (`xrefs.rs (data_rows)`). A word just past the instruction, such as a
  pointer table placed in `.text` after a `mov eax, offset f`, stays a pointer,
  and so does one inside an instruction the walk never decoded or whose reference
  it did not record, so dropping a row never leaves the word unanswered.
- **Fixup sites** (unlace, GH #1379,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/dynrelocs.rs (fixup_sites)`):
  the slots whose loaded bytes the two writers above may have rewritten, for a
  reader of the load image that must say which of its bytes are the file's. It
  lists every slot of the metadata `resolve` walks, the ones it leaves alone
  included: each chained-fixup rebase (with its target) and bind (with the
  import it names and its addend), and each dynamic relocation of a linked ELF.
  It also lists the packed `SHT_RELR` relocations `resolve` does not read
  (`relr_sites`, on any machine): each is a rebase whose target is the word its
  slot already holds, so there is nothing to write. A `RELATIVE` relocation is a
  rebase whose target is `B + A`; a `GLOB_DAT` or `JUMP_SLOT` one is a bind,
  valued `S + A` where the image defines the symbol and unvalued for an import;
  any other kind (`COPY`, `IRELATIVE`, an absolute word, TLS, and every
  relocation of a machine without the triple) is listed unvalued, because the
  loader rewrites the slot and unlace does not. Both callers share one
  per-relocation classifier (`ElfTable::classify`), and `resolve` writes exactly
  the valued rebases and binds, as before. The list is read regardless, so a
  reader compares the loaded bytes with the file's
  to learn what was applied. The coverage is `Partial` when some of an ELF's
  tables, or of a Mach-O's chains, were not read, by the same accounts
  (`unread_tables`, the `SHT_RELR` bound, `ChainedFixups::damage`) the data-held
  pointers use: their slots are absent from the list and hold the file's bytes,
  since `resolve` did not read them either. That account is of the tables a
  dynamic loader applies, so an image without a dynamic section (a static
  executable, whose `.rela.plt` of `IRELATIVE` entries links `.symtab` and is
  applied by its own startup code) has none to miss. Any other image lists
  none, under coverage `none`.
- **ELF GOT data imports** (unlace, `elfgotimports`, committed under `importdata`,
  default on; `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elfgotimports.rs`):
  the complement of the `dynrelocs` walk above. A `GLOB_DAT` slot whose symbol is *undefined*
  is skipped there because its value lives in another object, and the PLT/import
  naming covers a *call* to it. A `-fPIC` *data* read is not a call: it loads the
  slot (the import's address) and then loads through it, and with nothing naming
  the slot that printed as `*dat_<slot>` — or, for a stdio stream `libctypes`
  types, as `*stdout_ptr`. `resolve` lists every such slot with its symbol, over
  the same relocation triple (x86-64, AArch64, i386, ARM). `ElfFormat::import_slots`
  reports them, so a slot is a pointer word and never a function body. The pass
  names each one for its import (a symbol-table `FunctionSymbol`, as the format's
  own import names are, but not a function-inventory entry, since the slot is not a
  function; the name goes through the `symbolnamechars` sanitizer like every name
  the loader mints) and paints it `externref`, so `PrintC::op_load`
  renders the read as the import (`importdata`, chapter [09](09-emission.md)):
  `return imported_counter;`, `return environ;`, `stdout`. Painting the slot also
  lets `ActionDeindirect` bind a call through it (`(*dat_e9f30)()` becomes
  `__cxa_finalize()`), the binding `peimportcall` gives a PE or Mach-O slot. A slot
  whose symbol the image defines is never taken. `dynrelocs` already fills it in and
  folds it to the object (`exported_value`, `&exported_value`), and `externref` would
  stop that fold. The same holds for a local GOT entry (`RELATIVE` to an in-image
  object) inside RELRO, which the fold above already renders as the object. A
  local entry outside RELRO stays a dereference for the reason given above.
- **Mach-O data-import slots** (unlace, `machodataslots`, committed under
  `importdata`, default on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/machodataslots.rs`): the
  Mach-O counterpart. The indirect-symbol walk (`macho_stubs.rs`) names every
  `__got` / `__la_symbol_ptr` entry after the import it holds and hands each to
  the function-symbol stream, so a call through the slot resolves and the slot
  is a canonical inventory entry (chapter [00](00-overview.md)). A symbol-pointer
  slot of a data object is a pointer word too, but never a callable one, and it
  was listed as a size-0 function all the same: 7,865 of a 72 MB Swift app's
  270,680 entries were `__got` words. The walk keeps out of the import stream
  every slot whose import's *mangling* says it is data (`is_data_import`): an
  Objective-C class, metaclass, ivar-offset, protocol or exception-type object
  by its `_OBJC_*_$_` prefix; a Swift symbol by the kind at the top of its
  demangling tree (`unlace_swift::is_data_symbol`: type metadata, a nominal type,
  protocol, conformance, opaque-type, method, property or enum-case descriptor,
  a witness table, a cache, a field offset, an async or coro function-pointer
  record, a variable's storage; an accessor, thunk, constructor or metadata
  accessor is code); an Itanium C++ symbol whose encoding carries no parameter
  list (a static data member, a vtable, typeinfo, guard variable). A plain C
  import carries no such mark and stays a callable slot, as before. The slot is
  still an import slot (`import_slots`, so `peimportcall` paints it `externref`),
  and the pass names it for its import exactly as `elfgotimports` names a
  `GLOB_DAT` slot — a symbol-table `FunctionSymbol`, demangled and sanitized as
  the function stream spells it, never an inventory entry — so `PrintC::op_load`
  renders the read as the import: `return OBJC_CLASS_$_NSObject;`,
  `return Swift.String.type_metadata;`. The app above lists 2,541 fewer entries;
  no other entry moves. The Swift metadata reader (`analyzers/swift`) still
  resolves a relative pointer through such a slot to the import it holds, so a
  witness of an imported protocol keeps its name on an image whose binds are
  classic `LC_DYLD_INFO` opcodes rather than chained fixups. The slot's name,
  like an ELF GOT data slot's, is a data alias (`lookup_data_alias`), so
  `unlace xrefs --to` and `unlace read` select the slot by the import's name. The
  walk runs on every read of the import stream, so each demangled
  classification is memoized per thread.
- **In-code literal pools** (unlace, `litpoolconst`, always on, DIV-136,
  `crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/litpoolconst.rs`): the
  third user of the same "constant by construction, not by policy" exception, and
  the one that needs no loader pass at all — only the section table the loader
  already reports.

  An ARM immediate too wide for the instruction encoding is not in the
  instruction: the compiler parks it in a **literal pool** in `.text` and loads it
  PC-relatively, so the value a function returns can be a word a few bytes past
  its own last instruction. `getReadonly` already covers that word — `.text` is
  `SHF_ALLOC` without `SHF_WRITE`, so every varnode reading it carries
  `Varnode::readonly` — but folding it is gated by the program-wide `option
  readonly`, which is off. The default C therefore said `v3 = dat_8458;` where
  `unlace disassemble` printed `0x8458 39050000 .word 0x00000539` in the same
  listing: the number the program returns was nowhere in the output, and reading
  it meant inspecting the pool by hand.

  `code_const_ranges` takes the `(vma, size, flags)` section snapshot and keeps
  the rows that are allocated, executable, non-writable and file-backed
  (`CODE|READONLY`, neither `UNALLOC` nor `NOLOAD`), falling back to the `PF_X`
  load segments when no section qualifies — the sectionless-ELF case. The merged
  ranges are carried on `Architecture::litpool_const`, and `ActionVarnodeProps`
  folds a read-only varnode that lies **entirely** inside one even with global
  propagation off (§3.4). Entirely, not merely starting there: a word straddling
  the end of `.text` is half instruction stream and half something else, and
  neither half is evidence about the other.

  The warrant is the mapping itself. Executable non-writable memory is mapped
  `r-x`, so a store to it faults and the image's copy of those bytes *is* the
  run-time value — the same standard `PT_GNU_RELRO` supplies for the slots above.
  What it deliberately does not cover is a non-writable *data* section —
  `.rodata`, `.data.rel.ro` — which stays behind `option readonly` unless the
  image maps it executable as well, as a firmware image with one RX region does.
  The warrant is the permission, not the section name. That is the direction that
  matters on a corpus of packers and protectors: a data section's flags are least
  trustworthy exactly where an image rewrites its own data, and a program that
  patches itself has to make the page writable first. An image whose
  loader reports neither sections nor segments — the XML `<binaryimage>` corpus,
  the raw-bytes loader — contributes no ranges, so the option is structurally
  inert for the datatest oracle and the whole feature is a no-op there.

  One property outranks the mapping warrant: an **external reference** is a slot
  the loader resolves, not a constant stored by the program. A PE is allowed to
  place its Import Address Table inside the same RX section as its code and import
  directory. Such a slot contains a hint/name RVA in the file, but the Windows
  loader overwrites it with the imported function address before execution.
  `ActionVarnodeProps` therefore never fills an `externref` Varnode from image
  bytes, under either `litpoolconst` or program-wide `readonly`; subtracting PE
  ranges here would wrongly couple this general invariant to one loader.
- **i386-PIE stubs** (angr, always on): a PIE i386
  PLT entry is GOT-relative (`jmp *disp(%ebx)`, bytes `FF A3 <disp32>`), so naming
  it needs the GOT base `%ebx` holds at run time; `elf_plt.rs (i386_got_base)`
  derives it once and threads it into the i386 decoder. Non-PIC, only the
  absolute `FF 25` form decodes, as upstream. Without this a 32-bit PIE's `exit`
  stays `sub_<addr>` and is never marked no-return — the spurious
  `do {} while(true)` symptom.
- **PE IAT** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/pe_iat.rs`, the
  `PeLoader.processImports` analog): PE exports enter the function-symbol
  stream only when their addresses lie in sections classified as code by the
  loader. A data export keeps only a lookup name (§1.2), so an explicit array
  or other object declaration can claim its address.
  The import path walks each import descriptor's INT (names) and
  IAT (slots) in lockstep — the i-th name belongs to the slot at
  `image_base + first_thunk_rva + i*ptr` — naming the slot (the GOT analog, folded
  through the read-only `.idata` page) and additionally decoding the MinGW `FF 25`
  thunk veneers so a direct `call thunk` also resolves. An import-by-ordinal has
  no name in the INT. (unlace) `peordinal` (always on,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/peordinal.rs (ordinal_name)`)
  names it from a built-in export table when the DLL is `OLEAUT32`, `WS2_32`,
  `WSOCK32` or `MSVBVM60`, whose ordinals are fixed by their `.def` files and which
  toolchains routinely import by ordinal (`OLEAUT32` #2 is `SysAllocString`, #6
  `SysFreeString`; `WS2_32` #23 is `socket`, #115 `WSAStartup`). Each table is the
  consensus of independent export listings: an ordinal is admitted only when every
  listing that has it agrees on the name. `WS2_32` is limited to the WinSock 1.1
  ordinals (1-23, 51-57, 101-116, 151, 500), the only ones stable across Windows
  releases, and `WSOCK32` has its own table because it swaps `inet_addr`,
  `inet_ntoa` and `ioctlsocket` relative to `WS2_32`. Any other ordinal, and every
  ordinal of any other DLL, synthesizes `<DLL>_Ordinal_<n>`. The resolved name is the import's name
  everywhere downstream (slot and thunk symbols, `unlace functions`, `unlace xrefs`),
  so `win32sigs` seeds its prototype when its table carries one.
  (unlace) `rexthunk` (always on,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/rexthunk.rs (is_rex_tail)`)
  keeps that thunk decode off compiler-emitted tail jumps. The decode is a byte
  scan for `FF 25 <disp32>` whose target is an IAT slot, and every PE linker
  (link.exe, lld-link, GNU ld) emits its import thunk bare, starting at the `FF`.
  MSVC, GCC and clang instead put a REX.W prefix on an indirect tail jump through
  `__imp_X` (`48 FF 25`), the epilogue form the Windows x64 unwinder recognises.
  The scan's match is then one byte into that instruction, and the slot still
  resolves, since a RIP-relative displacement counts from the end of the
  instruction both readings share. Each such tail jump therefore became an
  import-named function one byte into an instruction (35 in each of the MSVC `/Od`
  and `/O2` images of GH-468), and the function ending in that jump reported a
  size cut short at the phantom.
  On x86-64 a match whose preceding byte is `40`-`4F` is a REX tail and is
  dropped, unless one of two things makes the byte before a real thunk harmless.
  If the six bytes before the match are themselves an `FF 25` through an IAT slot,
  the byte is that neighbour's displacement high byte, as in a contiguous link.exe
  thunk table; both ends of a displacement lie in one image, so that byte can be
  `40`-`4F` only in an image spanning more than 1 GiB, and the look-back handles
  that layout directly. Otherwise the match is kept when the image references its
  `FF` byte
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/rexthunk.rs (referenced)`): a
  direct `call`, `jmp` or `jcc` rel32 or a RIP-relative `lea` in an executable
  section, the address as an eight-byte little-endian value anywhere in a section
  other than discardable data such as `.reloc` or MinGW's `.debug_*` (a relocated
  pointer, a function table, a `mov reg, imm64`, a pointer that `litpoolconst`
  folds), a `.pdata` `BeginAddress`, or an export. A real thunk can
  directly follow a function ending in `jmp qword ptr [rax+0x48]` (`48 FF 60 48`),
  and through any of those references it keeps its import name, so a call that
  reaches it keeps the name and the import's no-return fact. A thunk reached only
  in another way (a short branch, a 32-bit absolute or image-relative value, a
  computed address) loses its import name; a short jump into one still renders the
  import through the slot, as a plain call instead of a tail call. Short branches
  are not counted as references because a random `EB` or `7x` byte within 128
  bytes of a REX tail lands on it about once in 200 tails, which kept 13 of the
  corpus's tails below, and COFF has no 8-bit branch relocation, so no linker thunk
  is a short-branch target. A branch into a real REX tail at its `FF` would
  execute the bare jump, so the name is right there too. The evidence scans run
  once per image: `format::resolve_imports` is called about twenty times per load,
  so the result is remembered under a hash of the scanned bytes, the section
  addresses and the candidates, and a later call only rehashes.
  The prefix byte is not named in the tail's place: a function whose whole body is
  the tail jump is a compiler-emitted wrapper with a symbol of its own
  (`my_lconv_init` in `pe_imports.exe`, the CRT's `__acrt_FlsFree`), reached by an
  ordinary `call` and found by the call-target walk, and its body still renders the
  import through the slot. The 32-bit arm is unchanged, because there `40`-`4F` are
  the one-byte `inc`/`dec` instructions and say nothing about where the `FF 25`
  starts, and non-x86 images never run the scan. Across 944 x86-64 PEs (the RE
  dataset, Wine's MinGW-built DLLs, the other vendored fixtures, the GH-468
  testbed) the option removes 2,589 entries, every one at a REX `FF 25` byte, and
  adds or renames none. None of the 37,366 bare thunk matches in those images
  follows a `40`-`4F` byte, and no REX tail there is referenced in any of the ways
  above. Whole-binary decompiles of the affected images change no function's C;
  only the phantoms and the enclosing functions' sizes differ.
- **Mach-O stubs** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/macho_stubs.rs`,
  the `MachoProgramBuilder.processIndirectSymbols` analog): the `LC_DYSYMTAB`
  indirect-symbol table indexed by each `__stubs`/symbol-pointer section's
  `reserved1`, entry address `sec.addr + i*stride`. Calls target the stub
  *directly*, so naming the entry is sufficient and arch-independent;
  `__la_symbol_ptr`/`__got` slots are named too for `-fno-plt`-style indirect
  calls. `INDIRECT_SYMBOL_LOCAL`/`ABS` entries are skipped; the C-ABI leading `_`
  is stripped. The image's own exports (its external `nlist` entries and its
  export trie) join the stream only when they lie in a code section (§1.2,
  `data_exports`).
  (unlace `stubbinds`, default on) A stripped image can keep a stub whose
  indirect-symbol entry no longer indexes anything: a chained-fixups link
  records each import again as the bind on the slot its stub loads, so `strip`
  may drop the undefined `nlist` and write `INDIRECT_SYMBOL_LOCAL | ABS` over
  the entry, which is how the SwiftPM-built frameworks of an App Store app ship
  most of their Swift stdlib and runtime calls. The walk above leaves such a
  stub `sub_<addr>`.
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/stubbinds.rs (StubBindsPass)`
  decodes each stub of an `S_SYMBOL_STUBS` section the walk did not name to the
  slot it jumps through (`adrp; ldr; br` on arm64, the `adrp; add; ldr; braa` of
  an arm64e `__auth_stubs` entry, `jmp [rip+disp32]` on x86-64), reads the
  slot's addend-free chained bind (`chained.rs`) and names the stub after the
  import, one leading `_` stripped and the name demangled as the walk's names
  are, so `sub_fc80(0x28)` renders `Swift._StringGuts.grow(_:)(0x28)`. A stub
  that does not decode, a slot with no bind, and a bind with an addend are left
  alone, and the slot itself is not this pass's to name. The name is a pass
  function symbol, not a format-resolver import, so the built-in libc
  prototypes (which match the resolver's imports) are not seeded on it. The
  chains are walked only when the indirect-symbol walk left some stub unnamed.
  Mach-O only, inert without chained fixups or with a complete indirect-symbol
  table, so every datatest is byte-identical.
- **Export tries** (unlace, `exporttrie`, default on, env-bridged):
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho/exports.rs (parse_export_trie)`
  walks a Mach-O export trie (`LC_DYLD_EXPORTS_TRIE`, or the export range of
  `LC_DYLD_INFO`) iteratively, visiting each node once, and reports each name
  with its image-relative offset, its absolute value, or the dylib ordinal and
  name it is re-exported from. Two consumers read it. `macho_stubs.rs
  (trie_exports)` adds, as exports, the trie names a thin image's symbol table
  lacks, which is every export of a dylib whose nlists were stripped. In a dyld
  cache rebuild, `xrefs.rs (Names::adopt_imports_of)` resolves each undefined
  symbol of the rebuilt image through the trie of the dylib its two-level
  ordinal names. It follows `EXPORT_SYMBOL_FLAGS_REEXPORT` entries and, unless
  the dylib is `MH_NO_REEXPORTED_DYLIBS`, its `LC_REEXPORT_DYLIB` umbrellas, up
  to eight levels. A cross-image call or slot whose target exactly one import
  resolves to is then named after that import. On iOS 16.4.1 that renames 12 of
  CoreFoundation's 764 cross-image names and 29 of UIKitCore's 1,457 to the
  names the source called: `bzero` for `_platform_bzero`, `acos` for its alias
  `acosl`, `objc_release` for `objc_release_x0`. iOS 14's cross-image calls go
  through other images' stubs, whose indirect entries already carry the import
  name, so nothing changes there.
- **Bound pointer slots** (unlace, `machobinds`, default on):
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/machobinds.rs (MachoBindSlotsPass)`
  names every pointer slot a bind record fills that the indirect-symbol table
  does not: chained-fixup binds and classic `LC_DYLD_INFO` bind opcodes alike,
  the way IDA names each `<sym>_ptr`. A C function or data pointer initialized
  to an import, an arm64e `__auth_ptr`, a vtable or Swift witness slot all read
  as anonymous `dat_<addr>` without it. A bind with an addend is skipped (the
  slot holds `&sym + addend`), and so are `__objc_*` and `__cfstring`, whose own
  passes name their slots. The names go through the channel `elfgotimports`
  uses for ELF GOT slots: an `externref` paint and a symbol-table name committed
  at `read symbols`, which `query_function` resolves for a call through the slot
  (`peimportcall`, `ActionDeindirect`) or, with `importdata`, a read through it,
  and which never joins the function inventory. On the 84 MB Toyota app 71,257
  slots gain names (mostly Swift metadata and witness slots, ObjC metaclass and
  `_objc_empty_cache` words) while `unlace functions` stays byte-identical
  (314,038 entries).
- **dyld shared cache cross-image references** (unlace, `dyldcrossrefs`,
  default on, env-bridged): an image rebuilt from a dyld shared cache calls into
  other images past its own stubs. The cache builder sends a `bl` to a stub
  island in a `__TEXT_STUBS` sub-cache (iOS 16: `adrp x16; add x16; br x16`), to
  another image's rewritten stub (iOS 14), or straight to the callee. It also
  coalesces `__got` sections into plain sections with no indirect-symbol entries.
  None of those addresses is in the rebuilt image, so the stub walk above cannot
  name them, and a call renders `sub_<island>(...)`.
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/dyldcache/xrefs.rs (collect)`
  runs while the image is rebuilt. It scans an arm64 image's code sections for
  `b`/`bl` targets outside the image (an x86_64 image gets its GOT slots alone), and its untyped `__got`/`__auth_got` sections for
  slid pointers outside it. For each target it takes, in order, a symbol at that
  address, then the import an `S_SYMBOL_STUBS` entry there stands for (from the
  owning image's indirect-symbol table), then wherever the stub jumps. Up to four
  stubs are followed, decoding `adrp`/`add`/`ldr` (through slid data) to
  `br`/`braa`/`braaz`. An image's names come from its symbol table, exports
  winning over the locals in the `.symbols` file, and are built only for the
  images actually reached. The result rides in the rebuilt Mach-O as an
  `LC_NOTE` owned by `unlace.dyld.xrefs`, so `unlace unpack` writes it too, and the
  stub walk reads it back as imports: a call target becomes an import stub, and
  a slot becomes an import slot, so `peimportcall` binds a call through it. The
  gate is read at that point, so `off` leaves the note unread and every island
  call `sub_<addr>(...)`. On the iOS 16.4.1 cache, CoreFoundation's note names
  699 of its call targets and 65 GOT slots; `libobjc`'s `class_copyMethodList`
  calls `os_unfair_lock_lock_with_options` through an island on iOS 16 and
  through `HomeKit`'s rewritten stub on iOS 14, and both render the name.

- **Empty functions** (unlace `nullsubs`, default off,
  `crates/unlace-console/src/engine/thunknames.rs (name_nullsubs)`): after
  the thunks are named, a discovered function still named by a placeholder whose
  first instruction, after at most one that emits no p-code (`endbr64`, `bti`), is
  a return doing nothing but its own stack and link-register work (`LOAD`,
  `INT_ADD`, `INT_AND`, `COPY`) becomes `nullsub_<addr>` with the placeholder's
  address spelling, IDA's `AF_NULLSUB`. On MIPS and SPARC those ops would be the
  delay slot's, so the return must be alone. A name in use is left alone.
- **Jump thunks** (unlace `thunknames`, default on,
  `crates/unlace-console/src/engine/thunknames.rs`): a function
  whose first instruction is a direct unconditional branch is a thunk (a
  linker branch island, an identical-code-folding forwarder, an outlined tail
  call; one `b <target>` on arm64). No loader names it, so it stays
  `sub_<addr>` and every call through it is anonymous. While committing the
  entries, the engine decodes the first instruction of every discovered entry
  and keeps each direct unconditional branch to another address whose p-code
  is that one BRANCH. A delay slot is part of its branch, so a MIPS `j f`
  whose slot holds `addiu $a0,$a0,16` (a `this` adjustor) is not a thunk,
  while `j f; nop` is. After every
  other name source, a thunk still named by a placeholder is renamed
  `j_<target>` when its target's function has a name that is not a
  placeholder. A thunk to a thunk is named in the next round (`j_j_<name>`),
  for at most four rounds; a name already in use takes the first free `_<n>`
  suffix, in thunk address order within a round. After every prototype
  stream has run, each renamed thunk also takes what its chain's target
  carries for a call to it: the parked prototype and the bound prototype model (each
  only where the thunk has none of its own), and the target's Swift `self`
  classification, so a call through the thunk is typed as a call to the
  target. A thunk with a name of its own (`cmp3: jmp memcmp`) keeps its
  own prototype recovery, since its source signature need not be the
  target's. Under `lazyfuncs` only the
  thunks whose chain ends at an entry some fact names are made functions
  eagerly. Indirect stubs (`adrp; ldr; br`, arm64e `braa`) are named by the
  stub passes above, not here.

The import currency deliberately includes both executable linkage stubs and
pointer slots in data sections: the latter must be function symbols so indirect
calls resolve to a name and library prototype. They are not function bodies.
The complete canonical inventory retains both, while automatic whole-binary
decompilation selects only entries contained by a loader `CODE` section
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs
(ConsoleProgram::function_entries_executable)`). Explicit decompiling selection
uses the same body distinction: a lone IAT slot is refused with its import name
and address (among several selectors of one filtered run it is reported and
skipped, and the run fails only when the skips leave nothing to decompile;
`crates/unlace-cli/src/decompile_all.rs (resolve_targets)`), while a name shared by a stub and slot selects the sole body-bearing
stub. Generic lookup still resolves the slot for call binding and inventory
consumers. Loaders without section metadata keep the complete inventory.

(unlace) "In a data section" is the usual place for a slot and not a property of
one, so the section flags cannot carry that filter alone. A PE is free to put its
Import Address Table wherever it likes, and a packed image routinely puts it in
the one section it has: a round-9 crypter's first section is `0xe0000060`
(`CODE|EXECUTE|READ|WRITE`) and contains the whole import directory, so every
slot passed the `CODE` test and 50 of its 56 inventory entries decompiled to a
body dereferencing an uninitialized pointer — the pointer word read as
instructions, truncated by `funcboundflow` at the next slot. What tells a
pointer word from a function entry is not where it lives but who put the name
there, and the loader knows: each format reports the slot addresses it resolved
names at (`ObjectFormat::import_slots`, PE Import Address Table entries and typed
Mach-O lazy/non-lazy symbol-pointer entries) beside the names themselves, and the engine carries them
as `[lo, hi)` ranges (`ObjectLoadImage::import_slot_ranges` →
`ConsoleProgram::is_import_slot`). An entry inside one is excluded from the
batch set whatever the section says. Nothing else moves: the canonical
inventory, `unlace functions`, generic symbol resolution and the call naming the
slot exists for are unchanged. Decompiling `--addr`/`--functions` selection
refuses a slot before decode — on the crypter the batch goes
from 56 entries to its 6 real ones while the surviving body still renders
`ExitProcess(0)`. A caller-declared entry (`--define-function`) outranks this
test as it outranks the section-flag one, so an analyst who asserts a function
at an address the import directory claims still gets a body; that is also the
recourse if an image's import directory is a lie.

Each canonical entry also carries a byte **extent**, so the inventory answers
"how big" as well as "what is here" and a caller can order a binary's functions
by weight without decompiling any of them. unlace's model of a function is its
entry — the Listing is keyed by entry VMA and nothing in it records a body — so
the extent is reconstructed as the address-contiguous clip from the entry to
whichever comes first: the next canonical entry, or the end of the CODE section
containing the entry (`crates/unlace-console/src/funcextent.rs`). This
is the same reconstruction the FID extent generator
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/fid/extent.rs`) and the
discovered-no-return pass already apply where they need a body from an
entry-keyed model, and it reuses the entry list and the loader section table
rather than decoding anything, so the metadata-only `functions` surface stays
metadata-only.

The number is an upper bound, not the exact body: the clip runs to the neighbour,
so inter-function alignment padding is counted in, and against ELF `st_size` over
the symbolized fixture corpus it is never short. An entry in no CODE section — a
pointer slot, an undefined external — has no body to measure and reports zero,
the same value a synthesized entry carries when there is no program to measure
against. The loss is that the clip is address-contiguous rather than
flow-reachable: an outlined cold half living past the next entry is attributed to
its neighbour. Every whole-binary surface reports this one number under the one
name, including the decompiling ones; their alternative, the recovered
`Funcdata::get_size()`, is the *requested* flow bound rather than a measurement,
and a whole-binary run always requests an unbounded extent.

(unlace) The zero has that meaning only while a section table exists. An image that
publishes none — a sectionless ELF, or one whose section headers are corrupt
enough that the loader continues from the program headers — has no CODE section
anywhere, so every entry fell to the same answer and the whole binary reported
zero; size-based triage then discarded all of it, `--min-size 1` reporting a count
of none out of a total of twelve with no error to distinguish that from a binary
that really holds nothing. When the section table yields no CODE span at all, the
clip runs against the **executable load segments** instead, which the loader now
reports beside the sections
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loadimage_object.rs (ObjectLoadImage::get_segments)`,
reaching the console as `ConsoleProgram::segments`); a segment's CODE bit is its
execute permission, so the same filter reads both. The container is coarser, and
the last entry of a segment therefore runs to the end of it rather than to the end
of a `.text`, but that is the same kind of answer the field already gives: an
upper bound clipped at the next entry. The fallback is whole-table, never
per-entry. An entry that misses the CODE spans an image *does* publish is the
pointer slot the zero exists for, and choosing a segment for it would hand a body
to exactly those. The analyzer tier already degrades this way for entry point
discovery, which is where the shape comes from.

(unlace #1288) **On an x86 real-mode raw image the extent ends where the function's
flow does** (always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/rawextent.rs (measure)`). An
MS-DOS executable and a `--raw-image` real-mode program have no section table:
the loader publishes the whole load module as one CODE range, DGROUP and the far
data segments included, so the clip ran a function that data follows on to the
next entry. On the unpacked DAZZLE.EXE of issue #1288 a 28-byte function in
front of DGROUP measured 12,174 bytes, `unlace disassemble` listed DGROUP as its
instructions, and an address in DGROUP was reported `interior_to` it. Over the
descent the raw discovery already decoded (§1.6), each entry's flow is followed
along branches and fall-throughs wherever it goes short of another entry, since
a path can leave the span and come back into it; only what it reaches between
the entry and the next entry counts. A fall-through or jump into another entry
ends the path, where the decompiler's flow bounds the fall-through
(`funcboundflow`) and prints the jump as a tail call (`tailcalljump`); a
conditional branch into one is followed on, as the decompiler's flow follows it
(MS-DOS 4.0 C1L.EXE's `sub_1d56e`, a fragment of the routine at `sub_1d47a`,
reaches the rest of its span only through the loop head `sub_1d514`). A call is
not entered and falls through unless its callee is no-return, and a DOS exit
(§1.6) has no successor. A
computed branch the descent left unresolved is read from its p-code: a `cs:`
table that lies in the span (`jmp cs:[bx+table]`) reaches its words that name an
address in the span, decoded there when the descent did not decode them; a
fixed word (`jmp [2ef2h]`) leaves the function, as the decompiler prints it, a
tail call; anything else (a register, a table elsewhere, the displacement off a
pointer that a value search leaves in BX) has targets nothing names, so that
entry keeps the clip, as does one whose entry the descent never decoded. The
extent is the span from the entry to the end of the last instruction reached,
so bytes between reached instructions (a table in the body) stay in and a table
after the last instruction (where Turbo C and Borland C lay theirs out) does
not; it is never longer than the clip. An address that is not an entry is
bounded by its owner's flow, and one past it, or below every entry, is in no
function and has no extent: `disassemble` lists its 64-byte window there, and
`interior_to` no longer names the function in front of it; a selection there
gets a note naming the function whose flow ended before it instead. The rule
only bounds what the inventory reports: the `size` of every inventory surface
(`functions`, `decompile-all --json`, the project index), `disassemble`'s
default window (with a note naming the range it left out), `interior_to`, and
the `decompile-project` `.asm`, which prints a `; end of <name>` line where the
flow ends and still decodes the bytes after it. The decompiler's flow is not
bounded by it, so the C is unchanged. Over 72 DOS executables (MS-DOS 1.25 to
4.0 tools, FreeDOS, DAZZLE) 3,112 of 7,956 functions shrink, none grows, and
965,898 bytes are no longer attributed to a function whose flow reaches none of
them; for every shrunk function, no address of the decompiler's own p-code for
it lies between the new end and the clip. It is x86 real mode only: an image with a section table
already says which bytes are code (over stripped x86-64 ELF the clip's overshoot
is alignment padding, 694 of 1,093 functions; MSVC lays a switch table out after
its function in `.text`, and ARM a literal pool, both bytes of the function), and
another raw language would need its own table and literal-pool readers.

Naming a pointer slot is not by itself enough to bind a call *through* it. An ELF
PLT stub and a Mach-O `__stubs` entry are code, so the call is direct and the name
resolves at flow time. A PE Import Address Table slot, a Mach-O symbol-pointer
slot and an ELF `.got` slot are data, so `call [slot]` lifts to a `CALLIND` whose
target is the contents of a global. An ELF image reaches an import through its
`.got` slot whenever no PLT stub fronts it: `-fno-plt` code calls
`call *abort@GOTPCREL(%rip)`, and the linker leaves such a call through a
`R_*_GLOB_DAT` slot. `elf_plt.rs (resolve_imports_with_got_slots)` names those
slots after the PLT stubs: a word in a `.got*` section that a dynamic relocation
with no addend binds to an undefined `STT_FUNC` `.dynsym` entry, unless a decoded
PLT stub already jumps through it. The section test matters, because the same
relocation also fills a function pointer the program stores in its own data (a
`.data.rel.ro` table of `isalpha`-style callbacks), and that word is an object of
the program, not an import slot. MIPS and PowerPC are left out; their GOTs are
named through their own layouts. The only pass that resolves such a target is `ActionDeindirect`, and
its external-reference arm requires the target Varnode to carry
`Varnode::externref` — a flag Ghidra sets from an `ExternRefSymbol`
(`Scope::addExternalRef`) that unlace's port never carried. Without it a Windows API
call stays `(*dat_4112c4)(0)` and a direct Mach-O `__got` call to `objc_msgSend`
stays `(*dat_100004038)(...)`: no name, prototype, or no-return flow effect.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/peimportcall.rs (PeImportCallPass)`
(`peimportcall`, PE/COFF/Mach-O/ELF, always on; DIV-57, extended by DIV-171 and
to ELF `.got` slots) closes that with the
property map rather than a second symbol: `ObjectFormat::import_slots` reports one
exact pointer-width range per PE import-descriptor entry, Mach-O
`S_LAZY_SYMBOL_POINTERS`/`S_NON_LAZY_SYMBOL_POINTERS` indirect-symbol entry or ELF
`.got` import slot, and
the commit ORs `Varnode::externref` over each, the same
`Database::setPropertyRange` the loader's read-only section ranges use. The Mach-O
walk validates the typed section and indirect-symbol entry together, excluding
stub/export addresses, LOCAL/ABS entries, other pointer-section types, and
ordinary Objective-C data such as `__objc_msgrefs`.
`Scope::queryProperties` folds the property map into every global Varnode covering
the range, so the slot read now carries `persist|externref` and `ActionDeindirect`
resolves it against the `FunctionSymbol` the format's import resolver already
registered at that same slot VA — unlace's `Architecture::query_function` keys on the Varnode's own
address, where upstream indirects through `ExternRefSymbol::refaddr`, so no extra
symbol is needed. The flow half rides the same gate: `query_function` also carries
the resolved callee's no-return flag onto the prototype it hands `ActionDeindirect`
(the snapshot in
`crates/unlace-middle/src/p0_knowledge/database.rs (Database::build_global_query)`
dropped it, where upstream returns the callee's live `Funcdata`), which is what makes
the deindirect schedule the restart whose re-flow plants the artificial halt. The
extra upstream Win32 no-return-name list remains on the PE/COFF arm only. An ELF
slot named `abort`, `exit` or `_Unwind_Resume` takes the base ELF no-return list's
fact at the slot address, like a PLT stub. Off, PE, Mach-O and ELF import-slot
calls render byte for byte as before; other formats are unaffected either way. Code that
takes the slot's *address* (`lea slot(%rip)`, then `call *(%rax)`) keeps the constant:
`ActionConstantPtr` (`p9_emit/coreaction_render.rs (is_pointer)`) declines a code
Symbol whose address carries `externref`, because the slot and the function share one
Symbol and the function's name would state the wrong value.
A MIPS relocatable object's loader also makes import slots, the GOT entry of each undefined weak function: the engine stashes the
loader's ranges under this pass's id
(`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (object_import_slot_stash)`), so
they commit with that pass's facts and the call in `if (f) f(x);` binds to `f`.
Other images are unaffected.
An undefined symbol of a relocatable object is entered as an extern function
when a relocation that marks a branch or call reaches it. On x86 the opcode
bytes in front of a plain PC-relative rel32 field say so: COFF's
`IMAGE_REL_I386_REL32` and `IMAGE_REL_AMD64_REL32`, and ELF's `R_386_PC32`, carry
no call flag, so a field after `E8` (`call`), `E9` (`jmp`) or `0F 80`..`0F 8F`
(`jcc`) marks its symbol code
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/x86_relcode.rs (code_targets)`).
Before this a COFF object's `call _exit` reached an unnamed `sub_402010`, which
is not a no-return name, so flow ran past the call into the next section and
failed the function.
Undefined weak MIPS and x86-64 code-address operands in relocatable ELF objects
also retain their nullable identity before SSA. The relocation walker
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/nullable_reloc.rs (references)`
records exact instruction fields and one canonical dynamic slot per symbol.
The layout keeps one pointer per undefined weak symbol clear between the
synthetic extern slots and ELF COMMON storage, and a slot is allocated only
inside that reservation, so a slot never shares an address with a COMMON object
or an extern; a field address or slot that cannot be represented is skipped or
diagnosed, never wrapped. Other architectures reserve nothing and keep their
COMMON addresses.
`crates/unlace-lift/src/p2_lift/nullable_reloc.rs (materialize)`
replaces only a uniquely matched supported operand with a slot load and the
relocation's arithmetic. MIPS HI16/LO16/HIGHER/HIGHEST preserve rounding and
signed immediates; x86-64 absolute and PC-relative address forms preserve addends
and instruction-end bias. An x86-64 absolute field is one operand wherever its
value appears in its instruction, provided the instruction has no other weak
field and the value is not the instruction's own address or end: a register
displacement takes the slot read in place, and an immediate that reaches several
operations, as a compare's subtraction and flags do, takes one read made before
the instruction. Mixed GOT and ordinary forms share the binding.
Full-pointer weak relocations in read-only data retain the same binding and
addend when `RuleLoadVarnode` materializes the read, so read-only folding cannot
turn a genuine weak pointer into an unrelated numeric literal. Writable data,
partial pointer reads, other architectures and relocation families outside these
forms are not covered. Unmatched or unsupported code operands diagnose.
The binding represents the linker's weak-symbol choice, not arbitrary concurrent
mutation of an import slot.

Synthetic display addresses are not proof that an unrelated integer names the
import. A per-varnode literal marker protects coincidentally equal constants
through construction and cloning from pointer/name inference. Exact relocated
code operands explicitly clear it, and internal slot loads use their real slot
address. This keeps fixed numeric addresses and real imported calls distinct.
The nullable-relocations fixtures cover zero and bound imports, addends across
signed-low boundaries, mixed forms, defined functions and unrelated literals.

The `externref` mark also protects the slot until that resolution: P3 read-only
folding cannot replace it with an on-disk thunk/name RVA, even if a hostile or
single-section PE mapped the IAT executable and non-writable.

An arm64e Mach-O has one import table the indirect-symbol walk cannot see.
`__auth_got` backs the `__auth_stubs` and is an indirect-symbol section like
`__got`, so `peimportcall` covers it. `__auth_ptr` holds the signed pointers
code loads itself, for instance clang's `adrp; ldr x16; blraaz x16` call of
`___chkstk_darwin`. It is a plain `S_REGULAR` section with no indirect-symbol
entries; only its `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS` bind says which import a slot
holds. `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/authptrcall.rs (AuthPtrCallPass)`
(`authptrcall`, Mach-O only, always on) gives each `__auth_ptr` bind slot a
`FunctionSymbol` named after its import, with one leading `_` stripped as the
indirect-symbol walk does, and reports the slot as an `externref` range. The
commit and `ActionDeindirect` then treat the slot exactly like a `__got` slot.
A bind with a nonzero addend points inside the import rather than at it, so it
is skipped.

arm64e virtual calls are resolved by their signing context
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/rtti/arm64evcall.rs (resolve_signed)`,
`arm64evcall`, Mach-O only, default on). arm64e signs every C++ vtable slot
and every Swift class vtable entry with key IA, address diversity and a 16-bit
diversifier, the hash of the method's mangled name. The chained-fixup
resolver keeps that context for every authenticated entry
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/format/macho/chained.rs (AuthContext)`),
and a call site re-materializes the same constant to authenticate the loaded
slot: `movk x17, #d, lsl #48; blraa x8, x17`. So `(word offset from the
address point, diversifier)` names a method without any class type.

The index (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/rtti/arm64evcall.rs (Index)`)
has two sources. A Swift class metadata is found by its `Description` field,
signed key DA, address-diversified, diversifier `0xAE86`, 0x40 bytes past the
metadata's address point; `classSize` and `classAddressPoint` just before it
bound the metadata, and every IA-signed slot in it is filed under its word
offset from the address point. Every other run of consecutive IA-signed,
address-diversified slots in a `__const` section is a C++ vtable, whose
address point is its first method, so it is filed under `(index in run,
diversifier)`. A slot bound to another image, and a slot holding
`__cxa_pure_virtual` or `__cxa_deleted_virtual`, keeps its place in the run
but adds no method.

The pass then walks back up to 24 raw A64 words from each `blraa`/`braa` with
a register modifier; the walk reads instruction words because the lifted
p-code no longer carries the modifier. When the modifier's last write is the
`movk` that sets the diversifier, the walk follows the slot address along
`mov` copies, `add #imm`, `add` of a register a `movz` (and its `movk`s) set,
and pre-index `ldr` writebacks. It ends at the authenticated vtable-pointer
load (`autda`, `autdb`, `autdza`, `autdzb`, `ldraa`), which gives an index
key, or at an `adrp`, which gives the slot's fixed address: a static vtable
or a signed global. When the modifier's last write is a plain `movz #d`, the
discriminator is a constant and the slot is the one the called register was
loaded from, when that load's base is an `adrp` (plus `add #imm`). A fixed
slot resolves only if its own fixup is signed IA with the same diversifier
and address diversity, and it sits in a `__const` section or a `*CONST`
segment, where the load-time target is the only one the slot ever holds. A
slot in writable data is left alone. Any branch on the way, or any other
write to the tracked register, gives up. The one branch stepped over is the
`b.cond #8` across a `brk` that a kext's checked authentication puts between
the vtable-pointer load and the slot load (`autda x16, x17; mov x17, x16;
xpacd x17; cmp x16, x17; b.eq #8; brk #0xc472`), since its other path traps.

A kernelcache entry is cut out of its collection after the collection's
chained fixups are applied, so the entry's own image keeps no signing
context. The collection's signed slots, with every entry's `__const` and
read-only sections, are kept beside the image instead
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/kernelcache/fileset.rs (signed_image)`),
and the entry's call sites are resolved against all of them. So a kernel
call through a slot that a kext overrides names the kext's method too.

The result is committed as `call site → methods`. When flow builds the
CALLIND at such a site and the slot holds one method, the call is built as a
direct call to it
(`crates/unlace-decomp/src/infra/decompile_drive.rs (vcall_resolution)`).
When it holds several, the call keeps its indirect form and gets a warning
naming the candidates. A unique method is unique within the image, or the
kernel collection, only: a plugin or a third-party kext built against it
could override the method. The reference walk
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (XrefKind)`) reads the
same table: a site with one method is a `call` edge to it, a site with
several a `vcall` edge to each, and every method in the image's code is
walked as a function.
Stage test: `tests/stages/arm64evcall.toml`, each of three fixtures with the
option off and on.

Two arch-marker passes paint **decode context** rather than names, because a wrong
decode mode is unrecoverable downstream. `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/arm_markers.rs
(ArmMarkerPass)` (`arm_markers`) ports ARM's `ARM_ElfExtension`/`ArmSymbolAnalyzer`:
`$t`/`$a` mapping symbols and the STT_FUNC odd-address convention become `TMode`
paints, applied to the engine's `ContextDatabase` at commit, before any decode.
(unlace) Those are point paints: each fills up to the next address where the mode was
set, and so does the `TMode=1` a `blx` commits for its target. In an image with
function symbols but no mapping symbols nothing set the mode again at an A32
function placed after a Thumb one, so the Thumb mode reached it. The `armfuncmode`
pass (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/armfuncmode.rs (arm_func_mode_paints)`,
always on) sets `TMode=0` over each defined function symbol whose value is even, the
AAELF32 mark of an A32 function, when it lies in an executable section of a linked
ARM ELF after an odd function symbol, and sets `TMode=1` again where its extent ends.
The extent is the symbol's size cut at the next function symbol and at the end of the
section: an exported Thumb function whose symbol the linker moved onto its A32
interworking stub keeps the function's size, and must paint only the stub. The extent
then grows over every direct A32 `b`/`bl` target it reaches before the next function
symbol, up to the first return, unconditional branch, call to a function the
no-return list names (the image's own definition or its PLT stub), or literal-pool word
on that target's linear run, and over what that run branches to in turn: an A32 branch
target is A32 by its encoding, so an unsymbolized A32 static helper an A32 export calls
keeps A32. A run that reaches the next function symbol or the section end without such
a stop says nothing about where its code ends and adds nothing, and words a PC-relative
`ldr` in the scanned code loads are data, never read as branches. That data test is a
known limit: a pool word reached through `adr` + `ldr`, `vldr` or `ldrd` is still read
as a possible `b`, and a Thumb-2 `pop.w {..., pc}` at an address 2 mod 4 reads as an A32
`pop {..., pc}` stop, so a run over such bytes can still grow over a following
unsymbolized Thumb routine. Past the
extent the Thumb mode the symbol paint gave resumes, so a stripped library's
unsymbolized Thumb routines after an A32 one keep their mode. A symbol of size 0
states no extent and is skipped, and an image whose function symbols are all even
keeps the language default it already had, together with whatever modes its calls
commit. The pass paints nothing for an image with `$a`/`$t` mapping symbols, a
relocatable object, an image whose build attributes rule out A32 (M profile or
`Tag_ARM_ISA_use` 0), a Cortex-M image with a vector table, or an address that also
carries an odd function symbol. Its paints are committed and fed to the Listing's
context painter as well, and the Listing keeps the A32 extents: the
AIF gap walk rejects a Thumb walk (a 2-aligned candidate, or one whose first
instruction is 2 bytes) whose flow leaves the gap for a decoded instruction inside one
of them, since a Thumb branch cannot reach A32 code without an exchange. Without that
check a Thumb walk over the zero padding before an A32 routine was accepted once its
branches landed on the A32 instruction starts the extent now yields; an explicit `--isa` states the whole
image's mode and turns the pass off.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mips_markers.rs` carries the MIPS pair:
`MipsIsaModePass` (`mips_isa`) paints `ISA_MODE` at MIPS16e/microMIPS entries
(LSB-set or `st_other` STO-marked), and `MipsMarkerPass` (`mips_gp`) is a register
**value** seed, not a context bit — `t9 = func_entry` per function (the PIC
`jalr t9` convention, Ghidra's `MipsAddressAnalyzer`), committed as a tracked-range
so the S3 constant-base action emits `COPY #entry -> t9` at the entry block and the
prologue's `addu gp,gp,t9` folds to a real `$gp`. Both are doubly guarded: the pass
gates on its architecture, and the commit swallows an unregistered-variable /
unknown-register error, so a paint on the wrong language is a faithful no-op.
For ELF32, the marker pass sign-extends the pointer value when the selected
language's `t9` register is wider than 32 bits. It queries that register directly,
so explicit target overrides follow the same rule as automatic selection.
Function addresses remain in the ELF address space; only the seeded register
value changes. Native ELF64 values and 32-bit register seeds stay intact. Thus
an ELF32 entry at `0x80001000` supplies `0xffffffff80001000` to a 64-bit `t9`,
and a full-register signed comparison sees a negative pointer.
For an ELF loaded as MIPS, the same `mips_gp` policy also seeds `t9` when a
function is created without a symbol, including stripped and sectionless images.
That fallback requires a complete PIC address setup prefix: LUI, an ADDU/DADDU
using t9, and its matching ADDIU/DADDIU, optionally after stack-frame setup.
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsentry.rs` rejects unrelated
incoming t9 uses and does not scan through control flow. Zero words are not part
of the prefix: an address in alignment padding cannot borrow the setup of the
function after it. A discovered interior
block beginning with saved registers and a plain indirect call must retain the
incoming call target instead of acquiring its own address. The probe reads the
image bytes directly rather than through the load image's staging window, so it
changes no later read.
Symbol and fallback seeds share one value rule
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsentry.rs (class_pointer)`):
an ELF32 entry is sign-extended, as 32-bit code leaves a pointer in a 64-bit
register, and every tracked value is truncated to its register's width. N32,
and O32 under a 64-bit-register target, therefore see a sign-extended t9; a
32-bit-register target sees the address itself. Explicit
tracked values take precedence over this entry default; raw and XML images do
not acquire the ELF convention. N32 participates in MIPS ISA, entry, floating
ABI and GOT dispatch despite the object reader's separate architecture tag.

(unlace) `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/ppc64r12.rs`
(`ppc64r12`) is the PowerPC64 ELFv2 counterpart of the `t9` seed. The ELFv2 ABI
requires a caller entering a function at its global entry to pass that entry's
address in `r12`, and the global entry derives the TOC pointer from it
(`addis r2,r12,hi; addi r2,r2,lo`) before falling into the local entry. The pass
seeds `r12 = entry` at each defined PowerPC64 function symbol whose `st_other`
declares a separate local entry (field values 2 to 6, 4 to 64 bytes in), so
the prologue's `r2` folds to the TOC and TOC-relative globals resolve by
address. The seed is committed as a per-entry loader seed, as the ELFv1 TOC
is, not as a context-database range like `t9`: each function's snapshot of
that database would otherwise grow with the number of seeded functions. Only
the global entry address is seeded: a function decompiled from its local entry
keeps `r2` as an input. An
image whose `e_flags` declare ELFv1 is skipped, and a symbol without a local
entry gets no seed, so a stripped image seeds only the functions its dynamic
symbol table still names.

(unlace) **A PowerPC64 ELFv1 function symbol names a descriptor, not code**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/elfv1.rs (Descriptors::read)`, the
`.opd` half of Ghidra's `PowerPC64_ElfExtension`). Under ABI v1 a function symbol
and the image entry both point at a 24-byte `.opd` record — code address, TOC base,
environment — so selecting a function by name used to decode the record as
instructions. For a linked (`ET_EXEC`/`ET_DYN`) PowerPC64 ELF whose `e_flags` ABI
field is 0 or 1 and whose `.opd` is file-backed, the image entry, every
8-aligned function symbol defined in `.opd` and every `.dynamic` function pointer
(`DT_INIT`, `DT_FINI` and the `DT_INIT_ARRAY`/`DT_FINI_ARRAY` elements) are read as
descriptors. A descriptor
is used only when its code word is 4-aligned and lands on file-backed bytes of an
`SHF_ALLOC|SHF_EXECINSTR` section; the loader's symbol stream and image entry then
carry that code address, and every name at it is kept as an alias, so `answer`,
a `.answer` code symbol and a second descriptor for the same code select one
function. A descriptor word covered by a dynamic relocation takes the relocation's
value instead of the section bytes: an 8-byte RELA `R_PPC64_RELATIVE` resolves to
its addend (a linked image is mapped at zero bias), and any other type, a partial
overlap, or a second write to the word leaves it unresolved. An unresolved or
implausible code word leaves the symbol at its descriptor address, as before, and
ELFv2, 32-bit PowerPC, relocatable objects and every other machine read no
descriptors at all. Explicit numeric selections (`--addr`) stay literal. The TOC
word is the function's `r2` on entry, so the bootstrap records it per code entry as
a loader register seed (§0.5's per-function snapshot) that the S3 constant-base
action emits as `COPY #toc -> r2`, and a TOC-relative load resolves to the global
it names. A code entry whose descriptors disagree about the TOC, or where any of
them has an unresolved TOC word, gets no seed.

ELFv1 import markup recognizes complete descriptor-call stubs that save the
caller's TOC at SP+40, load the entry and TOC, and transfer through CTR.
A stub is named only when its decoded displacement and a validated function TOC
identify the same `R_PPC64_JMP_SLOT` import for every possible TOC. Only explicit
zero-addend relocations qualify: a nonzero addend selects the descriptor at
symbol address plus addend, whose identity cannot be inferred from the symbol's
name. Implicit addends are also unresolved here. Conflicting names and possible
TOCs without a matching import relocation are declined: an
unmatched TOC can select a returning local descriptor instead. Import matching
scans every 8-aligned word in `.opd` for a resolved, plausible code entry, so
symbol-less descriptors still contribute possible TOCs after stripping. It reads
the following TOC word without requiring an environment word; an unavailable
TOC is ambiguous. Unresolved potential code words also decline all these names
because they cannot exclude a descriptor. This conservative scan supplies only
import ambiguity, while symbol normalization and register seeding use the
validated image-entry, symbol and `.dynamic` descriptors described above. Possible
TOCs include aliases that disagree and cannot seed their shared code entry.
This resolver declines all descriptor-stub names if any validated descriptor's
TOC remains unresolved: without a caller-specific TOC, the unknown value could
select a different import and invalidate a no-return fact.
A stub addresses the descriptor from `r2` itself or from a base that `addis`
forms from `r2`, and it ends in `bctr` or in the GNU lazy-resolution tail.
The entry goes through `r11` or `r12`, an `addis` base is the other of the
two, and the move to CTR directly follows the entry load or the TOC load.
Loading the environment word into `r11` is optional. From an `addis` base it
is the last instruction before the ending. From `r2` it must directly follow
an early CTR move and precede the TOC load, which replaces `r2`. An environment
load in any other position is declined, as is a stub that does not load the
TOC. GNU ld's rarer forms also stay unnamed: an `addi` that moves the base when
the TOC or environment offset would cross into the next 64 KiB, the `xor`/`add`
pair that replaces the lazy tail when the resolver is out of branch range, and a
stub without the TOC save. A lazy
stub's zero-TOC branch must reach the matching import's resolver entry: its
relocation index, branch to the common glink code, and the common code's load of
`DT_PLTGOT` are validated against `DT_PPC64_GLINK` and `DT_JMPREL`. Returning
fallbacks, entries for another slot, and unknown resolver code or metadata are
declined. Currently only the two-instruction resolver entries with indices below
32768 qualify. A stub that ends in `bctr` needs no lazy resolver.
The existing known-no-return pass consumes these names, so a guard failure
import no longer introduces false fall-through or consumes the normal return.
ELFv2 decoding and ordinary returning imports retain their existing behavior.

The file front-ends also accept `--isa auto|arm|thumb`. An explicit ARM/Thumb
choice paints `TMode` across mapped CODE sections before decoding. If an ELF has
no section headers, it uses executable `PT_LOAD` memory extents, including their
zero-filled tails; non-executable segments and gaps remain unpainted. `auto` uses
the marker facts above, Cortex-M evidence, and Thumb-specific PE/COFF machine
values only when the resolved SLEIGH decoder is ARM32. Inferred container hints
therefore preserve an explicit non-ARM decoder selection; explicit `arm` or
`thumb` still fails for a non-ARM decoder. Explicit input state is retained on
the architecture so later Listing
and xref painters cannot replace it with ELF markers or Cortex-M metadata.
The analysis commit applies input paints after all other passes' context facts.
Before painting, the console checks whether the loaded ARM language exposes `TMode`.
Fixed-A32 languages without that variable accept explicit `arm` without any paint;
`thumb` fails with an unsupported-mode diagnostic even if there are no code ranges.
The generic PE ARM machine (`0x01c0`) is deliberately not a whole-image hint in
either direction, because such an image may mix ARM and Thumb; the THUMB
(`0x01c2`) and ARMNT (`0x01c4`) machines are Thumb-only by definition, so those
two do paint the image, with no flag and no option, where an unflagged run
previously decoded their bytes as A32. Without mode evidence, decoding uses the
selected language's default context. `--isa` is refused rather than dropped where
it could not reach a decode: `strings --no-xrefs` walks no references, so pairing
the two is a usage error.

## 1.4 Metadata analyzers

The always-on core, in pass order (`passes.rs (passes_for)`):

- **Strings** (`strings`, the `StringsAnalyzer` port,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/strings/mod.rs`): scan allocated,
  initialized sections for runs of printable ASCII (plus CR/LF/TAB) ended by a NUL,
  minimum visible length **4**; each hit commits a *typelocked* `char[len+1]` data
  symbol (`s_<addr>`) — the typelock is what carries the array type through type
  propagation, and the printer renders the literal, not the name. LOSS: Ghidra
  additionally scores candidates with a trigram model (`StringModel.sng`, not
  vendored), so unlace over-accepts random printable NUL-terminated runs; real
  literals are unaffected. Unlace uses four rather than Ghidra's default five so
  command and mode literals such as `quit`, `show`, `bind`, `fork`, and `dup2`
  do not remain raw addresses in stripped binaries. (unlace) A run that starts on
  a pointer slot is an entry of a pointer table, not text, and is not planted
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/strings/ptrslot.rs (PointerSlots)`).
  An image rebased at load time lists every pointer it holds, so on a
  position-independent ELF (its dynamic relocations) or a PE with base
  relocations the slot is exactly a relocated, pointer-aligned address. A non-PIE
  ELF or a PE without base relocations lists none, and there the slot is a
  pointer-aligned address whose pointer-sized value, read in the image's byte
  order, lies inside an allocated section. On an i386 image linked at
  `0x21414140` a function-pointer table reads `@AA!KAA!VAA!` up to its NULL
  entry, and planting it made the printer index and pass that literal where the
  code uses the table. Without relocations a genuine string can be refused only
  when its first pointer-sized bytes, NUL and padding included, spell an address
  of the image; it then prints as that address. A relocatable object has no
  image addresses yet, so nothing is refused there.
- **Rust `&str` records** (`fatstrrecords`, unlace, rustc-detected images only,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/strings/strrecords.rs
  (StrRecordPass)`, committed under the `fatstr` option's mode gate): Rust
  literals carry their length in the fat pointer, not a terminator, and rustc
  packs them back to back — so the NUL scan above GLUES adjacent Rust literals
  into one wrong row. The static `(ptr, len)` records that state every
  literal's length (a PIE's `R_*_RELATIVE` slots in `.data.rel.ro` with the
  length in the unrelocated companion word; absolute word pairs in read-only
  data on a non-PIE) are re-read as length-BOUNDED facts — exact extents, no
  terminator — and the commit plants them BEFORE the NUL stream, so the
  occupied-address guard retires the glued row and the symbol at each literal
  spans exactly the literal. Guards: target in read-only data, `1..=4096`
  bytes, valid UTF-8 at least 90% printable-or-whitespace, and the direct
  (relocation-less) arm additionally keeps the NUL scan's minimum of four.
  The engine half of the option is chapter [05](05-types.md)'s `RuleFatStr`.
- **Code-side `&str` lengths** (`strcodelen`, unlace, default on, rustc-detected
  images under the `fatstr` gate,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/strings/strcodelen.rs
  (scan)`): a literal that only code references has no static record, but the
  code loads its length beside it, because a `&str` argument or result is two
  scalar registers. The pass scans executable sections the way IDA 9.5's rust
  plugin does (rust.so 0xd200). On x86-64 the pointer is a `lea r64, [rip+d]`
  (or a non-PIE `mov r32, imm32`) into a SysV argument register, and the length
  is the nearest `mov r32, imm32` into the next argument register (`rdx` beside
  a returned `rax`) within 32 bytes, after the pointer first. On AArch64 it is
  `adrp`+`add` into x(N) and the nearest `movz w(N+1)` within eight
  instructions. The pair must then reach its consumer: a call or tail jump, or a
  `ret` for the result registers. That rejects a lookup table whose base and an
  unrelated constant happen to sit in `rax` and `rdx`. The target must be
  2..=4096 bytes of valid UTF-8 in read-only data. Pieces of one `fmt::Arguments`
  template are referenced inside each other, so a fact ends at the next fact's
  start. The facts join the record facts as bounded strings: they commit before
  the NUL stream and narrow its rows. In `std` (a 446 KB static rustc build) the
  pass finds 117 literals for +0.008% instructions over decompile-all, and on
  the 50 functions it changes the C output prints 160 string literals instead of
  78.
- **Rust panic `Location` records** (`panicloc`, unlace, default on,
  rustc-detected images only,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/strings/panicloc.rs
  (PanicLocationPass)`): every Rust panic site passes
  `&'static core::panic::Location { file: &str, line: u32, col: u32 }`, so a
  bounds check read `panic_bounds_check(a2,a1,0x51150)`. The pass scans
  read-only data (and `.data.rel.ro`) at pointer alignment for the record's
  shape: the `file` pointer reaches read-only text of `1..=0x1000` bytes that
  ends in `.rs` (rustc 1.89 counts the trailing NUL in the length; it is
  dropped) and passes the `&str` record text test, `1 <= line <= 0xffffff`
  and `1 <= col <= 0xfff`. Columns are 1-based, so a zero column rejects the
  look-alikes whose third word is the high half of a pointer or length: a
  `&str` table on a non-PIE, a `(&str, usize)` pair, the `log` crate's
  `(target, module, file, line)` record. On a PIE the pointer word is an
  `R_*_RELATIVE` slot, so its value is the relocation addend. Each record
  becomes a typed data symbol of type `core::panic::Location` (built once: a
  `&str { data_ptr, length }` field, then `line` and `col`) named from the
  last two path components and the position (`panic_loc_src_main_rs_10_5`),
  so the call prints `&panic_loc_tiny_rs_15_9`. The file name is also a
  bounded string fact of exact length. Pinned by
