  (swiftc 6.0's aarch64 output, and an Xcode-built macOS app), is not
  recognised. The facts are held apart (`AnalysisOutput::swift_helpers`) so `option
  swifthelpers off` drops them at commit. On a 72 MB third-party iOS app the
  arm names 278 helper copies (one pair per statically linked package), 818
  lazy accessors and 18,549 caches, for about 0.4 s of load time in a dev
  build. The stage test
  `tests/stages/swifthelpers.toml` runs the stripped
  `swift_helpers_arm64_elf` with both arms off and on.
- **Swift calling convention** (`swiftcall`, the calling-convention arm of the
  pass above, default-on and inert unless `swiftmetadata` and `swifttypes` are
  on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/swift/swiftcall.rs`):
  Swift passes a method's `self` in the `swiftself` register (x20 on arm64, r13
  on x86-64) when it is one pointer — a class instance, the address of a
  mutating or indirectly passed value, a thick metatype — and gets a
  non-mutating member of a loadable struct its `self` exploded into the
  trailing argument registers instead; a throwing function returns its error in
  the `swifterror` register (x21 / r12). Neither is a parameter under the
  platform's C model, so a method's `self` was an unnamed register read and a
  call dropped the `self` it passed. A `__swiftcall` model derived from each
  AArch64 and x86-64 compiler spec's default describes both (04 §4.4), and this
  arm binds it, with no signature, to every
  function it can place in a type: a class's vtable slots and overrides (an
  override of an imported method is a class member when its method
  descriptor's demangled entity is `static` or an allocating initializer), a
  conformance's witnesses (local rows by their requirement flags, resilient
  ones by the requirement descriptor), a protocol's default implementations,
  and — in an image that kept its symbols — every method, accessor,
  initializer and deinitializer the demangler places in a class, struct or
  enum, directly or through an extension, the throwing ones (a `throws` on the
  function type) to `__swiftcall_throws`, the `async` ones (an `async` on the
  function type, or an await/suspend resume partial of one) to
  `__swiftasynccall` / `__swiftasynccall_throws`, which also take the task's
  context in the `swiftasync` register (x22 / r14; hinted as
  `swift.AsyncContext *async_context`). A payload-less enum
  with a static layout is a C enum of its cases in declaration order (the
  values the runtime gives them, 0, 1, …) at the width its value witness
  table states, so a field or a return of that type prints its case by name;
  an optional of an integer, a float or a struct (a payload with no spare
  bit) is a two-field struct named after the instantiation, the payload then
  a one-byte `is_nil` tag; a Clang-imported type (`__C.CGSize`, `__C.NSString`)
  is the C type of that name when the image has one (DWARF, the Objective-C
  pass), inline for a struct and through a pointer for a class. Any other type
  — an enum with payloads, an imported value type (`Foundation.Date`), a
  generic instantiation without a known layout, a tuple, an existential — is
  `undefined<n>` over the bytes up to the next field, so the layout is always
  right and the names are always real; only the field's own type is withheld. An import stub (a PLT entry or a
  Mach-O `__stubs` entry, in a code section) whose symbol demangles to a
  throwing function of another image that is not `async`, a protocol
  requirement's dispatch thunk included, binds `__swiftcall_throws` with no
  `self` type: a throwing function calls such imports with the error register
  holding the zero its own caller passed, reloaded rather than stored, so the
  zeroing-store rule of 04 §4.4 does not see the call. Each binding carries a `self` hint
  (`AnalysisOutput::swift_types.models` / `input_hints` → the decompile
  drive): the name always, and the type where the layout arm has one — `Class
  *` for an instance member of a class, `swift.class_metadata *` for a class
  member or an allocating initializer, the address of the value for a witness
  (`T *` for a struct, `Class **` for a class, since a witness receives the
  address of the reference), `swift.type_metadata *` for a static
  requirement's witness. A struct member's `self` is typed `T *`, which is what
  the register carries when the member reads it at all. A body two types' members share (identical code
  folding) is not bound at all: it keeps only the name the pass gives it
  (`Namer::owners_disagree`), and a getter the layout arm has
  already pinned keeps that lock. A struct or enum member found by symbol is
  marked as one that may not take `self`, which the call side reads (04 §4.4);
  a method's own `self` handed on untouched is passed at a direct call, and an
  indirect call dispatched through an object's own isa passes that object.
  On the Toyota iOS app the arm binds 42,607 functions; decompiling them,
  23,153 take a `self` parameter and 18,058 a typed one (15,834 `T *`, 1,442
  `Class **`, 782 metadata), against the 6,837 the getter locks alone typed;
  8,777 calls pass an argument they dropped before (almost all a `self`) and 3
  pass one fewer, and the functions that test a call's error by releasing it
  grow from 84 to 235. It adds no measurable load time and about 8 MB, and the
  42,240 decompiles take 2.5% longer. The
  stage test `tests/stages/swiftcall.toml` runs the stripped
  `swift_call_elf` with the arm off and on, and its unstripped twin
  `swift_call_syms_elf` on.
- **Swift runtime prototypes** (`swiftruntime`, Swift-detected Mach-O and
  ELF, default-on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/swift/swiftruntime.rs`):
  the runtime's entry points carry the signatures its public headers give
  them (`swift/Runtime/HeapObject.h`, `Metadata.h`, `Casting.h`,
  `Exclusivity.h`), bound by name so an import stub, a GOT slot and an
  unstripped runtime all take them — about 180 rows: allocation and
  refcounting (the native, unknown-object, bridge-object, unowned and error
  families with their `_n` counts), boxes and errors (`swift.BoxPair`),
  metadata accessors and instantiation (`swift.MetadataResponse`, the
  metadata and its state, two words, so a caller's `x0` read is `.metadata`),
  casting (`swift_dynamicCast` is a `bool`), exclusivity, weak and unowned
  references, enum tags, array bulk operations, class/struct/enum metadata
  initialization and the task allocator. The runtime is C under the platform
  convention, so these are plain prototypes; the `swiftcc` entry points
  whose arguments ride in the Swift registers (the key-path accessors) are
  left to recovery. An object reference is a
  `void *`: its type is the metadata's, which the call site knows, and a
  `swift.HeapObject *` would hide the first stored property behind
  `obj[1].isa`. The stage test `tests/stages/swiftruntime.toml` runs the
  stripped `swift_types_elf` off and on.
  On arm64 the table also carries the runtime's register-specific retain and
  release entry points (`swift/Runtime/CustomRRABI.h`, instantiated for
  `swift_retain`, `swift_release`, `swift_bridgeObjectRetain` and
  `swift_bridgeObjectRelease`): `swift_retain_x<N>` and
  `swift_bridgeObjectRetain_x<N>` take the object in `x<N>` and return it in
  `x0`, the two releases read `x<N>` and return nothing, for `N` in 1–15 and 19–28 (`x0` is the
  plain entry point, `x16`/`x17` are call glue, `x18` is reserved, `x29`/`x30`
  the frame and link registers). An optimized caller releases a value through
  them without moving it into `x0`, where no convention places a parameter,
  so the one parameter is explicit storage on the prototype (the
  `objc_retain_x<N>` shape) and the call prints its argument:
  `swift_release_x20(v)` for the bare `swift_release_x20()`. The stage test
  `tests/stages/swiftrrregs.toml` runs `swift_rr_regs_macho`, an arm64
  Mach-O assembled against the iOS libswiftCore.
  The standard library's own C entry points are in the table too
  (`_swift_stdlib_*`, declared in the shims headers
  `stdlib/public/SwiftShims/swift/shims/AssertionReporting.h`,
  `RuntimeShims.h`, `LibcShims.h`, `FoundationShims.h`,
  `ThreadLocalStorage.h`, plus `swift_reportError`, `swift_reportWarning`,
  `swift_lookUpClassMethod` and `swift_deletedMethodError`): the fatal-error
  and unimplemented-initializer reporters take their strings as `char *`
  with `int` lengths and a `uint32_t` flags word and return nothing, the
  `strto*_clocale` parsers return the `char *` they stopped at, and
  `_swift_stdlib_operatingSystemVersion` returns the three-word
  `swift.NSOperatingSystemVersion` (`majorVersion`, `minorVersion`,
  `patchVersion`), which on arm64 comes back through `x8`, so a caller's
  `v1[0]` reads `v1.majorVersion`. The stage test
  `tests/stages/swiftstdlib.toml` runs `swift_stdlib_macho`, assembled
  the same way.
  The rest of the compiler's list of runtime calls
  (`include/swift/Runtime/RuntimeFunctions.def`) is in the table as well, for
  every entry whose arguments all ride in the platform's argument registers:
  the typed allocators (`swift_allocObjectTyped`, `swift_deallocBox`, …), the
  array and `swift_cvw_*` layout-string value witnesses, the metatype casts,
  the class-metadata initializers and the non-atomic reference counting. The
  three runtime entry points that never return (`swift_unexpectedError`, which
  a failed `try!` calls, `swift_errorInMain` and
  `swift_onceClosureDestroyedError`) are no-return functions on a Swift image
  in every format (`loader/noreturn.rs` `SWIFT_NORETURN`), so the code after
  the call is not printed as reachable.
  The concurrency runtime's entry points come from a second, generated table
  (`swiftconcurrency.rs`, from the Swift project's
  `swift/Runtime/Concurrency.h` by `tools/gen_swift_concurrency.py`, 64-bit
  images only): the plain ones join these prototypes, and the `swiftasync`
  ones, which take the caller's context in the `swiftasync` register, are
  carried as facts the `swiftcall` commit binds (§4, *Swift*).
- **Core Foundation constant strings** (`cfstrings`, Mach-O-only, default-on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/cfstring/mod.rs`): a `CFSTR("x")`
  compiles to a four-word `CFString` struct in `__cfstring` (`isa`, `flags`, a
  `char *` into `__cstring`/`__ustring`, and a character `length`). Code references
  the struct address, not the characters, so the constant-string route — which
  reads the bytes *at* the referenced address — sees the struct and prints
  `dat_<addr>`. The pass reads each entry, resolves its `char *` through the
  chained-fixup overlay (§1.2) on an arm64(e) image or as a raw word on a classic
  `LC_DYLD_INFO` image, and decodes the string (8-bit when the `flags` unicode bit
  `0x10` of the 32-bit info word is clear, UTF-16 otherwise). The walk stops at the end of the file, not at
  the section header's size, and the string bytes it reads over all entries are
  capped at the file's length: an entry is 32 bytes, but every entry may name the
  same 64 KiB run, and each fact owns a copy of its string (as does the
  `StringManager` seed), so an uncapped crafted section would grow memory about
  4096-fold. A real image's strings are distinct bytes of the file and never reach
  the cap. The walk also stops after a fixed budget of section-span checks, because
  each read scans the image's section spans and a crafted file can size both the
  entry count and the section count. An 8-bit string that is not UTF-8, invalid
  UTF-16, and a string holding a NUL (a trailing one included) are skipped, since
  the C literal would stop at that NUL and silently drop the rest. The commit seam then types the entry an
  opaque `struct __CFString` spanning the entry's own four words (never the
  string's length, which would overrun the next entry and hide it) and seeds the `StringManager` at the
  entry address with the resolved bytes, so a reference renders the string
  across the one indirection the printer cannot follow on its own. The entries are
  marked read-only (a CFString constant is immutable), which the route requires on
  the historical writable `__DATA,__cfstring` layout (`__DATA_CONST` is already
  read-only). An entry a data symbol already holds (debug info, another pass)
  keeps that symbol's name and type and gets no `__CFString` symbol, but its
  string is still seeded and recorded; the symbol, mapped before the entries
  were painted, takes the read-only flag when it lies inside the entry, so the
  reference still renders as the literal. An entry under a function is left
  alone. The commit also records each seeded entry address
  (`Architecture::cfstring_entries`), and the C printer wraps a literal found at one
  of them as `CFSTR("...")`
  (`crates/unlace-emit/src/p9_emit/cfstr.rs (wrap)`): the value is
  the entry, a `CFStringRef`, not the characters, so
  `NSLog(CFSTR("Reachability Flag Status: …"))` is what was written. The printer
  reads an entry's seeded string through a `char` element whatever the
  reference's type (`cfstring_char` in
  `crates/unlace-emit/src/p9_emit/printc.rs`), at both the constant
  arm and the global-symbol arm, so the entry's own type is free to say what the
  value is: the commit declares `struct __CFString` at the entry size and a
  pointer to it named `CFStringRef`
  (`crates/unlace-emit/src/p9_emit/cfstr.rs (declare_types)`),
  reusing a `CFStringRef` and `__CFString` the type factory already holds (an
  opaque one is completed to the entry size), and registers that pointer as the
  one the factory returns for any later pointer to the struct
  (`TypeFactory::unlace_prefer_named_pointer`). Type inference therefore types a
  reference to an entry `CFStringRef`, and the type propagates to the returns,
  parameters and locals that carry it: a getter is
  `CFStringRef get_greeting(void) { return CFSTR("cfstring hello"); }`. When an
  existing `__CFString` has another size, or an existing `CFStringRef` is not a
  pointer to it, the entry falls back to a `char[N]` and the reference to
  `char *`. The Rust and Go back-ends keep the plain literal, with the pointer to
  the struct as its type. `cfstrings annotate` runs the same pass and
  also follows each `CFSTR` with `/* cfstring@0x<entry> */`, the address a
  disassembler or hex view shows for the entry, which the literal otherwise
  replaces. The pass is on by default: it runs only on a Mach-O and only on the
  real-binary path, so the XML datatest corpus never reaches it, and on the 80 MB
  Toyota arm64 app one decompile is within run-to-run noise of `off`. `off`
  renders each reference as the entry itself: its symbol (`&_kGreeting`) where the
  image names it, its address on a stripped image.
- **IOKit classes** (unlace, `iokitclasses`, Mach-O arm64 XNU images only,
  default-on; `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/iokit/mod.rs`): every
  libkern class registers itself from a static initializer that calls
  `OSMetaClass::OSMetaClass(&X::gMetaClass, "X", &Super::gMetaClass, sizeof(X))`
  and then stores the `X::MetaClass` vtable into `X::gMetaClass`. The pass runs
  only on a kext (`MH_KEXT_BUNDLE`) or a kernel (a `__KLD` segment). It follows
  each `__mod_init_func` / `__init_offsets` initializer with a forward register
  tracker (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/iokit/a64.rs (trace)`)
  that models `ADRP`/`ADD`/`ADR`/`MOV`/`MOVZ`, loads from a constant slot, the
  PAC sign/strip instructions as no-ops, and calls (which clear the
  caller-saved registers, except that a constructor returns its `this`); any
  other instruction that writes a register makes it unknown. The constructor
  is the callee most calls share whose `x1` is a class-name C string and whose
  `w3` is a plausible size, so no symbol is needed. A class with its own zone
  registers through a second overload that takes three more arguments
  (`IOSurface` does); any other callee with such a call is accepted as a
  constructor too when the call is followed, before the next call, by the store
  of a vtable into the object it built (`mod.rs (constructors)`). Each such call gives a
  class (name, metaclass object, superclass metaclass, instance size); the
  first store into the metaclass object after the call is the metaclass
  vtable. A class's own vtable is a run of code pointers in a data section,
  behind two zero header words, whose first twelve slots hold
  `X::getMetaClass() const`: a leaf that returns `&X::gMetaClass` within five
  instructions. For a kext cut out of a collection a slot may point outside the
  image, at the kernel or another kext, so a run also accepts aligned pointers
  into unmapped addresses of the same 4 GiB region. Every unnamed vtable method
  is named after its owner, the nearest class that is an ancestor of every
  class whose vtable holds it, and the method the same slot has in the owner's
  nearest ancestor with a symbol there (`Derived::m2` for an override of a
  named `Base::m2`), else `X::vfn_<offset>`. A function found at two different
  slots (the pure-virtual trap, folded stubs) is not named. The metaclass
  vtable's destructors and its `alloc` (the slot past them whose function
  differs between the most metaclass vtables) are named too. Output: sized data
  objects `X::gMetaClass` (the gap between consecutive metaclass objects),
  `vtable for X` and `vtable for X::MetaClass` where the image has no symbol,
  placeholder-only function names, and every vtable slot as a function entry,
  which is what discovers methods reachable only through a vtable. Measured
  against the symbols of the iOS 16.4.1 kernelcache while ignoring them: all
  149 kernel classes, 22/22 IOSurface and 85/85 AGXG12P classes have the right
  metaclass object; every metaclass vtable and every class vtable with a symbol
  is found at that symbol's address; method names are right or a class-right
  `vfn_` wherever no ancestor slot is named, except where an abstract class has
  no vtable in the image (AGXG12P: 627 of 1,979 methods are credited to the one
  concrete subclass instead). The pass takes 13 ms on the kernel.
  With `iokitclasses on` (the default; `names` stops at the names above) the
  kernel-side classes are also reported as C++ types
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/iokit/cxx.rs (cxx_facts)`),
  in the shape the typed Itanium vtables use, so chapter 05 types them with
  the same machinery whatever `vtabletypes` is set to. Each class with a
  vtable and a name no other class of the image shares gives a record: its
  instance size, and per slot a field name and the functions the class and its
  descendants in the image hold there. A slot is named `dtor` and
  `deleting_dtor` for the first two, else after the method the nearest
  ancestor's slot names, else after the name of the function the class or a
  descendant holds there, else `vfn_<i>`; a name an earlier slot of the same
  vtable took gets the slot index appended (`release_5`, the overload of
  `release`). The pass also reports the class of `this` for every function a
  class vtable holds (the nearest class that is an ancestor of every class
  whose vtable holds it) and for every `C::C` / `C::~C` of a recovered class;
  the address point of each typed vtable; each metaclass object's own vtable
  slots; and which `X::MetaClass::alloc` allocates which class. `vtable for X`
  then covers only the two header words, leaving the slots to the typed
  object. The arm64e call-site walk (`arm64evcall`) reports, for a call whose
  vtable pointer was loaded from an `adrp`-addressed object, that object
  (`arm64evcall.rs (object_at)`): when it is a metaclass object, the
  commit resolves the call to the one method that metaclass's own vtable
  holds in the slot, so `X::gMetaClass.alloc()` is a direct call.
  Stage test: `tests/stages/iokitcxx.toml` (the typed classes, `names`
  against `on`).
- **XNU data tables** (unlace, `xnutables`, the same XNU images, default-on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/iokit/tables.rs`): three kinds
  of table that need no class knowledge to find. Each `__kalloc_type` record (a
  0x40-byte `kalloc_type_view`, its `site.<type>` name at +0x10) and
  `__kalloc_var` record (a 0x50-byte `kalloc_type_var_view`) becomes a sized data
  object under its symbol, or else `kalloc_type_view_<T>` / `kalloc_type_var_view_<T>`
  (`struct` dropped, `*` spelled `_ptr`); the typed allocator entry points
  (`kalloc_type_impl`, `IOMallocTypeImpl`, `OSObject_typed_operator_new`, their
  `var` and `free` forms) get prototypes whose first parameter is a pointer,
  parked by name and at every address the image calls one at, so the view an
  allocation passes renders by name. A fixed-size view also describes what it
  allocates: its `kt_signature` (+0x20) spells the type one character per
  8-byte granule (`1` a pointer, `8` a signed pointer, `2` data, `4` either,
  `0` padding; a data-only type has an empty signature) and `kt_size` (+0x2c)
  is `sizeof` the type. A variable-size view describes a header followed by
  elements: `kt_size_hdr` (+0x2) and `kt_sig_hdr` (+0x38) the header,
  `kt_size_type` (+0x4) and `kt_sig_type` (+0x40) one element. Its allocation
  is the header struct `<T>` when there is a header, else the element (an
  array of `void *` when the site names a pointer type, `site.T *`). The
  struct `<T>` of that size is laid out from the signature
  (`crates/unlace-bandb-base/src/p5_types/kalloctype.rs (view_struct)`): a `void *` field per pointer granule, an
  `undefined8` per data granule, a trailing `undefined1[n]` where the size is
  not a multiple of eight, each named `field_0x<off>` except the first pointer
  of a class `iokitclasses` recovered, which is its `vtable`; a name another
  size already holds becomes `<T>_<size>` (template instances, `ExpansionData`),
  and a same-size struct of the name is reused. The names are decided by the
  pass, in section order, so every surface agrees on them; the struct itself
  is interned the first time a decompiled call needs it, so the project `.h`
  declares only the view structs some exported function allocates (two
  kernel functions exported: 534 structs and 575 KB of `.h` before, 2 and
  2.4 KB after). The view-to-layout map is handed to the engine
  (`Architecture::unlace_kalloc_types`), where
  `TypeOpCall::getOutputLocal`
  (`crates/unlace-bandb-base/src/p5_types/kalloctype.rs (allocated_type)`)
  answers for a call to one of the allocators whose view argument folds to a
  known view with `<T> *`, ahead of the prototype's locked `void *`: the
  allocation is declared `<T> *` and the stores into it are field accesses.
  A run of at least four
  `IOExternalMethodDispatch` (0x18-byte) or `IOExternalMethodDispatch2022`
  (0x28-byte) records in `__const`, each a pointer into this image's code with
  at most 16 scalars each way and struct sizes up to 256 KiB or variable, at
  least one variable (the checks IDA's kcu applies), is a dispatch table: it
  becomes a typed data object (its symbol, else `<Owner>_sMethods`) whose type
  is an array of the record struct (`tables.rs (dispatch_struct)`:
  `function`, a pointer to `int (void *target, void *reference, void *arguments)`,
  the four `check…` counts, and for 2022 `allowAsync` and `checkEntitlement`),
  so a read of a slot is `sMethods[2].function`, and every unnamed
  handler `<Owner>::externalMethod_<selector>`, the owner being the class whose
  vtable holds a method that computes the table's address (`a64::constants`),
  else the class of the table's named handlers. A `__got` / `__auth_got` /
  `__auth_ptr` slot the indirect-symbol table does not name, whose rebased
  pointer reaches a function or object of this image named by a symbol or by
  `iokitclasses`, is named `<target>_ptr`, a further slot holding the same
  target `<target>_ptr_2` and so on (123 slots when the whole iOS 16.4.1
  collection is loaded as one image; none on the stripped iOS 12.4 and 14.8
  caches, whose slots point at functions nothing names). On the iOS 16.4.1 collection there are 6,953 `kalloc_type`
  views (4,140 distinct structs; the kernel's 1,088 views build 533), 1,687 var
  views (in IOSurface, 5 allocations newly typed from them, such as
  `IOSurfacePlaneInfo *`) and 56 dispatch tables (901 records); in IOSurface,
  `OSObject_typed_operator_new(0xfffffff007cffc68,0x38)` becomes
  `OSObject_typed_operator_new(IOSurfaceSharedEventListener_ktv,0x38)` and its
  result an `IOSurfaceSharedEventListener *`; 48 of the kext's 1,806 functions
  carry a view-derived type, and the struct building adds nothing measurable
  to the kernel's 4.9 s `unlace functions`.
- **DriverKit class records** (unlace, `osclassinfo`, Mach-O with an
  `__osclassinfo` section, default-on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/iokit/osclassinfo.rs (classes)`):
  a DriverKit extension lists every class it defines as pointers to
  `OSClassLoadInformation` records (0xa0 bytes: `description`, `metaPointer`,
  `version`, `instanceSize`, eight reserved words, `New`, eight more), each
  pointing at an `OSClassDescription` (`descriptionSize`, `name[96]`,
  `superName[96]`, then the size/offset pairs of the method-option,
  queue-name and method-name tables, 0x138 bytes before the tables). A record
  is used when it and its description are mapped, `descriptionSize` is at
  least 0x138 and the name is a C identifier. It yields sized data objects
  `<Name>_Class`, `<Name>_ClassDescription` and `g<Name>MetaClass` (the global
  `metaPointer` points at), and names `New` `<Name>_New`, adding it as an
  entry. The names come from the records, so nothing is inferred from code.
- **DriverKit IORPC dispatch types** (unlace, `dextrpc`, arm64 dexts, run at
  the commit point like `com`
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/passes.rs (run_dextrpc)`) when `dextrpc` and `osclassinfo` are on, because the
  load-time pass list sees the architecture's constructor defaults rather than
  the run's options, default on since unlace#581;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/iokit/dextrpc.rs (emit)`):
  every symbol the dext defines or imports that names `C::_Dispatch(C *,
  IORPC)` (`_ZN<n>C9_DispatchEPS_5IORPC`), `C::Dispatch(IORPC)`
  (`_ZN<n>C8DispatchE5IORPC`) or `X::M_Invoke(IORPC, OSMetaClassBase *,
  handler[, const OSMetaClass *])` gets its prototype by address: an `int`
  (`kern_return_t`) return, the `IORPC` as `IORPC *` (AAPCS64 passes the
  24-byte struct by reference to a caller copy), `self`/`this` as `C *` for a
  class of the dext and `void *` otherwise; `IORPCMessageFromMach` gets
  `IORPCMessage *(IORPCMessageMach *msg, bool reply)`. `IORPC` and
  `IORPCMessage` follow `IORPC.h`; `IORPCMessage.msgid` is an 8-byte enum
  `IORPCMessageID` whose values `C_M_ID` come from the descriptions (the
  method-options table holds the n message ids of the methods a class
  implements, then n option words; the method-names table the n
  length-prefixed names in the same order; the meta tables likewise; an id two
  classes list keeps the first name), so `_Dispatch`'s comparisons print the
  method names. Each class becomes a struct `C` of its `instanceSize`: iig
  gives every class one `C_IVars *ivars` after its superclass, so `ivars` sits
  at `instanceSize - 8`, behind the superclass's struct as `super` when the
  superclass is a class of the dext whose size leaves room for it (else those
  bytes stay untyped). `init`, `free` and every `M_Impl` take an unlocked
  `C *this` hint on `x0`. A table that does not parse adds no ids, a class
  whose `instanceSize` is not a multiple of 8 gets no struct, and a name the
  program already holds for another shape is left alone. Like IDA's dku it
  reads names from the symbol table, so a dext stripped of its C++ symbols gets
  only the types.
- **Swift slot names from `@objc` thunks** (`swiftobjcthunk`, the naming arm
  of `swiftmetadata` for Mach-O arm64, default-on and inert unless
  `swiftmetadata` is on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/swift/swiftobjcthunk.rs`):
  a Swift method descriptor carries no name, so in a stripped image the first
  arm names a class's vtable slots by position (`Sentry.SentryOnDemandReplay.vtable#20.method`)
  and every call through one prints that. An `@objc` member also has an
  Objective-C entry point. For each `__objc_classlist` class whose `class_t`
  data word carries a Swift bit (`FAST_IS_SWIFT_LEGACY|STABLE`) and whose
  metadata `Description` word (offset 0x40) is a local class descriptor, the
  arm reads the class's and metaclass's method lists and property lists. Each
  method's IMP is a bridging thunk; its `bl`/`b` targets are read up to the
  next stated function start (the load commands' and exports' function
  starts, every IMP and every slot implementation; at most 128 instructions).
  When the targets reach exactly one implementation the class's vtable or
  override table lists, and none of them sends an Objective-C message (a call
  into `__objc_stubs`, or a stub whose `adrp`/`ldr` (or arm64e `adrp`/`add`/`ldr`)
  slot is bound to `objc_msgSend*`), the slot is named after the member, if
  its kind fits the selector: a getter or setter after the property whose
  accessor the selector is (`Class.isFullSession.getter`), a method after its
  selector (`Class.addFrameWithTimestamp:label:`), an initializer after an
  `init…` selector; an instance slot takes only a `-` method and a class slot
  only a `+` one, while an initializer (whose descriptor is not an instance
  member) takes a `-init…` method. The send check matters for an override of
  an inherited Objective-C method (`layoutSubviews`): it has no vtable slot,
  and when `-O` inlines its body into the thunk, the thunk sends to `super`
  and then calls some other slot directly, which must not take its selector.
  The same holds for any `@objc` member whose body `-O` inlines into its
  thunk: under whole-module optimization the body's call to another member
  of the class is direct (`@objc func tap() { handle() }` gives a thunk that
  calls `handle()`), so the hit is only taken as the thunk's own slot when
  nothing points elsewhere. If one of the class's own vtable slots of the kind
  the thunk's selector names (a method or `init` selector: method or
  initializer slots; a getter or setter selector: that accessor kind) has no
  implementation, the member that owns it was inlined everywhere, its thunk
  included, so the thunk names nothing; and a hit that another implementation
  of the class calls or branches to directly (the member's own surviving body,
  when a subclass override or public visibility keeps it, is a call to what the
  thunk calls) names nothing either. A hit's kind must also be the selector's:
  a property accessor's thunk never names a method slot. An implementation that
  carries a Swift symbol (`_$s…`, say the exported symbol of a public method)
  keeps the positional claim, so the symbol's own name (`act(_:)`) is reported
  rather than the selector (`act:`). On the `-O -wmo` crate fixture
  `macho_swift_objcthunk_inlined_arm64` the two `handle()` bodies keep
  `vtable#3.method`; the cost is recall on whole-module builds, where a class
  whose members were inlined away names none of that kind.
  The name belongs to the method descriptor, so an override in a subclass
  takes it too (`Sub.addFrameWithTimestamp:label:`); a slot two thunks name
  differently keeps its position. The pass runs at load, before `option`
  commands, so it records each renamed function's positional name
  (`AnalysisOutput::swift_positional_names`), and the commit boundary
  restores those names when the gate is off. On Perplexity for iOS (an 84 MB
  arm64 app) the arm without the inlined-body checks named 346 of the 1,723
  positional slot implementations (178 methods, 6 initializers, 87 getters,
  75 setters) with no measurable load cost; with them, the OneSignal
  frameworks' `OneSignalUser` names 13 of its 75 positional slots and
  `OneSignalOSCore` 2 of 37, each a bridging thunk around a large body. The crate test `unlace-console/tests/verify_swiftobjcthunk.rs`
  runs the stripped fixture `macho_swift_objcthunk_arm64` with the arm on and
  off, and checks the inlined-body and symbol cases on
  `macho_swift_objcthunk_inlined_arm64`.
- **Swift value witnesses** (`valuewitness`, the value-witness arm of the pass
  above, default-on and inert unless `swiftmetadata` is on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/swift/swiftwitness.rs`,
  `crates/unlace-bandb-core/src/p5_types/valuewitness.rs`): the word
  before a struct's or enum's type metadata points at its value witness table,
  the functions the runtime and generic code call to copy, move and destroy a
  value whose layout they do not know (`initializeBufferWithCopyOfBuffer`,
  `destroy`, `initializeWithCopy`, `assignWithCopy`, `initializeWithTake`,
  `assignWithTake`, `getEnumTagSinglePayload`, `storeEnumTagSinglePayload`),
  then `size`, `stride`, `flags` and `extraInhabitantCount`, and when the flags
  carry `HasEnumWitnesses` `getEnumTag`, `destructiveProjectEnumData` and
  `destructiveInjectEnumTag`. A stripped image keeps the tables, so the arm
  finds each local struct's and enum's table — through the static metadata a
  non-generic accessor returns, the incomplete metadata a singleton-initialized
  type's descriptor points at, or the value witnesses of a generic type's
  default instantiation pattern — checking that the metadata's kind and
  descriptor are the type's before it reads the word before it. A slot the
  loader binds to another image (the runtime's builtin tables for trivial
  layouts, `$sBi64_WV` and kin) names nothing. Each function in a local table
  is named the way the demangler spells the value-witness symbol
  (`Module.Point.destroy_value_witness`); a body several types' tables share
  is named after the first with `.merged#N`, and a function another record
  claims (a method, an accessor) keeps that claim. A function the image's
  symbol table names (the shared `__swift_memcpy16_8` and
  `__swift_noop_void_return` helpers of an unstripped image) keeps that name
  and only takes the witness prototype. A function that is one
  witness and nothing else gets its runtime prototype (`swift/ABI/ValueWitness.def`)
  bound by address: `void *initializeWithCopy(void *dest, void *src,
  swift.type_metadata *self)`, `void destroy(void *object, swift.type_metadata
  *self)`, `unsigned int getEnumTagSinglePayload(void *value, unsigned int
  emptyCases, swift.type_metadata *self)` and so on. With `swifttypes` on, the
  layout arm types each table `swift.value_witness_table` (or
  `swift.enum_value_witness_table` when it has the enum witnesses), whose
  function slots are pointers of those signatures, and the decompiler types the
  table where code loads it: an 8-byte LOAD from `p + -8` whose result is read
  at a table offset votes `swift.value_witness_table *` (the enum layout when a
  read ends past offset 0x58, each read measured by its width, so the 4-byte
  `flags` and `extraInhabitantCount` and a byte of the flags end inside the
  common table) in type inference, and pointer arithmetic leaves a
  constant offset off a `swift.type_metadata *` that falls outside its 16-byte
  header (the `-8`, and the field offsets and generic arguments past it) a
  byte offset instead of rewriting it to `meta[-1].field` or `meta[1].kind`,
  and type inference does not carry the metadata pointer type to such a sum,
  so a generic argument reads as `((long *)meta)[2]`, not as the `kind` of a
  record at `meta + 0x10`. A witness call then prints as
  `(*(*(swift.value_witness_table **)(meta + -8))->initializeWithCopy)(dest,src,meta)`
  and an allocation as `->size`. The vote looks the table type up by name and
  only the Swift pass interns it, so code without Swift metadata is unchanged.
  A witness call takes the slot's prototype before parameter recovery, so type
  recovery does not have to force it later (which costs a restart once the
  call's inputs are fixed): `ActionDefaultParams` reads the call's lifted
  p-code back from its target (an address `INT_ADD` in either operand order,
  as the lifter writes `call *0x20(%r12)` constant first), through register
  copies, spills and reloads,
  calls that keep the register, and blocks with one way in, to a load at a
  table offset from a word loaded from `p + -8`, and copies the slot's
  prototype, input-locked. A slot call the walk misses and type recovery finds
  after the inputs are fixed keeps the inputs already recovered and does not
  restart the function.
  The witness facts ride in `AnalysisOutput::swift_witnesses`, which the commit
  drops under `option valuewitness off`. On a large third-party iOS app (268k
  functions) the arm names 27,667 functions, up from none, and load time is
  unchanged.
  On arm64 the arm also names the outlined value-witness helpers
  (`unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/swift/swiftoutlined.rs`). swiftc
  copies, moves and destroys a value of a type whose layout is only known at
  run time through a small helper per type and operation: fetch the type's
  metadata, load the table from the word before it, call one witness
  (`destroy`, `initializeWithCopy`, `assignWithCopy`, `initializeWithTake`,
  `assignWithTake`), hand the value back. Each function start is decoded by a
  register tracker that accepts only the forms such a helper uses (frame
  setup and teardown, register moves, `mov #imm`, `adrp`/`add`/`adr`, a load
  through a constant page, the `-8` table load, the slot load, one call for
  the metadata and the witness call, `ret`). The helper must return the
  address it was given (its `dest` for a copy or take), as swiftc's helpers
  do: a value witness function of the same shape (the `destroy` of a struct
  whose one non-trivial field is resilient calls that field's witness and
  returns nothing) is not a helper of the field's type, and a function the
  witness tables or a record already claim is skipped. The metadata must
  come from an accessor call with request 0 (a local type's accessor, or an
  import whose symbol is a type metadata accessor), a local type's static
  metadata (kind and descriptor checked), a pointer slot (a bound import's
  type metadata, or a rebased pointer to local static metadata), an accessor
  passed as an argument, or a call with the helper's own arguments (a merged
  helper's instantiation call). The witness's value arguments must be the
  helper's arguments and its metadata argument the fetched metadata. The
  helper is named the way the demangler spells the symbol,
  `Module.T.outlined_destroy`, `Module.T.outlined_init_with_copy`,
  `outlined_init_with_take`, `outlined_assign_with_copy`,
  `outlined_assign_with_take`; one whose type is its caller's choice (the
  linker merged the helpers of several types) is `outlined_destroy.merged`
  and so on. Its prototype is the one the body states: `void *f(void *value)`
  for a destroy, `void *f(void *src, void *dest)` for the others (the
  arguments in the order the helper takes them, the value it returns), plus
  the `swift.type_metadata *(*accessor)(unsigned long)` or the instantiation
  arguments a merged helper takes. A helper whose metadata comes from
  `__swift_instantiateConcreteTypeFromMangledName` at a constant cache is
  left unnamed: its type is in the mangled name the cache points at. On the
  same app the arm names 3,024 helpers (2,697 with their type, 327 merged),
  and 210 calls in a 390-function sample print as named helper calls. The
  stripped arm64 dylib `swift_outlined_macho` covers a per-type helper, two
  merged ones and one fed by the instantiation helper.
  The crate test `unlace-console/tests/verify_valuewitness.rs` runs the stripped
  swiftc-built `swift_witness_elf` (a struct, an enum and a generic struct, and
  a generic function that moves a `T`) with the arm on and off.
- **PDB** (`pdb`, PE-only, default-on;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pdb/mod.rs`): Windows' debug info
  lives in a separate `.pdb` the PE only fingerprints, so the pass reads the
  CodeView record, locates the file, applies a hard **fingerprint gate**, then walks
  the global symbol stream (S_PUB32/S_GPROC32) and renames stripped functions behind
  the label gate. Names only; the passes below add types and lines. A C++ public is
  decorated (`??0Box@app@@QEAA@H@Z`), so the pass reduces it with the same
  name-only demangler the loader applies to a COFF or ELF symbol: `app::Box::Box`,
  nested under its namespace. MSVC spells a compiler-generated member and a
  function-local entity with backtick-quoted phrases; those become identifiers
  (`` Box::`scalar deleting destructor' `` is `Box::scalar_deleting_destructor`,
  `` `ns::f'::`2'::<lambda_1> `` is `ns::f::lambda_1`), as the anonymous namespace
  already does.

  Locating it is a short ordered search
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pdb/locate.rs (pdb_candidates)`),
  most specific first: an explicit path in `unlace_pdb_path`, then the CodeView
  record's own filename resolved **beside the image**, then `<image stem>.pdb`
  beside the image. The middle tier is the one a `/Zi` build makes free — the
  linker writes the name of the `.pdb` it emitted into the binary, and in a normal
  build tree or release archive that file is sitting right there. What it does not
  do is trust that recorded string as a path: it is content written by whoever
  linked the image, so only its last segment is taken (splitting on `\` as well as
  `/`, since a Windows linker writes the former and a POSIX `Path` does not treat it
  as a separator), it must be a single ordinary `*.pdb` component, and it is only
  ever joined onto the directory the caller already opened the image from. A
  build-machine absolute path, a `..` run, and a Windows drive prefix therefore
  cannot escape that directory.

  The gate is what makes the search safe to run by default, and it runs per
  candidate: a `.pdb` is applied only when its GUID and age equal the PE's
  record. The age is the DBI stream's, which the linker writes with the image's;
  the PDB info stream's age is bumped by every later writer (`symstore`,
  `pdbcopy`, Mozilla's and Microsoft's symbol servers publish age 2 or 3 against
  the image's 1), so it is used only when the DBI stream states none. So a stale sidecar left beside a rebuilt binary, or an
  unrelated `.pdb` that happens to share the name, is skipped rather than applied —
  wrong names are worse than no names. A skipped-because-mismatched candidate gets
  one `[unlace pdb]` line on stderr naming it: once the search is automatic, silence
  would make "your `.pdb` is stale" indistinguishable from "there is no `.pdb`
  here". A candidate that simply does not exist is not reported; most images have no
  sidecar, and that is not a defect. The cost of the search is per *load* — at most
  three `open` attempts, only on a PE that carries a CodeView record — and the
  `.pdb` is parsed only when one of them opens and matches.

  A fourth tier is opt-in: `unlace_pdb_symsrv` names a symbol store, `<cache>` or
  `<cache>*<url>` (an `srv*` prefix as in `_NT_SYMBOL_PATH` is accepted). Only
  when the three tiers above find no match is the store's
  `<cache>/<name>/<GUID hex><age hex>/<name>` (the SymStore layout, `<name>` the
  same safe record name) tried, and with a URL a missing file is first fetched
  from `<url>/<name>/<key>/<name>` by running `curl` (300 s, 4 GiB at most),
  written beside its final name and renamed when complete, and tried at most
  once per process and path; a failed fetch gets one `[unlace pdb]` line. The
  fingerprint gate applies to it like any other candidate. Without the variable
  nothing is looked up or fetched.

  **(unlace) Types, prototypes and locals** (`pdbtypes`, PE-only, default **off**;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pdb/pdbtypes.rs`,
  `pdbtpi.rs`). From the same fingerprint-matched `.pdb`, the TPI type
  stream is mapped onto unlace types the way the DWARF mapper builds them:
  primitives by width and sign, pointers and references at the record's width,
  modifiers transparent, arrays flattened to their element, enumerations with
  their constants, and structures, classes and unions at the compiler's member
  offsets. A forward reference resolves to the definition with the same unique
  name; an aggregate is declared (`unlace_declare_record`) before its members are
  walked, so a pointer built to it meanwhile (a self-reference, or the structure
  reached first through a global that points at it) reads the completed layout. A class carries each base class as a `super_<Base>`
  member and its table pointer as a `__vftable` member at offset 0. A structure's
  bitfield (an `LF_MEMBER` of an `LF_BITFIELD` type) keeps its bit position, placed
  in the smallest byte span that covers it as `dwarfstructs` does (PE images are
  little-endian); overlapping members, members past the stated size and a union's
  bitfields are left out.
  Every procedure record in the module streams then gives its entry address a
  prototype from its type (a member function's `this` first), the parameter names
  coming from the procedure's own parameter records: the `S_LOCAL`s flagged as
  parameters, or for MSVC's unflagged `S_REGREL32`/`S_BPREL32` the ones above the
  return address, used only when their count matches the type's. On i386 the
  stated calling convention binds the `x86win.cspec` model of that name.
  Identical-COMDAT folding can put several procedures of different types at one
  address (MSVC's CRT folds `_get_initial_narrow_environment` with unrelated
  stubs); such an address gets no prototype and no locals. An argument list that
  is a lone `T_NOTYPE` (C's `int f()`) states no parameters, not `f(...)`. A
  variable's location comes from its def-range (`S_DEFRANGE_FRAMEPOINTER_REL`,
  its full-scope form, `S_DEFRANGE_REGISTER_REL`, `S_DEFRANGE_REGISTER`) or from
  the record itself (`S_REGREL32`, `S_BPREL32`, `S_REGISTER`). A frame-relative
  offset is placed in unlace stack coordinates only where the records fix the base:
  the x64 stack pointer in the body is the entry stack pointer less the
  `S_FRAMEPROC` callee-saved bytes and fixed frame (`cbSaveRegs + cbFrame`, the
  convention MSVC and LLVM both write), and the i386 `EBP` frame pointer is the
  entry stack pointer less the pushed `EBP`. An x64 frame register (`RBP`,
  `R13`) points where the function's `.pdata` unwind data puts it: the
  `UNWIND_INFO` names the register and its scaled offset, and the codes listed
  after `UWOP_SET_FPREG` ran before it, so the register is the entry stack pointer
  less their pushes and allocations plus `16 * FrameOffset`
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pdb/pdbframe.rs`); a chained record,
  an epilog code or an unknown one leaves it unknown. Under i386 frame-pointer
  omission (`S_FRAMEPROC` naming `VFRAME` for both locals and parameters) the
  virtual frame `$T0` is the address of the return address (the frame data's
  `$T0 .raSearch =`), and the i386 stack pointer is placed like the x64 one; a
  realigned frame (locals off `$T0`, parameters off `EBP`, as clang writes for an
  over-aligned local) leaves both unknown, since its locals sit at a run-time
  distance from the entry. A variable spilled in pieces (`S_DEFRANGE_REGISTER_REL`
  with `spilledUdtMember` or a nonzero `offsetParent`, or a subfield range) has no
  single slot and is skipped: clang scatters a scalarized array's elements in
  descending addresses. A slot below the return address that does not reach it
  becomes a named, typed stack local (the DWARF
  `LocalFact` channel); a register range of a non-parameter becomes a
  register-held local from the range's start; locals of an inlined call site
  belong to the inlinee and are skipped. `S_GDATA32`/`S_LDATA32` with a complete
  type become typed globals, and each `??_7` vftable public is typed as an array
  of code pointers, one per slot the virtuals its class or its primary base
  introduces occupy. A multiply-inheriting class's table for another base
  (`??_7C@@6BB@@@`, named `C::vftable_for_B`) gets that base's slots: the class's
  new virtuals go into its primary table. The raw symbol is read directly when
  every name in it is a plain identifier; any other spelling goes through the
  demangler, which types only a primary table. The pass runs at the commit, with the deferred entry passes, and only
  when `pdb` and `pdbtypes` are both on, so a default load never reads the type,
  module or line streams. Default off, since it changes the output of every PE
  with a matching `.pdb`; on in the `aggressive` preset. Measured with
  `decompile-all --mode aggressive` on Mozilla's MSVC-linked images with their
  published `.pdb`s, it names 1,795 of 2,069 parameters in `softokn3.dll`
  (2 without it), 2,880 of 3,186 in `firefox.exe` (82) and 2,546 of 2,802 in
  `mozglue.dll` (77), fully names 466, 965 and 1,007 signatures (1, 30, 28), and
  takes no more time; `firefox.exe` gains 2,647 pointer casts where MSVC STL
  `std::basic_string` locals reach their small-string union. Stripped public
  `.pdb`s (Microsoft's) carry no types or locals and change nothing. The clang
  fixtures `pdb_types_x86_64` and `pdb_types_i386`
  (`unlace-console/tests/verify_pdbtypes.rs`) pin the frame math.

  **(unlace) Source lines** (`pdblines`, PE-only, default **off**;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pdb/pdblines.rs`). The PDB twin of
  `dwarf_lines`: each module's C13 line program maps code to `file:line`, and
  every line entry inside a procedure becomes an instruction comment at its
  address, attached to that procedure. Only the file's base name is kept, the
  first entry per address wins, and the compiler's hidden line numbers
  (`0xfeefee`, `0xf00f00`) and line 0 are dropped. It runs at the commit, only
  with `pdb` and `pdblines` both on, and is left out of the `aggressive` preset for the reason
  `dwarf_lines` is.

  Every PDB pass (`pdb`, `pdbinterior`, `pdbtypes`, `pdblines`) runs under a
  panic guard: the `pdb` crate asserts on some malformed records (an `LF_ARRAY`
  whose dimensions are not followed by the end of the record), so a panic while
  reading the `.pdb` is caught, reported once as a `[unlace pdb]` line on stderr,
  and that pass contributes nothing, as if there were no `.pdb`.
- **CVF trace** (`cvftrace`, PE32 i386 only, default `on`;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/cvftrace/mod.rs`): Compaq
  Visual Fortran links a `.trace` section of traceback records into its images,
  and they name every routine even when the image keeps no symbols. A record is a
  16-byte header (type, file count, code base, code length, record size), the
  record's source-file names, then a line program: routine markers carry a name
  and a preferred virtual address, file selections step forward through the
  file table, and line and PC deltas describe inclusive address intervals. The
  decoder (`decode.rs`) bounds every read by its record and declines a record
  outright on anything it does not understand: an unknown opcode, a file index
  past the table, a routine outside the record's code range, a routine name that
  is not a Fortran identifier (letters, digits, `_` and CVF's `$`, at most 127
  bytes), a truncated record, or an incremental-link type-11 record. Size caps
  (a 16 MiB section, 65,536 file names charged only to accepted records, 262,144
  facts) stop decoding with one `[unlace cvftrace]` note on stderr rather than
  silently. A routine must start in an executable section, and a name the trace
  gives two addresses, or an address it gives two names, is dropped. What
  survives is the lowest-priority function name
  (`AnalysisOutput::fallback_names`), committed after the PDB, FID, Objective-C
  and Swift renames: it renames an existing `sub_<addr>` placeholder and nothing
  else. It never creates a function, so a routine marker that is not a real
  entry cannot split one, and it never takes a name that a function, data symbol
  or alias elsewhere already uses, so an export, COFF symbol, PDB name or
  `--define-function` keeps both its address and its name. `cvftrace lines` adds
  the second pass, `cvftrace_lines`, which comments each interval's start with
  `file.for:N`, the counterpart of `dwarf_lines` and off by default for the
  same reason. Anything other than a PE32 i386 image with a `.trace` section
  returns before a byte is read.
- **FID** (`fid`, default-off, Listing-gated, DB via `unlace_fid_db`;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/fid/mod.rs (FidPass)`): a
  byte-exact port of Ghidra's FunctionID hashing — the operand-masked FNV-1a64
  full hash over a function's instruction stream (mask via the SLEIGH
  `instruction_mask`, x86 NOP padding skipped) — looked up in a unlace `.fid`
  database built by `unlace fid build`. Only a bucket that collapses to exactly one
  name renames (never guess on a tie). With `fid strict`, at least one record
  for that unique name must also match both the specific hash and code-unit
  count; a mismatch declines the rename even when the name is correct. This
  gate does not prove identity and never resolves a multi-name bucket. `fid on`
  retains the full-hash-only behavior. A declined name is still held as FID's
  guess (`AnalysisOutput::signature_vetoes`): it joins the agreement check with
  FLIRT at that address but is never applied alone, so `strict` names a subset
  of what `on` names. The code-unit count follows from the full hash; the
  specific hash decides. It folds in operand values that differ between links
  (absolute addresses in non-PIE code), so it agrees mainly when the database
  was built from the same link as the target: against glibc 2.35's `libc.a`,
  strict kept 12 of the 390 correct names `on` gives a stripped static program
  and did not remove its one wrong name, and against a database built from
  another static program linked with the same `libc.a` it kept 8 of 432 and
  removed both wrong names. Renames are only through the placeholder label
  gate: the stripped-static-library recovery (`sub_4017c0` → `unlace_crc32`) with no
  way to clobber a real name.
  The database builder bounds linear decoding by both the next entry and a
  nonzero symbol size when one exists; ARM32 odd symbols decode as Thumb at
  their even address in a scoped context. Unsized symbols still use the next
  entry. Rebuilding a pre-change database can change records when the old
  extent included trailing padding; existing databases remain readable.
  The next-entry clip folded the alignment padding GCC emits after a function
  (`data16 cs nopw`, which the x86 skipper does not skip) into most glibc
  records, and a Listing-based query never decodes that padding after a
  return. Rebuilt from glibc 2.35's `libc.a`, the database gives the right
  single candidate for 396 instead of 216 of the 1,060 sized functions of a
  static test program, and no wrong single candidate instead of 5: code-identical
  twins whose padding differed now share an ambiguous bucket. Built from the
  Thumb-2 armhf `libc.a`, it went from 9 records to 3,078. A function that ends
  in a call the Listing does not know never returns can lose its match,
  because the Listing decodes the padding after that call and the bounded
  record does not.
  (unlace) **Prototypes.** A record may carry the function's prototype as one C
  declaration and the type declarations it needs
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/fid/db.rs`, format version 2:
  each record adds a prototype offset and a run in a table of declaration
  offsets, so records share a declaration's text). A version-1 file loads as
  before, and a database none of whose records has a prototype is still written
  as version 1, byte for byte what the builder wrote before. A load decodes each
  distinct run once and every record naming it shares that one copy, as does
  every match of such a record, so a database built from many variants of one
  library (each optimization level a new record over the same declarations)
  costs memory in proportion to its distinct text, and a binary with many
  identical functions does not copy a record's declarations once per match.
  Records name their strings by offset, so a small file can still name one long
  string many times, in names or in overlapping runs; a load stops with
  `invalid` once the text it has decoded (each distinct run counted once) passes
  the larger of 64 MiB and 128 bytes per byte of the file. `unlace fid build`
  fills a record from the prototype the object's own committed analysis parked
  on the function symbol of that name, which is its DWARF signature
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/fid/fidproto.rs
  (describe)`; the hashes are taken before that commit), and from `--assert
  'prototype <name> <declaration>'` with any `--assert 'typedef …'`, which
  replace what was read. The types of every match land in one program, so a
  record type that two objects define differently is left as its forward
  declaration in every record and named on stderr (`drop_disputed`), and an
  enumeration two objects define differently is left out of every record, so a
  prototype naming it no longer parses and is dropped at the match. The check
  runs over every input record before records with the same hashes and name
  are merged, so the definitions it compares, and the database written, do not
  depend on the order of the objects in the archive or on the command line; a
  type one
  object defines and another only declares (an opaque handle a library casts
  to its own private state) is defined for both, so a function of the second
  object reads the first object's members. On a match the pass emits the
  prototype of the record
  the specific hash and code-unit count single out, else the one prototype all
  describing records of the bucket agree on (`pick`), as a `FidProtoFact`. The
  commit applies it last
  (`crates/unlace-console/src/fidproto.rs (apply)`): only to a
  function that carries the record's name, whether FID renamed it or the symbol
  table already said so, and only when nothing else parked a prototype there, so
  DWARF and every library table win and a later `--assert` replaces it. The
  type declarations are parsed first; one that redefines a type the program
  already has is rejected by the parser and the program's definition stands. A
  prototype that does not parse is dropped with a header warning on the
  function, and so is one that passes or returns a structure or union by value
  whose definition the record left out (`opaque_by_value`): an opaque type has
  no size to assign storage from, and a sizeless return would be taken for a
  hidden return buffer, inventing a first parameter and shifting the real ones.
  A declaration whose brackets nest deeper than 64 is not handed
  to the parser at all, since the text comes from a file and the parser
  recurses once per level. The applied prototype is parked like a DWARF one, so
  the function's callers copy it too, and the drive checks it against the body
  (04 §4.2 "Seeding").
  `unlace fid query` exposes full-hash candidates as a read-only lookup, each
  with its record's `prototype`. It
  reports whether the entry was discovered or supplied by the caller, the
  Listing's instruction-boundary classification, and that identity is unverified;
  `single_candidate` means one distinct name, not a confirmed match. ARM32 odd
  pointers select Thumb at the even address. An ARM32 instruction whose context
  no longer reproduces the Listing makes the result unavailable. Multiple address
  queries reuse the initial Listing and database, preserve input order, and scope
  each decode context so one query cannot change another. An address not in the
  initial Listing gets a separate walk. It exposes whether any candidate's
  specific hash matches and whether each candidate's code-unit size matches.
  These are evidence, not identity proof. Specific hashes do not select a winner;
  a database that does not apply to the binary or has malformed bytes is an error.
  (unlace) **Which database applies**
  (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/fid/fidapply.rs (applies)`):
  a database is matched against an image only when its header language has the
  image language's processor, address size and instruction byte order, the rule
  of Ghidra's `FidFile.canProcessLanguage`. Those facts are read from the
  `.ldefs` entries the bootstrap can see
  (`crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/langfamily.rs (LanguageFamilies)`:
  every language of a shared database, or, for a database scanned for one
  load, the database's own language and any other read on demand; with the
  `instructionEndian` attribute the C++ decoder ignores), not from the
  id's fields, which differ for some languages: `MIPS:BE:64:64-32addr` is 32-bit,
  and BE8 ARM (`ARM:LEBE:32:*`) and big-endian AArch64 have little-endian
  instructions. The variant and the compiler spec take no part, because the hash
  covers only instruction bytes and operand masks; a header language no scanned
  `.ldefs` defines applies to nothing, as Ghidra ignores a library whose language
  it cannot find. An architecture built without an `.ldefs` scan falls back to
  exact language-id equality. Before this, the pass matched any database whatever
  its header said, so a database labeled `AARCH64:LE:64:v8A` named functions in
  an x86-64 image. `unlace fid build` applies the same rule to each input: an object
  whose own language the `--lang` label does not apply to is refused (a member of
  an archive is skipped, and an archive none of whose object members the label
  applies to is refused), since its hashes were computed with the object's
  decoder and the label would send them to other images. **Status.** The pass
  reports what became of the database `unlace_fid_db` names on
  `AnalysisOutput::fid_databases` — `loaded`, `missing`, `unreadable`, `invalid`
  (the bytes do not parse) or `incompatible` — with the header's record count,
  language and compiler spec when it was read. The engine keeps the last commit's
  reports (`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (fid_databases)`), and the
  CLI prints a stderr warning for every status but `loaded`, once per run (not in
  `--jobs` workers), and lists the reports as `fid_databases` in its JSON
  documents. The console's `read symbols` prints the same `warning:` line
  (`crates/unlace-console/src/ifacedecomp.rs (IfcReadSymbols)`), which
  the text `decompile` surface relays from its `decomp_dbg` session. A configured database that is not matched does not change the exit
  status: it only ever adds names, and a database set for a batch of
  mixed-architecture images is expected not to apply to some of them.
- **FLIRT** (`flirt`, default-off, Listing-gated, signatures via `UNLACE_FLIRT_SIGS`;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/flirt/mod.rs (FlirtPass)`): names
  library functions from IDA FLIRT `.sig` files (versions 5 to 11; raw, deflate,
  zlib or zstd bodies). Reading the files and the byte-level match (trie, CRC,
  tail bytes, instruction bits) is the `flirt-sig` crate; the pass adds the
  reference names, the rounds and the arbitration below. `UNLACE_FLIRT_SIGS` is a `:`-separated list of files or
  directories whose `*.sig` files are all taken. A startup signature (its module
  names are IDA scripts, not functions) and one whose header file-type mask
  excludes the binary's format are never loaded, so pointing the variable at all
  of a `sig/` tree loads only the libraries that can apply.
  The applicable files are applied in an order that puts the C runtime of the image's compiler first:
  a `.comment` record that names GCC or clang (`GCC: (GNU) 15.2.0`, `clang version 18.1.3`; not
  an image with a `rustc version` record) selects the files whose name or header library name
  is that compiler's runtime (libgcc, libstdc++; compiler-rt, libc++) (`analyzers/flirt/cruntime.rs`).
  The order does not change the arbitration, which scores candidates rather than taking the first. When
  signature files were given and none is that runtime, the pass reports the compiler and its release on stderr.
  A signature header records no release, so a release mismatch inside the family is not reported.
  `unlace flirt make` names the four GCC `crtstuff.c` helpers (`deregister_tm_clones`, `register_tm_clones`,
  `__do_global_dtors_aux`, `frame_dummy`; `flirtpat::CRT_HELPERS`) from their local symbols, so a signature built from a
  `crtbeginS.o`, `crtbegin.o` or `crtbeginT.o` names them in a stripped image. Any other local-only function still yields no pattern.
  With `flirttil on` (default off) the type libraries that the `ids` and `idsnames` files
  beside the applicable signatures name are read as sources of the `typelib` option: a line
  `<signature> <library>` autoloads `<library>.til`, from beside the `.sig` or from
  `UNLACE_TIL_DIR` (`analyzers/flirt/autotil.rs`). Nothing is read under `typelib off`.
  At every discovered entry the byte trie is walked over the first `pattern_len`
  bytes; a module matches when the byte-swapped CRC-16/X.25 of the `crc_len` bytes
  after the prefix, its tail bytes and its expected instruction bits agree. An
  entry with fewer bytes than the prefix left in its section is walked over
  zero-padded code and keeps only the modules whose length fits in what is left,
  so a short function that ends the section is matched like any other. A
  reference names a function when the instruction covering its offset points
  there: a branch or call target or, on x86, the address its 32-bit field encodes
  (an `ifunc` resolver references its implementations with `lea`, which the Listing
  records as no flow). A module with a reference is accepted only when the
  reference's target already carries that name, or when the target is not named
  yet and its own bytes match a reference-free signature of that name (the callee's
  own signature, `callee_named`; a callee discovery never created, reached only
  by a tail `jmp`, resolves this way). Such a target counts as an agreeing site
  in the arbitration below. Matching runs up to three
  rounds and names found in one round satisfy references in the next.
  The version-11 reference sites decide the rest. A module that lies wholly inside
  the trie prefix has no CRC to tell it apart, so it is dropped when one of its
  sites points at a differently named target, and waits for the last round unless
  one agrees. When the modules at one entry disagree on the name, each name scores
  +4 for a site whose target has the expected name, -4 for one whose target has
  another name and 0 for an unnamed target; the strictly best name wins and a tie
  waits for a later round. A round that names nothing new makes the next one the
  last, and in the last round a module whose CRC covers bytes past the prefix may
  keep its classic reference unnamed (`rand` calling an unmatched `__random`). An
  entry whose first instruction is a return is never named, nor one that returns
  right after an `endbr64`/`endbr32` or AArch64 `bti` landing pad (an empty
  function matches every empty-function module), nor an entry that lies inside an
  instruction decoded at an earlier address (a tail byte: IDA's `flirt: skip tail
  bytes`; a Thumb entry is compared with its mode bit cleared), a name found at two
  entries goes only to the strictly best scored one or to none, and a name the
  binary already carries is not given again. A module's name is the library
  object's linkage spelling, so it is demangled the way the loader demangles an
  installed symbol (`flirt/mod.rs (display_name)`): a Rust library's
  `_RNvNtCs…_4core6option13expect_failed` is `core::option::expect_failed`, and a jump
  thunk's `j_` prefix moves onto the leaf (`__rustc::j___rdl_alloc`) so the thunk
  and its target stay apart. A referenced name is compared both raw and
  demangled, since the binary's own names are demangled. Measured with a `.sig`
  made by `unlace flirt make` from the Rust 1.95 `libstd`/`libcore`/`liballoc` rlibs
  on the stripped rustc 1.94 nightly `json_typegen` (`--option listing on`): 137
  functions named, mangled before; against its unstripped twin 132 are right, 3 are
  the `__rust_alloc` jump stubs named `j_` for the `__rdl_alloc` they jump to, and 2
  are functions with another one's identical code. The names go out through the FID
  rename stream and its placeholder label gate. FID and FLIRT names are code
  signature guesses (`FidMatch::by_signature`): the commit applies the metadata
  renames (PDB, Objective-C, Swift) first, so a guess never replaces one, and
  applies a guess only when every FID and FLIRT name at that address agrees.
  A supplied function name is protected even when it resembles a `sub_` or
  `FUN_` placeholder. Before replacing a discovery placeholder, the engine
  checks both the signature spelling and its loader-style canonical spelling
  for existing name ownership. A collision leaves the placeholder and the
  established name available at their original addresses.
  A defined ELF object label inside an allocated, mapped section reserves its
  spelling for this check even when its declared size is zero. Its name
  provides ownership evidence only and supplies no data object extent.
  Eligible signature proposals at different entries that share a raw or
  canonical spelling all keep their placeholders. Ownership is checked before
  any of the proposals are installed, so traversal order cannot choose an owner.
  When the two passes disagree, the function keeps its placeholder rather than
  taking whichever name sorts first.
  Measured on stripped static programs against their unstripped twins (right/wrong
  names): x86-64 against Debian 12 `libc.a` with `glibc_amd64.sig` 338/0, Debian 13
  337/1, i386 with `glibc_i386.sig` 227/4, AArch64 Debian 13 with `glibc_arm64.sig`
  156/1. The stripped static-pie `/sbin/ldconfig` gets 229 of 1,647 functions
  named. The remaining wrong names are functions whose code is identical
  to the library function named. A `.sig` file whose tree and modules would take
  more than 256 bytes of memory per byte of the file is not loaded (IDA's take at
  most 81), and neither reading nor matching recurses, so a crafted file cannot
  overflow the stack and takes memory only in proportion to its size (up to about
  1.6 KB per byte, since the reader's stack of open tree nodes is not counted). It
  can still make the pass slow, because every module of a crafted file can match
  at every entry, so `UNLACE_FLIRT_SIGS` should name signature files from a trusted
  source.
  The opt-in report API in
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/flirt/rustprofiles.rs`
  compares an explicit set of Rust version/optimization candidates on the same
  caller-supplied Listing and entry set. It retains each external signature
  source's identity, inline/no-inline bank, header library name, and accepted
  `core::`, `std::`, or `alloc::` match addresses and full names. The shared
  matcher can report an already-named entry when its exact signature name agrees;
  this does not emit a rename or alter matching rounds. Name collisions,
  reference-site requirements, CRC checks and ambiguous module names still
  refuse. Ordinary `FlirtPass` renames retain their existing behavior and do not
  collect report records.
  Each candidate's score is the greater of its two bank counts, not their sum.
  An absent bank makes the comparison incomplete; duplicate banks are errors.
  An empty candidate set, all-zero scores and tied best scores report distinct
  unresolved outcomes. A unique positive maximum identifies only the best
  measured candidate, never an authenticated compiler version or permission to
  enable an ABI/layout recovery. The API accepts linked little-endian x86-64
  ELF images and checks external signatures' x86 processor, ELF applicability
  and non-startup status. The caller supplies the signature provenance and
  candidate set; no signature corpus is bundled or downloaded, and no candidate
  is inferred from a fixture's name or a nightly version number.
  `unlace functions --summary --json --rust-signature-manifest PATH` requests this
  report for one loaded image. The CLI validates the explicit corpus/candidate
  manifest and hashes each signature's bytes before constructing the request.
  The request is distinct from `UNLACE_FLIRT_SIGS` and does not turn on `flirt`,
  `listing`, or another analysis consumer. The console consumes it once during
  the deferred image-analysis commit; the observer in
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/passes.rs` receives the final accepted
  Listing after recovery and never applies the report's matches as names.
  If a Listing is already required, that same object supplies the report. If
  only reporting requires it, consumer gates retain their original values.
  Unsupported targets decline before a reporting-only decode. A repeated
  analysis commit retains the completed report without rescoring.
  The report considers function entries in each text section's final 128 KiB;
  summary presentation filters do not change its candidate set or evidence.
  `compiler_provenance` contains independently observed Rust `.comment` records
  and complete `/rustc/<40-hex-commit>/library/` source-path hashes, including
  conflicting records. No source path is translated into a nominal version.
  `rust_signature_profile` carries compatibility scores and explicit unresolved
  statuses, with the verified external manifest/source identities. These fields
  are absent unless requested; stable compiler and formatter-layout facts remain
  separate. Malformed manifests and hash mismatches fail before image analysis.
  The CLI can include `comment_profile_hint` based on consistent stable ELF
  `.comment` records and the availability of both requested O3 banks. It chooses
  the closest patch at or below the compiler in the same minor, or the newest
  complete O3 profile of the same major when the compiler minor is above the
  requested range. Prereleases, conflicting versions and changes in major
  version have no such hint. The report evaluates scores and ties independently
  of the hint. Compiler identity, ABI and layout recovery use their original
  evidence.
  The separate `--apply-rust-signatures PATH` request explicitly trusts the same
  hashed manifest for names. It is available on `functions` and one-function
  `decompile`, whose text and JSON forms share the in-process load. Application
  consumes the final accepted Listing once before selection; inventory uses the
  same analysis defaults as decompilation, and selecting an address does not
  implicitly disable discovery. Explicit analysis options still apply.
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/flirt/rustprofiles/application.rs`
  requires a positive unique profile after every requested candidate is complete.
  Each proposal must have the exact same raw symbol and address in both banks of
  that profile. The maximum bank score alone authorizes no names. Empty agreement,
  unresolved profiles, unavailable analysis and unsupported images fail explicitly.
  Agreed pairs become ordinary signature `FidMatch` records, sanitized before
  merging with all other analysis output. The normal commit requires an existing
  discovered function and arbitrates metadata, loader ownership, raw/canonical
  name collisions, other FID/FLIRT guesses and vetoes. Agreement proposes a name;
  it does not bypass those refusals or imply types, ABI, compiler identity or
  side effects. The ordinary runtime version and registry-crate fields remain
  sourced from the image, independently of the selected signature profile.
  Later caller declarations and assertions keep their precedence.
  Bytes overlays are refused before loading, and the console independently
  declines application after an effective overlay. Archive inputs are refused
  before member selection or fan-out, including an archive holding linked ELF
  members. Ordinary archive commands retain their behavior. Slice/target/ISA and
  image-selection overrides are refused. Batch and worker application is not
  supported: ordinary inventory replay cannot replace existing placeholders or
  preserve all accepted aliases without a separate image-bound fact transport.
  No request changes the normal load. Report-only requests retain their original
  shape and behavior and cannot be combined with application in the same run.
  `unlace rust-signatures check` validates a local installed or explicit manifest
  before any image is opened. The command uses the same hash, signature format
  and applicability checks as a report and requires both banks for every
  candidate to indicate availability. The check reads only the requested
  manifest location and its referenced banks. Reports and application each
  obtain their own explicit manifest inputs.
- **Rust standard-library signatures** (`ruststdsigs off|exact|nearest`, default
  off; `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/flirt/ruststdsigs.rs`): adds a
  `.sig` for the Rust `std`, `core` and `alloc` to the FLIRT pass, built from an
  installed rustup toolchain. A Rust binary links its rustc's precompiled standard
  library, so those functions match the toolchain's rlibs up to relocations. The
  image's `.comment` names its compiler (`rustc version 1.94.0-nightly (b68e16cfc
  2026-01-11)`), and each toolchain under the rustup home (`RUSTUP_HOME`, else
  `~/.rustup`) names its own in the `.comment` of its `libstd` objects. `exact` takes
  the toolchain whose record equals the image's; `nearest` takes that one, else the
  one whose record's date is closest, then the closest version. Its three rlibs go
  through the `unlace flirt make` pattern and `.sig` writers once and the result is
  cached (`XDG_CACHE_HOME`, else `~/.cache`, at
  `unlace/ruststdsigs/<version>-<target>.sig`). Only an x86-64 or AArch64 Linux ELF
  with a `rustc version` record is considered, and the matching is the FLIRT pass's
  own, so it needs `flirt on` and the Listing. The choice travels as
  `UNLACE_RUSTSTDSIGS`, since the pass reads its signatures while the image loads.
  Measured on stripped release binaries against their symbol tables (names, right,
  `j_` jump stubs named for their target, wrong): a probe built by 1.95.0 with the
  1.95.0 toolchain 140/135/3/2, one built by 1.100.0 with 1.100.0 150/145/3/2; with
  the other of the two 70/63/3/4 and 71/64/3/4. The cargo-installed `fclones`
  (1.101.0-nightly of 2026-11-05) takes 1.100.0 under `nearest` and gets
  239/233/3/3; `json_typegen` and `wasm2es6js` (1.94.0 nightlies) take 1.95.0 and get
  137/132/3/2 and 67/66/0/1. A wrong name is a function with another's identical
  code.
- **FLIRT signature writer** (`unlace flirt make`, a build-time command that no
  decompile reaches;
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/flirt/flirtpat.rs (patterns_from_object)`,
  `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/flirt/flirtsig.rs (build_sig)`):
  writes the `.pat` and `.sig` files the FLIRT pass above reads, from object files
  or the members of a static library. One pattern is made per function start that
  carries a global name (aliases at one address share it, a strong name before a
  weak one, fewer leading underscores first): the function's bytes, up to its
  symbol size or else to the next function symbol of the section, with every byte
  a relocation rewrites left variable. On the fixed-width instruction sets
  (AArch64, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC, LoongArch) the whole instruction word is
  variable. On x86 the bytes a linker may rewrite when it relaxes the relocation
  are variable too: the opcode and ModRM in front of a `GOTPCRELX`, `GOT32X` or
  initial-exec TLS field, and the whole general-dynamic and local-dynamic TLS call
  sequences. On x86-64 and i386 a `call`, `jmp` or `jcc` with a 32-bit displacement
