that is itself code. An instruction is *trusted* when it is reachable from a
function entry over static branch and call targets and over the fall-through of
instructions that are not calls, or are conditional calls, or are direct calls to
a function some path of which provably reaches a `RETURN`
(`poolextents.rs (returning_entries)`, a least fixpoint propagated backwards
from every `RETURN`: a computed jump, an indirect call or a user operation never
proves a return, so a PLT stub stays unproven, and a function the no-return list
names never returns). A callee proves its call's fall-through only if it
returns *there*: libgcc's Thumb-1 switch helpers (`__gnu_thumb1_case_uqi` and
kin) read the case table that follows their `bl` and return past it with `add
lr,r1; bx lr`, so the table would be trusted as code and a table halfword can
spell `ldr rN,[pc,#imm]`. A `RETURN` through `lr` (`bx lr`, `mov pc,lr`) therefore
reaches back only over instructions that leave `lr` alone; a data-processing
write to `lr` or a load of it from anywhere but the stack stops it, a reload
from the stack (`pop {..,lr}`, `ldr lr,[sp],#4`) makes it a return through the
stack, which reaches back over anything, and a return to an address computed
from `lr` (`subs pc,lr,#4`) proves nothing. The helpers (`__gnu_thumb1_case_*`,
`__ARM_common_switch*`, `__ARM_switch*`, `__aeabi_switch*`) are also excluded by
name. Everything reached only by falling through an unproven
call or a user operation is provisional (`poolextents.rs
(trusted_instructions)`). A pool word is then a 4-aligned executable word that a
trusted `ldr`/`ldrd`/`vldr` reads at a fixed address — the resolved `[0x…]` and
`[pc,#imm]` operand forms the `poolentry` scanner parses, both words of a 64-bit
literal, but not a post-indexed or write-back form such as `[pc],-r2` that a
Thumb body decoded as A32 can spell; a byte or halfword read proves nothing — covered by no trusted
instruction and the static target of none. That judgement is made twice, under
two notions of trust, and a word that passes either is a pool word: the one
above, and a strict one whose trust crosses no call fall-through at all. The
strict witness is what sees a pool after a call to a function that does return
— gcc places one there when `__builtin_unreachable()` follows the call — since
under the first notion the word is reached and so excluded. Trust is only as
good as the Listing's function entries and returning callees, and both admit
data: discovery in a stripped library can seat an entry on a pool word whose
low halfword spells `push {..,lr}`, and the pool after a returning call ahead of
`__builtin_unreachable()` is trusted under the first notion. Such a word that
spells `ldr rN,[pc,#imm]` names live code past an unproven call, and bounding
that call deleted the rest of a real function (armhf glibc's
`__resolv_context_get_preinit` after its `malloc`, static glibc's
`__malloc_info` after an `fprintf`). So a witness must also pass two tests every
real literal load passes (`poolextents.rs (Loads::witnesses)`): no
fixed-address whole-word load anywhere in the Listing, trusted or not, reads
the witness's own bytes as data, and no known function entry lies between the
witness and the word it reads, because a compiler's pool belongs to the
function that loads it. Maximal stride-4 runs of the union are the extents
(`AnalysisOutput::arm_pool_extents`), which the commit parks on the
architecture. It adds no entry and no decode to the walk, and a provisional
instruction's reads cannot shield a word or vouch for one: the junk after `bl
die` in the reported shape covers nothing, while the loads before the first
import call witness the pool; a pool constant that spells a load of live code
past a returning call is at best reached past a call, so it is no strict
witness, and the live code it names is covered under the first notion.

A context painter applies the ARM/MIPS decode-mode paints per address before each
decode, so a Thumb or MIPS16 body disassembles in the right ISA. Each instruction
is decoded with a capturing p-code sink
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/decode.rs (decode_one)`). When
assembly text is requested, `Translate::one_instruction_with_assembly` captures
both results: SLEIGH reuses the p-code parse when safe, retaining its post-lift
assembly fallback for context commits and delay slots. Other translators use the
trait's sequential fallback. Assembly errors remain best-effort after a successful
lift; a lift error ends the decode without an assembly retry. Without text, the
walk calls `Translate::one_instruction` once. The resulting instruction is
classified by a lifted transliteration of the S2 flow rules
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/classify.rs (classify)`), whose three
load-bearing gotchas are worth restating: a constant-space branch operand is
p-code-relative (an intra-instruction branch), never a VMA; fall-through is decided
by the *last* op only; and delay slots are already folded into the reported length.

(unlace, GH-299) A predicated call — an A32 `blgt`, or a `bl` inside a Thumb `it`
block — lifts to a `CBRANCH` to the next instruction (the skip when the condition
fails) followed by the `CALL`. `classify` collects the target of every branch op,
and the walk makes every target of a call instruction a function, so the
instruction after each such call became a `sub_<addr>`: a mid-body entry that cut
its own function short, and evidence for the no-return discovery pass, which
counts the calls to a callee that are followed by a function start and at three
marks it no-return, truncating every caller in the image. The skip is the call's
fall-through and is now dropped from a call's targets; a call to the next
instruction (the i386 `call $+5` idiom), which carries no such branch, keeps its
target. Over 26 images (ARM, x86-64, i386 PE, AArch64, MIPS, PowerPC and RISC-V)
only the ARM inventories change: 37 entries fewer in all, 23 of them right after a
predicated call and the rest mid-body entries that sat in the functions those
entries had cut short, with no symbol-table start lost.

(unlace, GH-1632) The same holds for any other branch a returning call instruction
carries. The instruction at the end of an ARC zero-overhead loop is prefixed
with the branch back to the loop start (§2); when that instruction is a `bl`,
the back-edge is a jump inside the caller, not a second callee, so a call
instruction that falls through keeps only its `CALL` targets. The loop body is
still reached by the fall-through of `lp`.

The instruction model stores records in 1,024-row chunks. Its private address
index groups sorted `(address, row number)` pairs into 4 KiB pages, with a B-tree
of populated page keys for ordered lookup
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/insnstore.rs (InstructionStore)`).
Exact lookups binary-search one page; range queries visit only intersecting pages
and slice the boundary pages at their search positions. Growing the walk allocates
bounded chunks without copying a whole-image buffer. Every record retains its
flow targets, assembly and lazy p-code fields. Exact, range and interior queries
still borrow the original record in address order. The index key remains
independent of mutable instruction addresses. Replacing an address reuses its row.
Rebuilds that preserve ARM frames copy the paged address index but share immutable
record chunks. A shared chunk is copied only when a write reaches it through
`get_mut` or replacement, or when the walk appends into a shared partial tail
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/insnstore.rs
(InstructionChunk::clone)`). The copy retains full chunk capacity and leaves the
prior Listing independent. Serial and parallel walks use the same store. This
changes allocation and lookup layout, not the instruction partition or the facts
any consumer receives.

The optional lazy p-code list is an owned boxed vector, so an instruction with
no retained p-code reserves a pointer-sized slot rather than a vector header
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/model.rs (Insn)`). Populated lists
keep the same order and mutable vector operations, and cloning a record clones
its owned list. This changes the public `Insn.pcode` field from
`Option<Vec<RawOp>>` to `Option<Box<Vec<RawOp>>>`; a populated constructor uses
`Some(Box::new(ops))`. The usual Listing walk leaves the slot empty. A populated
slot adds the box allocation in exchange for reducing every record's fixed
storage; instruction contents and discovery remain unchanged.

After loading, committing analysis and applying caller assertions, the in-process
CLI returns unused glibc heap pages before selecting and decompiling functions
(`crates/unlace-cli/src/allocrelease.rs (after_analysis)`). Dropping
the Listing ends its ownership, but small tree and string allocations can leave
resident pages in allocator arenas. A single `malloc_trim(0)` at this boundary
releases free pages without discarding live program facts or imposing a memory
budget. This applies on GNU/Linux; other platforms retain their allocator's
ordinary release policy. It reduces post-analysis residency, while the chunked
instruction store reduces the construction peak on every platform. Worker
admission still uses the measured high-water mark, not the trimmed current RSS.

Three things the walk deliberately does **not** always produce. First, the human
assembly text on each instruction: capturing it means rendering every
instruction's assembly (`Translate::one_instruction_with_assembly`, which still
falls back to a second SLEIGH parse where the p-code parse cannot be reused), a
real per-instruction cost on top of the lift. Operands remain one owned string
per instruction, while repeated mnemonic spellings share one immutable text
allocation per decode lane. Capturing assembly is still pure waste whenever
nothing reads the text. Every bulk consumer of it — `noreturn_propagate`'s
call/NOP idiom checks, `tailcallentry`, and `poolentry`'s literal-load operands —
sits behind `listing`, so the walk captures text exactly when `listing` is on and
leaves the fields empty on the `fast_funcdisc`-only path, which is the path a
whole-binary export takes on any image large enough for `--mode auto` to resolve
to `fast`. The one other reader is AIF's function-start fingerprint (§1.5), which
needs the mnemonics of just the first two instructions of each *discovered*
function; rather than force whole-image capture for that, it falls back to
re-decoding those addresses through its own gap decoder when the Listing carries
no text. That the re-decode reproduces the walk's own reading is checked rather
than assumed: decoding an instruction commits the `globalset` context writes its
constructor asks for, and both the ARM and MIPS specs globalset a decode mode
(`TMode`, `ISA_MODE`) at a branch target, so a *later* decode can leave an address
in a different mode than the walk read it in — and the re-decode would then hand
back a mnemonic belonging to a different instruction while the stride and total
length still came from the Listing. Instruction length is the observable of
exactly that disagreement, since an alternate-ISA reading is a different width, so
the fingerprint compares the re-decoded length against the Listing's and declines
to fingerprint the function at all when they differ. Declining is the safe
direction: a function that contributes no fingerprint only makes the histogram
smaller, which can never admit a gap candidate the text-carrying path would have
rejected. Where the two agree the histogram — and every gap-walk and
pointer-target decision keyed off it — is unchanged, which is what keeps the
pointer-only entries `fast_funcdisc` exists to find.

Second, the cross-reference model itself, on the same reasoning and the same
gate. An edge is filed for every control-flow successor of every instruction, a
plain fall-through included. The walk collects each edge once in a contiguous
buffer, including edges whose destination is not decoded. After the walk, it
sorts and deduplicates that buffer by `(source, target, kind)` and makes one copy
sorted by `(target, source, kind)`
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/compactrefs.rs (ReferenceIndex)`).
Stable sorting preserves the first edge's operand metadata when duplicates are
removed. Incoming and outgoing queries binary-search the corresponding buffer
and borrow the matching slice; source iteration skips adjacent equal sources.
There is no separate map node or growable vector for each instruction's
fall-through. The reference model keeps the same edges, ordering, distinct-site
counts and absence queries as the former bucket maps. Serial walks, decode-lane
merges and ARM frame-preserving rebuilds all use this representation. During
index construction, the deduplicated buffer is trimmed to its length before it
is copied, and the copy is sorted in place, its keys being unique; every rebuild
still owns its instruction partition.

The readers, including `noreturn_disc`, `tailcallentry` and static format-string
analysis, are `listing` consumers, so a `fast_funcdisc`-only walk — again, the whole-binary export's path
on any image `--mode auto` resolves to `fast` — builds neither reference buffer and every xref
query answers "none" for every address. What must hold is that nothing else about
the walk changes, and nothing does: the reference filing is a pure sink, so the
instructions decoded, the functions discovered and the executable ranges are
identical either way, and `Listing::has_refs` reports which model was built rather
than leaving a caller to read an empty map as an answer. On a 147 MB C++ server
image (20.2 million instructions, 392,814 functions) the skipped model is 23.3
million edges: the whole `unlace functions` run drops from 12.9 GB resident to 6.0
GB and from 90.9 s to 73.7 s. The output of that command is byte-identical:
`unlace functions` carries no per-function budget, so nothing it prints can depend
on how long the run took. The whole-binary decompile surfaces do carry one —
`decompile-all`, `decompile-project` and `decompile-graph` under `--mode fast`
abandon a function after ten seconds of WALL CLOCK
(`crates/unlace-console/src/project.rs`,
`FAST_WHOLE_BINARY_FN_BUDGET_SECONDS`) — so a run that spends less time
elsewhere legitimately finishes functions a slower one gave up on: measured on
this image, 4 of 2,233 A/B function pairs differ, in both directions, every one
of them at that budget. Those surfaces are byte-identical at a fixed budget
(`--max-fn-seconds 0`), and the wall-clock watchdog is the documented exception
— the same exception for any change that moves the clock.

Third, instruction-byte coverage, which is *derived* from the instruction map
rather than mirrored into a range list: because a range list merges overlapping
but not adjacent ranges, a straight-line run of instructions would cost one node
per instruction, and the undefined-gap queries already answer from the
instruction map.

**Fast function discovery with conservative pointer validation** (`fast_funcdisc`, default-off;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/fast_funcdisc/mod.rs
(pointer_table_seeds)`) reuses that one walk without enabling the full Listing
tier. Its initial roots are only the loader-backed function symbols and the §1.5
format oracles; full `funcstart_patterns` roots are included only when both
`listing` and that option are on. The Listing walk recursively follows every
static CALL from those trustworthy roots, and `fast_funcdisc` commits all
resulting function entries.

On a Go image the walk leaves out the roots the pclntab already accounts for
(always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/pclntab/mod.rs
(function_entries)`). The pclntab names every Go function and gives its extent,
and the `gopclntab` pass puts each in the inventory. Walking them finds those
same functions again, and on an x64 PE it is expensive: Go's Windows linker
writes a `.pdata` record for every Go function, so with those records as roots
the walk decoded the whole Go text. A root at a pclntab function entry is
therefore dropped before the walk, and every other root is kept, so cgo's C
code and anything else the image's own records name is still walked. (Go's
internal linker lists a cgo image's C functions in the pclntab too, so there
they reach the inventory through the table; an external link leaves them out of
it, and they stay roots.) The cost is what the walk could reach only through a
pclntab function's body: it is no longer found unless something else names
it. Go code calls C only through function pointers (`asmcgocall`, the cgo
wrappers' data words), so this takes Go assembly that CALLs C code directly, in
an externally linked image whose C carries neither symbols nor unwind records;
there the called function and its callees are lost and the function before them
absorbs their bytes. Measured on four Go images (gh 2.89.0 for Windows and
Linux, two other Go PEs), on cgo builds (internal and external link, the race
detector, c-shared, plugin) for Linux and Windows, and on Go builds for macOS
and the BSDs, the inventory's addresses, names and sizes do not change. What changes is that a
Go function the walk reached only by a call no longer also carries a
`sub_<addr>` alias; a function another source of entries names (a `.pdata`
record, an entry oracle) keeps its alias as before; the decompiled C is the
same. The pruning applies only where `fast_funcdisc` builds the walk without
the full Listing, which is fast mode on every surface. With the Listing on,
every root is walked as before. The pruning applies only when the load-time
verdict is Go (the verdict that chose the pass set, so a `sourcelang` force
issued after the load does not count), since only then does the `gopclntab`
pass put the dropped roots' functions in the inventory.

The second source covers indirect-only callbacks. On non-ARM objects, scan
allocated, initialized, non-executable data for pointer-width runs of at least
two absolute values into executable ranges. Ignore a table longer than 256
slots. If the remaining tables produce more than 512 unique targets, discard
targets referenced by fewer than two distinct tables. Rank the survivors by
independent-table count and validate at most 4096. A candidate must still be
undefined in the Listing and must satisfy both AIF corroborators: its first two
decoded instruction mnemonics and their byte length form a fingerprint seen at
least four times among already-reached functions, and the bounded
`check_valid_subroutine` probe must cover more than two instructions without a
bad decode or out-of-image flow and reach either a terminal/computed jump or an
informative call/edge into known code. Accepted bodies are claimed so a later
candidate cannot split them. The walk then resumes with the accepted targets,
and the entries the load-time passes committed (a Delphi VMT method, say), as
roots, so their direct-call closure is discovered and committed too. On x86 the
functions a pass names, such as an MSVC vtable slot RTTI names or a constructor,
are roots as well (`engine.rs (commit_pending_analysis)`). On ARM they are not,
because their decode mode is not settled at that point. The
functions the walk had before the resume are kept, so the resume only adds
entries. A Delphi image's System memory-manager record is the case it was
written for: the record in writable data holds `GetMem`, `FreeMem` and
`ReallocMem`, which are reached only by indirect calls through that record, and
before the resume they were listed without any of the allocator code they call.
ARM instead reuses the existing Thumb-pointer
oracle: an aligned odd code pointer is accepted only at an undefined
frame-establishing prologue that passes the same valid-subroutine probe.

**Headerless-image function discovery** (`rawdiscover`, always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/rawdiscover.rs`) is the raw
analog of that walk. A `--raw-image` load has no `object::File`, so the whole
tier above declines: the consumer entry point opens by parsing the object, and
every §1.5 oracle under it reads a symbol table, an exception table or a section
list. The inventory is then exactly the `--entry` addresses the caller named,
which on a firmware image is one function spanning the file.

Neither of the two things that actually find functions needs that metadata, so
both run over the raw loader's synthetic `CODE` section instead. A **linear
call-target sweep** decodes each executable range end to end and collects the
statically derivable target of every direct call, dropping targets outside the
executable ranges; on a failed or zero-length decode it advances by the code
space's addressable unit rather than stopping, so a run of data costs
resynchronization instead of the rest of the range. Those targets join the
caller's seeds as roots of the ordinary recursive descent, which decodes each
for real and promotes the direct-call closure. Seeds are never dropped, so the
inventory can only grow.

The three walk inputs that come from the object file take the values a
headerless image honestly records: the executable universe is the raw loader's
single `CODE` section, the decode-mode painter is empty (there are no ARM `$t`
markers or Cortex-M vector table to read, and `--isa arm|thumb` has already
painted any whole-image mode claim), and the PPC64 local-entry fold is empty.
The gap-filling AIF walk is not run: it needs at least 20 already-discovered
functions to build its prologue fingerprint histogram, which is a corpus a raw
image does not have until this pass has already produced one.

Because a seed no longer bounds the run, `--entry` seeds a raw load without
*selecting*: with a discovered inventory beyond it, an entry that also filtered
would hide everything found from it. `--addr` continues to do both. What this
cannot recover is what the input does not record: a function no direct call
reaches and no seed names stays undiscovered, and `--define-function` remains
the way to assert it. Raw and TE containers only (a TE seeds the walk with its
container entry and bounds it by its `CODE` sections), so every object-format
result is byte-identical.

A byte-addressed raw image also runs the object-file pass list
(`objectview`, default-on), through an ELF view
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/objectview.rs (raw_as_elf)`).
The view has one `PT_LOAD` and one `SHF_ALLOC | SHF_WRITE | SHF_EXECINSTR`
`.text` section covering the mapped bytes at `--base`, which is the read-write-execute
block Ghidra's raw importer makes. The mapped bytes are the file for a headerless
image, and the image the container builds for a load that strips a header or
relocates (a PS-X EXE's 0x800-byte header, a DOS load module, a CIL method run): a
view of the whole file would put every byte the header's length past its address, so
the prologue oracle named functions in unmapped memory. Its machine, class and byte order come from
the selected SLEIGH language, and its `e_entry` is the first seed. A processor
ELF assigns no number gets `EM_NONE`: the sections still scan, and only
`object`'s architecture is unknown. The view runs at the commit like a TE's,
so the strings, the prologue and entry oracles and the Listing tier join the
seeds and `rawdiscover`'s call closure. A word-addressed target (code-space
word size above one) keeps the old behavior, because its addresses are not
byte offsets.

(unlace) **On an MS-DOS executable the sweep keeps only the calls a DOS program
can make** (`mzsweep`, always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/mzsweep.rs (MzEvidence)`). An
`MZ` load reaches this pass as a raw image (§1.2), but unlike a
firmware image its load module is mostly data: a large-model program's far data
segments (bitmaps, fonts, tables) and its DGROUP sit beside its code, the sweep
decodes them like code, and every `e8`/`9a` byte pattern it reads there becomes
a call whose target is minted as a function, most often a run of zero fill that
decompiles as repeated `ADD [BX+SI],AL`. The loader therefore hands the sweep
its relocated module and the linear address of every word a relocation entry
adjusted, and three rules apply to the sweep alone. A far `CALL`/`JMP
ptr16:16` counts only when the relocation table names its segment word: the
linker cannot know the paragraph DOS loads the module at, so an unrelocated
segment is absolute and does not land in the module. A call read in a
straight-line run (the decode stream since the last call, branch or return)
that also read zero fill or an undecodable byte does not count, since it is a
decode of data rather than a call an instruction makes. And a target counts
only when its own straight-line run, read up to its first control transfer (at
most 32 instructions), reads no zero fill and no undecodable byte and does not
end in an unrelocated far branch: a function opens with code. The far-branch
arm needs a relocation table. A module whose header lists no relocation
(EXEPACK's, whose fixups its stub applies after unpacking, or one an unpacker
stripped) carries its far calls unrelocated, so there a function that opens
with one, as a large-model prologue's `call far __chkstk` does, is still
code; the far call itself still counts for nothing, since its segment was
never moved to the load address and its target is not where the call goes.
The second rule does cost a real call now and then: a
function that only the sweep reaches and whose first call follows data in the
code segment (a switch table that decodes to an undecodable byte) with no
decoded branch in between loses that call, and its callee goes with it when
nothing else names it. `HLT`, which
SLEIGH lifts as a branch to itself, does not end a run, because the CPU resumes
after it. The seeds are never filtered, and the recursive descent still
promotes every target that code it reaches calls, so a refused call drops only
a target nothing else names. On the deark-unpacked DAZZLE.EXE of issue #1288
this removes the 24 swept entries IDA classifies as data (23 in the four far
data segments in front of the code, one in DGROUP; 321 functions become 297,
functions whose decode hits bad instruction data go from 15 to 3, and the
zero-run bodies from 15 to none) and keeps every function IDA has; the bodies
of every function that stays are byte-identical. `MZ` loads only, so every other
input, `--raw-image` included, is byte-identical.

(unlace) **A DOS program exit ends the flow** (always on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/dosexit.rs (analyze)`). `INT
20h` and `INT 27h` terminate a DOS program, and so does `INT 21h` with AH = 00h
(terminate), 31h (terminate and stay resident) or 4Ch (terminate with a return
code); control never comes back from any of them. x86 SLEIGH lowers every `INT
n` to a call through the `swi` userop that falls through, so before this the
decompiler followed `mov ah,4ch; int 21h` into the bytes after it: on the
unpacked DAZZLE.EXE of issue #1288, Turbo C's `_exit` ran into the zero word that
follows it, and three of the functions that call it, at four call sites, decoded
zero fill as `ADD [BX+SI],AL` up to the next function: five of the image's eight
`funcboundflow` warnings. Over the Listing the raw
discovery built, every `INT 20h`/`INT 27h` is an exit site, and an `INT 21h` is
one when AH holds 00h, 31h or 4Ch on the one path into it: walking back along
fall-through edges, the nearest instruction that writes AH decides (`mov
ah,4ch`, `mov ax,4c00h`, `xor ah,ah`, evaluated over the constants the
instruction moves through its temporaries), and the walk answers "unknown" at a
call or interrupt, at a write it cannot evaluate, at an address a branch or call
targets, a function entry, or a second instruction falls into, and after 16
instructions. So an `INT 21h` that a branch reaches with another AH is not an
exit even where the fall-through path sets 4Ch. The Listing does not resolve a
real-mode switch (`jmp cs:[bx+table]`) while the decompiler does, so the words
of the table an unresolved computed branch or call reads through the `segment`
op count as branch targets too, read from `realCS:offset` until one names an
address outside the decoded code (at most 256): a hand-written dispatcher whose
table names both `mov ah,4ch` and the `int 21h` after it, reached there with AH
9, keeps the code after the interrupt. The sites are parked on the
architecture (`dos_exit_sites`) and flow ends at each (chapter
[02](02-lift-and-flow.md), *DOS exits are no-returns*). The
same sites then seed the `noreturn_propagate` fixpoint (§1.7) in place of the
Known list, which a DOS image has none of, so `_exit` and the `exit` that calls
it are no-return to their callers; that half rides `noreturn_propagate` and
`noreturn_reach` like every other conclusion of the fixpoint, and is marked on
the installed functions right after the raw entries are. Only the x86 real-mode
language has DOS below it, so every other language, raw or not, is
byte-identical. On DAZZLE 15 of 295 functions change: the five `funcboundflow`
warnings and their zero-run tails are gone, and the error and abort paths of
eleven more end at the exit wrapper they call instead of running on after it.

Table-derived roots are committed but are deliberately not fed through a
second recursive walk. Thus the bounded path obtains direct-call closure and
high-confidence callback/vtable roots while avoiding the full prologue scan,
the AIF cursor over every undefined code gap, and recursive expansion from
disconnected pointer roots. Turning on `fast_funcdisc` alone does not run no-return, FID, AIF, or any
other ordinary Listing consumer.

Executable-section operands use a narrower rule because instruction immediates
are not pointer tables. On x86, the walk records an address-like executable
constant only when p-code stores that constant as the instruction's value (not
as a LOAD/STORE address); it is promoted when the instruction is `PUSH`, a
straight-line run of at most sixteen instructions reaches the next call, the
target is not an existing instruction or an interior instruction byte, and the
strict bounded subroutine probe reaches a valid termination. Accepted stack
callback roots are added to the Listing seeds and the walk is rebuilt, up to
four rounds and 1,024 roots, so a dialog callback that registers a second
callback contributes both bodies to one project inventory. Other code-looking
immediates, targets already claimed by a body, and targets that only happen to
decode without a valid return path remain unpromoted.

Candidate provenance is deduplicated by target before storage and bounded to
4,096 target/source pairs per walk. Only a constant STORE value earns the
on-demand mnemonic decode, preserving the reference-free Listing detail used by
fast discovery. A stable hash rank samples the bounded set across the address
space without traversal-order or low-address bias; the root budget and
four-generation limit still prefer bounded load time over complete recovery of
adversarially deep or unusually callback-dense registration graphs.

The full Listing **consumers** run over the built model and are individually gated before
invocation (with the commit gate retained defensively): the
no-return consumers of §1.7 (`noreturn_disc`, and `noreturn_propagate` carrying
the `noreturn_error`/`noreturn_reach` sub-rules), the FID matcher (§1.4), the AIF
gap-walk, and (unlace) the recursive-descent promotion `funcdisc_recursive`, which
commits the walk's discovered CALL targets as real functions (coupled to the
`funcstart_patterns` flag; this is what finds call-only targets with no
recognizable prologue). **AIF** (`aif off|on|strict|precise`, default `off` with
upstream's own "IT MAY CREATE A LOT OF BAD CODE!" warning;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/mod.rs (run_aif)`) speculatively
decodes each undefined gap between discovered functions and accepts a gap start
only when it both disassembles into a valid subroutine (a clean flow to RET, more
than 2 instructions, no bad byte or out-of-range flow) *and* its prologue matches a
start fingerprint shared by at least 4 already-discovered functions
(`FINGERPRINT_THRESHOLD`) — the exhaustive gap oracle for functions with no
static or accepted pointer-table root. The option's four values are cumulative
settings of one walk (`crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/aif.rs`):
`off` runs no walk, `on` runs it with the byte-granular cursor, `strict` with the
aligned cursor described below, and `precise` adds upstream's second fingerprint
test to `strict`. The `aggressive` preset sets `strict`; the whole-binary drivers
inject `on` on a non-x86-64 image when the selected mode names no value.

The gap cursor caches its current undefined span instead of repeating Listing
lookups at every candidate. The next known instruction still bounds subroutine
validation; an executable-range boundary only bounds cursor advancement. Once
the cursor advances, cached decode successes and failures below it are retired:
validation never decodes below its candidate. Forward results retain their first
decode, including across processor-context changes. This bounds retention on long
rejected padding runs without imposing a discovery cutoff or a universal cache
size limit on branch-heavy inputs. Shared immutable records avoid copying text
and flow vectors on cache hits; fingerprint equality remains two mnemonics and
their total instruction length. The validation walk reuses its visited-address
hash set and work stack, preserving successor order and the 4,000-step limit.
Accepted bodies are converted back to address-sorted sets. One already-decoded,
fixed-stride fall-through prefix can stand in for its visited addresses on the
next overlapping validation. Its deferred branch targets and information flags
are replayed in their original order under the same validation policy. All prefix
instructions still count toward the step limit; backward edges into the prefix
are already visited, and accepted bodies include every prefix address. Terminal
instructions, missing fall-throughs and stride changes end the prefix. Cache
retirement trims it, so reuse never skips a new decode or a context update.

AIF obtains flow and assembly through `Translate::one_instruction_with_assembly`
(`crates/unlace-sleigh/src/translate.rs`). Its default implementation
performs the original lift followed by best-effort assembly. SLEIGH reuses the
resolved parse for instructions without context commits or delay slots; otherwise
it reparses assembly after the lift, preserving the context updates and consumed
length. P-code errors still fail the probe, while assembly errors do not replace
a successful lift. Emitters must leave the image and translation context unchanged.
The combined SLEIGH path retains at most eight constructor decisions keyed by the
full instruction buffer, context words, table and operand offset. Each address
still evaluates operands, applies context changes and generates p-code normally;
this is not a cache of lifted instructions. Pattern-mask capture bypasses the
cache, and changing the processor spec invalidates it.

(unlace, GH-299) That gap walk slides its cursor **one byte at a time**, because the
undefined partition is byte-granular by construction, so every byte of every hole is
a candidate function start and both acceptance tests are applied to addresses that
cannot be instruction boundaries — a candidate starting mid-instruction reads the
tail of one encoding plus the head of the next, and that synthetic pair matches a
common prologue about as often as a real one. On a large stripped i386 PE the walk
plants roughly 2,100 entries in the middle of a function body, a third of them inside
a function the discovery set already has an entry for. `aif strict` (the setting
the `aggressive` preset carries;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/aifstrict.rs`) narrows the
cursor: it advances to the next 4-byte boundary rather than the next byte, and a
candidate is probed only when it is 4-byte aligned **or** it is the first byte of its
hole. The hole-start exemption is the whole distinction the setting draws — a hole
boundary is evidence, since the recursive-descent walk decoded up to exactly there
and stopped, while an interior byte the cursor slid onto is a guess. The stride is 4
on every architecture deliberately: 16-byte alignment kills nine tenths of the bad
Cortex-M entries but takes four fifths of the real ones with it. Declining a probe
also *recovers* entries rather than only removing them, because an accept advances
the cursor past the accepted body — a phantom accepted one halfword inside a literal
pool consumes the real function behind it. `aif on` keeps the byte-granular cursor
exactly.

(unlace, GH-299) The complementary reject the issue asks for — refuse a candidate
bracketed by a known function — is the bracket rule of
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/aifbracket.rs` (always on
with `aif`; formerly the `aifbracket` option). Some holes
are not gaps between functions but blocks inside a function the walk already knows,
behind a dispatch it could not follow, an undecodable instruction, or a call it
believes does not return; a block there that opens with a common prologue and
branches back into the function's decoded code passes both acceptance tests, since
the validity walk counts that branch as adding information. The Listing's function
model is entry-ordered and carries no extents, so "this hole lies inside one body"
cannot be read off the interval between known entries — on a sparsely discovered
image nearly every hole lies between two of them, and an interval test swallows
whole unexplored regions. (Where a defined function symbol states its size, the
extent is known and no accept strictly inside it is emitted at all, the rule of
`funcstart_patterns` in §1.5.) It is the `fdeinterior` question (§1.5) asked of an image
with no unwind extents, and the candidate's own speculative body answers it instead:
an accept is a fragment of its enclosing function when that body falls through or
jumps (not calls) into an instruction the walk decoded that is not a function entry
and lies in the same entry interval as the candidate. A fragment is refused unless
boundary evidence says a function starts there anyway: the walk files a reference to
it, or an aligned pointer-sized word in an allocated section holds its address; it
lies within the first word of a hole that a return, a direct unconditional jump or a
no-return call opens (the word admits the function behind a one-word A32 literal
pool); or the instruction ending exactly at it is alignment padding (`nop`, `int3`,
a self-move or self-`lea`), a return or an unconditional jump. A hole a computed jump
opens has no such boundary, which is exactly the unresolved-switch case. Like an
uncorroborated refusal under `aif precise`, a refused fragment still consumes its
body so the cursor
does not resume inside it. The refusal runs only in the plain gap walk (both the
Listing and the reference-walk callers); the frame-prefix reconciliation, which
replaces one accepted root by another, is untouched. Scored against unstripped twins
it removes 1,291 to 2,874 mid-body entries per corpus and mode (ARM ELF, i386 PE)
without losing or gaining a true function start; most of the mid-body entries that
remain never touch decoded code — the tail of a function that ends in its own return
— and are outside what a flow-join proof can see.

(unlace, GH-299) No gap entry starts on filler
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/aifnoppad.rs`, always on
with `aif`; formerly the `aifnoppad` option). The holes
between functions are mostly alignment padding, which the fingerprint test normally
refuses because no four discovered functions open with two `nop`s. Some images do
have them — Wine's exported unimplemented-function stubs open with nine `nop`s — and
then the `nop` run between each relay thunk's `ret` and the next thunk's
hot-patchable `mov edi,edi` entry passes both tests (a fingerprint match, and a valid
subroutine that falls through into decoded code) and becomes a function of its own
in front of one unlace already has; zero halfwords around ARM literal pools are
accepted the same way, and an accepted zero run swallows the function behind it. A
candidate whose first instruction is filler is therefore classified by the run of
filler it opens. Zero fill (x86 `add [eax],al`, A32 `andeq r0,r0,r0`, Thumb
`movs r0,r0`) is never probed. Padding — `nop` of any width, `int3`, a self-`lea`,
or a register self-move on a 32-bit target — is not probed when the run ends
exactly at a known function entry; when it ends at undecoded code the candidate is
probed as before, but an accept is planted on the first instruction after the
padding, since that is where the function the walk just validated begins. Padding
is never refused outright in front of undecoded code because it is also a
legitimate first instruction: symbol tables start 903 functions with `nop` in the
i386 PE corpus and 56 in the ARM one (Wine's stubs, an empty `-O0` function's
`nop; bx lr`), and `-fpatchable-function-entry` starts every function with one.
`mov edi,edi` is never padding — it is the MSVC hot-patch prologue that opens 7,827
true starts in the PE corpus — and neither is any self-move on a 64-bit target,
where a 32-bit one zero-extends its register. A self-`lea` on a wide target is
padding only when both operands name the same full-width x86-64 general-purpose register.
`lea esi,[esi]` and `lea r8d,[r8d]` clear the upper half of their destination, so
entry discovery retains them even though the printed register names match. A
full-width `lea rsi,[rsi]` still counts as padding. A refusal is a plain reject, not a
body claim, so the cursor moves on through the filler. Like the bracket rule it runs
only in the plain gap walk. Scored against unstripped twins in the default mode it
loses no true function start on any corpus and gains 50 on the i386 PEs (the
function behind padding, now at its own address) and 38 on the ARM ELFs (the
function a zero run used to swallow); it removes 7,446 non-start PE entries and a
net 77 mid-body ARM ones, and leaves i386 and x86-64 ELFs unchanged.

(unlace) A SPARC32 large-frame entry starts at its frame-size constant
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/sparcprologue.rs`, always on
with `aif`, inert on every other target). A frame larger than the signed 13-bit
immediate is built in a register first, `sethi %hi(-N), r; or r, %lo(-N), r;
save %sp, r, %sp`, and the function begins at the `sethi`. The fingerprint test
usually refuses the `sethi` candidate, because few discovered functions open that
way, so the cursor slides on and accepts the `save`, leaving an entry whose frame
size is an undefined input and two orphan instructions that truncate a decompile
from the real start. An accepted `save %sp, r, %sp` candidate therefore owns the
two still-undefined, unclaimed words in front of it, in the same executable range
and with no function entry on them, when they are exactly that fall-through pair:
the same register throughout (not `%g0` or `%sp`), and an eight-byte-aligned
negative frame size outside the immediate range. Only the entry and its body move;
acceptance and fingerprint stay the `save` candidate's, and only the plain gap walk
applies it. Over 117 Debian SPARC32 images it moves 12 entries in 11 images back
eight bytes, each onto a true start, and changes no count; GCC 14 stripped
`-m32` images scored against their unstripped twins move 29 entries, all onto the
symbol address. Two prefixes are not recognised: a frame size whose low ten bits
are zero, which GCC builds with a lone `sethi`, and SPARC64's `sethi; xor`, since
the pass runs only where `%g1` is four bytes.

(unlace, GH-299) No gap entry starts on a literal-pool word: `aifpoolslide`
(default-on; `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/aifpoolslide.rs`).
ARM code keeps its constants in pools right after the code that loads them, so a
pool usually sits between one function and the next, and the walk never decodes
it. The gap walk then reads a pool word as an instruction — an A32 image address
`0x608xxxxx` as `addvs`, the high half of a Thumb SRAM pointer `0x2000xxxx` as
`movs r0,#0` — whose pairing with the next function's prologue matches the
fingerprint, and whose speculative body runs into that function and validates. The
entry lands a word or half a word early, and because an accept consumes its body,
the function behind it is never probed: on a stripped A32 u-boot this hid 334 real
functions. `poolentry` repairs the same shape after the fact, but only in
`--mode aggressive`, only for a pool behind a return (u-boot's often follow a call
to a no-return function), and only by adding a second entry. Here the walk keeps a
set of literal words: every word an `ldr` or `vldr` of the decoded Listing loads
PC-relatively (its absolute `[0x...]` operand or its `[pc,#imm]` form, both words
of a 64-bit load; an `adr` only takes an address, so a function whose address it
takes is not a pool), extended with the literal words of each body the walk
accepts or consumes, so the pool behind a gap-found function is known by the time
the walk reaches it. A candidate inside a run of adjacent literal words is probed
as before, but its accept is planted on the first address after the run when its
body decoded an instruction there, and it is rejected otherwise, so the cursor
reaches the code after the pool and probes it on its own. When that address is
data — bytes that begin a printable NUL-terminated string, or an even address some
literal word of Thumb code holds, since a Thumb code address carries bit 0 — the
candidate is refused but still consumes its body: a body the walk accepts over a
string table decodes text as `ldr`s, and those bogus literal words must not move an
entry onto a string the code passes as an argument. A bracket refusal also keeps
consuming its body. It is 32-bit ARM only and runs only in the plain gap walk.
Scored against unstripped twins in the default mode: over the 93 non-u-boot ARM
ELFs of the decbench corpus mid-body entries 4,375 to 1,866 net and true starts
+222; on the two u-boot images 1,415 to 1,081 and +334; no true start lost, and
`CMSIS_DAP.axf`, the i386 PE corpus and x86-64 images unchanged. Besides the 556
true starts, the new entries are 5 mid-body entries and 63 on data (none on a
string start), against 88 such data entries removed, 77 of them on a string. It
shares `poolentry`'s one disclosed split: a literal
reference that resolves onto a function's own first word (the SPLIT shape of
`cortexm_poolentry_le32`) moves that function's entry four bytes in, which the
gap walk without this option gets right in `--mode reliable`; the corpus
measurement has no such case.

(unlace, GH-313) Upstream applies a **second** fingerprint test that unlace's port
dropped. Its analyzer refuses a candidate twice — once on the shared-prologue count
alone, and again after the validity walk, where a routine that adds no information
must match a prologue shared by fifty discovered functions rather than four. unlace
ported the first refusal and the "no two-instruction routines" half of the second,
so a self-contained routine that calls nothing, jumps nowhere known, and merely
reaches a return is accepted on a two-mnemonic coincidence. `aif precise` (the
aligned cursor of `strict` plus this test, set by **no preset**;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/aifcorroborate.rs`) restores
it: an accept must either add information — a call, or a jump into already-discovered
code — or match a prologue that fifty discovered functions share. The corroborating
fact is recomputed the upstream way rather than reusing the flag the
valid-subroutine gate already carries, because that one also counts a plain
fall-through out of the hole into decoded code, which is the *signature* of a
mid-body phantom rather than evidence against one. And a refused candidate still
consumes its body: the gap cursor advances past an accepted routine but only one byte
past a rejected one, so an accept-side refusal that released the cursor would hand it
back to the interior of the same hole, replacing one bad entry with a worse one.

No preset sets `precise` because it was **measured out of the default path**, not
because it is unevaluated. Over the same corpus, compared with `strict`, it cuts
roughly a third of the remaining mid-body entries but costs about half a real
function for each one removed, raises recall on none of the images, and takes real
functions off the A32 targets AIF's remaining justification rests on — which is the
finding, not the failure: upstream's guard assumes a function worth finding calls
something the analyzer already knows, and on bare-metal firmware the functions only
AIF can find are precisely the leaf helpers that call nothing. The per-image numbers
are in the option's catalog row, and the instrument that produced them is
`scripts/decbench/entrysweep.py` (§ the decbench loop), which scores unlace's function
entries for a stripped image against its unstripped twin's symbol table — the
discovery-tier measurement the GED loop cannot make.

`operand_refs` (default-off, matching
upstream's ELF-off default) shares the deferred slot for the same
decoder-availability reason but does its own linear decode rather than reading the
Listing, planting `char[N]` facts for immediate operands that point into read-only
data. (unlace) An immediate the instruction adds to a value it does not know, to
form the address of a load two or more bytes wide, is left out
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/operand_refs/mod.rs
(IndexedBases)`): `jmp *table(,%rax,8)`, `call *tbl(,%rdi,8)` and
`movzwl map(%rdi,%rdi)` index an array of wider elements, a jump table, a table
of function pointers or a word map, and typing its first bytes `char[N]` because
they happen to be printable made the printer index a short literal
(`*(unsigned long *)&"7A@"[i * 8]`) instead of the table. That test sees one
instruction, so a table the code reaches any other way still began with a
printable run: `movabs $tbl,%rax` before the indexed call (`-mcmodel=large`),
`mov $tbl,%edi` to pass it, or `movq $vtable+16,(%rax)` in a constructor, and a
non-PIE x86-64 entry such as `26 42 40 00 00 00 00 00` (0x404226) reads `"&B@"`.
Once one scalar planted the `char[4]`, every use of the table printed the
literal: `pick("&B@",a0)`, `*(char **)operator new(8) = "dB@"`. So the target is also refused when it
is a pointer slot, the same test the strings pass applies
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/strings/ptrslot.rs (PointerSlots)`).
On a PE with base relocations that test is exact: an MSVC i386 image's vtable
entries are relocated and refused, while its 4-aligned `"INF"` is not and keeps
its literal.

(unlace) A run as short as one character is also the first element of many arrays
whose elements are wider than a byte: `static const int arr[] = {65, 66, 67, 68}`
starts `41 00`, which is `"A"`, and `L"hellow"` starts `68 00`, which is `"h"`, so
`sum(arr,n)` printed `sum("A",a0)` and `lenw(L"hellow")` printed `lenw((int *)"h")`.
Two more refusals cover them. A sized data object of the image's symbol tables that
starts at the target with a size other than the run's says what the bytes are
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/operand_refs/mod.rs (DataObjects)`):
`arr` is a 16-byte object at the target, and the reference prints as its name. An
object that only contains the target, such as a table of `char` rows, does not
refuse the string it holds there. Without symbols the bytes decide
(`wide_element_neighbour`): at an address aligned to the width, two 4-byte elements
that are each one printable byte followed by zeros (a `wchar_t` or `char32_t`
string, an `int` table of character codes), or three 2-byte ones, the third
possibly the terminator (`char16_t`, a `short` table), open an array of character
codes. A merged string section lays one-character literals side by side in the
same 2-byte shape (`78 00 79 00 77 00` is `"x"`, `"y"`, `"w"`), and a literal that
ends a block at a 4-aligned address can sit right before an `int` table in the 4-byte
one, so the run is refused only when nothing marks its second element as a thing of
its own: no declared object starts there, no operand the scan found points at it,
and the image holds no pointer to it (`held_pointers`) -- in a pointer-aligned slot
of an allocated section or as the addend of a dynamic relocation. Beside a 2-byte
run of an ELF image, the merged-literal case, an entry of a table of 32-bit offsets
from the table's own start at an operand target counts too: the shape of clang's
position-independent lookup table of string addresses (`.long .str - table`,
`relative_string_table`). Such a table must not itself open a string, and its
entries are read up to the first that is zero, a small positive character code
(the first unit of a wide string or code table the read has run into), points back
into the table or lands on no string, with at least two remaining. A 4-byte run
never consults one: read as offsets, a struct's leading `int`s or a wide string's
units can land on the second unit of any wide string nearby. A 2-byte run of
`char16_t` or `short` data can still be kept that way, as on main, when a struct
holding it starts with `int`s that equal the offsets of its own units. A literal beside the
first is usually referenced from one of those places; the second element of an
array is not. When nothing visible refers to it the literal loses its string with
the array and prints as its address: a neighbour left behind by code that
`--gc-sections` removed, or, stripped, the 4-byte case before an `int` table, which
only that table's symbol tells apart. The other way round, a wide or `char16_t`
string whose suffix is referenced on its own, such as a tail-merged `L"xbind"`
whose `L"bind"` another call passes, or `u"b"` inside `u"xb"`, still prints as its
first character, as on main; only a scan for strings of the matching width would
recover it, which `widestrings32` does for the 4-byte case (its `wchar4` fact
commits first and takes the address). The scans run once, and only when some run is about to
be refused. Refusing drops the fact and nothing else, so the
reference prints as the array's symbol or address (`sum(arr,a0)`,
`lenw(&dat_2004)`), never as a different value. A stripped array whose second
element is no character code, such as `int {65, 1000}`, still reads as `"A"`.

(unlace) Three ARM-only seed scans run between the walk's first pass and those
consumers, each re-seeding the walk and rebuilding the Listing when it finds
anything, all gated by the `funcstart_patterns` flag: the existing raw unpaired
Thumb scan
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/thumbframes.rs`),
the code-pointer-table scan
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/mod.rs (code_pointer_table_seeds)`
— every 4-byte-aligned odd word in any allocated section whose masked target lands
in an undefined gap, *and* opens with a frame-establishing Thumb prologue, *and*
passes the same probe), and the AIF gap walk above. The additional default-off
`armframes` option walks shared validated ARM/Thumb frame roots in place of the
Thumb scan
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/mod.rs (raw_arm_prologue_seeds)`):
mode-matched LR-saving `STMDB SP!`, `PUSH` or `PUSH.W` in an undefined gap must
pass the strict valid-subroutine probe. It keeps the entries the Thumb scan and the
gap walk would have reported (see the ARM reference walks later in §1.6), and when it validates
no frame at all the Thumb scan runs exactly as with the option off.

A start that only the raw Thumb scan found is withdrawn after the
code-pointer-table scan when the Listing enters it by straight-line flow
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/passes.rs`, the rule of
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/frameflow.rs` that frame
recovery already applies to its roots). The instruction just before the start must
be a non-call that falls through or conditionally branches into it, on a run that
begins at a function entry or a branch target, and no call may target the start.
GCC shrink-wraps Thumb code: the routine tests its argument, returns with `bx lr`,
and only then runs `push {r4, lr}`. Scanned on its own, that `push` looks like a
function entry, and the routine it belongs to ended there with a `funcboundflow`
warning, leaving two near-empty halves. A start that a load-time pass committed is
never withdrawn. That covers every `<patternpairs>` start, which the deferred
`funcstart_patterns` pass commits before the walk, as well as vector-table handlers
and symbols. The rule does not run when frame recovery rebuilt the Listing. The
rebuild that withdraws a start reuses every decode of the raw-scan rebuild
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/decodememo.rs`), so it walks the
image again without decoding it again. On stripped Cleanflight O2-noinline it withdraws 25 of 2,679 starts, none of them a
symbol of the unstripped image; `Handle_USBAsynchXfer` (0x803b95c) is whole again.
Over the 92 distinct stripped ARM firmware images of DecBench (O0, O2 and
O2-noinline) it withdraws 398 of 42,937 starts, each inside the symbol of the
routine that absorbs it. The rule cannot tell a trap from a test: a routine that
ends in `svc` or `bkpt` runs straight into the next one, so a following routine
that only the raw scan found and that no call targets is joined to it.

**Pointer-referenced entries** (`ptrentry`, on by default, ARM-only; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/ptrentry.rs`) re-admits
what the second of those throws away. Measurement over the ARM Cortex-M corpus
found its two shape predicates — a frame prologue, and more than two instructions —
reject the bulk of the pointer-referenced population: 93% of the missed entries
establish no frame at all, and 41% are leaves of eight bytes or less, down to a
bare `bx lr`, which is a perfectly valid Cortex-M exception handler. Deleting the
two predicates is not an option on its own: it admits `ldr pc,[pc,r]` switch tables,
whose slots point *into* the function that holds the table, so a fifth of the new
entries split a real function body — a cost the per-ground-truth-function benchmark
cannot see and a real user pays in full. With the option on, a target is instead
admitted on **containment** evidence: no word referencing it may overlap a decoded
instruction (such a word is an instruction's operand bytes read four-aligned, not a
table slot), and none may lie in the same discovered function as the target itself
(that pairing *is* the switch table). The length floor is replaced by a
terminating-routine check — the same speculative walk, accepting when it reaches a
clean `RET`/computed jump or a call into discovered code with no undecodable byte,
no flow out of the image and no escape into another dark region, with no minimum
instruction count. This is the unlace form of the line Ghidra draws between
`OperandReferenceAnalyzer`, which creates functions from *instruction operands*, and
its data-side sibling `DataOperandReferenceAnalyzer`, which overrides
`createFunctions` to a no-op; unlace cannot use Ghidra's version directly because the
Listing records only control-flow references, so the containment pair recovers the
same discrimination from the code/data partition the walk leaves behind. Table-run
corroboration — requiring a run of consecutive code-pointer words — was measured
and is dominated: the switch tables it targets are runs themselves, so it removes
almost no additional split while costing a fifth of the recovered entries. Unlike
the three scans above, the accepted targets are emitted as an additive entry-fact
stream and **never** re-seed the walk: measured, re-seeding drops hundreds of
already-recovered entries through the same tail-call absorption that constrains
`cortexmvectors` (§1.5), so keeping the pass purely additive makes "never removes
an entry" a property of the wiring rather than of a heuristic. Output-changing
(more functions), hence default-off; ARM-only and Listing-tier, so it is a strict
no-op on every other architecture, with `listing off`, and on the XML datatest path.

**Call tables** (`calltable`, on by default; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/calltable.rs (scan)`). A
table a computed transfer indexes is either a switch or a table of functions.
The tables are read with the register-chain fold the switch reader uses
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/switchtable.rs
(register_targets)`), which also answers for a `CALLIND` and reads a pointer
table with no range check up to 256 entries, stopping at the first word that
is not code of the section the transfer is in; such a read is flagged
`unbounded` and is never taken as a switch. Nothing marks where a table with
no range check ends, so a function table followed by another switch's table
reads on into its case labels: such a read is cut before the first target
that is a case of a range-checked switch or already code inside a function
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/calltable.rs
(call_table_run)`), and the walk behind `unlace xrefs` reads its unchecked
indexed calls only once its queue has drained, when those switches have been
decoded. A switch reached only through the call table itself is not decoded
by then, so a table with no range check also ends before the first word that
code names as an address, decoded or not: every pointer-aligned read-only
address that four bytes of a code section spell (the displacement of `jmp
*tbl(,%rdi,8)`, a pool word) is collected once, on the first such read
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/poolref.rs (code_named)`).
The walk reads a switch whose operand names its table up to the first word
that is not code, with no count, and votes that read by the strict rule for
an unchecked table, so a switch table that runs on into a table of known
functions stays a switch. The vote (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/calltable.rs
(is_call_table)`): an indexed call calls every entry; a jump through a
range-checked table whose distinct targets are 40% or more other functions'
entries is a table of tail calls; a jump through an unchecked table is one
only when every target is already another function's entry, so it never adds
a function. An unchecked switch (gcc drops the range check under
`__builtin_unreachable()`) and a computed goto read exactly like a table of
tail calls, and gcc aligns their labels to 16 bytes as it does functions, so
an unchecked jump to targets that are not yet functions is left alone. The
targets of a call table become entries, and in the `unlace xrefs` walk they are
call references of the dispatcher rather than its switch cases. The other way
round, a discovered, non-symbol entry that sits on a case of a switch and that
no call reaches is dropped at the commit (`AnalysisOutput::case_entries`): a
case body that opens `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp` looks like a function to a
prologue scan. On the fixture `calltable_x86_64` the two functions of the
called table are found, its read stops at the next switch's cases, the
labels of an unchecked jump table are not functions, and the prologue-shaped
case is no longer a function. On the fixture `calltable_split_x86_64` the
function `h0` of a called table is found, and neither the cases of `bsw`,
whose table follows and which only `h0` reaches, nor those of `sw`, whose
table runs on into a table of functions, are functions or call targets. Over
529 stripped decbench ELFs, 1,150 ELF and PE fixtures and four sqlite3 builds
the function lists do not move; over 200 generated non-PIE gcc/clang programs
without unwind tables it finds 257 table-only functions and adds no false
start, and over 320 generated multi-file non-PIE gcc, clang and i386 programs
1,944 and none. A table reached only through an unchecked jump is no longer
found by running into it from the table before.

**Tail-call entries** (`tailcallentry`, on by default, ARM-only; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/tailcallentry.rs (tail_call_entries)`)
closes the walk's other structural blind spot. The recursive-descent walk
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/walk.rs`) makes a new function entry
at a CALL target and treats every other flow target as a same-function successor,
so a routine reached only by a tail `B` is absorbed into whichever function
branched to it and never becomes a function at all — the second largest class of
the ARM entry-recall gap. Splitting at a tail call cannot change *which*
instructions the walk decodes: a function entry is walked, hence decoded, either
way, so moving a target from the instruction worklist to the function worklist
leaves the walk's closure fixed and only grows the function set. The split is
therefore computed **after** the walk, where complete predecessor and region
information is available instead of whatever the worklist order happened to
expose, and — like `ptrentry` — emitted as an additive entry-fact stream that
never rebuilds the Listing. Recognising the tail call is easy; telling one from a
rotated loop head is the whole problem, and the naive rule (split at every
unconditional-branch target whose predecessor ends the flow) measures 39%
precision, splitting a real function body more often than it finds one. Four
guards, each measured on the corpus, take that to 94.6% with no split bodies:
every predecessor of the target must be an unconditional branch (a fall-through or
conditional-branch predecessor means the caller's straight-line code runs into it,
which is ordinary intra-function flow); the branch must **leave the caller's
entry-ordered function region**, so at least one other discovered entry lies
between the branch and its target; the target's flow region must reach a `RETURN`
or a computed jump, the same terminating-routine validity `ptrentry` uses and with
the same absence of a length floor; and the target must not open with a stack
restore, because a function does not begin by tearing down a frame it never built
— that shape is the caller's shared epilogue. The region crossing is the
load-bearing one: dropping it costs 43 points of precision and splits over five
hundred real bodies, while a stack-discipline model (reject a branch taken with an
unmatched `PUSH`/`SUB SP` still open) was implemented, measured, and dominated by
it on both precision and recall. As with `ptrentry`, the region is the
entry-ordered one — the nearest preceding discovered entry — which is the
granularity the tier has and errs conservative on a sparsely discovered image.
An accepted target becomes a region boundary for the next pass, and the scan
repeats until it finds nothing new (at most eight rounds). A routine reached by
a tail branch from another tail-branch target lies inside the first one's region
until that one is accepted. libopencm3's `_usbd_standard_request` is found in
the first round, and the `_usbd_standard_request_device`, `_interface` and
`_endpoint` it tail-branches to are found in the second. Before, their bodies
printed inside it.
Two of the four guards are satisfied by an *absent* model rather than by
evidence: the predecessor test reads the reference model and the epilogue test
the disassembly text, and a walk can be told to capture neither (above), which
would leave the naive rule — and on the fixture it accepts the shared epilogue
the full model rejects. So the pass checks for both models up front and yields
nothing without them. In production the gate that enables the pass is the same
one that enables the models, so the check is invisible there; it is what keeps a
later change to either gate from quietly reducing the four guards to the rule
they replaced. Output-changing (more functions), hence default-off; ARM-only and Listing-tier, so
it is a strict no-op on every other architecture, with `listing off`, and on the
XML datatest path. `tailcallentryall` (default-off; unlace) lifts the ARM gate for AArch64, x86
(32 and 64 bit) and RISC-V, IDA's tail-call split on every processor. The four
guards do not depend on the instruction set; only the stack-restore test reads
mnemonics, and it also knows x86 `pop` / `leave` / `add rsp`, AArch64
`ldp x29,x30` and post-indexed loads off `sp`, and RISC-V `ld`/`lw ra,(sp)` and
`addi sp,sp,+n`. Measured against the symbol tables of unstripped twins, Lua 5.4.8
built `-O2` gains 5 functions on x86-64 and 12 on AArch64, every one a real
function start, with no entry lost.

**Rename facts** (always on, no option;
`crates/unlace-console/src/engine.rs (apply_renamed_library_facts)`):
when a FID or FLIRT rename (the FLIRT pass is described under §1.4 above)
replaces a placeholder, the function also gets the libc prototype of its name
(or a `nameladder` spelling) and the no-return flag when the no-return lists
name it, as IDA applies the type and `noret.cfg` on a FLIRT rename. The lists
read there are the ELF, PE/Mach-O and Windows-only ones together
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/noreturn.rs (listed_noreturn)`): FLIRT names a
statically linked MSVC CRT `__CxxThrowException@8` or `___report_gsfailure`,
which only the Windows list carries.

**Data-object width** (`globalwidth`, default-on; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/accesswidth.rs (access_widths)`):
a symbol-table data object (`STT_OBJECT` with a size) has no type, so it was
mapped as `undefined<size>` and an element access rendered as
`*(short *)&g3[(i & 7) * 2UL]`. Over the decoded Listing every `LOAD`/`STORE`
whose address is a constant or a constant plus something, and every direct
data-space operand (branch and call targets excluded), that lands in an object
is read at the width of the value moved. An object all of whose accesses use
one width `w` that divides its size, with some access indexed or past the first
element, is mapped as `undefined<w>[size / w]` (or `undefined<w>` when `w` is
the size); a lone narrowing read (`(int)g1` of a `long`) changes nothing. IDA
sizes items from the referencing operand (`insn_create_op_data`). The same scan
gives **the AIF data veto** (`aifdataveto`, default-on;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/accesswidth.rs (data_targets)`):
a discovered entry (not a symbol, and not the target of a decoded call or
branch) whose first instruction the code reads or writes as data is dropped from
the entry stream, and an AIF gap entry likewise, IDA's roll-back of a
speculative run with a `dr_R`/`dr_W` xref. A register a constant was put in
stays known for the next eight straight-line instructions, until something else
writes it or a branch, call or user op ends the run, and two known addends sum,
so an AArch64 `adrp x17, P; add x17, x17, #o; ldrsw x16, [x17, x16, lsl #2]`
reads its jump table at `P + o`. Apple's linker lists such an inline `__text`
table in `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS`, where it decodes as a `sub_` entry the dispatch
then indexes (`sub_4060[a0 * 4]`), and the veto removes it
(`tests/stages/relswitch-a64.toml`). On a Thumb literal-pool image an
AIF-only entry whose first word a literal load reads is dropped too (the
`poolentry` fixture's `F`, the split shape its corpus measurement disclosed). On the stripped
Lua (x86-64, AArch64), ld.so, llvm-nm and llvm-objdump images it removes
nothing; on the fixture it removes the function-shaped table the code reads.
The veto also drops a discovered or AIF entry whose bytes are a string
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/aifstringveto.rs (is_string)`):
at least six printable characters, ASCII or UTF-16LE, and then the NUL that ends
them, followed by `int3` padding or another string of at least four characters
(printable code up to a zero byte, `push ebx; push 0xa; push 0x2b67`, goes on
with more code). A Windows driver keeps its `DbgPrint` formats in the code
sections it pages with the code and pushes their addresses as immediates, which
read as function pointers. In the Silicon Labs CP210x bus enumerator (x86) 109 of
its 227 functions were such strings. Over 85,000 functions of /usr/bin,
/usr/lib64 and the Holley PEs the test holds for 111 entries, each a string.
**Incremental walk** (`incrementalwalk`, default-on): the x86 callback rounds
resume the Listing from the accepted roots instead of rebuilding it, the
`addrtakenentry` way; on a 300-callback i386 fixture the function set is
identical either way.

**Call tables** (`calltable`, default-on; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/calltable.rs (scan)`): the
tables computed transfers index are read with the `switchtable` register-chain
fold (`register_targets` now also answers for `CALLIND`, and reads an unchecked
pointer table up to 256 entries, flagged `unbounded`) and voted as IDA's
`check_flat_jump_table` does: an indexed call, a jump whose distinct targets are
40% or more other functions' entries, or on x86 an unchecked table whose targets
all sit on 16-byte boundaries, is a call table. Its targets become entries (and
call references in the `unlace xrefs` walk, instead of switch cases); a
discovered, non-symbol entry on a case of a real switch that no call reaches is
demoted. On the fixture the two table functions are found and the
prologue-shaped case is no longer a function; on stripped Lua (x86-64, AArch64),
ld.so, llvm-nm and llvm-objdump the function lists are unchanged.

**Function chunks** (`funcchunks`, default-off; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/funcchunks.rs (ChunkModel::build)`)
gives a discovered function a body. The Listing keys a function by its entry,
and every consumer that needs a body clips `[entry, next entry)`; that clip
mis-assigns the two shapes compilers produce most: a tail several functions jump
into (a shared epilogue or error path) and a part placed after another function.
The chunk model is IDA's `func_t` with tails, computed after the walk from the
decoded flow. A function's body is the flow closure of its entry over
fall-through and branch targets; a call target is never followed, and neither is
another function's entry, because a jump there is a tail call. The body is cut
into address runs, where up to 16 undecoded bytes of alignment padding join two
runs and any decoded instruction between them splits them. The run holding the
entry is the main chunk and every other run is a tail. An instruction reached
from several entries is shared, and the model keeps the list of every function
that reaches it, as IDA's tail keeps its referers. With the option on, the FID
matcher hashes this body (all chunks, ascending, Ghidra's `func.getBody()`
order) instead of the clip. Analysis-tier and Listing-only; it changes FID's
input and nothing else, so it is inert on the XML datatest path. The inventory `size` the console reports (`unlace functions`) is the
chunk body under the option (the sum of the chunks, shared tails included)
instead of the clip's upper bound; on the fixture a function placed before a
shared tail reports its own 6 bytes instead of 12.

**Literal-pool inference** (`poolentry`, on by default, ARM-only; unlace;
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/poolentry.rs`) is aimed at
the gap walk itself rather than at what the walk misses. AIF advances its cursor by
**one byte** on a reject, with no instruction-alignment filter, because the
undefined-gap query it drives is byte-granular by construction. An ARM PC-relative
literal pool is data, so it *is* an undefined gap, and the cursor probes every byte
of it. On a Cortex-M image the pool words are SRAM addresses `0x2000_xxxx` whose
high halfword decodes as `movs r0,#0`, which clears the two-mnemonic fingerprint
gate as reliably as a real prologue does; AIF therefore accepts an entry one
halfword *before* the real function, falls through into it, reaches its return, and
on accept jumps the cursor past the whole body — so the true entry is never probed
at all. In A32 there is no halfword granularity and conditional execution makes
almost any word a legal instruction, so the same mechanism plants the phantom on the
pool word itself. Upstream Ghidra does not have this defect and needs no equivalent
of this pass: its reference analyzer defines pc-relative literal targets as **data**
before AIF runs, so those bytes are not an undefined gap there. unlace's Listing has no
literal-pool data-definition step, and this pass reconstructs the missing definition
after the fact.

The reconstruction is **reference-driven**. A word counts as a literal only when
some instruction actually loads it: either the resolved absolute `[0x…]` operand the
ARM disassembly prints for `ldr rN,[pc,#imm]`, or the unresolved `[pc,#imm]` form
that `vldr`/`ldrd` print because they compute the target in the semantic body — plus
the second word of a 64-bit literal, which nothing loads on its own. Completing that
second form is not a detail: without it every pool holding a float or a 64-bit
constant under-runs and the additive consumer below plants its entry *on* a pool
word, which is the difference between 19 split bodies at 89.7% precision and one at
98.4% over the measured corpus. The `[pc,#imm]` base needs the decode mode, which is
read from the engine's context database — the same `TMode` the bytes at that address
were decoded under, whichever pass painted it — so a language with no such context
answers "no mode" and the form is disabled outright, which is one of the reasons the
predicate is vacuous off ARM. The scan reads the decoded Listing **and** the
speculatively-decoded bodies of the gap-discovered routines, because a pool
sandwiched between two gap-discovered functions is referenced only from inside one
and a Listing-only scan silently finds nothing at exactly the shape being targeted.
A pool is then a **maximal run of adjacent referenced words**: unreferenced words
break the run, which makes the inference strictly more conservative than an ELF `$d`
mapping-symbol oracle, and bridging them was measured and rejected — a bridged run
swallows short real functions and destroys reachable bodies.

Two consumers hang off that one predicate, and they rest on different warrants. The
**recall** consumer emits an entry fact at the first address after a pool that abuts
a *return-class* terminal, when that address is still undefined and passes AIF's own
fingerprint and valid-subroutine tests. The return class is what separates an
inter-function pool, which follows a `bx lr` or `pop {..pc}`, from an intra-function
pool, which follows the unconditional branch the compiler emits to jump over it; and
because the fact is purely additive and never re-seeds the walk, "never removes an
entry" is a property of the wiring here exactly as it is for `ptrentry` and
`tailcallentry`. The **precision** consumer drops an AIF accept that lies inside an
inferred pool — but only when that pool's end carries a replacement entry, one this
pass just added or one another stage already found. That pairing clause is the whole
safety argument: the predicate's soundness (no accept inside an inferred pool was
ever a real function address, across 4,220 removals on the measured corpus) says
nothing about whether the *body* the phantom was decompiling survives, and unpaired
suppression leaves 531 real functions with no entry at any address while paired
suppression leaves zero. A paired removal is a MOVE, which restores a wiring-level
guarantee to the half that removes.

One residue is disclosed rather than gated away. When a literal reference resolves
onto the first word of a function the Listing never decoded, the inference cannot
tell that word from a pool word, and the entry moves four bytes into a real body.
It happens once in the measured corpus, and the only guard that removes it —
refusing to emit at a known branch target — costs 108 of 189 recovered entries, so
it is dominated. Output-changing (it both adds and relocates functions), hence
default-off; ARM-only in effect and Listing-tier, so it is a strict no-op without
