`listing`, without `aif`, on the XML datatest path, and on every architecture whose
constants live in `.rodata` rather than in `.text` interstices.

**The four ARM entry passes ship on** (DIV-93 measured them in the preset first).
`cortexmvectors`, `ptrentry`, `tailcallentry` and `poolentry` are on in the catalog and
ARM-gated, which is what keeps the XML datatest corpus byte-identical; the last three
are Listing consumers, so they act only where `listing` (and, for `poolentry`, `aif`)
is on -- the whole-binary surfaces (`decompile-all`, `functions`, `decompile-project`,
the WASM front-end and the benchmark) inject both on non-x86-64, and the `aggressive`
preset still lists all four with `listing` and `aif` ahead of them, so it owns them.
They were evaluated jointly because they compose: measured over the 110 stripped non-x86-64
decbench twins (50,724 symbol-table function starts), entry recall rises 44,957 ->
47,330 (88.63% -> 93.31%) while mid-body false entries *fall* 8,333 -> 7,117. 98.8% of
the 2,402 added entries are real function starts, no ground-truth entry is lost, and
`poolentry`'s 1,217 removals contain no ground-truth address — so the combination
improves recall and precision at the same time rather than trading one for the other.
Off ARM the flip is a measured no-op, not merely an intended one: entry sets are
identical over 90 x86-64 twins and the 12 i386 PE images inside the ARM corpus, and
emitted C is byte-identical over 8 x86-64 binaries. Three of the four enforce that
with an explicit architecture early-return; `poolentry` instead keys on PC-relative
literal pools, which no non-ARM target in the corpus produces. The cost is real work for real
output — discovery-only `unlace functions` runs about 6% longer on a Cortex-M image
because it discovers and reports more functions — and is amortized away end to end,
where the extra bodies dominate the extra discovery.

Driver defaults (unlace): `unlace decompile-all` and `unlace decompile` inject
`option listing on` unless the caller names `listing` (DIV-15/DIV-22) — without it
the default-on no-return propagation is a structural no-op and a stripped binary's
unnamed exit wrappers swallow the functions after them. Under the `fast` preset
(DIV-41), those full-tier injections stay off and `fast_funcdisc` is on for
unfiltered `decompile-all`, `decompile-project`, and `functions` inventory runs.
An explicit address selection suppresses the preset-provided walk unless the
caller spells `--option fast_funcdisc on`. Text-surface name selection also
suppresses a preset-provided walk on the first attempt and restores it in a
retry a name miss triggers, ahead of the held-back non-x86-64 discovery-bundle
retry, so a miss is diagnosed exactly as with the walk on; when the preset
leaves the walk off there is nothing to defer and no extra attempt. A placeholder
spelling (`sub_<hex>`, `FUN_<hex>`, `func_0x<hex>`) keeps the walk from the
start, since its entry may exist only because the walk found it. Selection remains exact even when
analysis is forced on. Under `reliable`, `unlace functions` keeps the Listing off: metadata-only
name enumeration gains nothing from the 0.21 s → 5.7 s full decode measured for a
stripped tar (DIV-15). The console and XML datatest paths never build either model
by default, which keeps every parity gate byte-identical.

(unlace) **The on-demand cross-reference query**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (build)`) is a second reader
of the same bytes, and is not an `AnalysisPass` at all: it is the read-only index
behind `unlace xrefs` and `unlace strings`, built after the caller has already
committed a program, and it commits nothing back. It repeats the Listing's
two-worklist descent but keeps every input varnode of every p-code op rather than
just `in0`, because the data references an RE agent navigates by — who reads this
global, who takes this string's address — are exactly the part the Listing model
drops. Two rules carry the weight. First, a **direct** flow op's `in0` is the
branch target and is filed as control flow, but an **indirect** one's is not a
target at all: `JMP qword ptr [__imp_VirtualProtect]` lifts to a single
`BRANCHIND` whose `in0` is the import slot, and treating that like a direct
branch's operand made every import veneer in a program reference nothing. Second,
an import has **two addresses under one name** — the IAT/GOT slot and the
forwarding veneer that jumps through it, both of which `pe_iat` (§1.3) names —
so the query joins them into an alias class along the decoded forwarding jump
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (veneer_at)`) and answers
`--to` over the whole class, with the forwarding jump itself excluded. A veneer
is recognised only when its indirect jump reads a **decode-time constant**
address, which is what distinguishes it from a jump table (whose address is
computed, and which therefore lifts to a `LOAD` through a temporary); the class is
never derived from a shared symbol name, which would fold genuinely distinct
same-named functions together. A shared library that calls its own export
through `name@plt` adds a third address: callers reach the body only through the
stub and its GOT slot. When the query selects a function **by name**, its class is
widened by every veneer whose slot carries a dynamic relocation against a symbol
the image defines at that body's address
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (export_alias_class)`). The
join is again the relocation's binding, not the name, and a query by address keeps
the plain class.

An x86-64 ELF memory-indirect call can have a proven local target through an
immutable GOT slot. `crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/gotcall.rs`
uses the loader's `fixup_sites` result. It requires complete relocation
coverage and an unambiguous, aligned eight-byte relative rebase within
`.got`. The full slot must be file-backed in one readable PT_LOAD
mapping and either read-only or wholly within the protected GNU_RELRO
extent. The loaded word must equal the relocation target. The target
must match a defined `STT_FUNC` entry within its declared executable section
and file-backed executable code.
An IFUNC alias, unmodeled relocation span, overlapping mapping or fixup,
mutable slot, or symbol bind prevents the inference.

The single CALLIND must take the slot directly or through a bounded chain
of exact-width COPY definitions in the same instruction. Other control
transfers, partial writes and a pointer carried from an earlier instruction
keep the existing listing behavior. A user-stated callee at the instruction
also keeps that path. The listing files references by instruction address,
including when several functions can reach it. A proven call enters the
existing call worklist and gets a Call reference to the actual callee.
The physical slot gets a separate Read, and other proven operand reads
and writes remain. A previously projected slot Call from that instruction
becomes a Read. The instruction still contributes to `hasIndirectCalls`
because the machine instruction is indirect. The reference index leaves
the decompiler's flow and stored assertions alone.

(unlace) The **call** spelling of that first indirection needs a third rule, because
it does not arrive in the shape the first one reads. `CALL qword ptr
[__imp_HeapAlloc]` — what MSVC emits for every Win32 call — does not put the slot
in the flow op's own `in0` the way `JMP` does: SLEIGH lowers it as `$U = COPY
(ram,slot,8); ...; CALLIND $U`, so the slot reaches the generic
direct-memory-operand arm and was filed as a `Read` of a pointer. A read is not a
call-graph edge, so on the filing image — a Windows PE — a function Ghidra lists
33 callees for came back with 9, and every one of the 24 missing was an imported
API the function plainly calls. The walk now resolves a `CALLIND`'s destination
back through the single-instruction `COPY` chain that materialised it
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (is_indirect_call_slot)`)
and files the slot it lands on as a `Call`. The chain is bounded at four copies
and never leaves the one instruction, so the rule can only re-label an operand
that instruction genuinely fetched its destination from; every other data operand
of the same instruction is judged exactly as before. The `Call` row **replaces**
the `Read` rather than joining it: one instruction makes one reference, carrying
the strongest claim it supports, which is already the collapse rule the
whole-binary graph states (§9.7). The cost is that a caller filtering `--kind
read` for data readers no longer sees the slot, which is the right trade — the
instruction is a call site, and the slot is where the callee is named. The same
rule files a `BRANCHIND` directly through a slot as `Jump`, making a forwarding
veneer a call-graph edge to the import. That edge and `forwardsTo` describe the
same relation; the alias-class query still excludes the forwarding instruction
from inbound results, so asking who calls the import does not count its own
veneer. This intentionally changes the public xref `kind` for PE `FF 25` veneers
and x86 ELF PLT stubs from `read` to `jump`.

(unlace) A call materialises its own **return address**, and the constant scan must
not read it as a reference: it is the instruction's fall-through, which x86 pushes
as a constant, A32 copies into `lr` and MIPS into `$ra`, so a call's fall-through
is never filed as `Data`. AArch64 spells it differently — `bl` and
`blr` lift `x30 = inst_start + 4` to one `INT_ADD` of two constants — so the
fall-through never appears as a constant and the scan filed the first addend, the
`bl`'s own address, as a `Data` reference from every call site to itself (and,
`--to` a call site, as an incoming one). In an instruction that calls, an op that
adds two constants into the fall-through is that same return address, and neither
addend is filed
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (is_return_address_sum)`).
The rule names the call's sum, not the instruction's own address: `adr x0,.`, a
constant equal to the instruction's address, a PC-relative sum that lands anywhere
but the fall-through, and the same sum outside a call — a Thumb-2 `vldr
s0,[pc,#8]` reads `pc` as `inst_start + 4`, which is its fall-through only by
width — are reported as before.

(unlace, GH #1360) Not every constant equal to the fall-through is a return address:
`adr x0,.+4` forms the address of the next instruction exactly as `adr x0,.` and
`adr x0,.+8` form theirs, and the scan dropped it along with the return
addresses. The fall-through is now skipped only where the instruction leaves a
return address
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (is_return_address)`).
One that **links**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (links)`) transfers
control: a `CALL`, `CALLIND`, `BRANCH` to an address, `BRANCHIND` or `CALLOTHER`.
That covers the links SLEIGH spells without a `CALL`: x86 `call $+5` is a push
and a `BRANCH`; PowerPC `bcl 20,31,$+4`, `bl` to the next instruction, RISC-V `jal
t0` and MIPS `bal` past its delay slot write the link register and `BRANCH`; a
RISC-V PLT entry's `jalr t1,t3` is a `BRANCHIND`; x86-64 `syscall` saves the
address in `rcx` beside a `CALLOTHER`. The AArch64 sum rule above applies in
the same instructions. An instruction that does not branch can still leave a
link value, in two shapes. A32 `mov lr,pc` lifts `lr = inst_next + 4` for the `bx` after it, so a
fall-through combined with another constant in one op is not an address the
instruction forms. MIPS `nal` (`bltzal $zero`) is a branch that is never taken
and lifts to nothing but `ra = inst_next`; it is told apart by its delay slot
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (has_delay_slot)`): its
fall-through lies past the slot, beyond its own encoding, and only a branch has
one. The compiler spec is no help here, since MIPS64's names no
`<returnaddress>`. A slot behind an instruction that does branch — a `RETURN`
or a `CBRANCH` to an address (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (branches)`)
— is an ordinary instruction, so SuperH `rts; mova` and `bt/s; mova`, which form
the address right after the slot, file it. The slot is asked only of an
instruction that moves the fall-through whole and does not branch, so the walk
pays the second decode almost nowhere. Anything else that moves the fall-through whole — a copy or an extension
of it, or a store of it — files it as `Data`: AArch64 and A32 `adr`, Thumb-2
`adr.w`, x86-64 `lea rax,[rip]`, `mov eax,offset next`, `push offset next`, SuperH `mova`. The
register-pair carry and the PIC base harvest below made the same assumption
about a value they compose, and skip it only in an instruction that calls (the
carry) or links (the harvest), so an `auipc`+`addi` pair that ends right before
the label it forms files the label. Over 112 images (x86-64, i386 ELF and PE,
AArch64 ELF and arm64 Mach-O, A32/Thumb, MIPS, PowerPC, RISC-V) no row changes:
armel libc's 1,130 `mov lr,pc`, PowerPC libc's `bcl` thunks, x86-64 libc's 436
`syscall`s, every RISC-V PLT `jalr t1,t3` and the `nal` in MIPS64 `ld.so.1`'s
`_dl_start` still file nothing, and no image there forms an address at its own
fall-through, so only the fixtures gain rows.
Emitted C is unchanged; the query is not on the decompile path.

(unlace) An edge also has to survive being resolved to a **node**, and the walk's
function set is the wrong authority for this one. The walk calls nothing outside
an executable section a function — an IAT slot lives in `.rdata`, so it is never
one — while the inventory does name it, because `pe_iat` (§1.3) registered the
import there. For PE, the graph therefore falls back from the walk's function
set to the inventory extent containing the target
(`crates/unlace-cli/src/callgraph.rs (CallGraph::callee_of)`), which
is the same fold it already applies to every callee it reports. ELF historically
inventories the PLT veneer only, not its GOT slot, so the graph admits the slot
half of each decoded forwarding relation as a zero-extent node; `decompile-graph`
materializes that missing node as a bodyless row with the veneer's name. The
ordinary named import case classifies as `import`, while an unnamed linkage
target such as ELF PLT0 classifies as `data`. Its `forwardsTo` target and
jump-edge endpoint are therefore the same row on both formats. This is
deliberately confined to the graph model: `unlace functions`
keeps its established loader inventory, while an ELF `decompile-graph` document's
`functionCount` and `functions` array gain the recovered GOT-slot rows. An address
in neither the inventory nor a decoded forwarding relation is still not an edge.
Measured over 120 in-tree images, seven changed and none lost an edge: on
`pe_imports.exe` the functions reachable from the entry point went 47 -> 52 and
those with no caller 115 -> 103.

(unlace) The same two addresses make the import's **name** a selector that matches
two entries, and the selector model's answer to that is a refusal naming every
candidate — which would refuse a question that has exactly one answer, since either
address alone answers it. So a contested name is not decided at lookup time at all:
whether its candidates are one callable is a property of the decoded forwarding
jumps, which only exist once the walk has run. The candidates are carried into the
walk as its focus set, so every one of them is decoded, and the ambiguity is settled
afterwards against the alias class
(`crates/unlace-cli/src/xrefs.rs (Resolution::settle)`). Candidates that all
lie in one class are one callable and the query proceeds at the class's code half —
the forwarding veneer rather than the pointer slot, because that is the address the
answer will next be disassembled at, with the lowest address breaking a tie between
several veneers through one slot. Candidates that do not all share a class are
distinct functions and keep the refusal, with every candidate still named. The fold
therefore still rests on the decoded jump and never on the shared name; the name only
selects which addresses to check.

(unlace) Because the query runs that descent **itself**, it takes its own analysis
bundle rather than a decompiling surface's. `unlace functions` and `unlace decompile-all`
inject the DIV-15/DIV-20/DIV-68 defaults (the Listing, the prologue-pattern scan,
AIF); the query surface takes the two *discovery* flags and declines the Listing,
because the Listing's walk is this walk — a second recursive descent over the same
bytes, decoded a second time. On a 466 KB obfuscated i386 image that walk, plus
`operand_refs`' third linear decode, was 1.66 s of a 3.4 s answer that is
byte-identical without either.

The two discovery facts the Listing fed are produced from the query's own decode
instead. The `<patternpairs>` prologue starts are handed straight to the walk as
seeds (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (discovery_seeds)`,
gated by `funcstart_patterns` and to the non-x86-64 architectures the injection
covered, so x86-64's seed set is exactly the caller's inventory). The speculative
gap-walk (`aif`) is run over the instruction partition the query's own walk leaves
behind (`gap_entries` → `Listing::from_partition`), and every function it accepts is
walked like any other seed, so the references inside it join the index. That recall
is not optional decoration: a function whose only inbound edge is an indirect call
through a data table has no CALL edge for any descent to follow, and without the
gap-walk a `--to` query loses every call site that lives inside one — measured on a
stripped i386 PE as 61 of one function's 174 callers.

(unlace) ARM reference walks also recover the
LR-saving frame roots used by the Listing when both `funcstart_patterns` and
`armframes on` are enabled. The default `armframes inventory` recovers A32 frames
for the function inventory only, and no CLI discovery bundle or mode preset
selects `on`. Below `on`, reference discovery keeps its existing seeded/AIF walk;
with `off`, the Listing also keeps its Thumb-only inventory recovery.

Frame recovery never drops an inventory entry the option-off pipeline reports
without evidence against it
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/frameretain.rs`). Once
at least one root validates, the Listing pass first computes that frameless
inventory under a discarded decode context: the walk after the Thumb prologue
scan, plus the AIF, pool and pointer entries over it. Two mechanisms would
otherwise lose those entries. A recovered frame's walk follows a tail branch into
a routine the gap walk had found on its own and absorbs it as same-function flow;
on a stripped U-Boot this dropped `invalidate_dcache_range`, reached by `b` from a
newly recovered caller. And the prefix scan below can replace a root with
literal-pool words in front of it that happen to decode as straight-line code,
which dense Thumb encodings do readily. So a root the frameless walk already has
is replaced by a prefix only when it lies inside one of the prefix's instructions,
as the false `PUSH.W` halfword of a `LDR.W` does, and after the last rebuild every
frameless entry the recovered inventory lacks is published unless the evidence
contradicts it:
the entry is data or lies inside a decoded instruction; a fall-through or a
conditional branch runs into it; its first instruction is predicated, with a flow to
its own fall-through, which no function entry can be because the condition flags
are undefined there (literal-pool words in front of an A32 frame decode this way);
an accepted body of the post-frame gap walk runs into it, a body that walk refused
covers it, or a later interworking call contradicted its decode mode; or non-call flow from it reaches decoded code that is no function entry,
as a switch case does when its function's computed jump stayed unresolved. A
shrink-wrapped `cmp; ble` prefix still replaces a push the gap walk had reported,
because the push then has a fall-through predecessor. Over the 98 stripped ARM
images of the DecBench dataset, scored against their original `STT_FUNC` symbols,
the option dropped 1,756 symbol starts the default inventory found and now drops
34; nearly all of the rest are still entered by a fall-through from literal-pool
words in front of them. It keeps 1,738 of the 1,746 starts it adds. Entries without
a matching symbol go from 8,528 to 8,583, 54 of them on three Cortex-M images where
no frame validates and the option now reproduces the default inventory exactly.
Computing the frameless inventory adds about 12% to frame recovery on the 5.4 MB
U-Boot image.
The shared
`raw_arm_prologue_seeds` scan matches unconditional A32 `STMDB SP!, {…,lr}`
only at word-aligned ARM addresses and Thumb `PUSH` / `PUSH.W` only where the live
`TMode` selects Thumb, in the selected decoder's instruction byte order.
This includes BE8 images whose ELF data are big-endian and instructions are
little-endian. A Thumb-shaped halfword inside
an ARM instruction is not a Thumb prologue. Metadata and explicit `--isa` paints
therefore control both ordinary decoding and root recovery.

A matching prologue is only a candidate: its bounded validity walk must stay in
executable memory, avoid known instruction overlap and unclaimed escapes, and
reach a valid termination. Claims cover every byte of each reachable instruction,
including the second halfword of a Thumb-2 instruction. Candidate admission
rechecks those spans after earlier roots or explicit focus addresses have walked.
A conditional return records a terminating path, and the frame probe keeps
following its not-taken successor so the rest of the function is claimed. A
computed jump ends its path. Code reached only through a call's fall-through is
speculative, because the callee may never return and literal-pool words often
follow such calls: an undecodable word, an invalid flow or the step cap on a
speculative path ends that path instead of rejecting the candidate, and a
speculative path stops at another prologue candidate rather than absorbing the
next function. Invalid flow reached directly, without an intervening call, still
rejects the candidate, and a push on a valid direct successor path remains body
code. Only frame probes follow a conditional return this way; the AIF gap walk,
pool, pointer and referenced-target validators stop at every terminal
instruction exactly as before (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/mod.rs (follow_subroutine)`).
With `aif` enabled, a fingerprint-supported prefix outside the claimed frame bodies
that reaches a recovered push replaces that push as the root before either the
Listing or the reference query finalizes boundaries. Interior AIF candidates
remain owned by the earlier frame that reaches them. Prefix probing is restricted
to gaps containing frame candidates. After the frames and explicit focus are
walked, prefixes are rechecked using the expanded fingerprint corpus and the
original gap partition, where the whole prefix-plus-frame body is still available
for validation. Both prefix guards use that original partition to exclude
established code; the expanded corpus supplies fingerprint evidence, not new
coverage boundaries. A prefix reached only through a provisional call remains
eligible for validation and replacement of its interior frame.
Direct calls protect a frame only when their source is reachable
independently of the proposed obsolete bodies. Reconciliation considers all
validated frame candidates, including ones first reached as speculative callees.
It substitutes validated prefix instructions into the recorded successor graph,
then follows branches, fall-through and calls from the original entries,
admitted explicit focus, surviving frames and validated prefixes. Unreached
call cycles cannot establish their own boundaries; a reachable independent
caller protects the whole recursive call chain. Both Listing and xref consumers
use this same support rule
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/framecalls.rs`).
Any replaced provisional frame is removed from the function and graph seed sets.
When replaced bodies cannot be retained, the reference walk rebuilds from
the supplied seeds, original query focus and reconciled frame roots before the
ordinary AIF gap pass. Its decoded partition, references, discovered callees,
successor graph, indirect-call sites and switch records are rebuilt together;
instructions reached only through a discarded speculative body cannot survive
as ownerless references or seed unrelated callees. Queries with no replacement
reuse their existing walk.
The rebuild reconsiders every independently validated frame candidate, including
ones already reached as callees before their candidate was processed. Admission
checks the surviving bodies again, so a discarded caller cannot hide a real
unreferenced frame, and an interior candidate does not become a boundary.
Both consumers recheck prefixes after each rebuild, until no roots change.
Discarding a speculative call can make its former callee eligible for prefix
replacement on the next pass. Reconciled candidates replace the prior candidate
set, so removed roots are never reinstated; replacements move roots strictly
toward earlier validated prefixes, ensuring progress. Ordinary queries without
late replacements perform no extra rebuild; compatible ARM prefix extensions
can also keep unrelated bodies, as described below.

A provisional frame can also have been decoded in the wrong ISA before a later
interworking call establishes its mode. Both walks record the decoded spans of
each candidate's reachable body and the `TMode` used for each span. A direct call
into any covered byte, including the interior of a former instruction, withdraws
the candidate if its newly established mode disagrees. Rebuilding removes its
instructions, references and derived callees together. Prefix replacements run
first, so calls from discarded interiors cannot settle a frame's mode.
The saved context and mode checks remain available through the ordinary AIF gap
pass. The inventory walks accepted pointer-table and checked AIF roots before
publishing Listing consumers, so their calls can invalidate provisional frames
as well. Each inventory rebuild copies the original independently decoded
instructions, function records, references and proven mode corrections before
walking speculative roots.
Recovered calls publish their modes only over successfully decoded instruction
spans, so they cannot repaint retained callers. New callees keep their
interworking evidence outside that partition. Only the original partition is retained: discarded
frames and their derived callees are still rebuilt from surviving roots.
Pointer-table additions refresh the corpus before AIF runs. Before any
AIF body is walked, `ptrentry` and `poolentry` inspect the pre-AIF partition. Their
accepted pointer entries, pool-end additions and filtered AIF entries are retained
as one result. Only surviving AIF entries seed the interworking rewalk; pointer
and pool entries remain additive facts. This prevents speculative coverage from
rejecting a pointer target or hiding a pool boundary, and prevents a filtered AIF
entry from being recommitted by `funcdisc_recursive`. A frame replacement or ISA
invalidation discards the cached checks and recomputes them against the rebuilt
partition (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/entrychecks.rs`).
Mode correction also runs with AIF disabled
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/framemode.rs`).

Frame recovery retains its original validation records across reconciliation.
When `aifpoolslide` is enabled, frame-prefix reconciliation uses the same literal
word evidence as the ordinary AIF gap pass, including loads from validated frame
bodies before any prefix is considered. An accepted prefix on a referenced pool
word moves to the code after the pool. Its retained decode records exclude the
pool instructions, so neither their register writes nor their calls can supply
frame evidence. If the corrected address is already a frame root, that root
keeps its place; reconciliation never replaces an entry with itself
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/framepool.rs`).
A prefix pass reuses frame validity and claimed spans, and retains accepted prefix
bodies directly from the gap scan instead of validating them again. An unchanged
root set and unchanged fingerprint acceptance thresholds reuse the prior scan;
independent call support is still checked against the current graph. Corpus growth
that crosses a threshold triggers reconsideration
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/framecache.rs`).
For an ARM prefix whose validated body contains every old frame instruction with
identical decoding, and which contains no BLX, unrelated bodies can survive the
replacement. Both the saved and live context must select ARM throughout the
prefix body, the old body must have decoded in ARM, and the new entry must remain
undecoded. Only the affected callers' partition, references, flow, switch records
and fingerprint-context records are removed and rewalked. This recomputes data
references whose values originate in the newly admitted prefix. All other
replacements, including Thumb instruction interiors and changed modes, retain the
full rollback and rebuild
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/prefixreuse.rs`).

The reference walk can reuse a validated instruction's p-code only when the
translator certifies that the lift commits no context and depends on no other
instruction. The immutable image, address, translator and complete context words
must match. Instructions without that certificate are translated normally;
interworking and IT-state writes therefore still execute. Prefix probes apply the
same context check before reusing such decode records
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/decodereuse.rs`).

ARM frame and prefix probes use private decoder-context scopes. They preserve
the selected `TMode` while allowing local commits such as Thumb IT conditions,
then discard all probe writes. Provisional reference and Listing walks also
retain their pre-walk context: late replacement restores it before rebuilding;
otherwise accepted walks keep their legitimate interworking changes. Prefix
validation temporarily restores the saved pre-walk context. The xref corpus
instead retains the context words seen before each instruction's translation,
stored as runs in decode order. Only the two fingerprint instructions per entry
are rendered, each under its recorded context in a private scope. This retains
new callees' legitimate interworking modes as well as earlier fingerprints that
a later speculative branch could repaint, including callees identified after
their instructions were already decoded as body code. Rebuilds discard these
records with the obsolete partition. Rendering checks instruction lengths and
restores the live context afterward
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/fingerprintcontext.rs`). These
scopes preserve context defaults, split-point values and explicit-set masks,
tracked registers, and cache write settings, including across nested scopes
(`crates/unlace-sleigh/src/contextscope.rs`).
Prefix reconciliation compares roots with complete instruction spans, including
roots inside Thumb-2 instructions rather than only at their starts.
The ordinary AIF gap pass runs after the
recovered roots and explicit focus have been walked: their function count and
fingerprints can cross acceptance thresholds that the initial partition did not.
Mode changes from recovered calls remain confined to decoded instruction spans,
including discontiguous callee blocks. Undefined gaps retain their input modes
for this pass; no separate restoration scan or repeated body decode is needed.
Both reference queries and the inventory retain pre-frame validation bounds
for the later AIF check. AIF still admits starts only in current gaps, but its
non-strict body validator may follow a branch across a new frame boundary within
the same original gap. Pointer and pool checks still use the pre-AIF partition.
This preserves previously discoverable discontiguous callers without extending
validation across independently established code boundaries. Strict frame and
pointer validation keep their existing limits.
This admits rare frame prologues without a fingerprint-frequency requirement,
retains calls after an early return on another path, and assigns those calls to
the entry that reaches them. Discovery probes use the existing partition; only
late root replacement or contradicted frame mode rebuilds the reference walk. Disabling either `funcstart_patterns` or `armframes` disables this scan;
disabling `aif` does not. Recovery remains heuristic and bounded: frames with other
prologues, undecodable paths or uncorroborated flow escapes can remain undiscovered.

The `inventory` value is the default: it validates A32 frame starts in the
function inventory while retaining the existing Thumb-only inventory path.
The `on` value also validates Thumb frames and expands independent reference
walks; `off` restores the prior discovery path. The same function-start and
Listing prerequisites still apply. In the optimized DecBench U-Boot pilot,
full frame recovery adds 770 listed bodies and loses none; the corresponding
Betaflight pilot exchanges one gained body for one lost body. Default recovery
therefore targets A32 inventory roots. Short callbacks and vector-only handlers
remain separate discovery sources.

With `armframes` enabled (`inventory`, the default, or `on`), the Listing walk
also follows an A32 jump table. Unlike frame recovery, table following needs no
other option: not `funcstart_patterns`, which is off by default, and in the
reference walk not `listing` either. GCC
lowers an A32 switch to `cmp rN,#n` and a predicated `ldrls pc,[pc,rN,lsl #2]`
with its table of case addresses 8 bytes past the dispatch, or to `addls
pc,pc,rN,lsl #2` followed by one `b` per case. The dispatch's p-code is folded
with the switch-table lattice; only those two PC-relative shapes answer. The
case count comes from the guard, read as a Thumb `tbb` guard is, with the
dispatch's own condition as the range branch when it is predicated. An
unguarded dispatch reads nothing. Word-table entries must lie in the
dispatcher's executable section. The cases become successors and code
references of the dispatch
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/a32switch.rs`). Without this,
frame recovery left every case block undefined. The AIF fingerprint histogram,
which frame recovery fills with the whole program, then accepted case blocks as
function entries and cut the dispatcher apart. Following a switch also decodes
the code its cases reach, and the walk absorbs a routine reached only by a tail
branch into the code that branches to it, as it does everywhere else. On stripped
U-Boot O2-noinline that absorbs 7 of the 2,836 functions, all of which frame
recovery without switch following lists: four tail-branch targets of `pointer`'s
cases, and `memalign_simple`, `efi_process_event_queue` and `malloc_trim`, the
tail-branch targets of functions the walk now reaches through a followed case.
`tailcallentry` splits such routines off.

A frame root is also withdrawn when the frame-expanded Listing enters it by
straight-line flow, the way a contradicted mode withdraws it. The instruction
just before the root must be a non-call that falls through or conditionally
skips into it. Tracing back, its run must start at a function entry or a branch
target. A shrink-wrapped routine saves LR a few instructions after its entry,
and once a caller reaches that entry, its fall-through runs into the `push`. A
run that begins at a call's fall-through is speculative and keeps the root: a
literal pool after a no-return call decodes as such a run into the next routine
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/frameflow.rs`). A
retained prior entry that a jump-table dispatch reaches is a case block and is
contradicted too. On the stripped U-Boot O2-noinline image these rules leave
recall at 92.0% and raise precision from 92.6% to 98.6%; `parse_label` and
`malloc` stay whole.

A `ptrentry` target is checked against the raw Thumb scan's roots the same
way (`ptrentry.rs (shrinkwrap_roots)`). Its decoded run, following
fall-through only for at most eight instructions and stopping at a call, a
return or an unconditional branch, may reach a root no call targets. Then the
target is the routine's real entry and the root its shrink-wrapped `push`: the
root is withdrawn, the target becomes a walk root, and the Listing is rebuilt.
libopencm3's `dwc_poll` (`ldr.w r12,[r0,#0xdc]; push.w {...}`, reached only
through the driver table) was a 4-byte stub and a separate 472-byte
`sub_8001718` before.

One inventory recovery shares its decodes. Frame validation, the AIF gap walks
(including the prior inventory's), prefix reconciliation and every Listing
rebuild decode the same image again. A decode is kept only when SLEIGH certifies
it context-free, together with the effective context words it read. It is reused
only while its address still reads those words, so a reused record is the
record a fresh decode makes, and it reports no context commits. These records
keep no p-code: the inventory never replays a frame body into a reference walk,
so the inventory's own validation records keep none either. A record is a
fixed-size slot per halfword of executable code, with its text and flow targets
in shared arenas, so the whole image's records cost about 16 bytes per halfword
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/decodememo.rs`).
A `--jobs` worker does not search at all. The parent's recovery leaves a record of
its final roots, code-pointer and AIF entries and retained prior entries
(`AnalysisOutput::arm_frames`). The worker builds the final Listing from that
record under the same context lifecycle
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/aif/framereplay.rs`).

Full reference expansion can substantially increase query cost. In a historical
measurement on a 400,556-byte stripped ARM BusyBox ELF,
`xrefs --to puts --kind call` initially reached 2,271 instructions; frame
recovery expanded the walk to about 74,000. The recovered query found 70 call
references instead of 43 and took roughly twice as long. Disabling `aif` with
`armframes` enabled retained 66 references at lower cost. Speed comparisons use
release builds, one new process per query and warm filesystem caches; a repeated
query does not reuse an index from another process.

ARM runtime reference queries with `funcstart_patterns` enabled retain decoded
fall-through, branch and switch successors to resolve caller ownership after all
entries are known. Each entry owns only
instructions it reaches without passing another entry; shared blocks prefer the
greatest entry that reaches them. An unrelated function in a gap cannot absorb
another caller's discontiguous block merely by preceding it in memory. A later
direct call can still establish a separate callee in previously decoded code.
Incoming owner labels, outgoing buckets, intra-function branch filtering and
indirect-call flags all use these same body owners. This graph walk reuses the
decoded instructions and does not invoke the decoder again.
CLI call-graph ownership projects these reachable owners onto the canonical
inventory too, so direct callers, callback references and graph edges agree with
the reference index for discontiguous bodies. Where no reachable owner is
available, bounded inventory extents still resolve undecoded import slots.
Graph seeds are appended during discovery, then sorted and deduplicated once
when the index is finalized, before any instruction-count query reads them.

(unlace) A reference query also seeds the walk with **the address it was asked
about**. The same structural gap applies to the query target itself: `--from <entry>`
about a function no descent reaches answered `count: 0` about a function that plainly
has references. The named address is walked after the seeded descent and the
recovered prologue candidates are merged with explicit focus addresses in address
order. A recovered frame's walk stops at another pending frame candidate unless
its own validated body claimed that instruction, so a frame whose call never
returns cannot absorb the function placed after its literal pool.

ARM runtime xref walks with both `funcstart_patterns` and `armframes`, and inventory rebuilds that
admit recovered frames share one context lifecycle
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/walkcontext.rs`):

- Independent seeds, frames, AIF entries and focuses select their input mode
  from the context captured before the walk. A queued direct callee retains
  its call's mode, even if another seed is walked first.
- Branches, fall-through and switch successors carry the decoding instruction's
  mode. A SLEIGH mode commit at the successor supplies an explicit change;
  ordinary calls inherit the caller's mode. Thus a distant block does not
  inherit the mode of a different function placed between it and its entry.
- Automatic SLEIGH `TMode` writes are masked throughout the walk. Their recorded
  commits remain available as control-flow evidence. Other context fields,
  including Thumb IT state, keep their existing decode semantics.
- Each instruction uses a temporary effective read mode without changing database
  boundaries. Failure publishes no selected mode. Success publishes it only over the
  instruction's complete byte span. Fingerprint and decode-reuse keys observe
  the same effective context as the instruction.
- Speculative frame scopes retain their bodies, references and bounded context
  changes together. A full rebuild rolls them back and clears queued mode
  evidence. Prefix extension reuses only compatible ARM bodies; replaced
  instruction/reference records are removed before the extension walks.
- Final publication needs no gap or body repair pass: only surviving decoded
  spans changed mode. Unclaimed bytes retain their input modes with AIF off,
  below its corpus threshold, or enabled. Repeated queries and later
  decompilation therefore see the same unrelated instruction streams.

Initial Listing discovery keeps its own context behavior, `armwalkmode`'s
carried modes and the optional `flowmode` proof policy. Already established Listing bodies are retained during
a recovery rebuild. Provisional
bodies contradicted by direct interworking, including calls into instruction
interiors, are invalidated using the recorded call mode. Inventory rebuilds
retain these rejected heuristic entries for the rest of the discovery run;
later AIF scans and prefix replacements cannot restart the same stale retry.
Pointer and pool checks continue to use the partition preceding the AIF rewalk.
Frame and AIF probes are scoped, and original-context prefix validation remains
separate from the expanded fingerprint corpus. Scoped read and write policies
are restored on exit. Ordinary ARM AIF scans, including recovery-disabled xref
gap scans and their fingerprint rendering, also run in a context scope. Speculative
`TMode` writes are masked while other fields, including Thumb IT state, remain
active inside the scan. Dropping the scope restores values, write boundaries,
and read/write policies on every exit. Accepted entries are returned as facts;
the subsequent real walk supplies their interworking effects. Non-ARM walks
retain their existing context behavior.

A focus preceding its frame claims
the reachable push as body code before it can become a boundary; an earlier
recovered root still owns an interior focus.
An address the natural walk already claimed is already in `decoded` and attributed
exactly as before — the focus pass can only add
coverage, never re-attribute an instruction another entry owns. An address that does
not decode is dropped rather than recorded as a function, so a byte in the middle of
a string does not become `sub_<addr>`.

(unlace, GH #1406) A focus address is decoded only where the walk decodes at all: in
a section the linker marked as code. The loader obeys the segment instead, so memory
can be executable without being marked. An Apple toolchain links a function placed
in `__TEXT,__const` with no instruction attribute although `__TEXT` is `r-x`, a
bare-metal link script leaves `.ramfunc` flagged `WA` in an `RWE` `PT_LOAD`, and GNU
ld links AArch64 `.rodata` into the `R E` segment. `unlace xrefs --from` such an
address answered `count: 0`, the same document a function with no references gets.
The walk still does not decode that memory on its own account: most of it is
strings and tables, and the Mach-O inventory keeps its symbols out of
`unlace functions` (GH #1339). An explicit `--from` source there is decoded as code when the image
says it is code
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (build_with_unflagged_focus)`).
The section holding it must lie wholly inside a segment the image maps executable
(ELF `PF_X`, Mach-O `initprot` execute) and have a type that can hold instructions
(ELF allocated `SHT_PROGBITS` that is neither TLS nor merged strings; Mach-O
`S_REGULAR`, `S_SYMBOL_STUBS` or `S_COALESCED`)
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/unflaggedcode.rs (placement)`).
An ELF symbol table must not declare a data object at the address, and something
must say the address is code: a symbol names it and a direct call or branch the
seeded walk decoded targets it (checked when the focus pass reaches it, after that
walk has drained), or an ELF symbol table declares a function there, an ARM
`STT_FUNC`'s Thumb bit aside
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/unflaggedcode.rs (declared_function)`).
The symbol is any Mach-O `nlist` or ELF function or untyped label, never a mapping
symbol (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/unflaggedcode.rs (named_at)`).
A call alone is not enough: on a static ARM glibc image the Thumb `_start` read in
A32 is a `bleq` into the `.rodata` strings, and that target is no more code than any
other string.
Selection alone is not enough, because the same memory is mostly data: GNU ld put
x86-64 `.rodata` in the `R E` segment until `-z separate-code` became its default
(binutils 2.31), and still does on AArch64, and a string there decodes to a run of
plausible conditional jumps. A Mach-O `nlist` carries no type,
so a symbol alone is not evidence there. Only the source's own body is decoded: its
branches are followed while they stay in that section, and a call out of it is
filed and walked under the ordinary rules. The seeded descent can reach the address
first, as a callee, and stops at it as before; only the focus pass decodes it.
`--to`, and every other surface built on the walk, decodes nothing new. A PE
section is its own mapping unit, executable and walked or not executable at all, so
PE has no such gap.

Every answer also carries a `coverage` object
(`crates/unlace-cli/src/xrefs.rs (coverage_of)`): whether the walk decoded
the queried address, the section it is in, whether that section is marked as code
and whether its memory is executable, and the call and jump targets in executable
memory not marked as code that the walk filed but did not decode and a symbol names
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (undecoded_flow_targets)`).
The references those targets make are missing from every answer. Only a direct
call or branch counts, never a call through a slot: Go's closure call `MOV
RAX,[funcval]; CALL RAX` is a `call` row to the funcval word in `__rodata`, which
holds a code address and is not code. A `--from` answer
about anything other than code decoded in a code section, and a `--to` answer while
such targets exist, say so in a note.

(unlace) Both of those rules read a reference out of *one instruction's* p-code,
which is the whole answer on x86-64 and no answer at all in 32-bit
position-independent code. There the address of a string, a global or a function
pointer is never a constant in the instruction that uses it: the program
materialises the GOT pointer at run time — `call <next instruction>; pop ebx; add
ebx,imm`, an idiom that exists for no other purpose — and every literal is reached
as base-plus-displacement, so the address occurs nowhere in the image and the
constant scan reports that every string in the program is referenced by nothing.
**PIC base folding** (`picbase`, always on,
`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/picbase.rs`) closes that with a
deliberately tiny abstract machine over the same whole p-code the query already
keeps: a value is a constant or an offset from the stack pointer, memory is
modelled only at stack offsets (enough to follow the `call`'s push into the
`pop`), a constant is tainted as PC-derived when it equals its own instruction's
fall-through, and only a tainted value may establish a base — so a plain
`mov ebx,imm` cannot. GCC's out-of-line form is covered by the same machine: a
direct call whose callee delivers the return address in a register (probed like a
veneer, at most two instructions) hands that register the call's own
fall-through. Three shapes are then read off each instruction *independently*, with
the base seeded and nothing else assumed, so no state crosses a control-flow
edge: the address a `LOAD` reads, the address a `STORE` writes, and a constant
that lands in a register, which is the address-taken case. A value computed only
into a temporary is deliberately not reported — in an indexed access the array
base lands in one, and filing it would claim a reference the instruction does not
form.

Two claims hide in that and they are licensed differently. A function that runs
the idiom *itself* computes the value and assumes nothing. A function that only
uses an inherited base — which is the case that matters, because unlace's own
inventory splits the filing crackme's prompt routine at its `int3` traps and the
`lea` that forms the prompt lands in a different entry from the idiom that set the
register up — is relying on the i386 System V ABI reserving that register as the
module's GOT pointer, so the recovered value is cross-checked against the image's
own `_GLOBAL_OFFSET_TABLE_` (the `.got.plt`/`.got` address) and every idiom in the
program must agree on one register and one value; absent that, nothing is claimed
module-wide. The rule that keeps ownership honest is refusal rather than
guesswork, because attributing a string to a function that merely sits near it is
worse than reporting nothing and no parity gate could see it: the base is offered
to a function whose body never writes the register at all, or from its own
establishment up to the next write of it (in GCC output, the epilogue's restore),
and to no other function. A body that reuses the register for its own purposes
contributes no references rather than wrong ones. The pass runs only on a
32-bit image: a 64-bit one (x86-64, AArch64) forms PC-relative addresses
directly, which the constant scan already reads, so the walk never probes its
prologues for the idiom.

(unlace) One indirection further out is the same defect on ARM, and PIC base
folding does not reach it: an ARM immediate cannot hold an arbitrary address, so
the compiler parks the constant in a **literal pool** in `.text` and the code
loads it PC-relatively (`ldr r0,[0x86e4]` at 0x862c, and the word at 0x86e4 is
the string). SLEIGH resolves the pool address at decode time, so the walk files
that read — and stops, because 0x86e4 is all the instruction says. The literal
itself is referenced by nothing, and on the filing image `unlace strings --json`
reported `xrefs_count: 0` and no owning function for a string
`__libc_start_main` plainly prints. **Literal-pool following**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/poolref.rs`) closes that with
exactly one dereference, of content that cannot change: a `Read` of a
pointer-sized, pointer-aligned location in an **allocated, non-writable** section
with file content, whose word passes the same `checkOperands` value filter the
constant scan uses and lands in a mapped section, files a second edge to that
word's value. The edge is filed from the **instruction**, not from the pool word,
which is the whole point — a pool word is data and belongs to no function, so
attributing the reference to it would answer the question with another address
instead of a name.

Each clause is a refusal that would otherwise be a fabricated reference. The read
must be pointer-*sized*, and the width has to come from the access rather than
from the address varnode, because a `LOAD`'s address is pointer-sized whatever
the access is — without that, `ldrh r0,[pool]`, which is reading a number out of
a pool, reads as a pointer dereference. The section must be non-writable: a GOT
entry or a `.data` pointer holds whatever the loader or the program last wrote
there, and the image's copy of it is not evidence. And the value must clear the
address floor, so a read-only word holding 42 stays a number. The kind filed is
`Data`, the address-taken case, because that is what the load did. Measured over
a 15-image sweep: zero edges added on every x86-64 ELF and PE in it (a RIP-relative
load already encodes the address it forms), zero attributions lost anywhere, and
on the ARM images 2,239 new string-to-function attributions on u-boot and 763 on
the filing crackme — of which an independent capstone-plus-symtab oracle
corroborates 2,234 and 761 as real PC-relative pool loads, with every one of the
remainder confirmed by hand as a load the oracle's own sweep missed.

(unlace) Literal-pool following assumes the pool holds a *pointer*, and in a
position-independent ARM image it holds no pointer at all. There the pool word is
the signed distance from the instruction that consumes it to the datum, and the
address exists only once the two are put together: `ldr r0,[0x6a0]` at 0x660 and
`add r0,pc,r0` at 0x664 form 0x66c + (-0x1c1) = 0x4ab, the success string of the
filing crackme. The word is not an address and lands in no section, so following
it as a pointer correctly declines, and every string reference in the function is
lost — the reported `xrefs_count: 0` and empty owner list were not one site but
all four the function makes. **PIC pool composition**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/picpool.rs`) closes that by
composing the two decode-time constants the pair already carries. It is PIC base
folding with a per-site base rather than a module-wide one: there the base is a
register a prologue establishes once and the whole function inherits, so there is
something to detect and to scope; here each reference carries its own base — the
PC of its own `add` — so there is nothing to detect once, and what the walk
carries instead is the pool word itself, from the load to whatever composes it.

A pool word is admitted as a *displacement* only where it comes out of the same
read-only, pointer-sized, pointer-aligned slot literal-pool following already
vouches for, whatever the word itself looks like: in an ARM executable linked at
a fixed low address (0x10000) a displacement often lands in a mapped section by
chance, and only the PC fold below decides that it is one. A32 reads the slot
with a `LOAD` from a constant address; Thumb's literal loads, the 16-bit `ldr`
and `ldr.w`, export the slot itself with the word-aligned PC already folded in,
so they lift as a `COPY` out of the image, and both forms are read. Both of
these, the mapped-looking word and the Thumb `COPY`, are admitted only in an
image that has a GOT (`.got` or `.got.plt`) or a `.dynamic` section, which is
what position-independent code links into; a static image with none of them,
which is what bare-metal firmware is, admits only an A32 `LOAD` of a word that
is not a mapped address. That keeps the walk on such firmware, whose Thumb code
is dense with literal loads of pointers, at the cost it had before Thumb was
read, and its output is unchanged: over the 98 decbench ARM firmware images, their
stripped copies, and firmware relinked at 0x0, the wider admission formed no
reference. It is then
carried forward along fall-through alone, for a bounded run of instructions, and
dropped at the first write of its register, at any branch or return, and at a
call unless its register is callee-saved (GCC schedules the load before a call
and its `add` after). A user-defined operation ends it too, except inside a
call, where it is the Thumb `bl`'s instruction-set switch and the call's own rule
decides — the walk is breadth-first, so the values are keyed by
the address they reach rather than held as "the previous instruction's state",
which is what makes the carry independent of the order the queue happens to visit
a function in. The composition itself is a one-instruction constant fold over
`COPY`/`INT_ADD`/`INT_SUB` and nothing else, and it reports a value only when
**both** a pool word and a constant the instruction materialised from its own
address contributed to it (`inst_start + 8` on A32, `+ 4` on Thumb). That second taint is the whole guard: `add r0,r0,#4`
on the same word can land on a real literal, and only the missing PC separates it
from a reference. A value that stays in a temporary is not reported, for the same
reason PIC base folding does not report one — the GOT idiom `ldr r1,[pool]; ldr
r1,[pc,r1]` composes its slot address into a temporary and dereferences it, and
the slot is not what the instruction formed.

The `checkOperands` address floor is deliberately not applied to the composed
value. That floor asks whether an *immediate* is an address or an integer; here
the PC has already settled the question, and the filing image is an Android PIE
whose whole layout lives under 0x2828 — applying the floor there would discard
every reference in the program. Landing in a mapped section is the whole test the
result has to pass. Measured over a 417-image sweep of the crackme corpus, the
vendored fixtures and a set of host binaries: no edge is added on any x86-64 or
PE image (a RIP-relative load already encodes the address it forms), no
attribution is lost anywhere, and the composed edges are all on ARM images.

When a pool word that is itself a mapped address is carried on, literal-pool
following's pointer edge for it is held until the function's walk ends and is
filed only if no PC fold consumed the word, so a displacement is never also
reported as an absolute pointer from its load.

ARM `-fPIC` code also reaches data and functions through the GOT. The function
makes the GOT address once with the same pair (`ldr r4,[pool]; add r4,pc,r4`) and
keeps it in a callee-saved register; each use loads a GOT offset from the pool
and reads the slot (`ldr r2,[r4,r2]`). A composed value that lands in `.got` is
therefore tracked as a **GOT base** along every edge of the function, branches
included, and across a call when its register is callee-saved, until the register
is written. A load whose address is a GOT base plus a carried pool word files a
read of the slot and, when the slot's file word is a mapped address, a data
reference to that word from the load. `.got` is writable, so literal-pool
following does not hold it; its file bytes are what the loader starts from, and
in a non-PIE executable the linker writes a local function's or object's address
there with no relocation (an import's slot holds 0 and names nothing). Only base
plus a pool word (the GOTOFF form) is an address: base plus an immediate is
arithmetic on the base and names nothing, and a plain copy of the base files
nothing but is itself a base, so `mov r5,r4; ldr r3,[r5,r3]` still finds the
slot. A switch's case bodies are the dispatcher's own code, so each case target
receives the bases the dispatch holds. On ARM a Thumb function's slot word, and a
Thumb function's PC-composed address, carry bit 0. Whether an odd address whose
even half lies in an executable section is such a pointer or a datum at an odd
address (a string in a `.rodata` linked into `.text`) is decided once the whole
walk is done: it names the function, bit 0 cleared, when the walk decoded an
instruction or knows a function at the even address, or when the nearest ARM
mapping symbol at or below it is `$t`; a `$d` or `$a` there leaves it at its own
address. An image with no mapping symbols says nothing either way, and the
Thumb pointer, by far the commoner of the two, is assumed.

(unlace) **Accesses through a held address** (ARM only, always on):
the slot's word, a PC-composed address and a GOTOFF address are each the address
of a datum, and the program goes on to read and write it through the register
(`ldr r3,[r4,r2]; str r0,[r3,#0x20]`), as code built without `-fPIC` does with a
literal-pool word (`ldr r5,=g_cfg; ...; str r4,[r5,#0x14]`). Filing only the
instruction that loads the address left `unlace xrefs --to` a global with none of
its reads and writes, all of which IDA and Ghidra list. Each such address that
lands in a register outside `.got` is therefore tracked as a **pointer** the way
a GOT base is: along every edge, across a call when its register is callee-saved,
through a copy and through the addition or subtraction of constants, until the
register is written with anything else. The slot's word becomes one when it is a
mapped, even, pointer-width word; a pool word becomes one when it is a mapped,
even address outside `.got`, in an image with a GOT or a `.dynamic` section,
whose pool words are already carried. A `LOAD` or `STORE` whose address is a
pointer plus constants files a `Read` or `Write` of that address from the
instruction, so an `ldm` or `stm` files each word it moves. A pointer plus a pool
word, plus another register, or plus the PC names nothing. A pool word can be a
displacement that happens to be a mapped address, so an access through it is
filed only if no PC fold in the body consumes the word, the same test its pointer
edge from the load passes. The rows are `Read` and `Write` rows, which the call
graph does not read, so `decompile-all` is byte-identical with the option on and
off; off files only the addresses, as before. Like a base, a pointer the
function did not form itself (one a caller passes in, or one reloaded from the
stack) is not tracked.

Because the walk decodes each instruction once, breadth-first, it can decode a
join before it has seen every edge into it, so what it carries is only a
candidate. Each instruction that sees a tracked value is recorded with the
values it was handed, what it passes on and which addresses it forms, each
naming the incoming values it was computed from; every edge is recorded as it is
taken, switch cases included, whether or not the dispatch carried anything. When
the walk of the function ends, a value is kept at an instruction only if every
recorded predecessor passes on the same one, and everything computed from a
dropped value goes with it, repeated until nothing changes. Only addresses whose
inputs all survived are filed. The entry needs no rule of its own: the walk
decodes it first, so nothing is carried into it. This is stricter than Ghidra's
`SymbolicPropogator`, which follows each path with its own copy of the state and
keeps the union of what the paths find.

A predicated instruction lifts as a branch to the next instruction when its
condition fails, ahead of its body, so it reaches the next instruction along two
edges: the one where it ran and fell through, and the one where it did not run,
which carries what it was handed less what its condition wrote. A base meets
both, so a conditional write to the base ends it after the instruction, while a
predicated return such as `popeq {r4-r6,pc}` leaves the base to the path that
falls past it. Pool words follow the instruction when it falls through, because
a predicated pair (`ldrne; addne`) runs under one condition.

Nothing is recorded before a body's first pool load, since nothing can be in
flight; this keeps the walk's cost on bodies, and architectures, that never form
one of these pairs to one scan of each instruction's operations. Soundness does
not need the earlier edges: at the first load, everything the walk has queued and
not yet decoded was queued by an instruction that carried nothing, so nothing
holds there, which is exactly what the meet over every edge would answer. An
instruction that a recovered frame's walk refused to enter is treated the same
way, because the frame's edge into it is in no other body's record.

Six shapes are not covered, or not exactly. A GOT base inherited from a caller
(one the function never forms itself) is not tracked: on ARM the register that holds it is
only callee-saved, not reserved, so assuming it would need every caller to
agree. A pool word does not cross a branch, so a slot load reached by a branch, as when
GCC merges the tails of switch cases into one shared `ldr r3,[r6,r3]`, files
nothing, even when every path brings the same offset. Code that a function walked
later reaches by jumping into a body already walked is not part of that body's
meet. A pool word the PC meets only inside an address (`ldr r3,[pc,r3]`, the A32
read of a TLS initial-exec slot) composes nothing a register holds, so the slot is
not read, and a word that is itself a mapped address keeps its pointer edge from
the load. A position-independent static image with no GOT and no `.dynamic`
section (code that touches only its own strings and statics) is read as
firmware. And in an image stripped of its mapping symbols, a datum at an odd
address inside an executable section is filed one byte low.

(unlace) PIC base folding and PIC pool composition each recognise one idiom; the
general form of their defect is any ISA whose instructions cannot hold an address.
AArch64 builds one as a page (`adrp x0,0x100000000`) plus a twelve-bit offset
(`add x0,x0,#0x488`, or the offset of an `ldr`/`str`), RISC-V as `lui`'s or
`auipc`'s high twenty bits plus an `addi`/`lw`/`sw`/`ld` offset, MIPS as `lui` plus
`addiu`, PowerPC as `lis` plus `addi`; neither instruction names the datum, so the
constant scan reported a static string that a function returns, a global that it
reads and a function pointer that it loads as referenced by nothing, on arm64
Mach-O, AArch64 ELF and RV32/RV64 ELF alike. **Register pair carrying**
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/regcarry.rs`) carries a
register's constant to the instructions that fall after it. A register an
instruction leaves holding a constant that passes the `checkOperands` floor is
handed to its fall-through, and each instruction that receives one evaluates its
own p-code with it seeded, over the same small integer fold PIC base folding uses.
The three shapes that machine reads are read here too, with one difference in
kind: the address a `LOAD` reads is a `Read`, the address a `STORE` writes a
`Write`, and an address an `INT_ADD`/`INT_SUB` composes into a whole register is
`Data` — forming an address is not reading it. Only a value a carried register
contributed to is reported (the instruction's own constants are the scan's), and a
value that stays in a temporary is not, for the indexed-access reason above.

A carried value lives for at most eight instructions, is dropped when its
register is written with anything the fold cannot follow, and survives a call only
in a register the default prototype leaves unaffected and the call instruction did
not itself write (ARM's cspec lists `lr` as unaffected, yet the `bl` writes it). An
instruction whose p-code branches inside itself — a predicated A32 instruction, an
x86 `rep` — passes on no register it writes, and nothing it computes past a
p-code-relative label is filed, because a value there may come from either side
of the label (`cinc x0,x0,eq` leaves `x0` or `x0 + 1`). Values travel only along
fall-through, and the walk is breadth-first, so each reference records the
instructions its value passed through; once the whole walk has drained, a
reference is filed only if none of them is a branch target, a switch case or a
function entry. A join is where another path may hand the register a different
value, and two `adrp`s meeting at one `add` therefore form nothing. This gives
up a value that every path agrees on, which the meet PIC pool composition runs
would keep; the carry is meant for the two halves of one pair, which a compiler
keeps in one straight run.

The `Data` shape is narrower than the other two because nothing dereferences the
value to vouch for it, and the same pair builds integers. A copy of a carried
value (`mv a1,a0`, which RISC-V spells `addi a1,a0,0`) is the reference its source
already was. Bitwise composition (`movk`, `ori`, `movt`) and an add narrower than
the register it lands in (RV64 `addiw`, which truncates through a `SUBPIECE`) are
how a program builds a number. A value formed only to form the next one — the
middle `add` of an A32 PLT entry, whose register the very next instruction uses as
a base and overwrites — is a step, not an address, and an access that writes its
own address back (`ldr pc,[ip,#0x2f0]!`, `lwzu`) is one reference, the access. And
in an ELF `ET_DYN` image, which is relocated as a whole, an absolute immediate is
a number, never an address (`lui s2,0x3; addi s2,s2,-5` in a RISC-V shared object is
12283, and a PJSIP library forms thousands of `70000`-range status codes that
way), so there a constant starts a carry only when it was computed from the
instruction's own address: `auipc`'s `imm + inst_start`, A32's `pc` read as
`inst_start + 8`. x86-64 and AArch64 are exempt, because SLEIGH folds their
PC-relative operands (`lea [rip+…]`, `adrp`) into a plain constant, so the PC is
not visible, and neither builds a number from an add of two immediates. RV32 is
where the two shapes coincide in an executable: `li a1,70000` assembles to
`lui a1,0x11; addi a1,a1,0x170`, exactly the `%hi`/`%lo` pair of an address, so in
an RV32 `ET_EXEC` a number that lands in a mapped section files a `Data` row — the
same floor the constant scan applies to a lone immediate. RV64 builds that number
with `addiw` and is not affected. The page or high half on its own is not a
carried reference.

(unlace, option `movwpairs`) A 32-bit address built in two 16-bit halves
starts no carry by the rule above, because the low half is usually below the
floor: `movw r0,#0x1cc; movt r0,#3` (A32 or T32) or `mov x0,#0x230; movk
x0,#0x22,lsl #16` (AArch64 `movz`/`movk`, `-mcmodel=large`) left the global it reads
and writes, the string it passes and the callback it registers referenced by
nothing. With `movwpairs access` an instruction whose encoding is a low-half move
(A32/T32 `movw`, AArch64 `movz` with no shift) and whose p-code writes a register
from a constant leaves that register as a *half*: carried like any value, but
naming nothing while it is below the floor. The high-half move that completes it
(`movt`, `movk` with a shift, recognised by encoding too) leaves the whole value,
which is then an ordinary carried address, so a `LOAD` or `STORE` through it is a
`Read` or a `Write`. `movwpairs on` also files the completed value as `Data` at the
completing instruction where it lands in a mapped section (IDA's "valid addresses
only" reading of `MOVT` pairs), which is a judgement: a number built the same way
that lands in a section names it. Everything else of the carry applies unchanged
(eight hops, no joins along the run, a `movk` that only re-inserts zero upper
halves changes nothing), and big-endian code is not read. `on` is the default;
`off` is the behaviour above. GCC for Cortex-M builds addresses from literal pools, so the
default changes the Listing of those images not at all; clang's `movw`/`movt` pairs are the
case it changes.

A constant subtracted from a carried address biases that address rather than
naming another one. Swift builds a string literal's object as `adrp/add` of the
literal, `sub x8,x8,#0x20`, then `orr x1,x8,#0x8000000000000000`, and the literal,
not the 32 bytes before it, is what the code references: so the `sub` files no
`Data` row and does not make the literal's `add` a step (with the `add` folded
into `adr x8,lit; nop` by the linker, the `adr` is the row). Over the Mach-O sweep
above this drops 294 rows naming whatever lay 32 bytes before a literal and
restores 14 rows naming the literal. Only a subtraction is a bias: an add of a
negative constant is how RISC-V and MIPS complete a `%hi` whose `%lo` is negative.

An AArch64 `adrp` page that is a mapped address is also a `Data` row of the
constant scan's own, which names whatever datum the page starts with: `adrp
x8,_hook@PAGE` in a function that only goes on to `add x8,x8,#0x8` and read
`_pair` is no reference to `_hook`. So the carry tracks the page, and when an
instruction it holds across completes the page into a different address — the
`add`, the `ldr x1,[x1,#0x5a8]` of a selector reference, the `ldr x16,[x16,#0x18]`
of a stub — the page was a step to that address and the scan's row is withdrawn.
A page the run also uses at offset 0 is the datum itself and keeps its row,
whatever else completes it: an access at the page (`ldr x16,[x16]`, the first
register of `ldp x0,x1,[x8]`, a post-indexed `ldr x0,[x8],#8`), or the `add
x0,x0,#0` that is the `:lo12:` half of a page-aligned symbol. That `add` is the
only trace of a symbol at the page that is used by address: clang compiles
`s.d = 5; use(&s)` for a page-aligned `s` to `adrp x0,s; add x0,x0,#0; str
x8,[x0,#0x18]; b use`, and the `str` alone would withdraw the only row naming `s`.
A page nothing completes, or that is completed only past a join, keeps its row
too. What the carry cannot see is a use of the page itself on a path it does not
follow (the far side of a conditional branch, past a join) or the page stored,
compared or returned without that `add`; a page completed elsewhere on its run
then loses its row. Compilers do not emit that shape — every such use in the
sweep below is a register spill the function reloads as a base — and keeping each
page live across a conditional branch would restore 458 false rows there to
recover none. Only an `adrp` is a page, read off its encoding: an `adr` of a
page-aligned label lifts to the same `COPY` and is the label's address. Over the
Mach-O sweep above (each universal binary split into its slices) and 79 ELF and
PE controls on eight architectures, 11,924 page rows are withdrawn: 6,627 on
AArch64 ELF, among them every `.plt` entry's `adrp x16` of the `.got.plt` page,
and 5,297 on Mach-O, most from `__stubs` and `__objc_stubs`. Every one is an
`adrp` whose completing instruction names another address, and no other row
changes.

(unlace) **A call through a loaded slot** (GH #1376). x86's `call qword ptr
[slot]` takes its destination out of a fixed slot in one instruction, and the scan
files it as a `Call` to the slot, which is where an import's name lives. A
fixed-width ISA spells the same call in three: `adrp x16,_malloc@GOTPAGE; ldr
x16,[x16,…]; blr x16`, and x86-64 sometimes in two, `mov rax,[rip+slot]; call
rax` (MSVC's i386 `mov esi,[__imp_X]; call esi`, GCC's `if (hook) hook();`). The
carry already read the `ldr` as a `Read` of the slot; the register it fills now
holds *the word at that slot*, and a `CALLIND` whose destination is that register,
or a copy of it, is a `Call` to the slot, filed from the call instruction on the
same join rule as every carried reference. Only a pointer-width load leaves such a
word, and a direct pointer-width memory operand copied whole into a register
starts one (`mov rax,[rip+slot]`). The word itself is unknown, so it is inert: an
add, a mask or a partial read of it is no value, and a load through it is no
reference. The load stays the `Read` it was, so an agent sees both observations,
the read and the call through what was read. `call [slot]` in one instruction is
still the scan's row alone. Over the Mach-O sweep above plus 30 x86-64 ELF images,
4 i386 PE and 45 ELF images across eight architectures, the rule adds 981 `Call`
rows and removes none: GOT and IAT slots (`blr x1` in `ld-linux-aarch64.so.1`,
`call esi` after `mov esi,[GetProcessHeap]`), function-pointer globals (`tar`'s
`error_hook`) and Go closures (`mov rax,[fv]; lea rdx,[fv]; call rax`). The
decompile graph gains the edge to a slot the inventory names, an import; a global
the inventory does not name gains none. An indirect *branch* through such a register (an arm64
stub's `br x16`, a tail call) is not filed: the forwarding relation is
the veneer walk's
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (veneer_at)`), which reads
the slot from the branch's own operand.

Most instructions never reach the evaluation. One is evaluated when a carry
reaches it, or when it could start one: it calls nothing, some modelled op yields
an address-like constant, some register is written by a modelled op from constants
and temporaries alone (the first register an evaluation can know is always written
that way), and in an `ET_DYN` image some modelled op reads a constant in the
instruction's PC window. An instruction failing any of these would leave nothing
to carry or keep, so the gate decides what is evaluated, never what is filed. A
register copied whole from a pointer-width direct memory operand also passes the
gate.

Measured over 86 images (AArch64 ELF and Mach-O, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, RISC-V,
x86-64, i386 PE and the vendored fixtures): no row is lost, and of the 14,550 rows
added, 10,994 on RISC-V match GNU objdump's own `lui`/`auipc` pair annotation
exactly, 895 more trace back through a base objdump annotated, 2,237 on AArch64,
MIPS, PowerPC and x86-64 match an independent capstone def-chain resolver, the 344
ARM PLT slot reads match the entries' own `add`/`add`/`ldr` arithmetic, and the
other 80 (Thumb `adr` + `ldrd` pool reads, a MIPS delay-slot `addiu`, a RISC-V
`c.lui` store and an `amoswap` on a lock) were checked by hand. The walk
itself costs about 2% more on x86-64 and ARM, where little is carried, 2-3% more
on MIPS and PowerPC, and 4-7% more on AArch64 and RISC-V, where a high half
precedes nearly every global access. Roughly half of that is the evaluation; the
rest is the new rows themselves, rendering each one's instruction text (about
2 µs a row on AArch64) and filing it (the 9,331 rows of a RISC-V PJSIP library).
Emitted C is unchanged.

(unlace) **Addresses below the floor** (GH #1364). The `checkOperands` floor tells a
number from an address among *immediates*, and a zero-based image keeps real
addresses under it: an arm64 Mach-O dylib's `__TEXT` starts at 0, ld.lld puts an
ELF shared object's or PIE's `.rodata` in its first page, GNU ld an older x86-64
or AArch64 PIE's `.text`, and firmware is linked at 0. There the floor dropped
every address a program formed into that page — `adrp x0,0x0; add x0,x0,#0x378`
naming a dylib's first function, `_start`'s `lea rdi,[rip+0xe6]` passing `main`.
Lowering the floor is no answer: `mov w0,#0x378` and `add x1,x1,#0x378` carry the
same constant, and in such an image nearly every small immediate lands in a mapped
byte (with no floor at all, the sweep below gained some 13,000 rows, almost all
`mov`/`cmp`/displacement immediates landing in `.dynsym`, `.rela` and their
neighbours). What separates the two is the PC, so a value computed from the
instruction's own address is exempt from the floor and has only to land in a
mapped section — the rule PIC pool composition already applies. SLEIGH folds most
PC-relative operands at decode time and leaves a plain constant in the p-code, so
**PC-relative forms** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/pcform.rs`)
recognises them from the instruction's encoding and recomputes their value from
its bytes: AArch64 `adr`/`adrp`; x86-64 RIP-relative `lea`, whose value is the
fall-through plus its last four bytes (an instruction that ends in an `imm32`
would need the value `next + imm32`, which it never carries); A32 and Thumb `adr`,
a four-byte ARM word being read both ways because the value must match. Only a
constant equal to the recomputed value is exempt, both in the one-instruction
scan and as a carried value. Register pair carrying also takes an instruction's
