  conversion to internal byte offsets. The complete nonempty file is published as
  one `CODE` section, and only caller-supplied entries are installed. ARM32 also
  requires an explicit ARM/Thumb state, painted across that section and preserved
  through the deferred analysis commit. Function pointers consume the ARM state bit,
  while data and property addresses preserve it. Presentation converts an address with
  its own address space's word size; data-space `dat_<hex>` tokens retain the coordinate
  emitted in C rather than inheriting the code space's word size, and merge with a named
  data label only when both the address space and presentation coordinate match. An
  ordinary load accepts XML only after parsing a document containing `<binaryimage>`;
  parse failures retain the headerless-image command guidance even when the first byte
  is `<`.

(unlace) **Firmware front ends.** `crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/firmware/`
holds the probes that turn a firmware file into raw-image arguments or into
modules. `cortexm.rs (probe)` reads a Cortex-M vector table the way IDA 9.5's
`cortex_m.py` does: word 0 an initial stack pointer in `0x10000000..0x40000000`
(SRAM or a CCM/TCM alias), the fifteen system words zero or odd pointers below
`0x20000000` with Reset non-zero (reserved slots are not checked, since NXP
parts keep a checksum there), then IRQ words to the first word that is neither,
at most 496, trailing zeros trimmed. The base is voted: every 2-byte-aligned
dummy handler after the table (`bx lr`, `b .`, `b.w .`, `nop; b .`) and every
handler target give the candidate `target - offset` when it is 0x1000-aligned,
and the most-voted candidate wins with at least 15 votes; else the first of
0x08000000, 0, 0x400000, 0x10000, 0x8000, 0x10000000 that holds every handler;
else the page below the lowest handler. Handlers are named `<Exception>_Handler`
and `IRQ<n>_Handler`, a target several IRQs share is `Default_Handler`. The CLI
(`unlace-cli/src/rawfront.rs (prepare)`) turns the table into `--raw-image`
arguments before a subcommand parses its own, so the engine sees an ordinary
raw load. `uefifv.rs (walk)` walks UEFI PI firmware volumes for `unlace unpack`:
FV header (`_FVH`, extended header), FFS files (24- or 32-byte headers, 8-byte
alignment, erase polarity from the volume attributes), sections (4-byte
alignment, extended sizes), nested volumes in `FIRMWARE_VOLUME_IMAGE` sections
and RAW files, compression sections stored uncompressed, and GUID-defined
sections for EDK2 LZMA (`lzma-rs`, the 13-byte LZMA-alone header), LZMA with
the x86 BCJ filter (decoded as the LZMA SDK `x86_Convert`), Tiano
(`tiano.rs (decompress)`, a port of EDK2 `BaseTools/Source/C/Common/Decompress.c`
with the 5-bit position set), Brotli (`brotli-decompressor`, after EDK2's
16-byte size header) and CRC32; a standard compression section of type 1 is
decoded as EFI 1.1 (4-bit position set) and retried as Tiano. Every
PE32/TE section is a module named by the file's UI section. `containers.rs (detect)` reads U-Boot
legacy images, Intel HEX, Motorola S-records,
uClinux bFLT v4 (rebasing GOT entries and relocations past the 64-byte header,
as `binfmt_flat` does), Qualcomm MBN/SBL wrappers, MediaTek `md1img` (the
`md1rom` section at 0x90000000 as MIPS32 LE, the LZMA `md1_dbginfo` symbol
records as function names, a nanoMIPS ROM reported because no SLEIGH spec
decodes it) and PC BIOS images (the reset-vector test of IDA's
`bios_image.py`; the last 128 KiB mapped below 1 MiB with `register CS`
assertions for segments E000 and F000, or with a 32-bit target the whole flash
ending at 4 GiB), and returns either one
flat image (lowest to highest loaded address, gaps filled, at most 256 MiB)
with the processor, base and entries its header states, or the ELF it wraps. `svd.rs (parse)` reads a CMSIS-SVD device with the unlace XML
reader: peripherals (`derivedFrom` reusing the base's registers and type),
clusters, `dim`/`dimIncrement`/`dimIndex` expansion, register sizes inherited
from the peripheral or device, and `<interrupt>` names. `Peripheral::c_struct`
lays a peripheral out as a C structure, dropping a register that overlaps an
earlier one and padding gaps. The CLI asserts the structure (`typedef`), the
peripheral as a typed global at its base (`data`) and its register range as
volatile, for an object file (an ELF, an ESP image, the ELF a container
wraps) as for a raw image, and names the IRQ handlers a raw image's vector
table found from the interrupts. A leading XML declaration is dropped before
the reader sees it (the vendors' files declare `standalone="no"`, which the
unlace XML grammar does not take). `svd.rs (bundled)` reads a device from
`svd_devices.br`, the descriptions `tools/gen_svd_bundle.py` cuts from the
vendors' device packs down to what `parse` reads and stores as one Brotli
stream (180 devices, 77 KiB); `--svd` takes a bundled name when no file of
that name exists, the bundled name equal to the argument or else the longest
that covers it (case-insensitive, `X` matching one character, the part number
going on past the name).

`bundles.rs (Bundle::parse)` lists the members of the inputs that hold several
images, without decoding them. A tar archive is recognized by its first
header's checksum, so a pre-POSIX archive without the `ustar` magic is one
too; members are the regular files up to the first all-zero block, named by
the `ustar` prefix and name, a GNU long-name record or a pax `path` record,
with sizes in octal or the base-256 form. A gzip stream whose first 512
inflated bytes are a tar header is inflated whole and read as that tar. A zip
archive is read from its central directory (the end record is searched in the
last 64 KiB; the zip64 end record and extended-information field are
followed); a member's data is located through its local header, stored (0) and
deflate (8) members decode, and an inflated member must match its stated size
and CRC-32. A flattened device tree with an `/images` node is a U-Boot FIT:
each child node is a member with its `type`, `arch`, `os`, `compression`,
`load` and `entry` properties (one or two cells), its data inline (`data`) or
external (`data-position`, or `data-offset` from the 4-byte-aligned end of the
tree, with `data-size`), and the member the default configuration's `kernel`
(else `firmware`) property names is the default. `Bundle::flat` turns an image
with a load address into the same flat image a U-Boot legacy image becomes,
with the processor from `arch`, the base from `load` and the entry from
`entry`; `gzip` data is inflated and any other compression is refused when the
member is selected. Offsets, sizes and counts come from the input and are
checked against it: a decoded member is at most 1 GiB, a listing at most
2^20 members, a device tree at most 32 levels deep. Member selection is the
CLI's (chapter [00](00-overview.md), `armember.rs (resolve)`).

(unlace) **Espressif application images and `esprom`.** An ESP32-family or
ESP8266 application image (`esp.rs (parse)`: `0xE9`, a segment count, the
entry, on ESP32-family parts a 16-byte extended header with the chip id, then
`address, length, bytes` per segment) is not flattened. Its segments load far
apart: on an ESP32-C3 the constants are at `0x3c000000`, the RAM code at
`0x40380000` and the flash code at `0x42000000`, so one flat image would be
100 MiB of padding or would drop every segment but the entry's. The engine
loads it instead as a raw image over separate runs
(`crates/unlace-sleigh/src/loadimage.rs (RawLoadImage::from_segments)`):
each segment is one section, an address between two segments is not mapped,
and the header's entry is the seed raw-image discovery widens from. The parse
refuses a segment that runs past the file, a segment outside
`0x20000000..0x70000000`, overlapping segments and an entry no segment holds;
the header allows at most 16 segments. A segment takes the properties of the
region of the chip's memory map it loads into (`esprom.rs (regions,
load_flags)`): DROM is read-only data, so its strings and tables fold as
constants; IROM and IRAM are read-only code, so the literal pool an Xtensa
`l32r` reads folds too; DRAM and RTC memory are writable data. The C6 and H2
map flash on one bus, so there the segment that starts with the application
descriptor (`0xABCD5432`) is the constants and the other flash segments are
code. The language is Xtensa or RISC-V by the chip id unless `--target` names
one.

`esprom` (default `auto`; `crates/unlace-lift/src/p1_partition/esprom.rs`
holds the value, `crates/unlace-console/src/esprom.rs (apply)`
applies it at the analysis commit) adds what the image does not carry. An ESP
application calls the routines of the chip's mask ROM at fixed addresses, and
without a name each call renders as a call through a literal
(`(*dat_40080504)(dst,src,n)`) or to a bare address. With a chip in force,
every ROM function of the chip is a function symbol at its address, with the
call fixup and the libc prototype its name selects, so the call renders as
`memcpy(dst,src,n)`; every ROM data symbol is a named untyped global unless a
symbol already covers the address; and every peripheral register range of the
chip's map that the image does not load into is volatile, so a register poll
keeps its read. A ROM function is a symbol only: it has no bytes in the input,
so it is not in the function inventory and nothing decompiles it. `auto` uses
the chip the image header names (an image without the extended header is an
ESP8266) and names no chip on any other input, which is what keeps the option
inert off-target. A chip name (`esp32`, `esp32s2`, `esp32s3`, `esp32c2`,
`esp32c3`, `esp32c6`, `esp32h2`, `esp8266`) applies that chip's ROM and
peripheral ranges to any input, such as the firmware's ELF; `off` applies
nothing. The tables under `loader/firmware/esprom/` are generated by
`scripts/gen_esprom.py` from the ROM linker scripts of ESP-IDF v5.5.6
(`components/esp_rom/<chip>/ld/*.ld`) and ESP8266_RTOS_SDK v3.4
(`esp8266.rom.ld`), both Apache-2.0: one name per address, the chip's main
script first, a symbol being a function when its address is in the ROM's code
range and the script does not list it under a `Data` heading. The memory maps
are the `SOC_*_LOW`/`SOC_*_HIGH` bounds of ESP-IDF's `soc.h`. A ROM revision
that moved a routine is not detected; the table holds the first address a
name was given.

The real-binary path of §1.2 is the fourth binding, console-side: `bootstrap_from_object`
plays the leaf role itself — it resolves the language from the object header
(with the compiler-model fallback retry), runs `build_engine_and_init`, attaches
the default code space to the loader (the `postSpecFile` contract), and hands the
loader to the engine as the byte source every subsequent instruction decode reads
through.

When the input explicitly selects an ARM ISA, frame recovery retains the
successfully decoded instruction spans from its final accepted walk as inventory
metadata. Inventory-seeded xref walks select those modes at matching seeds;
later direct-call evidence takes precedence. The hints survive recovery retries.
Ordinary decompilation context is not repainted by this metadata, and unrelated
roots retain the explicit input mode. Discarded rounds and unclaimed gaps publish
no hints. The behavior requires Listing, function-start patterns, and `armframes`.
Automatic ISA selection continues to use loader mode facts without extra hints.

Xref result formatting reuses the query's canonical inventory for names
and fallback ownership. ARM address normalization and discovered-entry naming
retain their existing precedence; formatting does not rebuild the inventory
for each endpoint of every result row.

### Stable Rust compiler-version evidence

The standalone loader also records an optional stable Rust compiler version from
ELF `.comment` in `Architecture::rustc_stable_version`. The record parser
in `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/sourcelang/rustversion.rs`
requires three numeric components and rejects prerelease suffixes, malformed
Rust records and conflicting versions. This image fact survives option resets and lets
versioned consumers such as the P9 `rustfmt` recoveries reject unsupported layouts.

An image whose `.comment` holds no `rustc version` record (the section was
removed, or the release profile never wrote one) still names its compiler: every
panic location the standard library carries is a source path of the form
`/rustc/<commit>/library/...`, where `<commit>` is the 40-digit hash of the
compiler build. For such an image, when the loader detected it as Rust, the parser
collects those paths over the whole file, accepting `/` or `\` after the hash. When they all name one commit, it is
looked up in `rustreleases.rs`, a table of the commit of every stable release
tag of rust-lang/rust, sorted by hash and regenerated by
`scripts/gen_rustreleases.py`. The match is on the full hash. A commit outside the
table (a nightly, a beta, a distribution build), paths that disagree, or no path
at all leave the version unknown, also when `sourcelang` is forced. A `.comment`
record always wins: the paths are consulted only when no record exists, so an
image with a rejected record (a prerelease, conflicting versions) stays unknown. An
image not detected as Rust is never scanned, so its load cost is unchanged.
The `rustfmt` pieces layout uses the same fallback and accepts the commits of
1.89.0, 1.90.0 and the one verified nightly.

`unlace functions --summary` reports the same evidence in the `rust` row of
`summary.runtime` for every container format: `version` is the `.comment` version
token (prerelease suffix kept) or the release found from the source paths. The row
also lists the registry crates the image names. `rustcrates.rs` scans for
`registry/src/<index>/<crate>-<version>/`, where `<index>` is a registry host
followed by `-` and 16 hex digits, and splits the crate directory at the first `-`
that begins a `major.minor.patch` version, so `sha-1-0.10.1` is `sha-1` at
`0.10.1`. Either path separator is accepted and the Cargo home prefix is not
matched, so images built in a container or on Windows list their crates too. The
list is sorted, each pair once, and holds only crates that left a source path in
the image.

For verified stable Rust 1.93.0/1.93.1 images, the standalone loader also retains
primitive integer Display callback types in `Architecture::rust_display_formatters`.
The reader in `crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/sourcelang/rustformatters.rs` accepts only linked 64-bit little-endian ELF images. It reads full demangled object-function symbols and their aliases before normal
symbol-name normalization removes trait qualifiers. Exact standard-library trait
identities qualify; conflicting aliases invalidate the address. The P9
`rustfmt` consumers independently check language, layout and call shape.
This evidence does not rename symbols or infer a generic formatter's pointee type.

The same symbol walk records integer formatting traits in
`Architecture::rust_integer_formatters` for P9 `rustfmt`. Display, Debug,
LowerHex, UpperHex, Octal, Binary, LowerExp and UpperExp retain exact type and
trait identity; the Display-only map is derived from these facts without another
object parse. Unknown or conflicting aliases invalidate the shared address.

### MIPS lazy-binding imports

`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/mipsstubs.rs` validates each
MIPS lazy-binding stub against its dynamic-symbol/GOT identity, executable
section and complete instruction sequence, in o32, n32 and n64 images. The
object loader records the validated stubs once per image (`MipsLinkage`). For a
MIPS language, bootstrap installs their resolver sites, and the GOT-proven
imports from the ELF function provenance, in the architecture; every Listing
walk, including a resumed one, and the reference walk behind `unlace xrefs`
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/xrefs.rs (descend)`) take only
the sites bootstrap installed.
The Listing models each resolver transfer, including the delay slot, as an
opaque computed jump. The walk applies this when it decodes the call
(`crates/unlace-analysis/src/listing/walk.rs (step)`), so it never
follows the call's fall-through into the next stub, section padding or a
following section, and files no reference along it. A stub's no-return status
still comes from its import's name, as no-return propagation above describes;
an unknown resolver destination supplies no terminal evidence. Ordinary
functions and unrecognized instruction sequences retain their original flow.
This applies to serial, parallel and resumed Listing construction. The same
validated resolver sites are passed to the decompiler's flow recovery, so a
stub decompiled alone ends with its tail call instead of falling through into
the next stub or section padding.

The real dynamic import name takes precedence over the linker-generated
`_MIPS_STUBS_` label at the same address; the label remains an alias, so a
call through the first stub names its import.
Without a callee prototype, a preserved incoming argument register cannot
establish import arity: calls with and without that argument can have identical
instructions. A declared prototype supplies that missing contract
(`gotimportproto.rs`, §4). A RISC-V call through an `auipc`/`jalr` pair to an
undefined symbol is the same case: the loader's undefined call relocations are
the proven imports, so the name-seeded libgcc and libc prototypes bind to it
(without this, `rv32.o`'s `fadd` prints `void fadd(void) { __addsf3(); }`).


### Weak import identity and slot membership

An undefined weak import has one FunctionSymbol, entered at its synthetic extern
address: the address every undefined function has, which direct calls and
address relocations reach and which a GOT relocation against the symbol
allocates as it does for any other symbol. Its import slot, the GOT entry or the
word allocated for its other address forms, is recorded as another address of
that same symbol. The function inventory, a cross-reference query by name and
the call graph therefore find the import and its direct references where they
would without a slot. The loader carries the SymbolIndex-based association
through bootstrap; the database maps both addresses to one symbol, so name
selection, renamed imports and edited prototypes do not split between two
independent functions. Distinct ELF symbols are not merged by their spelling.
The canonical inventory contains the import once; a lookup at the slot address
resolves the same entry. Import pointer storage remains bodyless unless a caller
explicitly declares a function there.

Import storage extents are normalized once at bootstrap: empty extents are
removed and overlapping/adjacent half-open ranges are merged in address order.
Membership queries use a binary search, including interior and missing addresses.
Executable-function enumeration therefore avoids a full slot-vector scan per
candidate, while preserving PE/Mach-O import slots inside executable sections and
caller-declared-entry precedence.

(unlace) **`__eh_frame` FDE starts on Mach-O** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/analyzers/entry/machoehframe.rs (MachoEhFrameStartsPass)`, option `machoehframe`, default-on). A Mach-O describes most functions' unwinding in `__unwind_info` and falls back to a DWARF FDE in `__TEXT,__eh_frame` for a function the compact encoding cannot describe (a variable stack adjustment, an unusual register save). Each FDE's `pcBegin` is a function start, exactly as on ELF, where the always-on discovery already reads `.eh_frame` (oracle 3); the pass runs that same walk (`scan_eh_frame_starts`, now accepting a Mach-O's `__eh_frame`) and keeps the starts that lie in an executable section and carry no symbol. Like `__unwind_info` the section lives in `__TEXT` and survives the strip of `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS`; unlike it, every FDE is a real function start with no folding, and the pass is cheap, so it is on by default, as IDA's Mach-O loader runs its `eh_frame` parse on every load. On an image that keeps `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` it adds nothing.

(unlace) **`LC_DATA_IN_CODE` runs are data to the Listing** (`crates/unlace-analysis/src/loader/machodataincode.rs (data_in_code_ranges)`, always on). clang lays an x86-64 switch's jump table and a Thumb `tbb`/`tbh` table into `__text` after the dispatch, and ARM literal pools between functions, and records each run as a `data_in_code_entry` (`offset`, `length`, `kind` 1 to 5: data, 8/16/32-bit jump table, absolute 32-bit jump table). The Listing build cuts those ranges out of the executable ranges the walk decodes (`listing/mod.rs`), so a table's bytes are neither decoded as instructions nor reach the gap and prologue sweeps; the jump-table readers take their own executable ranges and still read the tables. In a linked image `offset` is a file offset from the Mach-O header and is placed through the section holding it; in an `MH_OBJECT` it is a pre-link address. A table with an entry of any other kind is ignored whole (a dyld-cache image's `dataoff` names another sub-cache file).
